look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a student to make their thinking process visible
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks student to make the thinking or steps behind a response, prediction, or approach visible
* Asks student why they chose a particular strategy, step, or decision
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be asked before, during, or after the student completes the task
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "The darker gray area has more electrons." Teacher: "Why did you decide that darker gray means more electrons?"
* Student: "The two triangles are congruent." Teacher: "Walk me through your thinking. What did you do first, and how did you decide that told you they were congruent?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Are you confident that the answer is 4 grams?" [Why attempting: Yes/no, doesn't ask for process]
* "What part of the text did you use to answer the question?" [Why attempting: prompts partial but not full reasoning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Student: "The area near oxygen is darker gray." Teacher: "Right. That's because there's a greater concentration of electrons near the oxygen atom." [Why non-example: Explains instead of asking student to do so]
* Student: "The answer is 12." Teacher: "Great job." [Why non-example: No thinking prompt]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional Group B: counts toward the 2+ threshold, in any combination across group members, for understanding student thinking
look_fors.name: Prompt Interpretation or Explanation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a student to interpret or explain what something means
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks student to explain why or how something in the content occurs (e.g., a cause, pattern, or phenomenon)
* Asks student to interpret the meaning or significance of an ambiguous or non-obvious case
* Asks student to justify why a stated fact, answer, or interpretation is correct
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May ask about a typical, non-obvious, or ambiguous case (e.g., "why doesn't this fit either category?")
* Target may be a diagram, phenomenon, text, or previously stated fact
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Why are the crystal sizes in these two rocks different?"
* "Why is the character's decision to stay considered brave, even though he barely talks about it?"
* "Describe at least two causes of migration within the United States during the 1930s"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Is the theme about friendship?" [Why attempting: Yes/no, doesn't require interpretation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher: "The theme of the story is that friendship helps in hard times." [Why non-example: States rather than asks]
* Teacher: "The grey area doesn't have any charge because the electrons are spread out evenly across the molecule." [Why non-example: States rather than asks]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional Group A: counts toward the one-time threshold for assessing basic student knowledge
look_fors.name: Prompt Recall or Identification
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a student to recall, name, define, or classify content
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks student to recall a previously taught fact, term, step, or event
* Asks student to identify, name, or locate an element within a text, image, object, or problem
* Asks student to define or describe the meaning of a term or concept
* Asks student to classify or categorize an item
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May reference content already taught, or a text, image, object, or problem in front of the student
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Sort this word list into adjectives and adverbs. Be ready to explain how you know."
* "Look at the diagram. Where are the electrons located in this molecule?"
* "What does 'renewable' mean in this paragraph?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Take a look at the anchor chart. What's the first step?" [Why attempting: Student can read answer vs. stating their own answer]
* "Are the electrons near the oxygen atom?" [Why attempting: Yes/no, doesn't require student to locate independently]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "This word, 'reluctant,' means hesitant." [Why non-example: States rather than asks]
* "This dark gray area near the oxygen atom is where the electrons are concentrated." [Why non-example: States rather than asks]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional Group A: counts toward the one-time threshold for assessing basic student knowledge
look_fors.name: Prompt Student to Restate or Paraphrase
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt a student to restate or paraphrase a key idea in their own words
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks a student to restate or paraphrase a key idea, concept, or instruction in their own words
* Asks a student to restate or paraphrase another student's contribution
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target may be the teacher's explanation, a concept, an instruction, or a peer's contribution
* May ask the original student to restate their own idea or route the restatement to another student
* May provide a sentence stem to support the restatement
look_fors.strong_examples: "We just said slope is the rate of change. In your own words, what does that mean? Try the stem: 'Slope tells us…'"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Can someone tell me what slope means again?" <calls on student who repeats the exact definition verbatim> [Why attempting: Prompts repetition but not restatement in the student's own words]
look_fors.non_examples: "So what that means is the slope is the rate of change. Got it? Let's move on." [Why non-example: Teacher restates instead of prompting a student to]

skills.name: Assets-Based Approach
skills.description: Identify and build off students' current knowledge using assets-based language.

look_fors.name: Connect to Prior Knowledge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Activate students' existing knowledge of the topic or content.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Prompts students to recall what they already know about the topic or concept
* Links new content to previously learned content or familiar real-world concepts
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Background knowledge may be drawn from prior lessons or common experience
* May ask students questions, have them complete a practice item to demonstrate a previous skill, or otherwise engage students in the relevant prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "This story is about seeds. Remember when we learned how seeds grow into plants? Look, this character is planting a seed right here. What do you already know about what a seed needs?"
* "Today we will learn to calculate density. Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month, so your do now today is a speed problem. Pay attention to how you figure out the units in your answer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This story is about the ocean. Who has seen a picture the ocean or a picture of it?" <A few students raise hands and teacher moves on> [Why attempting: superficial connection to prior knowledge]
* "Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month. You divide one number by another and keep the units." [Why attempting: teacher-led connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "This story is about the ocean." [Why non-example: no connection to prior knowledge]

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Affirmation/Assurance
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Express confidence in student's ability to be successful
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in students' abilities (e.g., "I know you can do this," "You're capable of this work")
* May reference growth over time (e.g., "You already figured out..., now you just have to...")
* May be used after redirection, when giving feedback, or during instruction
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address whole class or individual students
* If used after a redirection, walks away rather than lingering to check compliance
* Redirect affirmations may be more concise (e.g., "You got this")
* Often paired with communicating high expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* After redirection: "You've got this - I'm excited to see your thinking when I come around again later" <walks away>
* During instruction: "I know you can master this concept"
* When giving feedback: "I'm giving you this feedback because I know you're capable of meeting high standards."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Okay great, get to work" [Why attempting: Positive and directive but not affirming]
* "Good job" [Why attempting: Generic praise]
* "You can do this if you focus" [Why attempting: Conditional]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Let's see if you can actually do it this time" [Why non-example: Doubts capability]
- "Just give it your best and see what you can do" [Why non-example: No affirmation/assurance of student's ability]
- States what student did wrong (e.g., “that’s not solving the equation”) without any follow up

look_fors.name: Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create conditions where students attempt challenging work safely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly invites students to try even if unsure (e.g., "Give it a shot, even if you're not certain, this will help you learn and help me see your thinking")
* Recognizes attempts and effort, not just correct answers
* Provides support structures that allow productive struggle (think time, partner talk, resources)

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
* Student shares incorrect answer [rationale: not clear evidence that student feels safe, they may have thought their answer was correct]
* Teacher asks follow up questions or asks students to build on others' thinking [rationale: not a bad practice, but does not explicitly create safe conditions for risk-taking]
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* When applicable, includes statements like "There's no right answer" or "Multiple approaches work here"
* May celebrate "wrong" answers that show sophisticated reasoning
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I want to hear your thinking even if you're not 100% sure. Your ideas will help us all learn"
* "We're figuring things out together rather than just looking for the 'right' answer"
* "Try it out in your voice and we can all learn from each other's writing" 
* "Turn and talk with a partner to share thinking before we discuss as a class"
* Remember, you have a toolbox for when you feel stuck. Consult the rubric or phone a friend!"  
* "I actually expect some of your first attempts to be unsuccessful. If you finish this without running into a single issue, you probably didn't take a big enough risk. I'm looking for how you pivot when things get messy, not just the final product."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you get it wrong" [Why attempting: no connection to learning value]
* "Be sure everyone participates!" [Why attempting: generic participation encouragement instead of explicitly encouraging academic risk taking]
* Validates partially correct answers [Why attempting: Implies recognition of effort, but not explicit]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher consistently calls on same few students who raise hands with confidence [type: missed opportunity]
* "Don't worry, this one is easy" [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarrass or demotivate a student from taking future risks (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Normalize Mistakes as Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state that errors are part of learning and respond to mistakes or misconceptions as opportunities to learn
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States that mistakes help learning 
* Responds to errors with curiosity rather than clarification alone
* Publicly acknowledges own mistakes as learning opportunities
* Thanks students for sharing mistakes that help class learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May frame revision as normal part of learning process
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections. Let's look at what this mistake can teach us"
* <Teacher makes and catches own error> "Oops! Can anyone find the mistake I just made?" <Student answers> "Thanks! Next time I will..."
*  <Student work shows two divided by zero is two> Teacher: "Oooh, interesting thinking here! Walk me through why you think two divided by zero is two." <Listens to student thinking, and connects to thinking when providing clarification>
* "This is a really interesting misconception. I used to think that the seasons were caused by Earth's distance from the sun, too. This is a logical guess, but it's not what's actually happening, which blew my mind a little when I learned the real answer!"<Teacher demonstrates misconception clarification and comes back to original student to share updated thinking>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you make a mistake" [Why attempting: Reassures but doesn't frame mistakes as valuable]
* <Student gives partially correct answer.> Teacher: "Good start. You're getting there" <does not explain why, calls on another student>. [Why attempting: Somewhat affirming but doesn't use error as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
- <student gives wrong answer> "No, that's not right. Who else?" [Why non-example: Dismisses error without learning value] [type: relational harm]
- Only acknowledges correct answers with praise [type: missed opportunity]
- "You mixed up the numerator and denominator AGAIN" <exasperated tone> [Why non-example: judgmental of error] [type: relational harm]
- Tells one student to explain to another why they are wrong [Why non-example: Negatively framed with emphasis on wrong vs. correct instead of what can be learned] [type: relational harm]

skills.name: Background Knowledge
skills.description: Build background knowledge or activate students' existing knowledge of a topic to support new learning.

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: Anticipation Guide
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students respond to statements about the topic before instruction/reading, then revisit their responses after.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a short set of statements related to the topic before instruction/reading
* Prompts students to respond to each statement (e.g., true/false, agree/disagree)
* Frames upcoming learning in terms of evaluating initial thinking in anticipation guide
* Returns to the statements after instruction/reading to discuss any changes in thinking
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * If there is only transcript/lesson/video evidence of before or after teaching/reading, only the corresponding portion of the look-for is expected
look_fors.strong_examples: "Before we read, mark each statement true or false based on what you think." <Students complete guide> "As we read, pay attention to your initial thinking on these statements. Try to figure out if you were right or wrong." <After reading> "Let's go back to the initial set of statements we responded to. Did any of your answers change? Why or why not? Turn and talk to your elbow partner for 2 minutes"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Read these statements and mark true or false." <Students complete guide> <No framing of connection to upcoming reading/instruction>
look_fors.non_examples: "Turn to page 5 and start reading the story about the bear."

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: Connect to Prior Knowledge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Activate students' existing knowledge of the topic or content.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Prompts students to recall what they already know about the topic or concept
* Links new content to previously learned content or familiar real-world concepts
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Background knowledge may be drawn from prior lessons or common experience
* May ask students questions, have them complete a practice item to demonstrate a previous skill, or otherwise engage students in the relevant prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "This story is about seeds. Remember when we learned how seeds grow into plants? Look, this character is planting a seed right here. What do you already know about what a seed needs?"
* "Today we will learn to calculate density. Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month, so your do now today is a speed problem. Pay attention to how you figure out the units in your answer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This story is about the ocean. Who has seen a picture the ocean or a picture of it?" <A few students raise hands and teacher moves on> [Why attempting: superficial connection to prior knowledge]
* "Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month. You divide one number by another and keep the units." [Why attempting: teacher-led connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "This story is about the ocean." [Why non-example: no connection to prior knowledge]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group B)
look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Predictions/Observations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to make their own predictions and/or observations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides time and structure for students to form predictions
* Explicitly invites student predictions/observations as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student predictions by revisiting or testing them against new information
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Predictions/observations may be gathered from a subset of students or the whole group
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Looking at this cover, what do you think might happen in this story? Turn and tell your partner your prediction." <Students predict; teacher notes a few and tells students they will return to them after reading>
* "Before we run the experiment, write down what you predict will happen to the balloon in the hypothesis box." <Students write> "Let's test it and see."
* "Take a moment to look at this photograph. What do you notice about the bear's fur? Turn and tell your partner what you notice. Say, I notice…" <Students share observations, teacher notes a few and tells students they will learn something special about bears' fur when they read>
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What do you think happens next?" <Accepts one or two predictions and moves on> [Why attempting: doesn't create broad prediction-generation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher states what will happen and/or what they see; students only listen
* "What do you think will happen?" with no time or structure for students to respond

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group B)
look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Questions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to generate their own questions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides dedicated time and structure for students to formulate questions
* Explicitly invites student questions as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student-generated questions by using them to drive learning (e.g., discussion or investigation)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student questions may be verbal or written
* Use of student questions may focus in on a small subset or consider all questions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading." <Students write> "Share your question with a partner." <Students discuss> Teacher uses student questions to frame the class discussion.
 * "We've been studying the water cycle. What's a question a scientist might still be trying to answer?" <Students generate questions> "I love this one — let's investigate it together."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What questions do you have?" and accepts and answers 1 to 2 student questions and moves on [Why attempting: doesn't create broad student question-generation]
 "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading" <Teacher moves on immediately> [Why attepting: Students have opportunity to ask questions, but they are not used for learning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher asks all questions; students only answer
* "Any questions?" with no time or structure for students to formulate them

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: KWL Chart
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use a K-W-L chart to record what students know (K), want to learn (W), and later learn (L) about a topic.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Before teaching/reading: records what students already know about the topic under "K"
* Before teaching/reading: records what students want to learn under "W"
* After teaching/reading: returns to the chart to record what was learned under "L"
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Chart may be completed whole-class, in small groups, or individually
* Teacher may transcribe responses or have students write their own
* If there is only transcript/lesson/video evidence of before teaching/reading, only K & W steps are expected
* If there is only transcript/lesson/video evidence of after teaching/reading, only L step is expected
look_fors.strong_examples: "What do you already know about volcanoes?" <Records under K> "What do you want to learn about volcanoes?" <Records under W> <After the lesson> "Let's go back to our chart and add what we learned under L."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "I want to hear from a couple different people. What do we already know about volcanoes? What questions do you have?" <Takes a few students' answers, but does not record>
* "What questions do you have about volcanoes? Everyone turn and talk to your partner about your questions, and then we will make a list." [Why attempting: Asks for questions but not what is already known]
look_fors.non_examples: "Today we're learning about volcanoes." <Begins lesson without referencing prior knowledge or questions>

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group B)
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group B)
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Participation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Vary the modes students use to respond.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses 2+ participation modes (e.g., saying, writing, gesturing, drawing, moving) across the lesson or lesson segment
* Varies the mode across activities or segments rather than defaulting to one
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May offer choice in how students communicate or demonstrate their understanding; this still counts as 2+ modes
* A single mode is fine in a moment, but multiple modes should be used across time
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Write your prediction on your sticky note." <Students write> "Now stand up and put your sticky note on the chart under the heading you picked." <Students move to chart> "Turn and tell your partner why you chose that one."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone write your answer in your notebook. If you finish early, you can draw a quick sketch of it." [Why attempting: second mode only for early finishers]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Every prompt across the lesson or lesson segment asks students to respond in writing with no opportunities for other modes like drawing or speaking
* "Turn and tell your partner what you predict." <Later> "Turn and tell your partner what surprised you."

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: Paired Text
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Introduce a shorter, topically related text to build vocabulary or background knowledge that scaffolds comprehension of the main text.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Introduces a second, shorter text (e.g., poem, song, short passage) related in topic or vocabulary to the main text being closely read
* Connects the paired text explicitly back to the main text (e.g., asks how the paired text relates to the main text)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Paired text may be introduced before reading the main text (to build background) or during/after (to reinforce or extend understanding)
* May take the form of a poem, song, short passage, or other brief text
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher reads the "She Sells Seashells" poem, then asks: "What does the 'She Sells Seashells' poem have to do with Mary Anning?" Student: "It's about her selling fossils to visitors at the beach."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <reads "She Sells Seashells" aloud> "Think about this poem while we continue learning about Mary Anning" [Why attempting: lacks explicit text to text connection]
look_fors.non_examples: "Let's read this fun poem about the seashore!" <reads "She Sells Seashells,"> "Ok, now let's read our story." [Why non-example: no connection made to the main text]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: Realia / Concrete Objects
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use physical objects or hands-on materials to build knowledge/background knowledge about an unfamiliar concept.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a physical object, model, or hands-on material related to the topic
* Prompts students to touch, examine, or manipulate the object
* Connects the object explicitly to the concept or vocabulary being taught
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Object may be a real item, replica, or manipulative
look_fors.strong_examples: <Passes around a real seashell> "Feel how hard and smooth this is. This shell protects the hermit crab inside. The article we are about to read will tell us why hermit crabs need shells like this for protection and how they get them."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* <Passes around a real seashell> "This is a seashell. Today's reading is about crabs. A hermit crab is a type of crab that lives in a shell." [Why attempting: builds some background knowledge but misses key details to support student understanding]
* "This is a real seashell. Notice how smooth and hard it is. This shell can protect a hermit crab inside" [Why attempting: students do not get to hold or touch the object; connection to reading/instruction unclear]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Turn to page 5 and start reading the story about the bear."
* "Today's reading is about crabs. A hermit crab is a type of crab that lives in a shell." [Why non-example: verbal preview only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Optional (Background Knowledge, Group A)
look_fors.name: Resource Exploration
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students explore one or more preselected resources to build background knowledge before reading or learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides one or more preselected resources related to the topic (e.g., short video, website, image set, article)
* Provides a focused question or task to guide students' exploration
* Structures time for students to explore the resource(s) independently, in pairs, or in groups
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Single resource or multiple
* Print or digital
look_fors.strong_examples: "In the next chapter, Esperanza arrives at a migrant worker camp in California. Let's watch this video showing photos of and describing life in a similar migrant camp before we read. As you watch, write down at least two things you notice about living conditions and how people were treated." <Plays video> <Students take notes> <Teacher calls on students to share what they noticed after video, then asks: "How do you think Esperanza will feel when she arrives at the migrant camp? Why?">
look_fors.attempting_examples: "In the next chapter, Esperanza arrives at a migrant worker camp in California. Let's watch this video showing photos of and describing life in a similar migrant camp before we read." <Plays video with no guiding question>
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Turn to page 5 and start reading the story about the bear."
* "Look up whatever you want about The Great Depression online" [Why non-example: no curated resource or focused question]

skills.name: Balanced Questions
skills.description: Ask a balance of procedural and conceptual questions to assess student understanding.

look_fors.name: Conceptual Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that requires reasoning about mathematical structure or relationships rather than computing one definite answer.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Poses a question with more than one valid response or approach, or that requires explaining why/how a procedure works
- Question reveals understanding of underlying structure, relationships, or meaning rather than just execution
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- May ask students to generate an example or context (e.g., a word problem) that fits a given expression or equation
- May reframe a procedural task by asking about it differently, e.g., asking for a possible next step when more than one is valid, instead of asking for the definite answer
- May ask a broad follow up question to further understand student thinking (e.g., "Can you tell me more about that?")
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Give me an equation like this one that would have infinitely many solutions instead of just one. How do you know?"
- Teacher: "Is 24 the lowest common denominator of 1/4 and 5/6? Why or why not?" Student: "No, 12 is the lowest common denominator." Teacher: "Tell me more about that. Why is it 12 and not 24?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Is 24 the lowest common denominator of 1/4 and 5/6?" <no follow up question> [Why attempting: student may include why in answer, but as posed, the question is just yes/no]
- "What's a possible third step in evaluating this expression?" <no follow up question> [Why attempting: open question, but doesn't surface the reasoning]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "This equation has infinitely many solutions because both sides simplify to the same expression." [Why non-example: teacher states the reasoning instead of asking the student to reason]
- "Solve 2x + 3 = 9 for x." [Why non-example: single definite answer, no reasoning required; this is not a bad question it is just not a conceptual question]
- Asks vague check for understanding question rather than a question that probes conceptual thinking (e.g., "does that make sense?", "do you have any questions?", etc.)

look_fors.name: Procedural Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question with one definite, accurate answer that requires efficient execution of a known procedure.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Poses a question with a single correct, definite answer
* Answering requires accurately carrying out a known procedure or computation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May ask for the final answer or for a specific step in a known procedure, as long as there is one correct response
* Efficiency and accuracy are the focus, not the reasoning behind the procedure
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "What is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are 9 and 12?"
* "Let's look at the equation x + 5 = 16. What should I do to both sides to solve for x?"
* "Look at our anchor chart for adding and subtracting fractions. Now that I have a common denominator, what do I do next?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Teacher solves x + 5 = 16 on the board, isolating x = 11> "So what does x equal?" [Why attempting: has a definite answer, but the teacher already executed the procedure, so answering doesn't require the student to carry it out]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "To solve x + 5 = 16, subtract 5 from both sides. x = 11." [Why non-example: teacher performs the procedure and states the answer instead of asking the student]
- "Why do you divide both sides by 2 here?" [Why non-example: asks for reasoning, not a definite computed answer; this is not a bad question it is just not a procedural question]
- Asks vague check for understanding question rather than a question that requires demonstration of procedural knowledge (e.g., "does that make sense?", "do you have any questions?", etc.)

skills.name: Caregiver Phone Call
skills.description: Call a student’s caregiver to offer praise or support

look_fors.name: Ask Caregiver About Student
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask what the caregiver has noticed or thinks about the topic
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks caregiver an open-ended question about what they've noticed, experienced, or think regarding the student
* Pauses to let caregiver respond
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May ask broadly (e.g., "how's reading going at home?") or narrow to the specific topic of the call
* May occur once or more than once during the call
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Why don't you tell me a little bit about what you're seeing when it comes to reading with Olivia at home?" 
- "You know him best. Does this match what you're noticing at home?"
- "I noticed Christian really loves hands-on activities. What else have you noticed that Christian loves when it comes to learning?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Have you seen Rahul’s most recent scores on the parent portal?" [Why attempting: question but does not invite caregiver’s perspective]
look_fors.non_examples: "I'll be honest, your child had a tough time on this assessment. They scored 0 out of 5." [Why non-example: shares data without ever asking for caregiver's perspective]

look_fors.name: Caregiver Conversation Closing
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Thank caregiver and close respectfully
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Thanks caregiver for their time and/or collaboration in support of the student
* Includes a respectful goodbye or well-wish
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May include statement about when they anticipate connecting again
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Thank you for your time, Mr. Johnson. Have a great night."
* Thank you for your collaboration in support of Brett. I will see you at the end of the month at parent-teacher conferences, but let me know if you need anything in the meantime!”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Bye" [Why attempting: Abrupt]
look_fors.non_examples: * "I hope I don't have to call again for this reason. Goodbye." [Why non-example: Negative/rude]

look_fors.name: Caregiver Conversation Collaborative Next Step
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Develop a next step with the caregiver
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Proposes a specific next step OR asks caregiver for input on next step OR both
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may ask caregiver for their input on the next step itself (e.g., "what do you think would help most right now?") or for what they think should happen next
* Teacher may propose action and ask for caregiver agreement
* Next step may involve teacher action, caregiver action, or both
* May ask if caregiver has questions or needs support
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I will talk to him in the morning, but could you also pass along the compliment?"
* <Caregiver shares challenge at home due to family member with cancer> Teacher: "I am so sorry to hear that! Thank you for telling me. Do you think that Jailyn would want to talk with someone at school about everything? I can ask our school social worker to check in with her." <Caregiver affirms this would be helpful> Teacher: "I understand. I will speak to the social worker tomorrow and ask her to meet with Jailyn. If there is anything else I can do, or the school can do, for you and your family, please let me know."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I will talk to him in the morning about it." [Why attempting: No caregiver involvement]
look_fors.non_examples: "Let me know if you have any questions." [Why non-example: No specific next step, vague]

look_fors.name: Caregiver Conversation Opening
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Open by greeting caregiver and checking timing if needed
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Greets caregiver by name
* Introduces self by name and role if not previously acquainted
* If conversation is not pre-planned (e.g., if conversation is phone call rather than discussion on conference night) ask if timing works (e.g., "do you have a few minutes?"
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include brief pleasantry (e.g., "How are you?")
*May offer to call back at another time
* May include time estimate (e.g., "I need about 5 minutes")
look_fors.strong_examples: "Hi, Mr. Johnson. This is Ms. Higgins, Brett's teacher. How are you?" <Mr. Johnson responds> "I'd like to take 2 minutes to share some good news about Brett. Is now a good time or would you like me to call back another time?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Hi, Mr. Johnson. This is Ms. Higgins, Brett's teacher. I hope you're having a nice evening." [Why attempting: Missing time check]
look_fors.non_examples: "Hello, this is Brett's teacher calling. I'm calling about his behavior today." [Why non-example: No names, no time check, launches into topic]

look_fors.name: Caregiver Conversation Purpose Statement
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: State the specific reason for the discussion with the caregiver
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States the reason for the discussion with necessary details
* Includes specifics of what happened or specific evidence (e.g., student work or scores)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise conversations: May include specific positive behavior, context where it occurred, and impact
* Support conversations: May include specific concern, pattern observed, and impact on learning or wellbeing
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I called to tell you that Brett did an excellent job collaborating with peers during our science lesson today. The lab required a lot of focused attention, communication, and team decision making. Brett was highly engaged and communicated well with his group. His efforts showed a great deal of determination and cooperation and led to a successful lab report."
* "I am calling because I am worried about Jailyn. She is missing valuable learning experiences because she frequently puts her head down, pulls up her hood and does not respond when I check in with her. This has happened in class each day so far this week."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I called to tell you that Brett did a great job in science today." [Why attempting: Missing context and specific behavior]
look_fors.non_examples: "I'm calling about Brett’'s behavior in class." [Why non-example: Vague, no specific details]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required only for support calls, where affirming the student's capability to the caregiver keeps the concern from reading as a judgment of the student's overall ability. Not required for praise calls.
look_fors.name: Caregiver Conversation Affirmation of Student
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell the caregiver you believe in the student's ability to succeed
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in the student's ability to succeed, addressed to the caregiver and referring to the student in third person (e.g., "I know Jailyn can catch up on this")
* References specific evidence, effort, or growth supporting that confidence
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May reference a specific skill/behavior or general capability
* May occur at any point in a support call
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "I know Sofia can catch up on this skill. She's already shown she can push through hard problems once she puts her mind to it."
- "I know Owen can meet our classroom expectations around respectful listening. He's already shown he can do it during small group work when he's really engaged."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I think he'll be okay." [Why attempting: Vague, no evidence]
look_fors.non_examples: "I'm not sure he's going to turn this around, but we'll see." [Why non-example: Doubts capability]

skills.name: Checking for Understanding Question
skills.description: Ask questions that directly reveal whether students have mastered the specific learning objective or related key concepts and skills from the lesson at strategic points in the lesson.

look_fors.name: Right Time (CFU)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Check for understanding at strategic moments in the lesson
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- CFUs after key points and key steps in content or skill instruction
- CFUs when instruction can still be adjusted based on results
- CFUs before releasing students to lengthy independent work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- May do a formative check for understanding to assess prior knowledge before instruction on key points or steps, but must also check for updated understanding after instruction in this case
- If key points do not require sequence and are short, check for understanding questions may be asked after each individual point or in a group after instruction on multiple key points
- A short stop and jot or independent task can be a well-timed check for understanding and should not be penalized as an example of releasing students to independent work without a check
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher explains metamorphic rock formation process, immediately checks if students can explain how heat and pressure create metamorphic rocks, adjusts explanation based on responses, then continues to next rock type
* Teacher models solving two-step equations, checks that students can identify which operation to undo first (trickiest part), adjusts based on CFU results, then has students practice
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Introduces three key steps for solving inequalities, checks for understanding after steps 1 and 2, but moves directly to practice after teaching step 3 without checking [Why attempting: CFUs at some strategic points but misses checking after the final key step before release]
* Conducts a pre-assessment on fractions before the lesson but doesn't check for understanding after teaching the new content [Why attempting: Uses formative check for prior knowledge but fails to check updated understanding after instruction]
look_fors.non_examples:
- Delivers a lecture on rock formation and then has students work on 5 independent practice problems without checking for understanding [type: missed opportunity]
- Checks for understanding after students have completed independent practice [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required when lesson plan available OR when it is clear from practice transcript what happened before the CFU
Else not required
look_fors.name: Right Question (CFU)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that reveals what you need to know about student understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question directly targets the learning objective/goal or related key concept or skill from the lesson
* Question reveals whether students can demonstrate the specific knowledge or skill being taught
* Question is aligned with the cognitive demand of the learning objective from the lesson (or scaffolds toward it) 
* When available, learning objective/goal from the lesson must be: 
===BEGIN LEARNING OBJECTIVE(S)/GOAL(S)===
[Learning Objective(s)/Goal(s) from external source]
{{learning_objective_s__goal_s_}}
===END LEARNING OBJECTIVE(S)/GOAL(S)===
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* For selected response questions, question includes appropriate number of answer choices for the concept being assessed
* Question may be related to prior knowledge (e.g., from an earlier lesson) necessary for success with the current lesson's objective
* Question may require less cognitive demand if used in a way that scaffolds toward the full cognitive demand of the lesson (e.g., teacher checks for student ability to identify figurative language types like metaphors before having students analyze an author's use of figurative language)
* Any question that asks students to demonstrate understanding (e.g., explain, apply learning to a new scenario, etc.) as opposed to doing something else like predicting can be a check for understanding question
* Student tasks themselves, when framed around prompts or questions that require students to demonstrate understanding, may be checking for understanding questions
* Questions may come directly from lesson plan or materials
* Questions may ask for students to respond verbally, in writing, in pictures, etc
* Questions may target anticipated misconceptions
* Do nows are often checks for understanding of prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how metamorphic rocks form. Teacher first asks students to define temperature and pressure in their own words [scaffold] before asking "How are metamorphic rocks formed? Use today’s key vocabulary words in your answer."
* Learning objective is to compare and contrast two characters; teacher asks "What are two similarities and two differences between Character A and Character B?"
* Learning objective is to compare and contrast two characters; teacher asks students to identify the character traits of the first character. Transcript or lesson plan indicates that later in lesson teacher asks students to compare and contrast two characters. [Why strong: Question scaffolds directly toward objective]
* Learning objective is "SWBAT determine why constellations in the night sky vary by season by using and analyzing a model". Teacher references specific questions for students to answer in writing in their handout. Uploaded lesson plan shows these questions to be: "Will someone in Buenos Aires ever see Ursa Major?", "Will someone in New York City ever see The Southern Cross?", "Would constellations still change throughout the year if the Earth did not revolve around the Sun?" and "Why don’t we see constellations during the day?" [Why strong: These questions require full understanding of the spatial reasoning required to master the objective and also require nuanced understanding relative to the objective]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how sedimentary rocks are formed. Teacher asks students to identify specific sedimentary rocks based on grain size [Why attempting: Related to objective and may imply formation environment, but does not directly align to objective]
* Learning objective is to solve two-step equations; teacher asks students to solve a one-step equation and does not move on to a two-step equation next or indicate it is a stepping stone to two-step equations [Why attempting: Lower cognitive demand than objective]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how metamorphic rocks form; teacher asks "What is your favorite type of rock?" [Why non-example: Doesn't target learning objective] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks vague question (e.g., "Any questions?", "Does that make sense?", etc.) [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Checking for Understanding Strategy
skills.description: Select and employ checking for understanding strategies that strategically match the type of data needed to make instructional decisions.

look_fors.name: Right Strategy (CFU)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Select a checking for understanding strategy that matches the data you need to gather
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Strategy aligns with whether teacher needs to know what students understand (conceptual) or what they can do (procedural)
* Strategy matches question type (open-ended explanation vs. selected response)
* Strategy choice reflects whether teacher needs to scan all students or sample some students
* Strategy allows teacher to gather process information when process is important to assess
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* For routine checks of familiar content, quicker sampling strategies may be appropriate
* For new or complex content, more comprehensive scanning strategies may be needed
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher needs to know if students can explain metamorphic rock formation; uses ask-ask-ask to hear multiple student explanations of the process
* Teacher wants to see all students' multi-step problem-solving process; uses whiteboards and gives adequate time to solve and hold up for teacher to scan
* Teacher wants to quickly check if all students can identify which of three answer choices is correct; uses gestures with adequate think time
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher asks for a detailed explanation from all students and uses whiteboards [Why attempting:potentially insufficient space for student writing and likely insufficient time for teacher scan of responses though teacher will get some desired information; teacher should use a strategy like everybody writes with observation or turn and talk with listen in instead]
* Teacher checks students' understanding of a yes/no concept; uses cold call on 3 students [Why attempting: could easily check understanding of the full group with a poll for more comprehensive data]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher wants to know if students can explain rock formation process; uses gestures with answer choices A, B, C [Why non-example: Gestures don't capture explanations, only selected responses]
* Teacher needs to see students' problem-solving process for multi-step math; uses ask, ask, ask to ask individual students to share the answer they got but not how they got it [Why non-example: Provides no insight into problem-solving process, teacher likely needs to see written work to evaluate problem-solving process]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Annotations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to mark up a text or document with notes, highlights, underlines, symbols, or comments to show their thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Gives clear annotation expectations (what to mark, how, time for task, etc.)
* Students mark up text (underlining, circling, margin notes, or symbols, etc.) simultaneously
* Circulates throughout the room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use sticky notes if can't write in books
* May be physical or digital annotations
look_fors.strong_examples: "As you read paragraph 2, I want you to use two annotation strategies. First, underline any evidence that supports the author's claim that recycling helps the environment. Second, put a question mark next to anything you don't understand. You have 3 minutes to read and annotate." <Students read and mark text; teacher circulates>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "As you read, underline important parts." [Why attempting: Unclear what important parts are]
* "Circle the main idea and underline supporting details." <Stands in one place> [Why attempting: Strong prompt but no monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Annotate the text" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher does not circulate [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Ask, Ask, Ask
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A verbal method of checking for understanding where the teacher asks the same or a similar question to several students to make an inference about students’ understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Calls on 3+ different students, asking the same root question repeatedly
* Evidence that teacher is strategically sampling rather than just calling on those who raise hands first or know answer (e.g., gives wait time to get 50% or more of hands up before calling on anyone, uses cold call instead of hands, builds on knowledge of previous writing/speaking - e.g., "Katja, you agreed that 0 is an even number, can you explain why?", etc.)
* Does NOT reveal correct answer until questioning sequence is complete
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use randomization tools to select students
* May ask the same root question in different ways (e.g., "Marco, what's one character trait of Amos?" then "Fatima, do you agree or disagree with Marco, why?" then "Arecely, what's one character trait **you** would choose for Amos?")
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the main idea of the paragraph, Eli?" <Student responds> "What do you think the main idea of the paragraph is, Maricruz?" <Student responds> "Christian, do you agree with Maricruz? Why or why not?" <Student responds> "Thank you for sharing!" <Teacher states correct answer>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Calls on some non-volunteers but only 1-2 students total
* Calls on 3+ students but always those who raise hands within first 3 seconds
* Calls on 3+ students using cold call, but asks different root question to each (e.g., "Marco, what's one character trait of Amos?", "Fatima, how does Amos feel about the ocean?", "Arecely, why do you think Amos packed two barrels of fresh water for his trip?") [Why attempting: Multiple students but different questions]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Only calling on students with raised hands or accepting responses from those who call out [type: missed opportunity]
* Always calling on the same 2-3 students [type: missed opportunity]
* Asking one student, getting correct answer, and moving on [type: missed opportunity]
* Revealing correct answer before end of questioning sequence (e.g., "you are close but not quite, Marco") [type: missed opportunity]
* Giving cues as to whether answers are correct before questioning ends (e.g., only saying "great" or nodding when correct; only frowning when incorrect) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Graphic Organizers
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to fill in a structured visual organizer to support and.or show their understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear prompt/purpose for graphic organizer
* Clear directions for parts of graphic organizer (e.g, sections of t-chart, Venn diagram areas of overlap and non-overlap, etc.) and completion (e.g., time, individual vs. pair/group work, etc.)
* Organizer matches prompt/concept/thinking skill
* Students fill out
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Different types of graphic organizer
- Graphic organizers familiar to students may require less specific directions (e.g., "Fill out the t-chart to compare and contrast facts and opinions. Try to get at least three items for each")
- Semantic and concept maps are types of graphic organizer particularly useful for vocabulary development
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "You each have a Venn diagram on your desk. In the left circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for amphibians. In the right circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for reptiles. In the middle overlapping section, write characteristics they both share. Try to include at least 3 items in each section. You have 4 minutes to work with a partner."
- "On your paper, you have a cause-and-effect chart with three boxes. In the left column, write three causes of World War I. In the right column, write one effect for each cause. Be specific - use dates or events when you can. You have 3 minutes, silent and solo."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Fill in this Venn diagram comparing amphibians and reptiles." [Why attempting: Uses organizer but lacks specificity for organizer or completion]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Do your graphic organizer" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Show the steps of mitosis in the Venn diagram" [Why non-example: Organizer does not match concept/prompt] [type: learning harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Poll
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question at the same time via a gesture or other tool.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks question with clear answer options (A/B/C/D, true/false, agree/disagree) and clear way to show answer (hand signals, standing/sitting, etc.)
* IF question has only two response options (e.g., true/false or agree/disagree) follows up with an additional strategy like ask-ask-ask to learn more about student thinking
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time
* Students respond simultaneously
* Scans all responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used for polls in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May combine with think time or turn and talk first
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let’s take a look at question 2. When I say “show,” hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false. <Gives wait time>. Ready…show! " <Asks 2-3 students to explain why they chose true or false after the show>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's take a look at question 2. Hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false" [Why attempting: Clear answer options but no in-cue, no follow up questioning with only two response options]
* "Raise your hand if you think it's A. Raise your hand if you think it's B. Raise your hand if you think it’s C..." [Why attempting: Uses hand signals but sequential, not simultaneous]
* "Not yet, but when I say go, hold up your answer. Take some think time. <pause> Ok, ready, go!" [Why attempting: Has in-cue but unclear how to show answer]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Any questions?" <waits for raised hands> [Why non-example: Not a poll - only volunteers respond] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Ok, show me your answer" [Unclear how to show; students reveal at different times] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Everyone say their answer" [No in-cue, teacher unable to evaluate individual student responses when all spoken at once] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Total Physical Response (TPR)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for or supporting understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question or prompt at the same time using their whole body or physical movements in a way that conveys meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond with physical movement
* Physical movement clearly corresponds to concept being taught or assessed
* Prompts students to do the movement at the same time
* Students do movement simultaneously
* Scans student movements
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If using to check for understanding, must have more than one possible response and be in response to a question (e.g., "Imagine the UV light is here in the room and you are a plant. When I say go, use your body to show the direction you will grow")
* If using to convey meaning, may have single motion without a question (e.g., "frigid means really cold. cross your arms and shake your body to show brrrrrrrrr...frigid!")
* If using to convey meaning, exact simultaneous response less important
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Conveying meaning: "At convergent plate boundaries, plates crash or push together. Push your arms together like I am and say convergent with me. My turn - convergent. Your turn."
* Checking for understanding: "I'm going to say a number. If it's greater than 50, stand up. If it's less than 50, crouch down. If it's exactly 50, freeze in place. Ready? Think first, and then stand up, crouch down, or freeze when I say go. The number is 73....go" <All students stand. Teacher asks 2 students how they knew 73 was greater than 50>.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Show me with your body what it means to freeze" [Why attempting: Body movement but no in-cue]
* "Use your arms to make a rectangle because the constitution was written on parchment" [Why attempting: Not conceptually meaningful]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Raise your arms in air to be a cell" [Why non-example: Does not match concept] [type: learning harm]
* "Move your body to show the answer" [Vague prompt, no in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Whiteboards
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student holds up their work via a whiteboard on which they have written a response to a question or prompt.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond by writing/drawing on whiteboards/paper
* Gives time for all students to write/draw their response independently
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time by holding up whiteboard or paper
* Students hold up simultaneously
* Scans responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used as whiteboards in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
* May narrate trends they see in student responses
look_fors.strong_examples: "Take 45 seconds to calculate 24 ÷ 6 on your board and show your work. If you finish early, look at me so I know you are done, but do NOT hold your board up yet." <pauses for work time; circulates> <after 45 seconds> "Markers down. When I clap twice, flip your board to face me. Ready?" <claps twice> <Teacher scans boards>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "On your whiteboard, solve for x. When you're done, hold it up." [No synchronized reveal]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Write on your whiteboard then show it to me" [Why non-example: Vague prompt, no clear in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher gives question and immediately says "boards up" [Why non-example: No wait time, students can't complete task] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Clear Standards for Success (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Ensure students understand what success looks like and can evaluate their own progress by sharing high expectations that are specific, clear, and concrete

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame tasks as challenging yet worthy while maintaining rigorous standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Acknowledges difficulty/high expectations but doesn't frame as worthy (e.g., "This is hard" or "Oooh, a spicy problem!")
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
* Assigning easier work to struggling students without scaffolding the grade-level content [Why non-example: Reduces rigor]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required for exemplary rating on Danielson 3d: Clear Standards for Success
Else not required
look_fors.name: Student Goal-Setting
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in establishing and tracking goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Facilitates process for students to set personal or collective goals
* Provides structure for students to monitor or reflect on progress toward goals
* Conferences with students about their goals
* Celebrates progress toward student-identified goals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Goals may be academic, behavioral, or both
* Can be short-term (daily/weekly) or long-term (unit/semester)
* May use goal-setting templates, trackers, or reflection protocols
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you'll each set a goal for what you want to improve. We'll check in on Fridays to see your progress"
* "Look at your data from the last assessment. Based on that, what's one skill you want to strengthen?"
* Students maintain goal-tracking sheets and regularly reflect on progress
* "Now that we've identified group strengths relative to our class norms, take 2 minutes to write a personal goal relative to our class norms. Refer to the examples on the board if you need some inspiration!"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What do you want to work on today?" [Why attempting: Vague]
* "Here are our class goals. Raise your hand if you would like propose any changes or additions" [Why attempting: Teacher-led with student input]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All goals set by teacher without student input
* Goals never referenced

look_fors.name: Checklist
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use a structured checklist of specific criteria while observing, listening to, or questioning students to systematically gather data on understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher holds/references physical or digital checklist
* Marks criteria for multiple students
* May make statements referencing checklist data
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May sample strategically rather than check every student
look_fors.strong_examples: Carries clipboard with checklist showing student names in rows and columns labeled: "Labels diagram correctly," "Uses at least 3 content vocabulary words," "Includes claim and evidence." Circulates systematically, looking at each student's work and marking checks or notes in appropriate cells. After circulating, shares patterns noticed.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Carries checklist but only marks 1-2 students [Why attempting: Insufficient data]
* References vague criteria like "understands concept"
look_fors.non_examples:
* Observing/listening in to students without any structured criteria [type: missed opportunity]
* Has/references checklist but does not use/make any marks on [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Criteria for Success
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide a visible list of the top 2-5 actions students need to successfully complete the task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides checklist or criteria visible to students
* Criteria include what students need to know and show or do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria may be co-created with students or teacher-provided
* May be referenced at different points: before task, during work, during revision, during peer review
* Criteria can be used by teacher for checking understanding while observing/listening in
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Review our checklist for success as you go through the problem to guide your work" <Points to visible checklist with 3-4 items>
* Before writing: "Your paragraph must: 1) State a clear claim, 2) Include 2-3 pieces of text evidence, and 3) Explain how evidence supports your claim"
* During revision: "Check your work against our criteria. Do you have all three branches labeled with their powers?"
* While observing: <Teacher uses criteria checklist to note which students have included required components>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember today's objective focuses on the impacts of the Nuremberg Laws. Be sure you show that in your response to the exit ticket prompt" [Why attempting: Too broad]
* Teacher provides criteria that only focus on format, not content 
* Criteria are written on board but never referenced
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher does not provide visible criteria
* "Remember to do your best work" [Why non-example: Vague, no specific criteria]
* Teacher provides 10+ criteria [Why non-example: Too many to be actionable]

look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Learning Goal(s)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to learning goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or points to learning goal
* Uses language like "Today you'll learn..." or "By the end of this activity, you'll be able to..."
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use to frame full lesson or activity in a lesson
* May reference during in struction to highlight connection (e.g., this helps us achieve today's goal of simplifying fractions by...")
* Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
* Learning goal may be for unit, lesson, or activity
* May refer to learning goal using different terminology such as objective, outcome, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you will learn how to identify the main idea and supporting details in nonfiction text. This will help you understand what authors want you to remember most"
* "By the end of this activity, you will be able to identify and explain each stage of the water cycle"
* "Our goal today is to master adding fractions with unlike denominators"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "We're going to learn about fractions" [Why attempting: Vague; does not specify specific goal related to fractions]
