* "The objective is on the board" <points but doesn't read or discuss> [Why attempting: Doesn't actively frame or reference]
* “Show your mastery of today’s objective on this exit ticket!” [Why attempting: References objective, but not in a way that reinforces the specific goal]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: Focuses on what students will do not learn]

look_fors.name: Use an Exemplar
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Show or reference a completed example that demonstrates mastery of a task, including thought or work process when applicable.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Shows completed example of strong work
* Highlights multiple approaches or methods when possible
* Explicitly references what makes the example strong
* Example aligns to rigor of lesson objective and standards
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be used during instruction (for analysis, think aloud) or as reference during student work
* If used as reference during student work, exemplar should be similar but not identical to student task
* Exemplar may be teacher-created or a previous student work sample
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Notice that in the strong example the writer first named a character trait to describe Amos. Then, they provided and explained text evidence to illustrate the character trait"
* Teacher creates exemplar during think aloud: "Watch me solve this problem. First, I identify my knowns and unknowns..." <writes on board showing work organization>
* "Before you start on problem 5, let's review our two examples from earlier. Notice how the first example arrived at a correct answer by drawing stick figures and counting on. The second example created a number sentence, used subtraction and ALSO arrived at a correct answer. There are multiple ways to solve problem 5. You can use either of our previous examples to guide your work or show a new way, but be sure to show your work."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher shows exemplar but doesn't explain what makes it strong
* Teacher references an exemplar during student work revisions, but does not explain how to use it
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Complete the essay using what we've learned" [Why non-example: No exemplar provided]
* Teacher shows exemplar that doesn't match the rigor of the lesson objective [Why non-example: Misaligned rigor]
* Teacher shows exemplar that exactly matches student task BEFORE students complete task [Why attempting: Gives answer away]

skills.name: Close Reading Rounds
skills.description: Plan and facilitate multiple purposeful rounds of reading a complex text to build understanding of the text's full meaning.

look_fors.type_explanation: Often the culminating, highest-order question across the rounds
look_fors.name: Elaborative Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that gets at the text's deeper understanding, theme, or overall meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question asks students to synthesize across the text (not a single detail) to identify a theme, lesson, or overall understanding
* Requires students to use evidence from the text to support a broader interpretive claim
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May ask students to state and defend a theme, lesson, or big-picture interpretation
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is this story teaching us about hard work? Use evidence from the text to explain."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What is the theme of this story?" <accepts a one-word answer with no evidence> [Why attempting: elaborative question, but no textual support required]
look_fors.non_examples: "Do you think hard work is important?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Generally earliest in the complexity progression across rounds
look_fors.name: Explicit Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question whose answer is directly stated in the text ("right there").
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question can be answered by locating information stated outright in the text
* Answer does not require inference or interpretation beyond locating/paraphrasing what is stated
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May ask students to quote the exact text or paraphrase what is stated, or locate it within the text
* May be posed before, during, or after reading a passage
look_fors.strong_examples: "What did Mary's mother do after her father died?" (Answer: she sold everything — directly stated in the text)
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What happened in this chapter?" [Why attempting: text-dependent, but too broad to pinpoint a specific explicitly-stated detail]
look_fors.non_examples: "What does 'sold' mean?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Each round must begin with this look-for
look_fors.name: Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview what will happen and state clear focus for student thinking and engagement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews what teacher and/or students will do
* States clear purpose, target question, or learning focus
* Gives students specific task or role during activity (listen for, analyze, record, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May check for understanding of the framing before beginning the activity
* Student task may be note-taking, analyzing, comparing, evaluating, or other cognitive engagement
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I have noticed that our understanding of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' sometimes breaks down because of all the pronouns that Zora Neale Hurston uses. When texts have tons of pronouns, there are steps readers can follow to avoid confusion. I will show you how I make sense of the pronouns so I can follow along with the story. As I am thinking aloud for you, I want you to record notes on the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean. Before I start sharing my thinking, remind me - what are you doing as I am thinking aloud for you?"

* "I want to highlight DeAndre's response. As I read it, think about what makes his argument strong." <Reads>

* "I'm going to show you each characteristic of parallel lines with examples. As I do, record the characteristic and an example in your notes. You will use your notes later to practice identifying examples and non-examples of parallel lines based on these characteristics."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "I am going to show you both methods for the sake of putting it out there, whichever you prefer. So let's start by using slope-intercept form. Which form are we starting with?" [Why attempting: Purpose unclear, no student task/goal]
- "This think aloud will be about dividing fractions." [Why attempting: States topic but not purpose or goal]
- "Take a look up here quickly and just pause what you're doing. I want to highlight a student response." [Why attempting: missing why they are highlighting specific student response]
- “Today we are going to continue our focus on fluency. I want you all to sit where you are and listen, then I want to hear you all read. [Why attempting: Fluency is too broad, purpose should be more specific]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, listen to me think aloud." [Why non-example: No framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "I'm going to show you how to do this. Pay attention." [Why non-example: 'Pay attention' too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as compliance (e.g., "Complete this task to earn your participation points for the day", "You must read") [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as for grades or test performance only (e.g., "This is on the state exam", "This exit ticket is like a quiz for your grade") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Generally increases in complexity after explicit questions across rounds
look_fors.name: Implicit Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question whose answer requires inference, because it is not directly stated in the text.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question cannot be answered by locating a single stated sentence
* Requires students to combine information from the text with their own knowledge and analysis to infer an answer
* Teacher asks students to point to what in the text supports the inference
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require inferring feelings, motivation, or an unstated cause/effect
* May draw on multiple parts of the text combined
look_fors.strong_examples: "The text never tells us how the hen felt when her friends said no. Based on what she did next, how do you think she felt, and what in the text makes you think that?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "How do you think the hen felt?" <accepts a one-word answer without asking what in the text supports it> [Why attempting: inferential question, but no textual support required]
look_fors.non_examples: "How do people usually feel when their friends reject them?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a round's stated purpose or format calls for this structure; else not required
look_fors.name: Annotations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to mark up a text or document with notes, highlights, underlines, symbols, or comments to show their thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Gives clear annotation expectations (what to mark, how, time for task, etc.)
* Students mark up text (underlining, circling, margin notes, or symbols, etc.) simultaneously
* Circulates throughout the room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use sticky notes if can't write in books
* May be physical or digital annotations
look_fors.strong_examples: "As you read paragraph 2, I want you to use two annotation strategies. First, underline any evidence that supports the author's claim that recycling helps the environment. Second, put a question mark next to anything you don't understand. You have 3 minutes to read and annotate." <Students read and mark text; teacher circulates>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "As you read, underline important parts." [Why attempting: Unclear what important parts are]
* "Circle the main idea and underline supporting details." <Stands in one place> [Why attempting: Strong prompt but no monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Annotate the text" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher does not circulate [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a round's stated purpose or format calls for this structure; else not required
look_fors.name: Choral Reading
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have the class or a group read a passage aloud together in unison.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Has the group (or whole class) read the same passage aloud together at once
Reads along with or sets the pace for the group to support accuracy and expression
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let's read this together, my voice with yours, nice and smooth." <Group reads the passage in unison at a steady pace.>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Has the group read together but at no set pace, so students drift apart and some fall silent. [Why attempting: unison not supported]
look_fors.non_examples: Calls on students one at a time to read aloud while others listen. [Why non-example: round-robin, not choral]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a round's stated purpose or format calls for this structure; else not required
look_fors.name: Partner Reading
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pair students to read the same text aloud, taking turns and giving feedback to each other.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Pairs students to read the same text, alternating readers
Gives the listening partner a clear role (follow along, help with a stuck word, give feedback)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Partners may alternate by sentence, paragraph, or page; pairing need not be by matched level.
look_fors.strong_examples: "Partner A reads page 1 while Partner B follows along and helps with any stuck word by stretching the sounds; then switch for page 2."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- Pairs students to read but gives the listener no role, so one reads while the other waits. [Why attempting: no listener role]
- Pairs students to read but only directs one partner to read and the other to listen. Never has them switch. [Why attempting: Both partners should read]
look_fors.non_examples: "Read silently to yourselves." [Why non-example: no partner oral reading]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a round's stated purpose or format calls for this structure; else not required
look_fors.name: Read with Expression (Prosody)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Read with expression, varying intonation and stress to match meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Varies intonation (pitch) and stress to match punctuation and meaning 
- Reads dialogue and emphasis with appropriate expression, not monotone
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
A student with a naturally flat affect may read with little expression; this is acceptable when comprehension is not impaired.
Expression is judged against meaning, not performance.
Reading with expression may apply to teacher modeling or student practice.
look_fors.strong_examples: Reads "He loves tigers!" with rising excitement and pauses at the exclamation point, matching the meaning of the sentence.
look_fors.attempting_examples: Reads with some expression but ignores a character's excited dialogue, reading it flatly. [Why attempting: inconsistent expression]
look_fors.non_examples: Reads quickly and accurately but in a flat, robotic monotone and cannot recall what was read. [Why non-example: no prosody, meaning lost]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a round's stated purpose or format calls for this structure; else not required
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Access Supports): teacher must use at least one Group A look-for to help students access the text
look_fors.name: Connect to Prior Knowledge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Activate students' existing knowledge of the topic or content.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Prompts students to recall what they already know about the topic or concept
* Links new content to previously learned content or familiar real-world concepts
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Background knowledge may be drawn from prior lessons or common experience
* May ask students questions, have them complete a practice item to demonstrate a previous skill, or otherwise engage students in the relevant prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "This story is about seeds. Remember when we learned how seeds grow into plants? Look, this character is planting a seed right here. What do you already know about what a seed needs?"
* "Today we will learn to calculate density. Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month, so your do now today is a speed problem. Pay attention to how you figure out the units in your answer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This story is about the ocean. Who has seen a picture the ocean or a picture of it?" <A few students raise hands and teacher moves on> [Why attempting: superficial connection to prior knowledge]
* "Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month. You divide one number by another and keep the units." [Why attempting: teacher-led connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "This story is about the ocean." [Why non-example: no connection to prior knowledge]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Access Supports): teacher must use at least one Group A look-for to help students access the text
look_fors.name: Explain Unfamiliar Terms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explain unfamiliar terms to support content understanding and vocabulary development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Defines new or unfamiliar words
- Provides synonyms or familiar language for unfamiliar terms
- NOT required when term is part of a classroom routine or procedure (e.g., "phonics time") or refers to a skill likely used repeatedly in a grade/subject (e.g., "calculate," "solve," "blend," etc.) unless the teacher indicates this is the first time with the routine or skill
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May provide or connect to word(s) in students' home language(s) to support explanation of target word when teaching multilingual learners
look_fors.strong_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries where earth’s plates move away from each other.”
- “A cake is the baked dessert in this picture. Cake in Spanish is ‘pastel’.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- “There are some new words that you're going to learn in this book. Same, recipe,  and unique. Alright, let’s get started and see what happens.” [Why non-example; Names but does not explain new terms]
look_fors.non_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- I am using expression, so you hear my voice. I have intonation and inflection. [Why non-example: expression is just more than hearing voice; no definition of intonation or inflection]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Graphic Organizers
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to fill in a structured visual organizer to support and.or show their understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear prompt/purpose for graphic organizer
* Clear directions for parts of graphic organizer (e.g, sections of t-chart, Venn diagram areas of overlap and non-overlap, etc.) and completion (e.g., time, individual vs. pair/group work, etc.)
* Organizer matches prompt/concept/thinking skill
* Students fill out
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Different types of graphic organizer
- Graphic organizers familiar to students may require less specific directions (e.g., "Fill out the t-chart to compare and contrast facts and opinions. Try to get at least three items for each")
- Semantic and concept maps are types of graphic organizer particularly useful for vocabulary development
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "You each have a Venn diagram on your desk. In the left circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for amphibians. In the right circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for reptiles. In the middle overlapping section, write characteristics they both share. Try to include at least 3 items in each section. You have 4 minutes to work with a partner."
- "On your paper, you have a cause-and-effect chart with three boxes. In the left column, write three causes of World War I. In the right column, write one effect for each cause. Be specific - use dates or events when you can. You have 3 minutes, silent and solo."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Fill in this Venn diagram comparing amphibians and reptiles." [Why attempting: Uses organizer but lacks specificity for organizer or completion]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Do your graphic organizer" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Show the steps of mitosis in the Venn diagram" [Why non-example: Organizer does not match concept/prompt] [type: learning harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Access Supports): teacher must use at least one Group A look-for to help students access the text
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Paired Text
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Introduce a shorter, topically related text to build vocabulary or background knowledge that scaffolds comprehension of the main text.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Introduces a second, shorter text (e.g., poem, song, short passage) related in topic or vocabulary to the main text being closely read
* Connects the paired text explicitly back to the main text (e.g., asks how the paired text relates to the main text)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Paired text may be introduced before reading the main text (to build background) or during/after (to reinforce or extend understanding)
* May take the form of a poem, song, short passage, or other brief text
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher reads the "She Sells Seashells" poem, then asks: "What does the 'She Sells Seashells' poem have to do with Mary Anning?" Student: "It's about her selling fossils to visitors at the beach."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <reads "She Sells Seashells" aloud> "Think about this poem while we continue learning about Mary Anning" [Why attempting: lacks explicit text to text connection]
look_fors.non_examples: "Let's read this fun poem about the seashore!" <reads "She Sells Seashells,"> "Ok, now let's read our story." [Why non-example: no connection made to the main text]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Scaffolding Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student is stuck or makes an error, ask a simpler or more foundational question to get them thinking, then use their response to bridge back to the original task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student is stuck or has made an error
* Teacher asks a simpler, more foundational, or more manageable question related to the original task or question
* Teacher connects the student's response back to the original task or question
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require more than one scaffolding question before returning to the original task
* Scaffolding question may break the task into a smaller chunk (e.g., "What's the first step?") rather than stepping down in conceptual complexity 
* Bridge back may be a statement rather than a question (e.g., "Ok, now that you've identified you need to multiply length x width, do that to find the area and finish the problem")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Let's start with what area means. What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something."  Teacher: "Yes, and why does that help us here?" Student: "Because we need to find how much space the rectangle takes up." Teacher: "Exactly. So what information does the problem give you that might help you figure that out?"
 * Student: <identifies an incorrect theme> Teacher: "What actually happens to the main character by the end of the story?" Student: "She decides to go back and help even though it's hard." Teacher: "Good. So what do you think the author wants us to learn from that choice? That's your theme."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something." Teacher: "It's the size, or how much space the rectangle takes up. Now find the area of this rectangle." [Why attempting: Asks one scaffolding question but does not check to see if student needs more in order to complete the problem]
look_fors.non_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Remember, the area of a rectangle is length x width" [Why non-example: Provides a cue rather than asking a question; thinking stays with teacher]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group B (Struggle Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group B look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Text Chunking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break the text into smaller, manageable parts to support comprehension of a longer or more complex sentence or passage.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Displays or reads aloud one chunk (word, phrase, sentence, or short section) of the text at a time, rather than the full sentence/passage at once
* Asks a question or prompts thinking about that specific chunk before moving to the next chunk
* Builds toward the meaning of the full sentence or passage across the chunks
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Chunk size may vary (word, phrase, or sentence) depending on text complexity and student need
* May chunk visually (sentence strips, highlighting, revealing text progressively) or verbally (reading and pausing)
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher displays and reads: "Mary" <pause> "Who is the sentence about?" <student responds: "Mary"> Teacher then displays and reads: "had few friends," and asks the following sequence of questions, taking student responses for each: "What did Mary have?"; "How many friends is 'few'?"; "What if we added the word a in front of few? Would that change the meaning? How?"; "Can you say this chunk in your own words? How?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: <displays the full sentence at once> "Let's break this down. Who is it about? Mary. What problem did she have? Few friends. Why? Because of her family's poverty and the teasing." [Why attempting: connection to exact text chunks implied instead of explicit]
look_fors.non_examples: "Mary had few friends because of her family's poverty and the other children's teasing. What does this sentence mean?" [Why non-example: full sentence given at once, no chunking]

skills.name: Collective Success (Saga)
skills.description: Create a collective feeling of success where every student contributes to and shares in the group's progress

look_fors.name: Emphasize Collective Success
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame learning as community endeavor where all contribute
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses "we" language when discussing learning and progress
* Frames individual success as benefiting the group
* Teacher and students celebrate whole-class achievements or growth
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use class goals or challenges
* May highlight how diverse perspectives strengthen collective understanding
* May create accountability to peers, not just to teacher
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We're all learning together, and each person's ideas make us all smarter. With that in mind, let's here from a few different perspectives to help us interpret the evidence we collected"
* "Our collective effort helped us reach this milestone. Everyone contributed"
* Creates team game structure where students work together toward shared goal
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Use of we/our language without explicit connection to goals, collective work, classroom community, etc. (e.g., "Welcome to our classroom!", "Today we will work together to learn....", etc.)
* Let's here from a few different perspectives on this one" [Why attempting: Implies but does not make explicit individual contribution to strengthen whole group learning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Only individual competition or achievement recognized
* "My classroom" language
* Emphasizes individual success without connecting to community

look_fors.name: Facilitate Student-to-Student Relationships
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structures and opportunities for students to interact positively with each other
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses instructional structures that require student interaction (turn and talks, partner work, group discussions)
* Creates opportunities for students to give each other recognition
* Students demonstrate respect when peers speak or share
* Students show care for each other (affirming comments, applause, support)
* Students demonstrate knowledge of one another as individuals (e.g., interests, events, traditions, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student-to-student interactions can occur through structured academic tasks, classroom routines, or social-emotional activities
* Can involve brief partner interactions or extended collaborative work
* May include sentence or question frames for productive discussion (e.g., "Can you explain...?," "I agree because...," "I disagree because...," etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Students respond positively to peers who share (e.g., hand signals to show encouragement, building on each others' ideas, etc.)
* "Let's take a moment for shout-outs. Who noticed someone doing something kind or helpful today?" <multiple students recognize peers>
* Teacher structures lesson with multiple turn-and-talks and small group work. Students proactively demonstrate respect for each other by not interrupting each other, waiting for speakers to finish, and building on each other's ideas. Students appear comfortable engaging with various classmates.
* Teacher or students refer to class norms either for praise or positively framed reminders
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Students work in pairs or groups but some students dominate the conversation or students do not recognize or encourage each other [Why attempting: Structure exists but lacks intentional development of positive relationships]
* Student-to-student interactions are rarely hostile or dismissive, but when a negative interaction does occur teacher does not respond
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lesson consists entirely of teacher-led instruction with no student-to-student interaction opportunities [type: missed opportunity]
* Student-to-student interactions are sometimes or often hostile or dismissive (e.g., "Ha, you don't know what you're talking about," "Ugh, do I have to work with Mariana?," students interrupt each other, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Any form of bullying goes unaddressed [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.name: Group Roles
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Assign and support specific roles to student group members to support collaboration
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns or has students assign specific roles within groups
* Names roles and responsibilities (e.g., facilitator, recorder, timekeeper, materials manager, reporter)
* Refers to roles during activity to support accountability
  Roles distribute responsibility across all group members
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Roles can vary based on task (discussion roles vs. task roles)
* May provide role cards or descriptions
* In a tutoring context, there may only be one group and group may be small (e.g., 2 students only)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "In your groups, assign these roles: facilitator to keep discussion moving, recorder to capture ideas, timekeeper to monitor pace, and reporter to share findings. Each person is essential to your success"
* "Today's roles are: reader, materials manager, and checker. I'll explain each job and then you will decide who will do what in your group." 
 * "You'll need a question-asker and a summarizer in each pair. Take 10 seconds to decide who does what"
 * Provides role cards with specific responsibilities for each group member
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Assigns only one role ("Someone be the recorder") 
* "Make sure each person in your group contributes something to the discussion"
look_fors.non_examples: * "Work with your table group" <no roles or structure provided>

skills.name: Comprehensible Input
skills.description: Deliver instruction in a way that maximizes comprehension and supports language development for multilingual learners.

look_fors.name: Enunciate
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pronounce words such that all component phonemes are audible.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Each word is pronounced distinctly
* Consonants and vowels are crisp and clear
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Variations in accent are fine and should not be penalized
look_fors.strong_examples: Distincly enunciates all or almost all words
look_fors.attempting_examples: Distinctly enunciates most words
look_fors.non_examples: Distinctly enunciates less than half of words

look_fors.name: Explain Unfamiliar Terms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explain unfamiliar terms to support content understanding and vocabulary development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Defines new or unfamiliar words
- Provides synonyms or familiar language for unfamiliar terms
- NOT required when term is part of a classroom routine or procedure (e.g., "phonics time") or refers to a skill likely used repeatedly in a grade/subject (e.g., "calculate," "solve," "blend," etc.) unless the teacher indicates this is the first time with the routine or skill
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May provide or connect to word(s) in students' home language(s) to support explanation of target word when teaching multilingual learners
look_fors.strong_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries where earth’s plates move away from each other.”
- “A cake is the baked dessert in this picture. Cake in Spanish is ‘pastel’.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- “There are some new words that you're going to learn in this book. Same, recipe,  and unique. Alright, let’s get started and see what happens.” [Why non-example; Names but does not explain new terms]
look_fors.non_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- I am using expression, so you hear my voice. I have intonation and inflection. [Why non-example: expression is just more than hearing voice; no definition of intonation or inflection]

look_fors.name: Gestures for Meaning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use gestures to demonstrate the meaning of a concept or a word, supporting understanding and language development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses hand movements, body language, or facial expressions that illustrate meaning
* Gestures match/support verbal content
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “These are all different types of acute angles that I am making with my arms”
* “Stand up for lava and duck down for magma”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “As I read, give a thumbs up every time you hear the word amendment" (Why non-example: Not clearly connected to meaning)
look_fors.non_examples:
* Does not use gestures
* “Give me a thumbs up if you understand” (Why non-example: Not paired with concept or word)

look_fors.name: Keep Sentences Short
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Keep sentences short to help students process words, concepts, and ideas.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sentences are brief (typically under 10-15 words)
* Complex ideas or instructions are broken into multiple simple sentences
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Slightly longer sentences acceptable when they include a paraphrased definition (e.g., “The cuisine, meaning the unique cooking and food types, of this region includes…”)
look_fors.strong_examples: “Now we will practice interpreting pronouns. A pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. Let’s look at an example sentence together. ‘The people all saw her come because it was sundown.’ I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is her. Her could be replaced by the person’s name. I will highlight her.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Now we will practice interpreting pronouns, or words used to replace nouns. Let’s look at an example sentence together. ‘The people all saw her come because it was sundown.’ I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun and so the first pronoun I see here is her. Her could be replaced by the person’s name so I will highlight her.” [Why attempting: Some sentences could be broken up without disrupting flow]
look_fors.non_examples: “Now we will practice, with some examples, interpreting pronouns, which we know are words used to replace nouns. Let’s look at this example sentence from ‘Their Eyes Were Watching God,’ our book for this unit, together: ‘The people all saw her come because it was sundown.’ The first pronoun I see is her because a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun and her could be replaced by the person’s name so I will highlight it.”

look_fors.name: Pause
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Brief pauses between sentences and ideas can help learners who need additional time to process language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Stops speaking for 1-3 seconds between sentences or between distinct ideas to break up the flow of information
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May pause longer after groups of sentences with related ideas are shared
look_fors.strong_examples: Regularly pauses for 1-3 seconds after sentences and ideas
look_fors.attempting_examples: Occasionally pauses for 1-3 seconds after sentences or ideas
look_fors.non_examples: No discernable pauses between sentences or groups or ideas

look_fors.name: Repeat or Paraphrase Key Information
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Strategically repeat or paraphrase key words or ideas
look_fors.observable_behaviors: - Says same idea or word multiple times when presenting key concepts, ideas, or instructions
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Repetition may be skipped for familiar concepts, ideas, or instructions
- Repetition and rephrasing may be applied to questions as well as statements
look_fors.strong_examples: “The slope, meaning the rate of change, of the graph increases here. Increases means the value of the slope goes up. I can tell the slope increases because the line gets steeper. The steeper line represents a greater rate of change or greater slope as compared to farther left on the graph.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “The slope, meaning the rate of change, of the graph increases or goes up here. I can tell because the line gets steeper.”
look_fors.non_examples: “The slope increases here because the line gets steeper.”

look_fors.name: Speak Slowly
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Speaking slowly can help learners who need additional time to process language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher's speech rate is noticeably slower than typical conversation while still flowing enough to hold students' attention
* Words are not rushed and do not run together
look_fors.strong_examples: Regularly speaks at about 90 words per minute or slower
look_fors.attempting_examples: Regularly speaks at about 91-125 words per minute
look_fors.non_examples: Regularly speaks faster than 125 words per minute

look_fors.name: Add Emphasis
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Emphasize key words in speech to help call attention to them.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Changes volume, pitch, stress, or pace on important words or terms
look_fors.strong_examples: "When we are reading, sometimes it is tricky to figure out how a character is **feeling** if the author does not tell us. I am going to walk you through the **two steps** I take when I am reading a story to figure out how a character **feels.** As I am thinking out loud, I want you to listen for the **two steps** I take to figure out how the character is **feeling.**
look_fors.attempting_examples: "When we are reading, sometimes it is tricky to figure out how a character is **feeling** if the author does not tell us. I am going to walk you through the **two steps** I take when I am reading a story to figure out how a character feels. As I am thinking out loud, I want you to listen for the two steps I take to figure out how the character is feeling." [Why attempting: Inconsistent emphasis]
look_fors.non_examples: Does not emphasize keywords

look_fors.name: Criteria for Success
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide a visible list of the top 2-5 actions students need to successfully complete the task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides checklist or criteria visible to students
* Criteria include what students need to know and show or do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria may be co-created with students or teacher-provided
* May be referenced at different points: before task, during work, during revision, during peer review
* Criteria can be used by teacher for checking understanding while observing/listening in
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Review our checklist for success as you go through the problem to guide your work" <Points to visible checklist with 3-4 items>
* Before writing: "Your paragraph must: 1) State a clear claim, 2) Include 2-3 pieces of text evidence, and 3) Explain how evidence supports your claim"
* During revision: "Check your work against our criteria. Do you have all three branches labeled with their powers?"
* While observing: <Teacher uses criteria checklist to note which students have included required components>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember today's objective focuses on the impacts of the Nuremberg Laws. Be sure you show that in your response to the exit ticket prompt" [Why attempting: Too broad]
* Teacher provides criteria that only focus on format, not content 
* Criteria are written on board but never referenced
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher does not provide visible criteria
* "Remember to do your best work" [Why non-example: Vague, no specific criteria]
* Teacher provides 10+ criteria [Why non-example: Too many to be actionable]

look_fors.name: Do Not Use Contractions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Avoid contractions to support speech comprehension for multilingual learners who may not yet be familiar with contractions.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Does not use contractions; says "do not" instead of "don't", "we are" instead of "we're", etc.
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Contractions where the expanded form is rarely used in speech or writing are acceptable (e.g., "let's")
look_fors.strong_examples: Does not use contractions
look_fors.attempting_examples: Avoids a commonly used contraction (e.g., says “cannot” instead of “can’t”) but also includes a contraction (e.g., don’t, wasn’t, etc.) [Why attempting: Partial implementation]
look_fors.non_examples: Includes multiple contractions

look_fors.name: Do Not Use Fused Forms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Avoid fused forms (e.g., gonna, wanna) to support speech comprehension for multilingual learners who may not yet be familiar with fused forms.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Does not use fused form; says "going to" instead of "gonna", "want to" instead of "wanna"
look_fors.strong_examples: Does not use fused forms
look_fors.attempting_examples: Avoids a commonly used fused form (e.g., says “going to” instead of “gonna”) but also includes a fused form (e.g., “dunno” or “lemme”)  [Why attempting: Partial implementation]
look_fors.non_examples: Includes multiple fused forms

look_fors.name: Do Not Use Idioms or Slang
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Avoid idioms and slang to support speech comprehension for multilingual learners who may not yet be familiar with them.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Does not use idioms or slang; avoids phrases like "piece of cake", "hit the books", "my bad", "no biggie", etc.
* Uses literal language
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Idioms or slang with an explanation (e.g., taught as part of a lesson) are acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples: Does not use slang or idioms
look_fors.attempting_examples: Uses one extremely common slang term, which students across stages of language acquisition are likely to have encountered multiple times from multiple people (e.g., "hang out") [Why attempting: Minimal, commonly understood slang]
look_fors.non_examples: Includes multiple slang terms or idioms

look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.name: Model/Demonstrate Task
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Model or demonstrate what success looks like for a task, routine, or procedure.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Demonstrates (e.g., physically models, shows on paper or screen, etc.) or has student demonstrate what success looks like
- Model/demonstration is accurate
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- For multi-step tasks, routines, or procedures, model is presented step-by-step
- Can use student volunteer to demonstrate with teacher guidance
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on as shown in our safety gear image. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why strong: Uses visual and body motion/modeling in addition to verbal]
- Teacher demonstrates turn and talk in specific steps (e.g., face each other, decide who goes first, etc.) with student volunteers while rest of class observes and checks off steps on handout. After model, teacher narrates what was done well and highlights hardest part.
- “Watch my mouth” <points to mouth> “B says /b/. Watch again for how I press my lips together. /b/.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- <Teacher asks for two volunteers to model turn and talk> "Thanks Randy and Rochely. Ok, show me the turn and talk procedure" [Why attempting: Not specific, not broken down into steps for longer procedure]
- "Look how strong table 3's lab set-up is" [Why attempting: References exemplar but vague about what makes it strong]
- “Listen to me. B says /b/” [Why attempting: accurate model but verbal only]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution." [Why non-example: Verbal only, no demonstration]
- “Listen to me. B says buh”  [Why non-example: model inaccurate and verbal only]

look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Participation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Vary the modes students use to respond.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses 2+ participation modes (e.g., saying, writing, gesturing, drawing, moving) across the lesson or lesson segment
* Varies the mode across activities or segments rather than defaulting to one
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May offer choice in how students communicate or demonstrate their understanding; this still counts as 2+ modes
* A single mode is fine in a moment, but multiple modes should be used across time
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Write your prediction on your sticky note." <Students write> "Now stand up and put your sticky note on the chart under the heading you picked." <Students move to chart> "Turn and tell your partner why you chose that one."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone write your answer in your notebook. If you finish early, you can draw a quick sketch of it." [Why attempting: second mode only for early finishers]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Every prompt across the lesson or lesson segment asks students to respond in writing with no opportunities for other modes like drawing or speaking
* "Turn and tell your partner what you predict." <Later> "Turn and tell your partner what surprised you."

look_fors.name: Point out Cognates
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Point out cognates in a student’s home language to help them learn new vocabulary words more quickly and easily.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly states when a word is similar in student's home language
* Makes connection between languages (e.g., "In Spanish, this word sounds similar")
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Use of cognates may be more or less frequent depending on instructional language and student's home language (e.g., more cognates between English and Spanish than English and Chinese)
look_fors.strong_examples: When applicable, points out cognates for key words (e.g., “Today we will share family traditions. In Spanish, we say tradiciones familiares - notice how similar tradiciones in Spanish is to traditions in English, and how familiares and family also start with the same sounds”).
look_fors.attempting_examples: When applicable, references cognates for key words (e.g., "Today, we will share family traditions, tradiciones familiares") [Why attempting: States cognate, doesn't highlight similarity]
look_fors.non_examples: Misses an opportunity to share a cognate for a key word.

look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Agenda
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to lesson agenda to reinforce key vocabulary and/or preview learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Refers to written agenda or schedule
* Makes connection to what students are learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
look_fors.strong_examples: “Let’s move on to our next activity on the agenda for today: the debrief. Our debrief discussion will help us explain how array models help us multiply.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Let's move on to our next activity [Why attempting: Vague]
* The agenda is on the board <points but doesn't read or reference specifics] [Why attempting: doesn't actively frame or reference]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: No information on flow of time or learning activities]

look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Learning Goal(s)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to learning goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or points to learning goal
* Uses language like "Today you'll learn..." or "By the end of this activity, you'll be able to..."
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use to frame full lesson or activity in a lesson
* May reference during in struction to highlight connection (e.g., this helps us achieve today's goal of simplifying fractions by...")
* Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
* Learning goal may be for unit, lesson, or activity
* May refer to learning goal using different terminology such as objective, outcome, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you will learn how to identify the main idea and supporting details in nonfiction text. This will help you understand what authors want you to remember most"
* "By the end of this activity, you will be able to identify and explain each stage of the water cycle"
* "Our goal today is to master adding fractions with unlike denominators"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "We're going to learn about fractions" [Why attempting: Vague; does not specify specific goal related to fractions]
* "The objective is on the board" <points but doesn't read or discuss> [Why attempting: Doesn't actively frame or reference]
* “Show your mastery of today’s objective on this exit ticket!” [Why attempting: References objective, but not in a way that reinforces the specific goal]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: Focuses on what students will do not learn]

look_fors.name: Teach Multiple Forms of New Words
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach multiple forms of new words to support students’ ability to use the word in context.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents related forms of new vocabulary (e.g., predict, prediction, predictable)
* Shows how word changes with different endings or uses
* Uses different forms of word in context (e.g., sentences)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May prioritize key vocabulary for teaching multiple forms rather than doing this for ALL words that may be new to students
look_fors.strong_examples: Teaches multiple forms of new words in context with examples of use.
look_fors.attempting_examples: References multiple forms of new words, but does not provide in context examples of use for each form.
look_fors.non_examples: Teaches only one form of a new word.

look_fors.name: Use an Exemplar
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Show or reference a completed example that demonstrates mastery of a task, including thought or work process when applicable.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Shows completed example of strong work
* Highlights multiple approaches or methods when possible
* Explicitly references what makes the example strong
* Example aligns to rigor of lesson objective and standards
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be used during instruction (for analysis, think aloud) or as reference during student work
* If used as reference during student work, exemplar should be similar but not identical to student task
* Exemplar may be teacher-created or a previous student work sample
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Notice that in the strong example the writer first named a character trait to describe Amos. Then, they provided and explained text evidence to illustrate the character trait"
* Teacher creates exemplar during think aloud: "Watch me solve this problem. First, I identify my knowns and unknowns..." <writes on board showing work organization>
* "Before you start on problem 5, let's review our two examples from earlier. Notice how the first example arrived at a correct answer by drawing stick figures and counting on. The second example created a number sentence, used subtraction and ALSO arrived at a correct answer. There are multiple ways to solve problem 5. You can use either of our previous examples to guide your work or show a new way, but be sure to show your work."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher shows exemplar but doesn't explain what makes it strong
* Teacher references an exemplar during student work revisions, but does not explain how to use it
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Complete the essay using what we've learned" [Why non-example: No exemplar provided]
* Teacher shows exemplar that doesn't match the rigor of the lesson objective [Why non-example: Misaligned rigor]
* Teacher shows exemplar that exactly matches student task BEFORE students complete task [Why attempting: Gives answer away]

look_fors.name: Use High Frequency Words
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use high frequency words, meaning words that occur most commonly in language, to support comprehension.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses common, everyday vocabulary when possible
 * Avoids unnecessarily complex or rare words
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Must still teach grade-appropriate academic vocabulary
 * Using a low frequency word with an explanation of the word is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples: Rarely uses low frequency words without explanation
look_fors.attempting_examples: Sometimes uses low frequency words without explanation
look_fors.non_examples: Often uses low frequency words without explanation

skills.name: Comprehensible Input: Vocabulary Instruction
skills.description: Introduce new vocabulary by naming the word, modeling pronunciation, prompting students to repeat the word to practice pronunciation, providing a concise, kid-friendly definition of the word, and engaging students interactively with the word.

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 2 of sequence
look_fors.name: Choral Word Repetition
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Cue students to say a target word aloud together.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Teacher says target word before asking students to repeat
- Teacher prompts students to repeat the word with a clear in-cue (e.g., "My turn. Evaporate. Your turn",  "Say the word on three: 1, 2, 3...")
- Students orally repeat the target word in unison
look_fors.acceptable_variations: For early learners or multilingual learners, may include syllable-by-syllable repetition or multiple repetitions before the full word
look_fors.strong_examples: <Teacher> "Our word is evaporate. My turn. Evaporate. Your turn. Go." <Students in unison> "Evaporate."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Teacher> "The word is evaporate. Everyone say evaporate." <Some students respond at different times> [Why attempting: No in-cue, response not in unison]
look_fors.non_examples: <Teacher> "The word is evaporate. Let me tell you what it means." [Why non-example: No student repetition invited]

look_fors.type_explanation: Applies throughout
look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.type_explanation: Applies throughout; particularly important during step 1
look_fors.name: Enunciate
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pronounce words such that all component phonemes are audible.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Each word is pronounced distinctly
* Consonants and vowels are crisp and clear
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Variations in accent are fine and should not be penalized
look_fors.strong_examples: Distincly enunciates all or almost all words
look_fors.attempting_examples: Distinctly enunciates most words
look_fors.non_examples: Distinctly enunciates less than half of words

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 3 of sequence
look_fors.name: Explain Unfamiliar Terms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explain unfamiliar terms to support content understanding and vocabulary development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Defines new or unfamiliar words
- Provides synonyms or familiar language for unfamiliar terms
- NOT required when term is part of a classroom routine or procedure (e.g., "phonics time") or refers to a skill likely used repeatedly in a grade/subject (e.g., "calculate," "solve," "blend," etc.) unless the teacher indicates this is the first time with the routine or skill
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May provide or connect to word(s) in students' home language(s) to support explanation of target word when teaching multilingual learners
look_fors.strong_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries where earth’s plates move away from each other.”
- “A cake is the baked dessert in this picture. Cake in Spanish is ‘pastel’.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- “There are some new words that you're going to learn in this book. Same, recipe,  and unique. Alright, let’s get started and see what happens.” [Why non-example; Names but does not explain new terms]
look_fors.non_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- I am using expression, so you hear my voice. I have intonation and inflection. [Why non-example: expression is just more than hearing voice; no definition of intonation or inflection]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4 of sequence
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 1 of sequence
look_fors.name: Name Vocabulary Word
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state the target vocabulary word as a focus item.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Announces the target word as a discrete focus (e.g., "The word is...", "Our word today is...")
* Sets the word apart from surrounding speech
look_fors.strong_examples: "Our vocabulary word today is evaporate. The word is evaporate."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Evaporate means..." [Why attempting: Implies focus on vocabulary word but does not name as the focus]
look_fors.non_examples: "Today we'll learn how water evaporates from the ocean." [Why non-example: Word embedded in content, not named as focus item]

look_fors.type_explanation: Applies throughout
look_fors.name: Pause
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Brief pauses between sentences and ideas can help learners who need additional time to process language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Stops speaking for 1-3 seconds between sentences or between distinct ideas to break up the flow of information
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May pause longer after groups of sentences with related ideas are shared
look_fors.strong_examples: Regularly pauses for 1-3 seconds after sentences and ideas
look_fors.attempting_examples: Occasionally pauses for 1-3 seconds after sentences or ideas
look_fors.non_examples: No discernable pauses between sentences or groups or ideas

look_fors.type_explanation: Applies throughout
look_fors.name: Speak Slowly
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Speaking slowly can help learners who need additional time to process language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher's speech rate is noticeably slower than typical conversation while still flowing enough to hold students' attention
* Words are not rushed and do not run together
look_fors.strong_examples: Regularly speaks at about 90 words per minute or slower
look_fors.attempting_examples: Regularly speaks at about 91-125 words per minute
look_fors.non_examples: Regularly speaks faster than 125 words per minute

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Annotations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to mark up a text or document with notes, highlights, underlines, symbols, or comments to show their thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Gives clear annotation expectations (what to mark, how, time for task, etc.)
* Students mark up text (underlining, circling, margin notes, or symbols, etc.) simultaneously
* Circulates throughout the room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use sticky notes if can't write in books
* May be physical or digital annotations
look_fors.strong_examples: "As you read paragraph 2, I want you to use two annotation strategies. First, underline any evidence that supports the author's claim that recycling helps the environment. Second, put a question mark next to anything you don't understand. You have 3 minutes to read and annotate." <Students read and mark text; teacher circulates>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "As you read, underline important parts." [Why attempting: Unclear what important parts are]
* "Circle the main idea and underline supporting details." <Stands in one place> [Why attempting: Strong prompt but no monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Annotate the text" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher does not circulate [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Ask, Ask, Ask
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A verbal method of checking for understanding where the teacher asks the same or a similar question to several students to make an inference about students’ understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Calls on 3+ different students, asking the same root question repeatedly
* Evidence that teacher is strategically sampling rather than just calling on those who raise hands first or know answer (e.g., gives wait time to get 50% or more of hands up before calling on anyone, uses cold call instead of hands, builds on knowledge of previous writing/speaking - e.g., "Katja, you agreed that 0 is an even number, can you explain why?", etc.)
* Does NOT reveal correct answer until questioning sequence is complete
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use randomization tools to select students
* May ask the same root question in different ways (e.g., "Marco, what's one character trait of Amos?" then "Fatima, do you agree or disagree with Marco, why?" then "Arecely, what's one character trait **you** would choose for Amos?")
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the main idea of the paragraph, Eli?" <Student responds> "What do you think the main idea of the paragraph is, Maricruz?" <Student responds> "Christian, do you agree with Maricruz? Why or why not?" <Student responds> "Thank you for sharing!" <Teacher states correct answer>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Calls on some non-volunteers but only 1-2 students total
* Calls on 3+ students but always those who raise hands within first 3 seconds
* Calls on 3+ students using cold call, but asks different root question to each (e.g., "Marco, what's one character trait of Amos?", "Fatima, how does Amos feel about the ocean?", "Arecely, why do you think Amos packed two barrels of fresh water for his trip?") [Why attempting: Multiple students but different questions]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Only calling on students with raised hands or accepting responses from those who call out [type: missed opportunity]
* Always calling on the same 2-3 students [type: missed opportunity]
* Asking one student, getting correct answer, and moving on [type: missed opportunity]
* Revealing correct answer before end of questioning sequence (e.g., "you are close but not quite, Marco") [type: missed opportunity]
* Giving cues as to whether answers are correct before questioning ends (e.g., only saying "great" or nodding when correct; only frowning when incorrect) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Graphic Organizers
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to fill in a structured visual organizer to support and.or show their understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear prompt/purpose for graphic organizer
* Clear directions for parts of graphic organizer (e.g, sections of t-chart, Venn diagram areas of overlap and non-overlap, etc.) and completion (e.g., time, individual vs. pair/group work, etc.)
* Organizer matches prompt/concept/thinking skill
* Students fill out
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Different types of graphic organizer
- Graphic organizers familiar to students may require less specific directions (e.g., "Fill out the t-chart to compare and contrast facts and opinions. Try to get at least three items for each")
