- Semantic and concept maps are types of graphic organizer particularly useful for vocabulary development
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "You each have a Venn diagram on your desk. In the left circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for amphibians. In the right circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for reptiles. In the middle overlapping section, write characteristics they both share. Try to include at least 3 items in each section. You have 4 minutes to work with a partner."
- "On your paper, you have a cause-and-effect chart with three boxes. In the left column, write three causes of World War I. In the right column, write one effect for each cause. Be specific - use dates or events when you can. You have 3 minutes, silent and solo."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Fill in this Venn diagram comparing amphibians and reptiles." [Why attempting: Uses organizer but lacks specificity for organizer or completion]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Do your graphic organizer" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Show the steps of mitosis in the Venn diagram" [Why non-example: Organizer does not match concept/prompt] [type: learning harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Participation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Vary the modes students use to respond.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses 2+ participation modes (e.g., saying, writing, gesturing, drawing, moving) across the lesson or lesson segment
* Varies the mode across activities or segments rather than defaulting to one
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May offer choice in how students communicate or demonstrate their understanding; this still counts as 2+ modes
* A single mode is fine in a moment, but multiple modes should be used across time
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Write your prediction on your sticky note." <Students write> "Now stand up and put your sticky note on the chart under the heading you picked." <Students move to chart> "Turn and tell your partner why you chose that one."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone write your answer in your notebook. If you finish early, you can draw a quick sketch of it." [Why attempting: second mode only for early finishers]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Every prompt across the lesson or lesson segment asks students to respond in writing with no opportunities for other modes like drawing or speaking
* "Turn and tell your partner what you predict." <Later> "Turn and tell your partner what surprised you."

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Poll
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question at the same time via a gesture or other tool.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks question with clear answer options (A/B/C/D, true/false, agree/disagree) and clear way to show answer (hand signals, standing/sitting, etc.)
* IF question has only two response options (e.g., true/false or agree/disagree) follows up with an additional strategy like ask-ask-ask to learn more about student thinking
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time
* Students respond simultaneously
* Scans all responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used for polls in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May combine with think time or turn and talk first
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let’s take a look at question 2. When I say “show,” hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false. <Gives wait time>. Ready…show! " <Asks 2-3 students to explain why they chose true or false after the show>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's take a look at question 2. Hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false" [Why attempting: Clear answer options but no in-cue, no follow up questioning with only two response options]
* "Raise your hand if you think it's A. Raise your hand if you think it's B. Raise your hand if you think it’s C..." [Why attempting: Uses hand signals but sequential, not simultaneous]
* "Not yet, but when I say go, hold up your answer. Take some think time. <pause> Ok, ready, go!" [Why attempting: Has in-cue but unclear how to show answer]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Any questions?" <waits for raised hands> [Why non-example: Not a poll - only volunteers respond] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Ok, show me your answer" [Unclear how to show; students reveal at different times] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Everyone say their answer" [No in-cue, teacher unable to evaluate individual student responses when all spoken at once] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Total Physical Response (TPR)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for or supporting understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question or prompt at the same time using their whole body or physical movements in a way that conveys meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond with physical movement
* Physical movement clearly corresponds to concept being taught or assessed
* Prompts students to do the movement at the same time
* Students do movement simultaneously
* Scans student movements
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If using to check for understanding, must have more than one possible response and be in response to a question (e.g., "Imagine the UV light is here in the room and you are a plant. When I say go, use your body to show the direction you will grow")
* If using to convey meaning, may have single motion without a question (e.g., "frigid means really cold. cross your arms and shake your body to show brrrrrrrrr...frigid!")
* If using to convey meaning, exact simultaneous response less important
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Conveying meaning: "At convergent plate boundaries, plates crash or push together. Push your arms together like I am and say convergent with me. My turn - convergent. Your turn."
* Checking for understanding: "I'm going to say a number. If it's greater than 50, stand up. If it's less than 50, crouch down. If it's exactly 50, freeze in place. Ready? Think first, and then stand up, crouch down, or freeze when I say go. The number is 73....go" <All students stand. Teacher asks 2 students how they knew 73 was greater than 50>.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Show me with your body what it means to freeze" [Why attempting: Body movement but no in-cue]
* "Use your arms to make a rectangle because the constitution was written on parchment" [Why attempting: Not conceptually meaningful]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Raise your arms in air to be a cell" [Why non-example: Does not match concept] [type: learning harm]
* "Move your body to show the answer" [Vague prompt, no in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: at least 1 optional look-for required
look_fors.name: Whiteboards
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student holds up their work via a whiteboard on which they have written a response to a question or prompt.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond by writing/drawing on whiteboards/paper
* Gives time for all students to write/draw their response independently
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time by holding up whiteboard or paper
* Students hold up simultaneously
* Scans responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used as whiteboards in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
* May narrate trends they see in student responses
look_fors.strong_examples: "Take 45 seconds to calculate 24 ÷ 6 on your board and show your work. If you finish early, look at me so I know you are done, but do NOT hold your board up yet." <pauses for work time; circulates> <after 45 seconds> "Markers down. When I clap twice, flip your board to face me. Ready?" <claps twice> <Teacher scans boards>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "On your whiteboard, solve for x. When you're done, hold it up." [No synchronized reveal]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Write on your whiteboard then show it to me" [Why non-example: Vague prompt, no clear in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher gives question and immediately says "boards up" [Why non-example: No wait time, students can't complete task] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Conceptual Focus (Saga)
skills.description: Convey mathematical content for deep understanding and ensure the full scope of problems or tasks is addressed.

look_fors.name: Address Entire Problem/Task
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ensure all parts of the problem or task are addressed, including the most challenging portions.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
During teacher modeling:
* Works through all parts of the problem/task, including the most difficult steps
* Does not skip, abbreviate, or gloss over hard portions
 
During student practice:
* Requires students to attempt all parts of the assigned problem or task
* Provides support (e.g., prompting, scaffolding) to help students persist through difficult portions rather than letting them stop short or giving them the answer
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Full scope is defined by the assigned problem or lesson plan; this look-for is evaluated against what was assigned
* Parts may be addressed in a different order than written, as long as all are completed
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During modeling:Teacher narrates through all three parts of a word problem, spending the most time thinking aloud through the hardest step: "This part is where it gets tricky. Let me slow down to explain the how and they why of my approach here."
* During practice: Student: "I finished parts a and b." Teacher: "Part c is the one I really want you to wrestle with. What do you know so far?" <supports student in persisting through the hardest part>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* During modeling: Teacher addresses all parts but rushes through the hardest one: "Part c is tricky, but you basically apply the same rule as before" [Why attempting: Acknowledges hard part but doesn't fully work through or explain it]
* During practice: Teacher notices a student stopped after part 2 of 3 and gives them a susbtantial part of the answer for part 3 [Why attempting: Ensures completion but removes cognitive lift]
* During practice: Teacher affirms student work with an answer for each part, but missing a critical component for one or more parts (e.g., missing showing work, citing evidence, etc.) [Why attempting: Affirms coverage of task but does not require depth or rigor]
look_fors.non_examples:
* During modeling: Teacher reaches the hardest step of a multi-part problem and says, "We won't get to part c today so let's move on"
* During practice: Students turn in work with a section blank; teacher accepts without requiring completion [Why non-example: Hard part omitted entirely]

look_fors.name: Mathematical Accuracy
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Convey mathematical content accurately
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explains and demonstrates mathematics correctly
* Calculations and procedures are correct
* No mathematical errors in explanations or examples
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May intentionally use incorrect examples to teach error analysis
look_fors.strong_examples: No accuracy errors; all problems are solved correctly
look_fors.attempting_examples: Makes a minor error that is unlikely to negatively impact students' skill development or understanding
look_fors.non_examples: Teacher does the math incorrectly

look_fors.name: Mathematical Conceptual Understanding
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Convey content in a way that fosters conceptual understanding and clarifies likely student misconceptions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explains WHY procedures work, not just how
* Connects concepts to visual models or real-world meaning
* Addresses underlying mathematical relationships
* Calls out and clarifies common misconceptions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Consistently explains and shows the why behind the math or example
 * Consistently explains and shows clarifications to misconceptions such that students understand why the misconception is wrong
look_fors.attempting_examples: Occasionally explains and/or shows the why behind the math, example, or misconception clarification
look_fors.non_examples:
* Focuses only on procedural fluency with no attention to conceptual understanding or application
 * Incorrectly explains or shows the why behind the math, example, or misconceptions clarification

skills.name: Confident Content
skills.description: Understand and internalize the content to facilitate learning with academic accuracy.

look_fors.name: Mathematical Accuracy
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Convey mathematical content accurately
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explains and demonstrates mathematics correctly
* Calculations and procedures are correct
* No mathematical errors in explanations or examples
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May intentionally use incorrect examples to teach error analysis
look_fors.strong_examples: No accuracy errors; all problems are solved correctly
look_fors.attempting_examples: Makes a minor error that is unlikely to negatively impact students' skill development or understanding
look_fors.non_examples: Teacher does the math incorrectly

look_fors.name: Mathematical Vocabulary
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Convey content using precise mathematical terminology
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses correct mathematical terms (e.g., "sum" not just "answer")
* Introduces and reinforces grade-level math vocabulary
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May use informal language first, then connect to formal terms
look_fors.strong_examples: Consistently uses key mathematical vocabulary appropriately in context
look_fors.attempting_examples: Occasionally uses key mathematical vocabulary appropriately in context
look_fors.non_examples:
* Rarely or does not use key mathematical vocabulary appropriately in context
* Misuses mathematical vocabulary

look_fors.type_explanation: Required except when the lesson's focus is exclusively fluency; not required during fluency-only instruction
look_fors.name: Mathematical Conceptual Understanding
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Convey content in a way that fosters conceptual understanding and clarifies likely student misconceptions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explains WHY procedures work, not just how
* Connects concepts to visual models or real-world meaning
* Addresses underlying mathematical relationships
* Calls out and clarifies common misconceptions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Consistently explains and shows the why behind the math or example
 * Consistently explains and shows clarifications to misconceptions such that students understand why the misconception is wrong
look_fors.attempting_examples: Occasionally explains and/or shows the why behind the math, example, or misconception clarification
look_fors.non_examples:
* Focuses only on procedural fluency with no attention to conceptual understanding or application
 * Incorrectly explains or shows the why behind the math, example, or misconceptions clarification

skills.name: Cooperative Learning (Saga)
skills.description: Use cooperative learning strategies to create a collaborative, energetic environment

look_fors.name: Hot Potato (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Direct students to alternate writing and verbally explaining each step of a problem.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns one student to write and explain the first step aloud
* Directs the next student to correct any errors in the prior step, then write and explain the next step
* Continues rotation until problem is complete
* Prompts students to verbalize reasoning, not just write (e.g., "Can you walk us through why you did that step?")
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Students may use different colors to distinguish each student's contributions
* Students may rotate by problem rather than by step when working through a set of shorter practice problems
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Let's use Hot Potato. Alexis, write and explain the first step out loud. Diego, your job is to correct any errors, then take the next step and explain your thinking too. Alternate roles until you have completed the problem. "Diego completes first step while explaining: "I'd distribute the negative to both terms in the parentheses because..." Alexis completes second step while explaining: "Okay, so now I'd combine like terms, which gives me..."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Take turns doing each step." <students alternate writing but explain little to nothing aloud>
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students work independently
* Teacher tells students to work together, but no structure given

look_fors.name: Pencils Down (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Before students begin writing, guide them to read, discuss, and plan together.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs students to hold off on writing before starting
* Guides students to read the task together
* Prompts discussion for clarity and initial ideas (e.g., "What's the first thing you notice?", "What do we already know that might help?")
* Gives explicit signal when students may begin writing and solving
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* After the discussion phase, students may work independently or together
* May use focusing questions to structure the pre-writing discussion; discussion length may vary based on task complexity
look_fors.strong_examples: "Pencils down for now. Let's read this one together first." <reads problem aloud> "What's the first thing you notice?" <students respond> "What do we already know that might help?" <students respond> "Great, use what we just discussed to get started"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Read through the problem once before you start writing." [Why attempting: Prompts reading but skips deeper thinking or discussion]
look_fors.non_examples: "Go ahead and get started." <students begin writing immediately without reading or discussing together>

look_fors.name: Rally Coach (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Assign alternating coach and writer roles so one student explains while the other records, switching for each new problem.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns partner roles (one explains while the other writes)
* Directs the writer to record only what the coach explains, not to add their own ideas
* Reverses roles for each new problem and continues rotating through the problem set
* Reminds the writer to follow the coach's lead if they begin contributing ideas (e.g., "Your job is to write what your partner explains — pause and listen first")
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* For groups of 3+, rotate through all students
* May prompt the coach to verbalize reasoning if they go quiet (e.g., "Talk me through your thinking")
* May prompt students to rotate step by step instead of problem by problem
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let's use Rally Coach. For problem 1, Alexis coaches and Diego writes. Diego, your only job is to write exactly what Alexis explains. Don't add your own ideas yet. Alexis, walk Diego through your thinking step by step." <Alexis explains each step; Diego writes without adding ideas> "Now switch — Diego coaches, Alexis writes. Problem 2."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Take turns explaining and writing." <writer begins adding their own ideas alongside what the coach says>
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students work independently
* Teacher tells students to work together, but no structure given

look_fors.name: Reciprocal Teaching (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have one student teach a concept to their partner in their own words, then switch roles.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns one student to explain a concept or skill to their partner in their own words
* Listens without intervening unless the student gets stuck
* Prompts the teaching student to break it down if they struggle (e.g., "Can you explain just the first step?", "Can you give an example?")
* Reverses roles so the second student teaches a different (or the same) concept
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * If one student was absent: the attending student teaches what was covered; roles do not need to reverse
look_fors.strong_examples: "Alexis, you were here yesterday when we worked on slope-intercept form and Diego wasn't. Can you teach Diego what he missed? Walk him through what it means and give an example." <Alexis explains; tutor listens only intervening to give Alexis short cues if she gets stuck> "Diego, what questions do you have for Alexis?" <Diego asks a clarifying question> Tutor: "Alexis, can you give an example to show what you mean?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Can you share what you learned yesterday with your partner?" <student gives a vague or short response; tutor jumps in to give full explanation> [Why attempting: Peer teaching initiated but tutor takes over too soon]
look_fors.non_examples: Tutor re-explains a concept to student who was absent from the last session and student who was present at the same time

look_fors.name: Think Ink Pair Share (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students independent think time and writing time before they share and discuss with a partner.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Poses a question or task and directs students to think silently before writing
* Signals students to write down their initial ideas (ink step) before any discussion begins
* Directs students to share and discuss with a partner or small group before sharing with the larger group
* May prompt students to return to their own work and revise based on discussion
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Think time and ink time may be combined for simpler prompts; keeping them separate supports students who need more processing time 
* Partner share may extend to groups of 3
look_fors.strong_examples: "Take 60 seconds to think about this silently — don't write yet, just think." <pause> "Now take another 60 seconds to jot down your initial ideas." <students write independently> "Share what you wrote with your partner. See where your thinking lines up and where it differs. You have 90 seconds"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Think about this for a moment." <brief pause> "Okay, go ahead and talk with your partner." [Why attempting: Insufficient independent think and/or ink time]
look_fors.non_examples: "Turn and talk with your partner about how you solved this." <students discuss immediately, without individual think or writing time> [Why non-example: Skips think and ink phases]

skills.name: Decoding
skills.description: Teach students to read words accurately by mapping letters to their sounds, blending those sounds, or chunking longer words into decodable parts.

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
Depending on the phonological or phonemic unit of the lesson….
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name(s) ("em") or "muh"
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces digraphs and vowel teams accurately (/ch/, /ee/, etc.)
* Segments syllables accurately
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
"Listen: /mmm/-op. The first sound is /mmm/."
"What is another word that sounds like 'bat'?"
"Which one doesn't belong? Weed, bead, pill, seed?"
"/tae/ /bl/ What's the word?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first sound in 'top' is /tuh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
"The first sound in 'mop' is 'em.'" [Why non-example: says letter not sound]
"There are five sounds in 'cheese': /c/, /h/, /e/, /e/, /z/" [Why non-example: not accurately pronouncing digraph /ch/ nor vowel team /ee/]
"Tiger has two syllables: /tieg/ /r/" [Why non-example: syllables not divided correctly]

look_fors.name: Map Letters to Sounds
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say the correct sound for each letter or letter pattern.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the correct sound while showing a letter or letter pattern
* Treats a letter team or digraph as one sound (e.g., English "sh" says /sh/; Spanish "ch" says /tʃ/)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., /c/ and /at/ for an onset-rime focus)
look_fors.strong_examples: <Shows "sh"> "These two letters work together. They say /sh/." <Points> "/sh/. Now let's read it in this word /sh/, /i/, /n/, shin."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "a"> "That says /a/, or sometimes /ay/." <does not specify which for this word> [Why attempting: gives a sound and letter, but leaves out of context of word]
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Shows the word "shine"> "The word is shine." [Why non-example: no mapping of specific letters to sounds]
* With no visuals: "Listen to me say /sh/. Now listen to me say /sh/ ine. Shine." [Why non-example: no connection to the actual letters, sound only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Apply Vowel Patterns is required when the word's vowel sound depends on a pattern or generalization (e.g., silent-e, vowel team); not required for simple CVC or fully regular short-vowel words.
look_fors.name: Apply Vowel Patterns
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Apply vowel patterns and generalizations to decide the vowel sound and read the word correctly.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Identifies the vowel pattern in the word or syllable (e.g., silent-e/vowel-consonant-e, vowel team, r-controlled, open or closed syllable)
Uses the pattern to decide the vowel sound rather than guessing or defaulting to the short sound
look_fors.acceptable_variations: The pattern may be named formally (e.g., "vowel-consonant-e") or described in student-friendly terms (e.g., "the silent e makes the i say its name").
look_fors.strong_examples: <Shows "bike"> "When a word ends vowel-consonant-silent e, the e is silent and the first vowel says its name. Here it's i, k, silent e, so the i says /ī/. /b/ /ī/ /k/, bike. Same pattern in 'kite' and 'time.'"
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "bike"> "There's an e on the end, so the i is long. /b/ /ī/ /k/, bike." [Why attempting: applies pattern, doesn't generalize]
look_fors.non_examples: <Shows "bike"> "The i here says /ī/." [Why non-example: gives the sound, no pattern]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required UNLESS focus of lesson is letter-sound correspondence only (
look_fors.name: Blend Sounds to Read
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Blend the sounds in order to read the whole word.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Says each sound in sequence, then blends them into the whole word
Blends left to right without long pauses that break the word apart
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., /c/ and /at/ blending to cat for an onset-rime focus)
* In Spanish, blending follows the sílaba → sinfón → fonema sequence (e.g., /m/ + /a/ blending to "ma"; /bl/ + /a/ blending to "bla"); onset-rime blending does not apply in Spanish
look_fors.strong_examples: "Watch me blend: /mmm/ /aaa/ /p/. /mmmmaaap/. Map."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "/mmm/ ... /aaap/ ... /p/ ... map" [Why attempting: blends but with long break in middle and combined sound at end]
look_fors.non_examples: "/m/ /a/ /p/." <stops; does not blend into "map"> [Why non-example: sounds are produced but never blended into a word]

look_fors.type_explanation: Chunk Multisyllabic Words is required when phonological unit is a chunk (e.g., syllable, prefix, suffix); else not required
look_fors.name: Chunk Multisyllabic Words
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break longer words into decodable chunks like syllables and when necessary highlight morphological units to support decoding and meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Divides a multisyllabic word into syllables or word parts
* When appropriate, highlights morphological units such as prefixes and suffixes
* Helps students identify compound words by recognizing familiar words within larger words
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Chunking may use syllable division, affixes and roots, or other known word parts
* In Spanish, chunks are syllables following Spanish syllable structure (open, e.g., ma-pa, or closed, e.g., pan-tas), including a sinfón as part of its syllable (e.g., ti-gre, not ti-g-re)
look_fors.strong_examples:
"napkin: I see two closed syllables, nap and kin. /nap/ /kin/, napkin."
<points to "rehacer"> "Antes de decir cada sílaba quiero que busquemos las partes de la palabra que ya conocemos. Veo el prefijo RE al frente," <covers the rest of the word so only re is visible> "y una palabra base al final" <covers the front so only hacer is visible>. "Ahora leamos ambas partes y las mezclamos: re…hacer. Ahora, leámosla dividiéndola en sílabas: re- ha- cer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "/na/ /pkin/. Napkin" [Why attempting: divides the word but not into decodable parts]
* "Vamos a leer re-ha-cer. Re-ha-cer. ¿Puedes ver una palabra familiar dentro de la palabra rehacer?" <Student responds: "hacer">. "Correcto. Rehacer se puede dividir entre re y hacer." <Teacher leaves it there and does not explain prefix or base word>
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Napkin has two syllables" [Why non-example: names syllable number but no actual chunking]
* "Vamos a leer re-ha-cer" [Why non-example: doesn't highlight the three syllables or the prefix re- and the base word hacer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Sound-to-Movement mapping is required in kindergarten and any early childhood (ECE/Pre-K) grade, else optional
look_fors.name: Sound-to-Movement Mapping
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pair each sound unit with one matching movement
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Assigns one physical motion to each sound unit (e.g., one clap per syllable, one tap per phoneme)
Keeps the movement-to-unit match consistent; no extra or missing motions
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Movement may be clapping, stomping, tapping, touching boxes on the board, moving magnets on the board, or similar
* Tapping and sweeping: one tap per sound followed by a single continuous sweep under the whole word to cue blending; the blend sweep is one glide across all sounds, not one motion per unit
* In Spanish, a sinfón (consonant blend) receives one motion as a single blended unit (e.g., one clap for the /gr/ in "grande"), not one motion per consonant within the blend.
look_fors.strong_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ms. (clap) Ah (clap) med (clap). Three claps for three syllables. Now let's stomp it: Ms. (stomp) Ah (stomp) med (stomp)."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ma (tap)(tap) ya (tap)" [Why attempting: motion-to-unit match inconsistent]
look_fors.non_examples: Claps several times while saying a word without matching one clap to each beat.

skills.name: Decoding (Spanish)
skills.description: Teach students to read Spanish words accurately by mapping letters to their sounds, blending those sounds, or chunking longer words into decodable parts.

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production (Spanish)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target Spanish sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name ("eme") or an added vowel ("muh")
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces the five Spanish vowel sounds consistently; pronunciation is always the same, never variable by word
* Segments syllables accurately, respecting Spanish syllable structure (open: ma-pa; closed: pan)
* Pronounces Spanish-specific digraphs (e.g., ll, rr, ch) and the ñ sound accurately
* Produces a sinfón as one blended onset, not two separated sounds (/bl/ in blanco, not /b/-/l/)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target sounds vary by lesson focus: sílabas (ma-pa) for chunking; phoneme /m/ for phoneme work; sinfón /tr/ for blend work; rhyming words (pan/gran) when used.
* Regional pronunciation (seseo vs. distinción, aspirated /s/) is a valid variation, not an error.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Escuchen: /mmm/-esa. El primer sonido es /mmm/."
* "¿Qué otra palabra suena como 'pan'?"
* "'Blanco' empieza con el sinfón /bl/, dos sonidos juntos."
* "'Tigre' tiene dos sílabas: ti-gre."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "El primer sonido en 'pan' es /puh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "El primer sonido en 'mesa' es 'eme.'" [says the letter name, not the sound]
* "'Chico' tiene cinco sonidos: /c/ /h/ /i/ /c/ /o/" [Why non-example: fails to treat /ch/ as one digraph sound]
* "'Tigre' tiene tres sílabas: /ti/ /gr/ /e/" [Why non-example: syllables divided incorrectly; the sinfón gr belongs with the following vowel: ti-gre]
* "Leamos 'idea'. /ai/ /de/ /a/" [Why non-example: incorrect Spanish pronunciation of /i/]

look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say the correct sound for each letter or letter pattern.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the correct sound while showing a letter or letter pattern
* Treats a letter team or digraph as one sound (e.g., English "sh" says /sh/; Spanish "ch" says /tʃ/)

look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "a"> "That says /a/, or sometimes /ay/." <does not specify which for this word> [Why attempting: gives a sound and letter, but leaves out of context of word]
look_fors.non_examples:

* With no visuals: "Listen to me say /sh/. Now listen to me say /sh/ ine. Shine." [Why non-example: no connection to the actual letters, sound only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the word's consonant sound depends on the c/g/qu/gü positional convention; not required for words without that ambiguity
look_fors.name: Apply Consonant Spelling Patterns (Spanish)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Identify consonant spelling patterns and generalizations that affect pronunciation to read the word correctly
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Identifies the consonant spelling pattern in the word (e.g., c or g before e/i vs. a/o/u; qu before e/i; gü before e/i)
* Uses the pattern to decide the correct sound rather than guessing or defaulting to the letter's most common sound
* Helps students identify when a letter pronunciation changes based on the vowel that follows
* Draws attention to Spanish orthographic markers such as the diéresis
* Draws attention to the letter ñ as a distinct letter in the Spanish alphabet, not as a variation of the letter n in English
look_fors.acceptable_variations: The pattern may be named formally (e.g., "la /gu/ antes de la e o la i siempre necesita una diéresis para mantener ese sonido de la /w/") or described using multiple valid approaches in student-friendly terms (e.g., "los dos puntitos encima de la u nos indican que la u suena. Si no hay puntitos, la u no suena").
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Shows "guerra"> "Cuando la g-u viene antes de la e o la i, la u es silenciosa. /G/, /erra/: guerra."
* <Shows "pingüino"> "Date cuenta de los dos puntitos encima de la u. Se llaman diéresis y nos dejan saber que debemos sonar la u así: pin-gÜi-no."
* "La palabra es ñame. /ña/ /me/. Qué bonita la letra ñ. Recuerda que la ñ es una letra independiente en el alfabeto en español. ¡No es una n con un sombrerito! Es muy distinguida pues es su propia letra."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* <Shows "guerra"> "/G/, /erra/: guerra." <reads correctly but never names why the u is silent>
* "La palabra es güero." <Points to the two dots but doesn't otherwise explain or draw attention to the diéresis or the way it impacts the pronunciation>
* "La palabra es ñame. /ña/ /me/" <reads correctly but does not name ñ as a distinct letter with its pronunciation>
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Shows "guerra"> "The g, u, e, r, r, a. g-w-erra." [Why non-example: applies the wrong pronunciation pattern]
* "La palabra es guerra." [Why non-example: reads the word for students without drawing attention to the pattern]
* "La palabra es güero." [Why non-example: doesn't call attention to the diéresis]
* "La palabra es ñame. Aquí la letra n tiene una línea arriba que hace que se convierta en una ñ." [Why non-example: ñ is a distinct letter in the Spanish alphabet; it is not an n with an orthographic marker]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the target word carries a written tilde; not required for words without one
look_fors.name: Apply Tilde-Marked Stress (Spanish)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Apply the tilde to decide which syllable is stressed and read the word correctly.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Identifies the tilde (written accent mark) in the word
* Uses the tilde to decide which syllable is stressed rather than defaulting to the standard stress rule
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Applies whether the word appears in isolation or in connected text
* A tilde may override the default stress rule (e.g., "árbol") or distinguish two otherwise-identical words (e.g., "el" vs. "él")
look_fors.strong_examples: "Miren, esta palabra tiene una tilde: 'árbol.' La tilde nos dice qué sílaba se dice más fuerte: ÁR-bol."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "árbol"> "Di AR-bol. ARbol" <stresses correctly but never names or points to the tilde>
look_fors.non_examples: <Shows "árbol"> "Di arbol. /ar/ /bol/" [Why non-example: ignores the tilde, defaults to standard stress, misreads the word]

skills.name: Diagnose Gaps
skills.description: Accurately assess misunderstandings and unfinished learning in student thinking.

look_fors.name: Listen In
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: During partner or small group discussions, circulate and listen to multiple student conversations to gather data about understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves between multiple groups/pairs
* Pauses near groups to hear conversation
* Makes statements about what was heard across groups (e.g., "A couple groups shared..." "Most of you discussed...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If discussion time is short (e.g., 1-2 minutes), teacher may listen in to a smaller number of pairs/groups
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific things they heard or patterns from student discussion indicating they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger, but Ellie and Max thought example 2 was stronger")
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Liam, you mentioned distance from the sun. Why?" [student responds] "Lara, can you share what you were discussing about intensity of sunlight with the whole class?")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I heard several pairs mention slavery, which is important. I also heard some pairs talking about states' rights and economic differences. Let's unpack how those ideas connect." [Teacher's summary matches evidence from trasncript about student multiple pair discussions]
* "Discuss with your table group: How is photosynthesis different from cellular respiration? You have 2 minutes" <Circulates, stopping briefly at each of 4 table groups> <After listening and calling class back to attention> "Table 3, can you share what you were discussing? I heard you making an interesting comparison about inputs and outputs."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Listens to 1-2 groups but not enough to identify patterns
* Spends entire time facilitating one group's discussion instead of gathering data
* Moves so rapidly between groups that can likely only hear that students are on-task, but not evaluate understanding
* "Nayeli and Lincoln though example 1 was stronger" [Statement matches what Nayeli and Lincoln discussed; Why attempting: single pair/group discussion focus, does not uncover patterns]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place during partner talk without listening [type: missed opportunity]
* Only intervening when students are off-task [type: missed opportunity]
* Listening to only one group for the entire discussion time [type: missed opportunity]
* Doing something else while students are talking [type: missed opportunity]
* Statement of what was heard does not match actual student discussion (e.g., stating "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger" IF Nayeli and Lincoln actually discussed example 2 being stronger) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Observation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Circulate or scan throughout the room to observe student work, looking for patterns in understanding across multiple students.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves to or scans multiple locations
* Looks at student work (written, kinesthetic, etc.)
* Makes statements about observations or patterns (e.g., "I'm noticing...", "Most of you...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific observations and/or patterns from student work indicating they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "I saw some of us got 90 and some of us got 9,000 for the answer." 
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "let's hear from two people who agreed and two who disagreed"; "Liam, tell me more about what you were thinking about distance from the sun," [student responds] "Lara, tell me more about why you wrote about intensity of sunlight")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I'm noticing several people are having trouble with step 2. Let's pause and address that together before continuing." [Teacher's observation matches evidence from transcript about multiple student responses]
* Teacher circulates during a science lab, stops to observe three different lab groups' setup of materials, then addresses whole class: "I see all three groups I checked have their graduated cylinders on a flat surface - excellent. Also, everyone check - goggles should be on your face, not on top of your head."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Circulates to see some student work but doesn't cover enough of the room to identify patterns
* Focuses on behavior management rather than academic work while circulating
* "Dante's board says 9x10 = 90" [Statement matches a single student response; Why attempting: single student focus, does not uncover patterns]
* Uses a visual strategy like poll, total physical response/gestures, or whiteboards, but no active evidence (e.g., scanning, narrating trends) of monitoring
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place for an extended period without looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Only checking work of students who raise their hands for help [type: missed opportunity]
* Circulating but not looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Observations do not match student work (e.g., stating "Dante's board says 9 x 10 = 900" IF Dante's board actually said 9 x 10 = 90) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Probing Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes an error or reveals a misconception, ask follow-up questions to understand the student's thinking and the root cause of the misunderstanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher asks follow-up question about student's thinking
* Teacher uses curious, non-judgmental language
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May probe publicly or privately
* May ask series of questions to get to root cause
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "The answer is 24." Teacher: "You got 24. Can you walk me through how you solved it?" Student: "I multiplied 3 times 8." Teacher: "You multiplied 3 times 8. What made you decide to multiply instead of add?" Student: "Because the problem said 'each' so I thought that meant times." Teacher: "You saw the word 'each' and knew that was a clue. Let's look at the problem together and figure out if multiplication is the right operation here."
* Student: "I think the main idea is that the girl went to the store." Teacher: "You said the main idea is that she went to the store. What part of the text made you think that was the main idea?" Student: "It was in the first sentence." Teacher: "Got it. How should we use the text to find the main idea?”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Check your answer against the key now. What would you change?" [Why attempting: Does not necessarily reveal student thinking]
* "And in step 3 did you multiply or divide?" [Why attempting: Does not reveal student thinking; may be leading]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Immediately corrects the student without asking any questions [type: missed opportunity]
* "Really? You think it's 7?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you remember we talked about this yesterday?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you think you should add instead of subtract?" [Why non-example: Leading question, does not reveal student thinking] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Discourse Routines (Saga)
skills.description: Set norms and routines for discourse so students build understanding together.

look_fors.name: Academic Discourse Norms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach how students should engage in academic conversations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly teaches and uses sentence stems or protocols for academic discussion
* Establishes and refers to expectations for listening and building on ideas
* Establishes and refers to expectations for ensuring all voices are heard
* Redirects discourse violations with reference to established norms
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Norms may be co-created with students or taught by teacher
* Can include visual anchor charts with discussion expectations
* May practice norms through fishbowl or role-play
* May model norms before use
* Norms may include distinct expectations for speakers and non-speakers (e.g., conduct norms for speakers, note-taking or listening norms for non-speakers)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When we disagree, we use the stem 'I disagree because...' and explain our thinking with evidence"
* "Our discussion norms are: listen to understand, build on ideas, and ask clarifying questions. Let's practice"
* Student: "I respectfully disagree because..." Teacher: "Notice how Tucker used our sentence stem for disagreement to express his response to Vanessa productively. What do you think Anya?"
* Student: "What do you think, Patrice?" <Student invites participation from other student>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Be respectful when you talk to each other" [Why attempting: Vague]
* Posts discussion norms but never references or reinforces them
* Several students use sentence starters for academic discourse, but conversation is limited to the same few students
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students interrupt or talk over each other without redirection
* The same few students dominate conversation
* Allows dismissive comments about peers' ideas ("That's dumb")
* No norms, sentence stems, or protocols related to academic discourse present

look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.name: Prompt Evaluation or Judgment
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to assess, critique, or make judgments about claims, work, or ideas
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students to evaluate the quality, accuracy, or strength of something (e.g., an argument, solution, peer response, or source)
* Asks students to weigh options, make a decision, and justify their choice
* Invites students to agree or disagree with a claim and explain why
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target of evaluation may vary (e.g., teacher-generated examples, student work, texts, or real-world claims)
* May be structured (written criteria) or open-ended (verbal judgment)
* May ask students to evaluate whether evidence is sufficient or complete, not only its quality or strength
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Here are two student responses to the essay prompt. Which is stronger, and what makes it stronger? Use our rubric to decide." 
* "The author claims social media is making teens less happy. Is that argument convincing? What evidence would you need to be sure?"
* "We got two different answers to this problem. Can both be right? How would you decide which one to trust?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Do you agree or disagree?" with no follow-up for reasoning [Why attempting: invites a stance but not evaluation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks students to recall or describe rather than evaluate (e.g., "What did the author say?")
* Asks recall questions

look_fors.name: Prompt Student to Restate or Paraphrase
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt a student to restate or paraphrase a key idea in their own words
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks a student to restate or paraphrase a key idea, concept, or instruction in their own words
* Asks a student to restate or paraphrase another student's contribution
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target may be the teacher's explanation, a concept, an instruction, or a peer's contribution
* May ask the original student to restate their own idea or route the restatement to another student
* May provide a sentence stem to support the restatement
look_fors.strong_examples: "We just said slope is the rate of change. In your own words, what does that mean? Try the stem: 'Slope tells us…'"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Can someone tell me what slope means again?" <calls on student who repeats the exact definition verbatim> [Why attempting: Prompts repetition but not restatement in the student's own words]
look_fors.non_examples: "So what that means is the slope is the rate of change. Got it? Let's move on." [Why non-example: Teacher restates instead of prompting a student to]

look_fors.name: Require Reasoning or Justification
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Establish the norm that answers must include reasoning or evidence
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sets or reinforces the expectation that students explain thinking, not just give answer
* Provides and references supports for reasoning and justification (e.g., sentence starters, posted norms)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Reasoning standard may be content-specific ("use evidence from the text") or general ("tell me how you know")
* May use follow up questions to push students who answer without reasoning to explain; however, for look-for to be strong, the expectation for reasoning or justification must be proactively established
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I don't just want to know what you think, I want to know why. So, remember to use our sentence frame: I think ___, because ___"
 * Student: "The answer is 12" Teacher: "You might be right — but I need the how you got there. Walk me through your reasoning." <student responds with reasoning> Teacher: "That's the kind of thinking I want to hear every time."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Can you say more?" [Why attempting: prompts elaboration but doesn't establish reasoning as a standing expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts correct answers without asking for reasoning (e.g., "Great answer! Who else?")
* Only asks for justification when an answer is wrong

look_fors.name: Support Student-to-Student Discourse
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Route conversation through students rather than always through teacher
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs students to respond to each other and build on peer ideas in discussion 
* Steps back during student-to-student exchanges
* As needed, reminds students to respond to each other ("What do you think about Maya's idea?")
* As needed, reminds students to build on peer ideas ("Add on to what Marcus said")
* Students respond to and build on each other's ideas
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May provide supports such as initial model or academic discourse norms
 * Can use structured prompts ("Do you agree or disagree with...?")
 * May redirect specific students to each other or open it to whole class
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Ok, let's discuss our key question for the day. For the next three minutes, I will step to the side unless I need to give a quick reminder. Use our academic discourse norms to discuss the key question as a group. In particular, Don't forget to respond to and build on each other's ideas and monitor your air time." 
 * "Marcus, what do you think about Keisha's explanation? Do you agree or see it differently?"
 * "Who can add to that idea?" <student responds to peer's thinking, not restating own idea>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus and a thumbs down if you do not" <most students give thumbs up, a couple give thumbs down> Teacher: "Yes, Marcus was correct" <teacher moves on> [Why attempting: Missed opportunity for student-to-student discussion]
 * <One student gives response> Teacher: "What do you think, Kim?" [Why attempting: Implies potential peer-to-peer response, but unclear]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All student responses go to teacher who then responds or calls on next student
 * "I’m sure we all agree with Marcus's great point about…" [Why non-example: Assumes student response rather than students giving response]

look_fors.name: Think, Share, Build (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Structure student discourse by pausing for think time, inviting one student to share, then prompting a second to restate or critique and build on that response.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Poses a question and pauses for silent think time before calling on anyone
* Asks one student to share their answer or approach
* Prompts a second student to restate (if in agreement) or critique (if in disagreement) the first student's response, then add on by explaining why, adding detail, or giving an example (e.g., "Do you agree or disagree with what Alexis said? Why?", "Can you restate what Diego said and explain what that means?")
* Does not evaluate or resolve the first response before the second student engages
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May begin with either student; strategy works whether the first student's answer is correct or incorrect
* May provide sentence stems to support the build step (e.g., "I (agree/disagree) with ___ because...", "___ said that..., which means...")
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher: "Take a moment to look at your work and think about what you did to get the answer." <pauses> "Can you share what you got and how, Alexis?" Alexis: "I got 4r + 8. I distributed the negative, so 3 + 5 = 8." Teacher: "Diego, do you agree or disagree with Alexis? Why?" Diego: "I disagree. I got 4r minus 2 because I subtracted instead of adding." Teacher: "Can you restate what Alexis did differently and explain why it matters?" Diego: "She distributed the negative first, which turns the minus 5 into plus 5.Oh, that's the step I missed. You have to do that before combining like terms."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Teacher: "What did you get, Diego?" Diego: "4r minus 2." Teacher: "Do you agree Alexis?" Alexis: "No, I got 4r + 8." Teacher: "Yes, Alexis is right. Remember, you need to distribute the negative, so you should add 5 instead of subtracting 5." <moves on> [Why attempting: Peer response but no build]
look_fors.non_examples: Teacher: "Alexis, what did you get?" Alexis: "4r + 8." Teacher: "That's right. Diego, take a look at Alexis's answer and remember to distribute the negative sign." <moves on> [Why non-example: Teacher evaluates and explains rather than prompting peer engagement]

skills.name: Dispositions for Learning (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Intentionally develop students' curiosity, critical thinking, reasoning, and reflection

look_fors.name: Create Problem-Solving Opportunities
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students problems to grapple with that require figuring out an approach, not just applying a known procedure
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Poses a problem students are not yet equipped to solve by formula or recall alone
* Explicitly invites students to use what they know to make progress (e.g., "What do you already know that might help here?")
* Holds off on providing a method or solution path, allowing students to struggle productively first
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Teacher may provide scaffolds (e.g., available tools, reference materials) without removing the problem-solving challenge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We've seen one possible approach to solving this problem. Now, with your partner, I want you to try to come up with a different approach to solving the problem. Show your steps and your work." 
* "Let's apply what we know about the water cycle to the challenge of desalination. How can you use the materials in front of you and the sun to remove the salt from saltwater? Draw and label a few different approaches you could test"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Poses a novel problem but walks students through it when they start to struggle [Why attempting: removes the productive struggle rather than providing supports for continued problem-solving]
* "Who wants to try?" with only volunteers engaging [Why attempting: not all students grapple with the problem]
look_fors.non_examples: * Teaches the procedure first, then assigns practice problems using that procedure

look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Questions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to generate their own questions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides dedicated time and structure for students to formulate questions
* Explicitly invites student questions as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student-generated questions by using them to drive learning (e.g., discussion or investigation)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student questions may be verbal or written
* Use of student questions may focus in on a small subset or consider all questions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading." <Students write> "Share your question with a partner." <Students discuss> Teacher uses student questions to frame the class discussion.
 * "We've been studying the water cycle. What's a question a scientist might still be trying to answer?" <Students generate questions> "I love this one — let's investigate it together."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What questions do you have?" and accepts and answers 1 to 2 student questions and moves on [Why attempting: doesn't create broad student question-generation]
 "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading" <Teacher moves on immediately> [Why attepting: Students have opportunity to ask questions, but they are not used for learning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher asks all questions; students only answer
* "Any questions?" with no time or structure for students to formulate them

look_fors.name: Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create conditions where students attempt challenging work safely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly invites students to try even if unsure (e.g., "Give it a shot, even if you're not certain, this will help you learn and help me see your thinking")
* Recognizes attempts and effort, not just correct answers
* Provides support structures that allow productive struggle (think time, partner talk, resources)

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
* Student shares incorrect answer [rationale: not clear evidence that student feels safe, they may have thought their answer was correct]
* Teacher asks follow up questions or asks students to build on others' thinking [rationale: not a bad practice, but does not explicitly create safe conditions for risk-taking]
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* When applicable, includes statements like "There's no right answer" or "Multiple approaches work here"
* May celebrate "wrong" answers that show sophisticated reasoning
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I want to hear your thinking even if you're not 100% sure. Your ideas will help us all learn"
* "We're figuring things out together rather than just looking for the 'right' answer"
* "Try it out in your voice and we can all learn from each other's writing" 
* "Turn and talk with a partner to share thinking before we discuss as a class"
* Remember, you have a toolbox for when you feel stuck. Consult the rubric or phone a friend!"  
* "I actually expect some of your first attempts to be unsuccessful. If you finish this without running into a single issue, you probably didn't take a big enough risk. I'm looking for how you pivot when things get messy, not just the final product."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you get it wrong" [Why attempting: no connection to learning value]
* "Be sure everyone participates!" [Why attempting: generic participation encouragement instead of explicitly encouraging academic risk taking]
* Validates partially correct answers [Why attempting: Implies recognition of effort, but not explicit]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher consistently calls on same few students who raise hands with confidence [type: missed opportunity]
* "Don't worry, this one is easy" [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarrass or demotivate a student from taking future risks (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Follow up Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use questions to push student thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Asks students to elaborate, explain reasoning, or provide evidence
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May direct follow-ups to original speaker OR redirect to other students
* May invite students to agree, disagree, or add on to peer responses ("Do you agree with ___? Why?")
* May ask for clarification or specificity ("What do you mean by...", "Can you show me where...")
* May probe connections between ideas ("How does this relate to...", "Why does this matter?")
* May scaffold incorrect responses toward correct understanding with targeted questions
* May focus on process ("How did you figure that out?") OR product ("Why is this answer stronger?")
* May be paired with a variety of question response formats (e.g., turn and talk, cold call, everybody writes, etc.)
* Often involves a sequence of questions to push for deeper thinking, but may not need multiple questions if initial student response is strong and detailed
* May be posed as a standalone/initiating question, not only in reaction to a prior student response
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Which student's response did you choose and why?" <Student: "Student B because it has more details"> "Say more about that - what kind of details make Student B's response stronger?" <Student explains> "Good. Maya, do you agree with that? Why or why not?" <Maya responds> "So you're both noticing that Student B shows what Amos actually did. How does that connect to our goal of using strong evidence?"

* "Why did I substitute in the values of x and y from the point given in the problem?" <Student: "Because it was in the problem"> "You're right that I used information from the problem. But why did I need to substitute those specific values? What was I trying to find?" <Student: "The b"> "Yes! I was solving for b, the y-intercept. I knew I could substitute 5 for x and 1 for y because the problem told me the point (5, 1) was on the line. So let's try again - why did I substitute those values into the equation?"

* "Water has a positive and negative side, but methane doesn't. How might that structural difference impact how each interacts with oil?" <Posed as an opening question, not in reaction to a prior student response>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Walk us through your answer [Why attempting: Too vague]
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus" [Why attempting: builds on one students' response, but doesn't require explanation of thinking]
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here?" <Points> [Why attempting: Provides related practice but doesn't ask students to explain their thinking process]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts first response and moves on without probing
* Asks vague check for understanding question rather than probing specific thinking (e.g., "does that make sense?", "do you have any questions?", etc.)
* Asks simple yes/no or recall question (e.g., "Did I figure out the pronoun correctly?", "What does precipitation mean?", "What value did I get for b?", etc.)

look_fors.name: Invite Generative Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to produce multiple ideas, possibilities, or original responses
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Frames the task as divergent; quantity and variety of ideas valued over a single correct answer (e.g., "How many ways can you think of...?")
* Explicitly withholds judgment or evaluation during idea generation
* Encourages original or unexpected responses (e.g., "What's an idea no one else might think of?")
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be structured (timed brainstorm, written list) or open (verbal, spontaneous)
* Generative phase may be followed by evaluation or selection
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Before we decide anything, I want as many ideas as possible. No evaluating yet. You have 3 minutes. Go." 
* "What's the most unexpected approach you can think of? I want something that might surprise me."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Any ideas?" without framing the task as divergent or explicitly valuing multiple or creative responses [Why attempting: opens space for ideas but doesn't cultivate generative thinking as a disposition]
* Accepts the first strong idea and moves on [Why attempting: doesn't create the expectation that generating many possibilities is itself the goal]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks for one correct answer
* Evaluates or narrows ideas as students generate them ("Good, but not quite what I'm looking for")
* "Brainstorm" framing with no actual divergent expectation (e.g., listing facts students already know)

look_fors.name: Model Enthusiasm and Curiosity for Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Demonstrate genuine excitement and curiosity about content and learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Shares own curiosity or interest in the topic
* Expresses excitement about student thinking or discoveries
* Models wondering and inquiry
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Enthusiasm may be calm or energetic depending on teacher style
* Can share personal connections to content
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I'm so excited to share this with you today. This is one of my favorite concepts because..."
* "Your thinking just blew my mind! I hadn't considered that perspective"
* "If you're all ready to strengthen your brains, say, Oh, yeah!" Students: "Oh, yeah!" <creates enthusiastic entry to learning>
* "I can't wait to see what you discover in this investigation!"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This is important and interesting" [Why attempting: Vague]
* Enthusiastic about behavior compliance but not about learning
look_fors.non_examples:
* Presents content as obligation ("We have to cover this")
* Shows no personal interest in topic

look_fors.name: Normalize Mistakes as Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state that errors are part of learning and respond to mistakes or misconceptions as opportunities to learn
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States that mistakes help learning 
* Responds to errors with curiosity rather than clarification alone
* Publicly acknowledges own mistakes as learning opportunities
* Thanks students for sharing mistakes that help class learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May frame revision as normal part of learning process
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections. Let's look at what this mistake can teach us"
* <Teacher makes and catches own error> "Oops! Can anyone find the mistake I just made?" <Student answers> "Thanks! Next time I will..."
*  <Student work shows two divided by zero is two> Teacher: "Oooh, interesting thinking here! Walk me through why you think two divided by zero is two." <Listens to student thinking, and connects to thinking when providing clarification>
* "This is a really interesting misconception. I used to think that the seasons were caused by Earth's distance from the sun, too. This is a logical guess, but it's not what's actually happening, which blew my mind a little when I learned the real answer!"<Teacher demonstrates misconception clarification and comes back to original student to share updated thinking>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you make a mistake" [Why attempting: Reassures but doesn't frame mistakes as valuable]
* <Student gives partially correct answer.> Teacher: "Good start. You're getting there" <does not explain why, calls on another student>. [Why attempting: Somewhat affirming but doesn't use error as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
- <student gives wrong answer> "No, that's not right. Who else?" [Why non-example: Dismisses error without learning value] [type: relational harm]
- Only acknowledges correct answers with praise [type: missed opportunity]
- "You mixed up the numerator and denominator AGAIN" <exasperated tone> [Why non-example: judgmental of error] [type: relational harm]
- Tells one student to explain to another why they are wrong [Why non-example: Negatively framed with emphasis on wrong vs. correct instead of what can be learned] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Prompt Evaluation or Judgment
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to assess, critique, or make judgments about claims, work, or ideas
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students to evaluate the quality, accuracy, or strength of something (e.g., an argument, solution, peer response, or source)
* Asks students to weigh options, make a decision, and justify their choice
* Invites students to agree or disagree with a claim and explain why
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target of evaluation may vary (e.g., teacher-generated examples, student work, texts, or real-world claims)
* May be structured (written criteria) or open-ended (verbal judgment)
* May ask students to evaluate whether evidence is sufficient or complete, not only its quality or strength
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Here are two student responses to the essay prompt. Which is stronger, and what makes it stronger? Use our rubric to decide." 
* "The author claims social media is making teens less happy. Is that argument convincing? What evidence would you need to be sure?"
* "We got two different answers to this problem. Can both be right? How would you decide which one to trust?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Do you agree or disagree?" with no follow-up for reasoning [Why attempting: invites a stance but not evaluation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks students to recall or describe rather than evaluate (e.g., "What did the author say?")
* Asks recall questions

look_fors.name: Require Reasoning or Justification
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Establish the norm that answers must include reasoning or evidence
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sets or reinforces the expectation that students explain thinking, not just give answer
* Provides and references supports for reasoning and justification (e.g., sentence starters, posted norms)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Reasoning standard may be content-specific ("use evidence from the text") or general ("tell me how you know")
* May use follow up questions to push students who answer without reasoning to explain; however, for look-for to be strong, the expectation for reasoning or justification must be proactively established
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I don't just want to know what you think, I want to know why. So, remember to use our sentence frame: I think ___, because ___"
 * Student: "The answer is 12" Teacher: "You might be right — but I need the how you got there. Walk me through your reasoning." <student responds with reasoning> Teacher: "That's the kind of thinking I want to hear every time."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Can you say more?" [Why attempting: prompts elaboration but doesn't establish reasoning as a standing expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts correct answers without asking for reasoning (e.g., "Great answer! Who else?")
* Only asks for justification when an answer is wrong

look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
