* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Monitoring and Self-Reflection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to do metacognitive checks or reflections on their own learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts students to monitor their own understanding, confidence, or progress
* Students pause to meta-cognitively reflect on their own learning in-the-moment or after a specific lesson, task, or goal is completed
* Students often identify when they're stuck, confused, or need help
* Students describe how their understanding or confidence has changed over time
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Monitoring tools vary by context (e.g., emoji check-ins for confidence ratings, answer keys for accuracy, progress trackers for completion, targeted questions for considering response quality, etc.)
* Students may track their own progress using provided tools (e.g., confidence scales, answer keys, completion trackers)
* May be embedded as a recurring routine (e.g., a daily exit ticket format, weekly reflection protocol) rather than a one-time prompt
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <At the end of a lesson> "Take 2 minutes to complete the statement 'I used to think... now I know...' based on what you have learned today."
* "On a scale of 1-5, how confident are you that you understand why the character made that choice?" <Students show fingers, teacher sees mix of 2s and 4s> "Turn to your partner and explain why you chose that number." <Students discuss their confidence levels>
* What was most challenging for you today? What helped you work through it?"
* "Place your green, yellow, or red circle on the top of the stack on your desk to indicate if you are ready to move on, need a little help, or are completely stuck"
* "Take a moment to reflect: What strategy did you use? How well did it work? What might you try differently next time?"
* "Now that you have peer feedback on your essay, turn and talk to a new partner about one major strength of your current essay and one next step you will take to revise it"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "During the work time, raise your hand if you need help" [Why attempting:Students are invited to self-monitor, but question is unlikely to lead to all students engaging in metacognitive monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Does everyone understand?" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher circulates and identifies confused students but students don't self-identify [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Surface Multiple Perspectives
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Deliberately introduce different or competing viewpoints or approaches
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents more than one interpretation, solution, or viewpoint on the same question or problem
* Asks students to consider or compare different perspectives
* Explicitly names that reasonable people or experts can disagree
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Perspectives may come from varied sources (e.g., texts, historical figures, peer responses, or teacher-generated examples)
* May be structured (e.g., assigned positions in a debate) or organic (e.g., surfaced from student responses)
* Perspectives must represent legitimate, reasoned positions. This look-for does NOT apply to harmful viewpoints (e.g., racist or discriminatory perspectives) or claims that contradict established fact (e.g., climate change denial, flat earth)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We have two interpretations of this poem — one from last period, one from this morning. Both classes used evidence. Can they both be right? Let's figure out what each assumes."
* <After students share one approach> "Here's how another mathematician approached the same problem." <Presents alternative> "What does this approach make easier? What does it miss?"
* "Historians disagree about whether this decision was justified. Here's the argument for, and here's the argument against. Your job isn't to pick a side yet — it's to figure out what each argument depends on."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Does anyone see it differently?" [Why attempting: opens the door to multiple perspectives but doesn't deliberately surface them]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Presents only one correct interpretation or approach
* Asks for student opinions without introducing any alternative perspectives
* Presents a harmful or debunked viewpoint as a reasonable point on which to disagree

skills.name: Encoding
skills.description: Teach students to spell words accurately by segmenting a word into its sounds, mapping each sound to letters, and applying spelling patterns.

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
Depending on the phonological or phonemic unit of the lesson….
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name(s) ("em") or "muh"
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces digraphs and vowel teams accurately (/ch/, /ee/, etc.)
* Segments syllables accurately
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
"Listen: /mmm/-op. The first sound is /mmm/."
"What is another word that sounds like 'bat'?"
"Which one doesn't belong? Weed, bead, pill, seed?"
"/tae/ /bl/ What's the word?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first sound in 'top' is /tuh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
"The first sound in 'mop' is 'em.'" [Why non-example: says letter not sound]
"There are five sounds in 'cheese': /c/, /h/, /e/, /e/, /z/" [Why non-example: not accurately pronouncing digraph /ch/ nor vowel team /ee/]
"Tiger has two syllables: /tieg/ /r/" [Why non-example: syllables not divided correctly]

look_fors.name: Map Sounds to Letters
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Write the correct letter or letters for each sound.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Matches each sound in the word to the letter or letters that spell it
Represents one sound spelled by multiple letters as a single unit (e.g., /sh/ spelled "sh")
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let's spell ship. For ship, /sh/ is s and h together, <writes sh>, /i/ is i <writes i>, and /p/ is p <writes p>. Notice that /sh/ is two letters for one sound."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Let's spell ship. For ship, /sh/ is s and h together, <writes sh> Then we add i and p. S-h-i-p." [Why attempting: partial mapping of sounds to letters]
look_fors.non_examples: "Map is spelled m-a-p" [Why non-example: names letters with no link to the sounds]

look_fors.name: Segment Words into Sounds
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Separate a word into its individual sounds before spelling it.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Says the word, then separates it into its individual sounds (e.g., tapping each sound)
Segments at the sound level, not by letter names alone
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Segments may be syllables when phonemic unit of focus is syllable
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let's spell map. Tap it out with me: /m/ /a/ /p/. Three sounds. Now let's spell." /m/ m. /a/ a. /p/ p. M-a-p spells map.
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Map has three sounds. Spell it" <does not say each sound> [Why attempting: counts the sounds but does not isolate each one]
look_fors.non_examples: "Spell 'map.'" <students write with no segmenting modeled or prompted>

look_fors.type_explanation: Apply Spelling Patterns is required when the word's spelling depends on a pattern or generalization; not required for simple, fully decodable words
look_fors.name: Apply Spelling Patterns
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Apply spelling patterns and generalizations to spell the word correctly.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Applies a relevant spelling pattern or generalization (e.g., suffix rules, syllable-junction patterns)
Uses the pattern to decide letter choices rather than guessing
look_fors.strong_examples: "Hop ends in one vowel and one consonant, so I double the p before adding -ing: h-o-p-p-i-n-g. Now let's try that same pattern with run to make running."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Hop ends in one vowel and one consonant, so I double the p before adding -ing: h-o-p-p-i-n-g." [Why attempting: states and uses doubling rule, but does not generalize to another word]
look_fors.non_examples: "Remember, hopping has TWO ps. It is spelled h-o-p-p-i-n-g." [Why non-example: not generalizable; no spelling pattern stated]

skills.name: Engaging Student Thinking
skills.description: Implement instructional routines that get all students actively thinking about the lesson's content.

look_fors.name: Align to Lesson / Objective
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Target instruction, tasks, and questions to the lesson's objective, reaching its full rigor by the end of the lesson.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Instruction, tasks, questions, and activities focus on the lesson's content or objective, not a tangential or off-objective substitute
* The cognitive demand of what the teacher and students do matches the rigor of the objective, or deliberately scaffolds toward it
* By the end of the lesson, students work at the full rigor of the objective, not only a lower-demand version of it
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May target the full objective or a prerequisite/lower-demand step, as long as it scaffolds toward and the lesson reaches the objective's full rigor
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Objective: infer a character's motivation from textual evidence; prompt: "What does Maria's choice in paragraph 4 reveal about what she wants, and which line shows it?"
* Objective: add fractions with unlike denominators; the task presents three such sums different from those modeled
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Objective: students explain how cooling rate affects crystal size; the task asks students to label rock types [Why attempting: related content, not the objective's relationship]
look_fors.non_examples: * Objective: students compare two strategies; the task instead has students copy the steps of one strategy [Why non-example: no comparison; off-objective]

look_fors.name: Engage All Students
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt every student to respond, not just volunteers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts every student to respond, not only volunteers or hand-raisers
* Every student produces a response (spoken, written, gestured, or signaled)
* Teacher follows up with non-responders rather than accepting partial participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Participation may be simultaneous — choral response, whiteboards, everybody writes / stop and jot, or turn and talk — or sequential (every student takes a turn)
* A student may pass in the moment if the teacher returns to them before the segment ends
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard. Then, when I say show me, hold it up." <Pauses, scans boards> "Dani, Sam, give me your best guess" <Pauses until all students have answer written> "Show me." <Scans all boards> "I've got all but three boards up, let's get to 100%" <Waits until all boards are up>
- "We're going around the circle — everyone gives one word describing the narrator. If you need time, say 'come back to me.'" <Every student contributes; teacher returns to the two who passed>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard." <Teacher scans the front two tables> "Great, moving on." <Several boards in the back are blank> [Why attempting: no follow-up on non-responders]
- "Talk to your partner. Partner closest to the door: share how you categorized the example and why. You have 1 minute." <Students talk; teacher never has second partner share> [Why attempting: Only tells one partner to share]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Who can tell me the theme of this chapter?" <Four hands raise; teacher calls on one student, affirms the answer, and moves on>
- "Look at this book. What do you see?" [Why non-example: No clear expectation that everyone responds, or for how to respond]

look_fors.name: Annotations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to mark up a text or document with notes, highlights, underlines, symbols, or comments to show their thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Gives clear annotation expectations (what to mark, how, time for task, etc.)
* Students mark up text (underlining, circling, margin notes, or symbols, etc.) simultaneously
* Circulates throughout the room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use sticky notes if can't write in books
* May be physical or digital annotations
look_fors.strong_examples: "As you read paragraph 2, I want you to use two annotation strategies. First, underline any evidence that supports the author's claim that recycling helps the environment. Second, put a question mark next to anything you don't understand. You have 3 minutes to read and annotate." <Students read and mark text; teacher circulates>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "As you read, underline important parts." [Why attempting: Unclear what important parts are]
* "Circle the main idea and underline supporting details." <Stands in one place> [Why attempting: Strong prompt but no monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Annotate the text" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher does not circulate [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Compare and Connect
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Present a task that can be approached in multiple ways or a situation that can be represented with different representations; guide comparison of different approaches, representations, and/or language
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a task that can be approached in multiple ways or represented differently
* Sequences multiple approaches or representations for class to see (often from different students/student groups after work time)
* Prompts students to identify similarities and differences between approaches
* Asks students to explain meaning of different elements of representations or solution paths (e.g., the evidence chosen, a strategy, a diagram, a calculation)
* Prompts students to reflect on and compare strategies, representations, or language
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Two main formats: (1) Teacher-led sequencing where teacher presents multiple approaches to whole class (e.g., less to more efficient, concrete to abstract, etc.), or (2) Gallery walk where students create displays and tour each other's work with guiding questions from teacher
* Teacher may think aloud (e.g., exploring why one might approach it this way, questioning an idea, wondering how ideas connect) or ask students to do the same
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's look at three different approaches to this problem. First, here's how Ari solved it by drawing 8 groups of 10 and circling five of the groups <displays work; asks students to explain meaning of different elements, "e.g., why did Ari circle 5 groups?"> Next, here's how Jamal solved using two different number sentences. First, 80 divided by 8 and then 10 times 5 <displays; asks students to explain different elements, e.g., "why did Jamal divide in step one?"> Finally, here's Maya's method using a single multiplication number sentence <displays; asks students to explain different elements, e.g., "what does the 5/8 mean?"> <Leads discussion on the three different approaches - compare & contrast, when you might use one approach vs. another, and how different elements of each approach connect>
* "Here are two ways classmates argued the theme. Group A used the narrator's dialogue; Group B used the final scene." <displays both; asks each to explain why that evidence supports the theme> "How do these two arguments compare? When might one piece of evidence be stronger than the other?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* <Displays two student solutions> "What's different about these two methods?" [Why attempting: Prompts comparison but doesn't ask students to explain reasoning behind approaches or connect ideas]
 * "Look at how Method 1 uses multiplication and Method 2 uses division. Which do you prefer?" [Why attempting: Identifies difference but doesn't explore why different operations were chosen or how they connect mathematically]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Shows only one solution or representation method
* Displays different approaches but doesn't prompt students to compare or contrast them
* States which method is best without thinking aloud or discussion

look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Predictions/Observations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to make their own predictions and/or observations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides time and structure for students to form predictions
* Explicitly invites student predictions/observations as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student predictions by revisiting or testing them against new information
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Predictions/observations may be gathered from a subset of students or the whole group
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Looking at this cover, what do you think might happen in this story? Turn and tell your partner your prediction." <Students predict; teacher notes a few and tells students they will return to them after reading>
* "Before we run the experiment, write down what you predict will happen to the balloon in the hypothesis box." <Students write> "Let's test it and see."
* "Take a moment to look at this photograph. What do you notice about the bear's fur? Turn and tell your partner what you notice. Say, I notice…" <Students share observations, teacher notes a few and tells students they will learn something special about bears' fur when they read>
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What do you think happens next?" <Accepts one or two predictions and moves on> [Why attempting: doesn't create broad prediction-generation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher states what will happen and/or what they see; students only listen
* "What do you think will happen?" with no time or structure for students to respond

look_fors.name: Isolate the Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give a task with a fixed start and end so students' thinking focuses on the path between.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sets a closed beginning: all students start from the same given point
* Sets a closed end: all students work toward the same answer, answer type, or goal
* Leaves the middle open: multiple valid approaches or paths between the two
* Prompts students to share or justify the path they took
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * The open middle may be one answer reached multiple ways, or multiple valid answers students must justify
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Everyone start from this claim: 'The setting shapes the narrator's fear.' Find the strongest piece of text evidence for it and be ready to justify why yours is best." <students select different evidence and defend their reasoning>
* "Everyone start with the number 24 and end at 6. Show a sequence of steps that gets there, and be ready to explain your path." <students share different valid routes: 24 ÷ 4; 24 ÷ 2 then ÷ 2; 24 − 18>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Start from 3 + 4 = 7. Write the matching subtraction fact." [Why attempting: only two obvious paths and no justification of thinking required]
* "Everyone start from the claim 'The setting shapes the narrator's fear' and find the best evidence for it." <collects work; no one shares or justifies> [Why attempting: open middle present, but students never share or justify their path]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Pick any topic and make an argument about it." [Why non-example: open beginning; thinking not isolated]
* Solve 6 x 7 using an array [Why non-example: single correct path; no open middle]

look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.name: Notice and Wonder
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Present a representation, text, or media and ask students what they notice and wonder
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Displays a representation, text, image, or other media to students
* Asks "What do you notice?" and "What do you wonder?" or similar questions
* Provides time for individual thinking and/or partner sharing
* Often records multiple student noticings and wonderings for class to see
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may steer conversation toward specific content focus after initial noticings and wonderings
* Noticings and wonderings may be recorded on board, chart paper, or digitally
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Here's a table showing how many rolls of paper towels a store gets with different numbers of cases. Take 2 minutes to think: What do you notice? What do you wonder? Then share with your partner." <after partner share> "Let's hear what you noticed and wondered." <records multiple student noticings on board: '3 cases = 36 rolls', 'The number of rolls goes up', '1 case = 12 rolls'> <records wonderings: 'How many rolls in 2 cases?', 'Is there a pattern?', 'What if they ordered 100 cases?'> "I noticed several of you are wondering about the pattern. That's what we're going to explore today."
* "Here's the opening paragraph of our story. Take 2 minutes: what do you notice? what do you wonder? Then share with your partner." <records noticings: 'the narrator is talking to someone', 'it's set at night'; records wonderings: 'who is she writing to?', 'why is she afraid?'> "Several of you wonder who she's writing to — that's what we'll track today."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Displays table and asks "What do you notice?" <records 2-3 student responses> "Ok, now let's move on to the lesson" [Why attempting: Records some noticings but doesn't ask what students wonder or provide adequate think/share time]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Look at this table. Now I'm going to tell you what's important to notice..." [Why non-example: Teacher tells rather than asks what students notice]
 * Asks "What did you notice and wonder yesterday" [Why non-example: Asks notice and wonder, but no specific representation/media]
* "Think about what you notice and then I will show you how to do the problem" <waits 5 seconds, then immediately moves on> [Why non-example: No time for thinking, sharing, or recording responses]

look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Evidence-Based Adjustments (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Respond to student errors or misconceptions by naming what was incorrect, addressing the misunderstanding, verifying that understanding has improved, and fostering conditions where students advocate for their own learning needs.

look_fors.type_explanation: Required after whatever other adjusting instruction look-for(s) are used
look_fors.name: Close the Loop
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: After addressing a misconception or error, return to the original student or sample additional students to verify that understanding has improved.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher previously addressed error/misconception
* Teacher returns to student(s) OR samples additional students
* Teacher asks similar question to verify understanding
* Occurs soon after adjustment (within same lesson segment)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May use whole-group CFU strategy to check broader understanding
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher asks a question that checks for updated understanding relative to a specific student misconception or mistake AND uses a checking for understanding strategy that targets the student(s) with the misconception
* After most students struggled with main and idea and teacher re-taught main idea: "Let's try main idea again. Everyone, write the main idea of paragraph 4 on your whiteboard. You have 1 minute." <Students write> "Boards up!" <Scans> "Excellent - I'm seeing most of you identified that the main idea is about adaptation. Much better than before."
* A few minutes after teacher cues student to correct 'runned' to 'ran' in oral reading: "Raya, let's come back to you. Can you read the next sentence for us? " Raya: "The cat ran up the tree."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Only checks with one student when multiple students had the misconception
* Check does not happen directly after the adjustment but later in the lesson
* Teacher asks a question about a related concept or skill but does not re-check understanding of the specific misconception or error
look_fors.non_examples:
* Moving on without checking if understanding improved [type: missed opportunity]
* Only checking with high-performing students (not the ones who had the misconception) [type: missed opportunity]
* Asking "Do you get it now?" or "Any questions?" [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Name the Error or Misconception
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state what was incorrect or misunderstood.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States the specific error, mistake, or gap in thinking clearly
* Contrasts the error with the correct understanding
* Connects the error to the root cause when possible
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May directly explain the correct understanding and/or root cause of the error or ask students to do so
* May use student work or examples to illustrate the error OR describe it generally without specific examples
* May be used reactively (in response to observed errors) or proactively (addressing predicted common misconceptions in advance)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "The misconception I'm seeing is that you're confusing mass and weight. This is a distinction I struggled with for a long time too! You said the object's mass would be different on the moon, but mass stays the same no matter where you are - that's the amount of matter in an object. What changes on the moon is weight, which is the force of gravity pulling on that mass."
* "Looking at Student A's response, the error is that this answer is too general. What makes Student B's response stronger?" <Student responds> "Yes, response A says 'Amos is determined' but doesn't prove it with specific evidence from the text. Looking at Student B's response, this answer includes specific actions such as 'worked on his boat in the daytime and studied navigation at night'. This shows us exactly how Amos demonstrated determination. The key difference is that Student A stated the trait without proof, while Student B connected the trait to specific textual evidence."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "You made a calculation error here." [Why attempting: Names that there's an error but doesn't specify what kind or where the thinking went wrong]
* "Remember, you need to show your work." [Why attempting: States what's missing but doesn't explain the underlying thinking error]
* "This isn't quite right yet." [Why attempting: Acknowledges incorrectness but doesn't name the specific error or misconception]
* "You swapped x and y. Try again." [Why attempting: Identifies the procedural error but doesn't explain why this matters or connect to conceptual understanding]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Vague feedback without naming a specific error or misconception (e.g.,"This needs improvement.", "Good try! Let's keep working on it.", "You didn't follow the directions", etc.) [type: missed opportunity]
* Shows correct work without addressing the error [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarass or demotivate a student (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required before longer reteach method like Narrate Your Thinking or Share Student Work
Else not required
look_fors.name: Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview what will happen and state clear focus for student thinking and engagement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews what teacher and/or students will do
* States clear purpose, target question, or learning focus
* Gives students specific task or role during activity (listen for, analyze, record, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May check for understanding of the framing before beginning the activity
* Student task may be note-taking, analyzing, comparing, evaluating, or other cognitive engagement
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I have noticed that our understanding of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' sometimes breaks down because of all the pronouns that Zora Neale Hurston uses. When texts have tons of pronouns, there are steps readers can follow to avoid confusion. I will show you how I make sense of the pronouns so I can follow along with the story. As I am thinking aloud for you, I want you to record notes on the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean. Before I start sharing my thinking, remind me - what are you doing as I am thinking aloud for you?"

* "I want to highlight DeAndre's response. As I read it, think about what makes his argument strong." <Reads>

* "I'm going to show you each characteristic of parallel lines with examples. As I do, record the characteristic and an example in your notes. You will use your notes later to practice identifying examples and non-examples of parallel lines based on these characteristics."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "I am going to show you both methods for the sake of putting it out there, whichever you prefer. So let's start by using slope-intercept form. Which form are we starting with?" [Why attempting: Purpose unclear, no student task/goal]
- "This think aloud will be about dividing fractions." [Why attempting: States topic but not purpose or goal]
- "Take a look up here quickly and just pause what you're doing. I want to highlight a student response." [Why attempting: missing why they are highlighting specific student response]
- “Today we are going to continue our focus on fluency. I want you all to sit where you are and listen, then I want to hear you all read. [Why attempting: Fluency is too broad, purpose should be more specific]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, listen to me think aloud." [Why non-example: No framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "I'm going to show you how to do this. Pay attention." [Why non-example: 'Pay attention' too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as compliance (e.g., "Complete this task to earn your participation points for the day", "You must read") [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as for grades or test performance only (e.g., "This is on the state exam", "This exit ticket is like a quiz for your grade") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required after longer reteach method like Narrate Your Thinking or Share Student Work
Else not required
look_fors.name: Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Articulate key learning in transferable terms.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States clear and accurate key point(s)
* Emphasizes when, why, how, or where to apply the learning
* Often framed as a next step
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher states takeaway OR asks students to state it OR co-creates with students
* Takeaway may be verbal only or in conjunction with writing on the board, anchor chart, and/or student writing
* Focus may be on content understanding, procedural steps, strategic approach, or transferable skill
* May connect specific example to broader principle or strategy
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When you are determining the central idea, always make sure it covers the entire text and references the specific topic."

* "Now that you have seen my model, what will you do next time you get stuck on a unit conversion?" <Student responds> "Yes - set up the conversion factor by putting the unit you want to get rid of in the denominator. That strategy is key for unit conversions."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember, in this problem we used slope-intercept form." [Why attempting: Specific to single problem, does not include when/why/how for transfer]
* "What did you learn from this?" [Why non-example: Too vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, let's move on to the next problem." [Why non-example: No takeaway]
* "So the answer is 42." [Why non-example: Specific answer without transferable principle]
* "Do you feel better about solving these on your own now?" [Why non-example: No takeaway]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required for exemplary rating on Danielson 3E: Evidence-Based Adjustments. 
Else not required.
look_fors.name: Student Agency for Learning Needs
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in voicing needs and making adjustments to their learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher asks students what they need (e.g., "What would help you right now?", "What resources do you need?")
* Teacher responds to student-initiated requests for support, resources, or changes
* Students articulate specific learning needs (e.g., "I need more examples," "I am stuck on the unit conversion," etc.)
* Students make adjustments to their approach based on self-monitoring or self-assessment (e.g., choose different resources, modify their strategy, seek help)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Needs may relate to: pacing, resources, supports, task modifications, clarification, or different learning pathways
* Teacher may offer menu of options or students may self-select without prompting
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During independent work, student raises hand: "If the photosphere is the visible surface of the sun, why is it on the inside of the diagram?" Teacher: "The key is the word visible. The photosphere is what the human eye can see. What do you think that means about the chronosphere?" Student "Oh, ok, it's above the photosphere but we can't see it". <Student goes back to work>.
* Student: "I'm stuck. I can't figure out why I keep getting my unit conversions wrong." Teacher: "Can you think of anything that would help you get unstuck?" Student: "Can I see another example of the joules to ergs conversion?" <Teacher directs student to exemplar, student reviews it and then goes back to their own problem set.>
* Students review criteria for success and make edits to their own work based on their self-evaluations.
* Teacher says "Some of you finished early and some need more time. Decide what you need: more practice, start the extension, or revise your work." <Students make different choices based on their self-assessment>
* During writing conference, student says: "I'm stuck on my introduction. Can I start with my body paragraphs first and come back to it?" Teacher affirms: "That's a great strategy - many writers do that." <Student adjusts their approach>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Student asks "Can you help me?" Teacher helps but doesn't prompt student to identify specific need [Why attempting: Student initiates but doesn't articulate specific need]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher assigns all students the same intervention or support without asking what they need [type: missed opportunity]
* Student says "I don't get it" or "I"m stuck" and waits for teacher to fix it [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks if there are any questions and moves on immediately or after a couple students say no [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Cue Missing or First Step
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Highlight a skipped step or emphasize which step comes first.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly states which step was missed or which step should be first
* Uses language like "first step," "remember to," or "before you [next step]"
* Provides time for students to take first step or add the missing step
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used to help students get started on procedure, process, or sequence OR in response to a procedural error
* Teacher may or may not provide additional explanation depending on student needs
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Don’t forget the first step. Check the anchor chart if you need to.” 
* "Remember that the first step is to check if the source is a primary source or secondary source."
* "Don't forget step 3, which is to convert to moles if needed. I see a few of us skipped this step in the ammonia example, so go back and check your own work and revise if needed."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * “Don’t forget to do all the steps. Double check your work.”
look_fors.non_examples: "You're missing something." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Cue with Anchor Chart or Notes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Direct students to reference visual aids or notes.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs student attention to specific anchor chart, poster, or notes
* Provides time for students to review and apply information
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may or may not provide additional explanation depending on student needs
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Reference our anchor chart if you need to remind yourself of each part in FOIL on problem 6."
* "Look at our chart to remember how to line up your ruler with the object."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Take two minutes to first look back at your notes at our definition of fitness and then silently adjust your answer. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Check the board as you work."
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't forget to use your resources if you need help." [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Cue with Definition, Rule or Procedure
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Remind students of a definition, rule or procedure to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or references a previously taught definition, rule or procedure
* Directs students to apply the definition, rule, or procedure
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may explain/provide the definition, rule or procedure or ask students to recall or find it
* General rather than specific cues (e.g., “Remember that we always read in one direction”) can put more cognitive lift on students, but teacher should get more specific if students do not self-correct after first cue
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Always measure the volume in a graduated cylinder by getting eye level and reading from the bottom of the meniscus. Everyone check your most recent volume measurement." <Students self-correct; Teacher moves on>
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle> “Ok, let’s get a little more specific. Remember that we always read from left to right. Watch my finger as I read on this page" <Teacher reads, moving finger from left to right>. "Now, turn the page and put your finger where you will start reading." <Teacher scans and circulates> "Next, move your finger in the direction you will read." <Teacher scans and circulates>
* "Remember, like terms have the same variable and exponent. Go back and make sure you have only combined like terms" <Students self-correct; teacher moves on>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle; Teacher repeats same cue>
* "Remember like terms share letters or variables, and also share exponents. That is, the exponents have to be the same" [Why attempting: Definition imprecise, no direction as to what to apply]
look_fors.non_examples: "Remember to measure carefully." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Cue with Example
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Reference specific examples to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References specific example(s) of knowledge and/or skill of focus in the moment
* Prompts students to apply the example
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may explain the example(s) or ask students to do so
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's revise our definitions of a prime number. Remember, one example is 7. Another is 11."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Let's think back to our examples of the sea turtle and the gray whale. The sea turtle had a lot more offspring, but what did the gray whale have that the sea turtle did not? Take 1 minute and turn and talk with your partner at a level two voice. Go." <Student turn and talk, teacher circulates>. "Alright, based on the conversation you had with your partner, take one minute to adjust your answer."
* "2 is more than 1. 1 is less than 2. Is 3 more than 4 or less than 4?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "It seems we are torn on this one. Think back to our sea turtle and gray whale example and then revise your answer" [Why attempting: References example but doesn't explicitly connect to misconception or guide students to do so]
look_fors.non_examples: "Think about what we learned before." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Playback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes a mistake, simply restate what the student said in a neutral tone, allowing them to hear their response and self-correct.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher repeats answer in neutral tone
* Teacher pauses (2-5 seconds)
* Student often self-corrects
look_fors.acceptable_variations: If playback doesn't work, use different strategy
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "3 + 4 is 8." Teacher: "You're saying 3 + 4 is 8." <pause> Student: "Oh wait, no, it's 7." Teacher: "Yes, 7."
* Student: "The answer is 52." Teacher: "52." <pause, looks at student> Student: <recalculates> "Actually, I think it's 62." Teacher: "Let me see your work. Yes, 62 is correct - nice job catching that."
* Student: "The setting is in a school." Teacher: "You said the setting is in a school." <pause> Student: "Well, it's in a classroom specifically." Teacher: "A classroom - that's more precise. Good."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student: "The capital of California is Los Angeles." Teacher: "Los Angeles? Common mistake, it's Sacramento." [Why non-example: No opportunity for student to self-correct first]
* Student: "7 times 8 is 54." Teacher: "You're saying 7 times 8 is 54..." <says it with a doubtful tone> [Why attempting: Playback but tone not neutral]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Are you sure about that?" [Why non-example: No playback] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Let me tell you the right answer..." [Why non-example: No opportunity for student to self-correct] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Share Student Work
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Display work publicly and acknowledge student's contribution.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Makes student work visible to all students (document camera, projector, copies, etc.)
* Uses language that frames work as learning opportunity for everyone
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Work may be shared in real-time OR prepared in advance (retyped, anonymized if needed)
* May display multiple pieces of work for comparison
* If work analysis is not anonymous, thanks student by name
* If work includes mistakes or misconceptions, frames positively (e.g., as examples of interesting thinking, opportunities to learn, etc.)
* Analysis may include strength(s) and or area(s) for growth
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Thank you so much, DeAndre, for allowing us to learn from your work." <Displays work on projector> "I want us to look at what DeAndre did really well here. I noticed that most of us included a claim and evidence, but DeAndre took it a step further. Let's look at what makes his argument statement so strong."

* "Thank you, Jasmine, for letting us use your work. I see that most of us are attempting to set up the equation, but there's some confusion. I'd like to use Jasmine's work to help us clear up that confusion together. Everyone makes this mistake when they're learning this, and working through it together will help all of us."

* "I want us to take a look at the two approaches to solving this problem that I have on the board up here. Thank you to both students who allowed me to share their thinking. Turn and talk with a partner for two minutes about the similarities and differences you see in these two examples" <Displays two student works side by side>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* <Projects student work> "Here's some student work for us to look at and learn from." [Why attempting: No acknowledgement of student]
* "Thank you, DeAndre." <Displays work on projector> [Why attempting: Thanks student but doesn't frame as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Look at this work." [Why non-example: Minimal framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Ok, let's look at Ellie's example. Ellie made a mistake we all need to avoid." [Why non-example: Negative framing] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher employs 1-3 optional look-fors to clarify misconception/misunderstanding; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
* Feedback may address content, process, or self-regulation
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Your thesis clearly states your position. To strengthen paragraph 2, add textual evidence like you did in paragraph 1, then explain how it supports your claim"
* "You accurately identified the problem. Now show your work step-by-step so I can see your mathematical thinking. Look at the example on the anchor chart for the format"
" Now, I want you to try holding your scissors with just your thumb and pointer finger from your right hand."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Your evidence is weak. Add more quotes" [Why attempting: Identifies issue but doesn't explain how to select strong evidence]
* "Nice work on the intro. The body needs more details" [Why attempting: Names strength and area for improvement but lacks concrete next steps]
* "This is better than last time" [Why attempting: Acknowledges growth but not specific about what improved or next steps]
*  "Keep working. Make sure that you use the visual anchors around the classroom to help you." [Why attempting: Lacks specificity as to what to improve or how to use visual anchors]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Good job" [Why non-example: Generic without specifics] [type: missed opportunity]
* "This needs work" [Why non-example: Identifies problem but no actionable steps] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You're not there yet - keep trying" [Why non-example: No specific guidance for improvement] [type: missed opportunity]
* Only marking errors without explanation or guidance [Why non-example: No actionable next steps] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Facilitate Student Discussion
skills.description: Facilitate group discussion so all students actively participate and respond to and build on each other's thinking.

look_fors.name: Align to Lesson / Objective
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Target instruction, tasks, and questions to the lesson's objective, reaching its full rigor by the end of the lesson.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Instruction, tasks, questions, and activities focus on the lesson's content or objective, not a tangential or off-objective substitute
* The cognitive demand of what the teacher and students do matches the rigor of the objective, or deliberately scaffolds toward it
* By the end of the lesson, students work at the full rigor of the objective, not only a lower-demand version of it
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May target the full objective or a prerequisite/lower-demand step, as long as it scaffolds toward and the lesson reaches the objective's full rigor
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Objective: infer a character's motivation from textual evidence; prompt: "What does Maria's choice in paragraph 4 reveal about what she wants, and which line shows it?"
* Objective: add fractions with unlike denominators; the task presents three such sums different from those modeled
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Objective: students explain how cooling rate affects crystal size; the task asks students to label rock types [Why attempting: related content, not the objective's relationship]
look_fors.non_examples: * Objective: students compare two strategies; the task instead has students copy the steps of one strategy [Why non-example: no comparison; off-objective]

look_fors.name: Engage All Students
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt every student to respond, not just volunteers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts every student to respond, not only volunteers or hand-raisers
* Every student produces a response (spoken, written, gestured, or signaled)
* Teacher follows up with non-responders rather than accepting partial participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Participation may be simultaneous — choral response, whiteboards, everybody writes / stop and jot, or turn and talk — or sequential (every student takes a turn)
* A student may pass in the moment if the teacher returns to them before the segment ends
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard. Then, when I say show me, hold it up." <Pauses, scans boards> "Dani, Sam, give me your best guess" <Pauses until all students have answer written> "Show me." <Scans all boards> "I've got all but three boards up, let's get to 100%" <Waits until all boards are up>
- "We're going around the circle — everyone gives one word describing the narrator. If you need time, say 'come back to me.'" <Every student contributes; teacher returns to the two who passed>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard." <Teacher scans the front two tables> "Great, moving on." <Several boards in the back are blank> [Why attempting: no follow-up on non-responders]
- "Talk to your partner. Partner closest to the door: share how you categorized the example and why. You have 1 minute." <Students talk; teacher never has second partner share> [Why attempting: Only tells one partner to share]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Who can tell me the theme of this chapter?" <Four hands raise; teacher calls on one student, affirms the answer, and moves on>
- "Look at this book. What do you see?" [Why non-example: No clear expectation that everyone responds, or for how to respond]

look_fors.name: Academic Discourse Norms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach how students should engage in academic conversations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly teaches and uses sentence stems or protocols for academic discussion
* Establishes and refers to expectations for listening and building on ideas
* Establishes and refers to expectations for ensuring all voices are heard
* Redirects discourse violations with reference to established norms
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Norms may be co-created with students or taught by teacher
* Can include visual anchor charts with discussion expectations
* May practice norms through fishbowl or role-play
* May model norms before use
* Norms may include distinct expectations for speakers and non-speakers (e.g., conduct norms for speakers, note-taking or listening norms for non-speakers)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When we disagree, we use the stem 'I disagree because...' and explain our thinking with evidence"
* "Our discussion norms are: listen to understand, build on ideas, and ask clarifying questions. Let's practice"
* Student: "I respectfully disagree because..." Teacher: "Notice how Tucker used our sentence stem for disagreement to express his response to Vanessa productively. What do you think Anya?"
* Student: "What do you think, Patrice?" <Student invites participation from other student>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Be respectful when you talk to each other" [Why attempting: Vague]
* Posts discussion norms but never references or reinforces them
* Several students use sentence starters for academic discourse, but conversation is limited to the same few students
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students interrupt or talk over each other without redirection
* The same few students dominate conversation
* Allows dismissive comments about peers' ideas ("That's dumb")
* No norms, sentence stems, or protocols related to academic discourse present

look_fors.name: Cold Call
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Call on any student after giving everyone time to think, not just volunteers.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Poses a question to the whole group before naming a student
* Pauses after the question to give all students think time before naming anyone
* Calls on a student who did not raise a hand or volunteer
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May call on 2-3 students in a row for the same question
* May tell students in advance that cold calling will happen
* May tell students not to volunteer/raise hands
* Student selection method (randomizer, pre-planned list, in-the-moment judgment) doesn't need to be visible
* Calling the name of a student who volunteers is permissible when all hands are up or in a series of questions when a mix of volunteers and non-volunteers are called
look_fors.strong_examples: "What evidence from paragraph two supports your idea? <pauses, scans the room> Marcus, what did you find?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What's the setting of the story, Marcus?" <names the student in the same breath as the question, no pause for others to think first>
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks a question and calls only on students with raised hands. [Why non-example: hands-only, no cold call]
* "Marcus, what's the setting of the story?" [Why non-example: student name before question]

look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.type_explanation: Should be paired with another look-for requiring student discussion; can give students think time before discussion, but is not a stand-alone look-for for this skill.
look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Leadership
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Allow students to lead activities, discussions, or demonstrations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Invites students to lead parts of lesson or activity
* Has students teach or demonstrate for the class
* Assigns formal or informal leadership roles
* Student takes charge while teacher observes or supports
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May scaffold leadership with preparation or support first
* Leadership may be brief (leading one example) or extended (leading full activity/presentation)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Jamal, will you come up and lead the class through your example?"
* "Who can be the teacher and explain this to the class?"
* Student leads call and response letter-sound review while teacher observes
* Teacher assigns student to lead small group through specific protocol or procedure
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student comes to board to share answer but teacher talks through most of the solution [Why attempting: Teacher still leading most]
* Leadership opportunities only for select students [Why attempting: Not equitable access]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher directs all activities and discussions
* Students only respond when called upon, never take charge
* "Who wants to share?"  [Why non-example: Invites participation but not leadership]

look_fors.name: Support Student-to-Student Discourse
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Route conversation through students rather than always through teacher
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs students to respond to each other and build on peer ideas in discussion 
* Steps back during student-to-student exchanges
* As needed, reminds students to respond to each other ("What do you think about Maya's idea?")
* As needed, reminds students to build on peer ideas ("Add on to what Marcus said")
* Students respond to and build on each other's ideas
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May provide supports such as initial model or academic discourse norms
 * Can use structured prompts ("Do you agree or disagree with...?")
 * May redirect specific students to each other or open it to whole class
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Ok, let's discuss our key question for the day. For the next three minutes, I will step to the side unless I need to give a quick reminder. Use our academic discourse norms to discuss the key question as a group. In particular, Don't forget to respond to and build on each other's ideas and monitor your air time." 
 * "Marcus, what do you think about Keisha's explanation? Do you agree or see it differently?"
 * "Who can add to that idea?" <student responds to peer's thinking, not restating own idea>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus and a thumbs down if you do not" <most students give thumbs up, a couple give thumbs down> Teacher: "Yes, Marcus was correct" <teacher moves on> [Why attempting: Missed opportunity for student-to-student discussion]
 * <One student gives response> Teacher: "What do you think, Kim?" [Why attempting: Implies potential peer-to-peer response, but unclear]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All student responses go to teacher who then responds or calls on next student
 * "I’m sure we all agree with Marcus's great point about…" [Why non-example: Assumes student response rather than students giving response]

look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Feedback
skills.description: Respond to student practice attempts by naming specific observed behaviors with specific praise or providing actionable guidance for improvement

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a student has made an error; not required when no errors are observed during practice
look_fors.name: Close the Loop
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: After addressing a misconception or error, return to the original student or sample additional students to verify that understanding has improved.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher previously addressed error/misconception
* Teacher returns to student(s) OR samples additional students
* Teacher asks similar question to verify understanding
* Occurs soon after adjustment (within same lesson segment)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May use whole-group CFU strategy to check broader understanding
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher asks a question that checks for updated understanding relative to a specific student misconception or mistake AND uses a checking for understanding strategy that targets the student(s) with the misconception
* After most students struggled with main and idea and teacher re-taught main idea: "Let's try main idea again. Everyone, write the main idea of paragraph 4 on your whiteboard. You have 1 minute." <Students write> "Boards up!" <Scans> "Excellent - I'm seeing most of you identified that the main idea is about adaptation. Much better than before."
* A few minutes after teacher cues student to correct 'runned' to 'ran' in oral reading: "Raya, let's come back to you. Can you read the next sentence for us? " Raya: "The cat ran up the tree."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Only checks with one student when multiple students had the misconception
* Check does not happen directly after the adjustment but later in the lesson
* Teacher asks a question about a related concept or skill but does not re-check understanding of the specific misconception or error
look_fors.non_examples:
* Moving on without checking if understanding improved [type: missed opportunity]
* Only checking with high-performing students (not the ones who had the misconception) [type: missed opportunity]
* Asking "Do you get it now?" or "Any questions?" [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a student has made an error; not required when no errors are observed during practice
look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
* Feedback may address content, process, or self-regulation
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Your thesis clearly states your position. To strengthen paragraph 2, add textual evidence like you did in paragraph 1, then explain how it supports your claim"
* "You accurately identified the problem. Now show your work step-by-step so I can see your mathematical thinking. Look at the example on the anchor chart for the format"
" Now, I want you to try holding your scissors with just your thumb and pointer finger from your right hand."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Your evidence is weak. Add more quotes" [Why attempting: Identifies issue but doesn't explain how to select strong evidence]
* "Nice work on the intro. The body needs more details" [Why attempting: Names strength and area for improvement but lacks concrete next steps]
* "This is better than last time" [Why attempting: Acknowledges growth but not specific about what improved or next steps]
*  "Keep working. Make sure that you use the visual anchors around the classroom to help you." [Why attempting: Lacks specificity as to what to improve or how to use visual anchors]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Good job" [Why non-example: Generic without specifics] [type: missed opportunity]
* "This needs work" [Why non-example: Identifies problem but no actionable steps] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You're not there yet - keep trying" [Why non-example: No specific guidance for improvement] [type: missed opportunity]
* Only marking errors without explanation or guidance [Why non-example: No actionable next steps] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Feedback (ECE)
skills.description: Respond to student practice attempts by naming specific observed behaviors with specific praise or providing actionable guidance for improvement

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
* Includes details about what made the contribution valuable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be directed to individuals, small groups, or whole class
look_fors.strong_examples: "I noticed Christopher kept the same beat each time — clapping, stomping, and tapping. He went nice and slow to match each syllable."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Nice work keeping the beat!" [Why attempting: References the skill but doesn't name specifics]
look_fors.non_examples: "Great job, Christopher!" [Why non-example: No specific behavior identified]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a student has made an error; not required when no errors are observed during practice
look_fors.name: Close the Loop
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: After addressing a misconception or error, return to the original student or sample additional students to verify that understanding has improved.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher previously addressed error/misconception
* Teacher returns to student(s) OR samples additional students
* Teacher asks similar question to verify understanding
* Occurs soon after adjustment (within same lesson segment)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May use whole-group CFU strategy to check broader understanding
look_fors.strong_examples: <After correcting Riley's /sh/ deletion> Teacher: "Let's try that again. Say 'ship' without the /sh/." Riley: "ip." Teacher: "Way to make that adjustment — you only said the sounds that were left."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <After correcting Riley's /sh/ deletion> "Did you get it that time, Riley?" [Why attempting: Checks back in but verbal confirmation doesn't verify the skill was applied]
look_fors.non_examples: <After correcting Riley's /sh/ deletion> "Good try. Cristina, say 'mask' without the /m/.'" [Why non-example: Moves to next student without checking if Riley's understanding improved]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when a student has made an error; not required when no errors are observed during practice
look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
