Circulates systematically, looking at each student's work and marking checks or notes in appropriate cells. After circulating, shares patterns noticed.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Carries checklist but only marks 1-2 students [Why attempting: Insufficient data]
* References vague criteria like "understands concept"
look_fors.non_examples:
* Observing/listening in to students without any structured criteria [type: missed opportunity]
* Has/references checklist but does not use/make any marks on [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Graphic Organizers
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to fill in a structured visual organizer to support and.or show their understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear prompt/purpose for graphic organizer
* Clear directions for parts of graphic organizer (e.g, sections of t-chart, Venn diagram areas of overlap and non-overlap, etc.) and completion (e.g., time, individual vs. pair/group work, etc.)
* Organizer matches prompt/concept/thinking skill
* Students fill out
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Different types of graphic organizer
- Graphic organizers familiar to students may require less specific directions (e.g., "Fill out the t-chart to compare and contrast facts and opinions. Try to get at least three items for each")
- Semantic and concept maps are types of graphic organizer particularly useful for vocabulary development
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "You each have a Venn diagram on your desk. In the left circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for amphibians. In the right circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for reptiles. In the middle overlapping section, write characteristics they both share. Try to include at least 3 items in each section. You have 4 minutes to work with a partner."
- "On your paper, you have a cause-and-effect chart with three boxes. In the left column, write three causes of World War I. In the right column, write one effect for each cause. Be specific - use dates or events when you can. You have 3 minutes, silent and solo."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Fill in this Venn diagram comparing amphibians and reptiles." [Why attempting: Uses organizer but lacks specificity for organizer or completion]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Do your graphic organizer" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Show the steps of mitosis in the Venn diagram" [Why non-example: Organizer does not match concept/prompt] [type: learning harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Optional Group B
look_fors.name: Listen In
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: During partner or small group discussions, circulate and listen to multiple student conversations to gather data about understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves between multiple groups/pairs
* Pauses near groups to hear conversation
* Makes statements about what was heard across groups (e.g., "A couple groups shared..." "Most of you discussed...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If discussion time is short (e.g., 1-2 minutes), teacher may listen in to a smaller number of pairs/groups
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific things they heard or patterns from student discussion indicating they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger, but Ellie and Max thought example 2 was stronger")
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Liam, you mentioned distance from the sun. Why?" [student responds] "Lara, can you share what you were discussing about intensity of sunlight with the whole class?")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I heard several pairs mention slavery, which is important. I also heard some pairs talking about states' rights and economic differences. Let's unpack how those ideas connect." [Teacher's summary matches evidence from trasncript about student multiple pair discussions]
* "Discuss with your table group: How is photosynthesis different from cellular respiration? You have 2 minutes" <Circulates, stopping briefly at each of 4 table groups> <After listening and calling class back to attention> "Table 3, can you share what you were discussing? I heard you making an interesting comparison about inputs and outputs."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Listens to 1-2 groups but not enough to identify patterns
* Spends entire time facilitating one group's discussion instead of gathering data
* Moves so rapidly between groups that can likely only hear that students are on-task, but not evaluate understanding
* "Nayeli and Lincoln though example 1 was stronger" [Statement matches what Nayeli and Lincoln discussed; Why attempting: single pair/group discussion focus, does not uncover patterns]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place during partner talk without listening [type: missed opportunity]
* Only intervening when students are off-task [type: missed opportunity]
* Listening to only one group for the entire discussion time [type: missed opportunity]
* Doing something else while students are talking [type: missed opportunity]
* Statement of what was heard does not match actual student discussion (e.g., stating "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger" IF Nayeli and Lincoln actually discussed example 2 being stronger) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Optional Group B
look_fors.name: Observation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Circulate or scan throughout the room to observe student work, looking for patterns in understanding across multiple students.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves to or scans multiple locations
* Looks at student work (written, kinesthetic, etc.)
* Makes statements about observations or patterns (e.g., "I'm noticing...", "Most of you...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific observations and/or patterns from student work indicating they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "I saw some of us got 90 and some of us got 9,000 for the answer." 
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "let's hear from two people who agreed and two who disagreed"; "Liam, tell me more about what you were thinking about distance from the sun," [student responds] "Lara, tell me more about why you wrote about intensity of sunlight")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I'm noticing several people are having trouble with step 2. Let's pause and address that together before continuing." [Teacher's observation matches evidence from transcript about multiple student responses]
* Teacher circulates during a science lab, stops to observe three different lab groups' setup of materials, then addresses whole class: "I see all three groups I checked have their graduated cylinders on a flat surface - excellent. Also, everyone check - goggles should be on your face, not on top of your head."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Circulates to see some student work but doesn't cover enough of the room to identify patterns
* Focuses on behavior management rather than academic work while circulating
* "Dante's board says 9x10 = 90" [Statement matches a single student response; Why attempting: single student focus, does not uncover patterns]
* Uses a visual strategy like poll, total physical response/gestures, or whiteboards, but no active evidence (e.g., scanning, narrating trends) of monitoring
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place for an extended period without looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Only checking work of students who raise their hands for help [type: missed opportunity]
* Circulating but not looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Observations do not match student work (e.g., stating "Dante's board says 9 x 10 = 900" IF Dante's board actually said 9 x 10 = 90) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A to strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Poll
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question at the same time via a gesture or other tool.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks question with clear answer options (A/B/C/D, true/false, agree/disagree) and clear way to show answer (hand signals, standing/sitting, etc.)
* IF question has only two response options (e.g., true/false or agree/disagree) follows up with an additional strategy like ask-ask-ask to learn more about student thinking
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time
* Students respond simultaneously
* Scans all responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used for polls in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May combine with think time or turn and talk first
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Let’s take a look at question 2. When I say “show,” hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false. <Gives wait time>. Ready…show! " <Asks 2-3 students to explain why they chose true or false after the show>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's take a look at question 2. Hold up a 1 if you selected true and a 2 if you selected false" [Why attempting: Clear answer options but no in-cue, no follow up questioning with only two response options]
* "Raise your hand if you think it's A. Raise your hand if you think it's B. Raise your hand if you think it’s C..." [Why attempting: Uses hand signals but sequential, not simultaneous]
* "Not yet, but when I say go, hold up your answer. Take some think time. <pause> Ok, ready, go!" [Why attempting: Has in-cue but unclear how to show answer]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Any questions?" <waits for raised hands> [Why non-example: Not a poll - only volunteers respond] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Ok, show me your answer" [Unclear how to show; students reveal at different times] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Everyone say their answer" [No in-cue, teacher unable to evaluate individual student responses when all spoken at once] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Optional Group B
look_fors.name: Probing Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes an error or reveals a misconception, ask follow-up questions to understand the student's thinking and the root cause of the misunderstanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher asks follow-up question about student's thinking
* Teacher uses curious, non-judgmental language
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May probe publicly or privately
* May ask series of questions to get to root cause
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "The answer is 24." Teacher: "You got 24. Can you walk me through how you solved it?" Student: "I multiplied 3 times 8." Teacher: "You multiplied 3 times 8. What made you decide to multiply instead of add?" Student: "Because the problem said 'each' so I thought that meant times." Teacher: "You saw the word 'each' and knew that was a clue. Let's look at the problem together and figure out if multiplication is the right operation here."
* Student: "I think the main idea is that the girl went to the store." Teacher: "You said the main idea is that she went to the store. What part of the text made you think that was the main idea?" Student: "It was in the first sentence." Teacher: "Got it. How should we use the text to find the main idea?”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Check your answer against the key now. What would you change?" [Why attempting: Does not necessarily reveal student thinking]
* "And in step 3 did you multiply or divide?" [Why attempting: Does not reveal student thinking; may be leading]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Immediately corrects the student without asking any questions [type: missed opportunity]
* "Really? You think it's 7?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you remember we talked about this yesterday?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you think you should add instead of subtract?" [Why non-example: Leading question, does not reveal student thinking] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A to strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A to strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Total Physical Response (TPR)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for or supporting understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student responds to a question or prompt at the same time using their whole body or physical movements in a way that conveys meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond with physical movement
* Physical movement clearly corresponds to concept being taught or assessed
* Prompts students to do the movement at the same time
* Students do movement simultaneously
* Scans student movements
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If using to check for understanding, must have more than one possible response and be in response to a question (e.g., "Imagine the UV light is here in the room and you are a plant. When I say go, use your body to show the direction you will grow")
* If using to convey meaning, may have single motion without a question (e.g., "frigid means really cold. cross your arms and shake your body to show brrrrrrrrr...frigid!")
* If using to convey meaning, exact simultaneous response less important
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Conveying meaning: "At convergent plate boundaries, plates crash or push together. Push your arms together like I am and say convergent with me. My turn - convergent. Your turn."
* Checking for understanding: "I'm going to say a number. If it's greater than 50, stand up. If it's less than 50, crouch down. If it's exactly 50, freeze in place. Ready? Think first, and then stand up, crouch down, or freeze when I say go. The number is 73....go" <All students stand. Teacher asks 2 students how they knew 73 was greater than 50>.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Show me with your body what it means to freeze" [Why attempting: Body movement but no in-cue]
* "Use your arms to make a rectangle because the constitution was written on parchment" [Why attempting: Not conceptually meaningful]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Raise your arms in air to be a cell" [Why non-example: Does not match concept] [type: learning harm]
* "Move your body to show the answer" [Vague prompt, no in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A to strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A: Teacher employs 1-3 look-fors from optional Group A to strategically to check for understanding via strategic sampling or full group response; does not need specific or all look-fors
look_fors.name: Whiteboards
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for understanding where, on the teacher’s cue, each student holds up their work via a whiteboard on which they have written a response to a question or prompt.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond by writing/drawing on whiteboards/paper
* Gives time for all students to write/draw their response independently
* Prompts students to reveal answers at the same time by holding up whiteboard or paper
* Students hold up simultaneously
* Scans responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Digital tools may be used as whiteboards in virtual or tech-integrated settings
* May ask follow up questions (e.g., "why?", "how do you know?", "what's an example?", etc.)
* May narrate trends they see in student responses
look_fors.strong_examples: "Take 45 seconds to calculate 24 ÷ 6 on your board and show your work. If you finish early, look at me so I know you are done, but do NOT hold your board up yet." <pauses for work time; circulates> <after 45 seconds> "Markers down. When I clap twice, flip your board to face me. Ready?" <claps twice> <Teacher scans boards>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "On your whiteboard, solve for x. When you're done, hold it up." [No synchronized reveal]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Write on your whiteboard then show it to me" [Why non-example: Vague prompt, no clear in-cue] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher gives question and immediately says "boards up" [Why non-example: No wait time, students can't complete task] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Monitoring Understanding
skills.description: Systematically gather data about student understanding.

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for for skill
look_fors.name: Checklist
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use a structured checklist of specific criteria while observing, listening to, or questioning students to systematically gather data on understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher holds/references physical or digital checklist
* Marks criteria for multiple students
* May make statements referencing checklist data
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May sample strategically rather than check every student
look_fors.strong_examples: Carries clipboard with checklist showing student names in rows and columns labeled: "Labels diagram correctly," "Uses at least 3 content vocabulary words," "Includes claim and evidence." Circulates systematically, looking at each student's work and marking checks or notes in appropriate cells. After circulating, shares patterns noticed.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Carries checklist but only marks 1-2 students [Why attempting: Insufficient data]
* References vague criteria like "understands concept"
look_fors.non_examples:
* Observing/listening in to students without any structured criteria [type: missed opportunity]
* Has/references checklist but does not use/make any marks on [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for for skill
look_fors.name: Listen In
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: During partner or small group discussions, circulate and listen to multiple student conversations to gather data about understanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves between multiple groups/pairs
* Pauses near groups to hear conversation
* Makes statements about what was heard across groups (e.g., "A couple groups shared..." "Most of you discussed...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If discussion time is short (e.g., 1-2 minutes), teacher may listen in to a smaller number of pairs/groups
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific things they heard or patterns from student discussion indicating they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger, but Ellie and Max thought example 2 was stronger")
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they heard multiple student responses (e.g., "Liam, you mentioned distance from the sun. Why?" [student responds] "Lara, can you share what you were discussing about intensity of sunlight with the whole class?")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I heard several pairs mention slavery, which is important. I also heard some pairs talking about states' rights and economic differences. Let's unpack how those ideas connect." [Teacher's summary matches evidence from trasncript about student multiple pair discussions]
* "Discuss with your table group: How is photosynthesis different from cellular respiration? You have 2 minutes" <Circulates, stopping briefly at each of 4 table groups> <After listening and calling class back to attention> "Table 3, can you share what you were discussing? I heard you making an interesting comparison about inputs and outputs."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Listens to 1-2 groups but not enough to identify patterns
* Spends entire time facilitating one group's discussion instead of gathering data
* Moves so rapidly between groups that can likely only hear that students are on-task, but not evaluate understanding
* "Nayeli and Lincoln though example 1 was stronger" [Statement matches what Nayeli and Lincoln discussed; Why attempting: single pair/group discussion focus, does not uncover patterns]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place during partner talk without listening [type: missed opportunity]
* Only intervening when students are off-task [type: missed opportunity]
* Listening to only one group for the entire discussion time [type: missed opportunity]
* Doing something else while students are talking [type: missed opportunity]
* Statement of what was heard does not match actual student discussion (e.g., stating "Nayeli and Lincoln thought example 1 was stronger" IF Nayeli and Lincoln actually discussed example 2 being stronger) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for for skill
look_fors.name: Observation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Circulate or scan throughout the room to observe student work, looking for patterns in understanding across multiple students.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Moves to or scans multiple locations
* Looks at student work (written, kinesthetic, etc.)
* Makes statements about observations or patterns (e.g., "I'm noticing...", "Most of you...") that match actual student responses
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Audio only evidence: teacher narrates specific observations and/or patterns from student work indicating they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "I saw some of us got 90 and some of us got 9,000 for the answer." 
* Audio only evidence: teacher may ask follow up questions of multiple students that indicate they saw multiple student responses (e.g., "let's hear from two people who agreed and two who disagreed"; "Liam, tell me more about what you were thinking about distance from the sun," [student responds] "Lara, tell me more about why you wrote about intensity of sunlight")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I'm noticing several people are having trouble with step 2. Let's pause and address that together before continuing." [Teacher's observation matches evidence from transcript about multiple student responses]
* Teacher circulates during a science lab, stops to observe three different lab groups' setup of materials, then addresses whole class: "I see all three groups I checked have their graduated cylinders on a flat surface - excellent. Also, everyone check - goggles should be on your face, not on top of your head."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Circulates to see some student work but doesn't cover enough of the room to identify patterns
* Focuses on behavior management rather than academic work while circulating
* "Dante's board says 9x10 = 90" [Statement matches a single student response; Why attempting: single student focus, does not uncover patterns]
* Uses a visual strategy like poll, total physical response/gestures, or whiteboards, but no active evidence (e.g., scanning, narrating trends) of monitoring
look_fors.non_examples:
* Standing in one place for an extended period without looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Only checking work of students who raise their hands for help [type: missed opportunity]
* Circulating but not looking at student work [type: missed opportunity]
* Observations do not match student work (e.g., stating "Dante's board says 9 x 10 = 900" IF Dante's board actually said 9 x 10 = 90) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for for skill
look_fors.name: Probing Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes an error or reveals a misconception, ask follow-up questions to understand the student's thinking and the root cause of the misunderstanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher asks follow-up question about student's thinking
* Teacher uses curious, non-judgmental language
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May probe publicly or privately
* May ask series of questions to get to root cause
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "The answer is 24." Teacher: "You got 24. Can you walk me through how you solved it?" Student: "I multiplied 3 times 8." Teacher: "You multiplied 3 times 8. What made you decide to multiply instead of add?" Student: "Because the problem said 'each' so I thought that meant times." Teacher: "You saw the word 'each' and knew that was a clue. Let's look at the problem together and figure out if multiplication is the right operation here."
* Student: "I think the main idea is that the girl went to the store." Teacher: "You said the main idea is that she went to the store. What part of the text made you think that was the main idea?" Student: "It was in the first sentence." Teacher: "Got it. How should we use the text to find the main idea?”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Check your answer against the key now. What would you change?" [Why attempting: Does not necessarily reveal student thinking]
* "And in step 3 did you multiply or divide?" [Why attempting: Does not reveal student thinking; may be leading]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Immediately corrects the student without asking any questions [type: missed opportunity]
* "Really? You think it's 7?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you remember we talked about this yesterday?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you think you should add instead of subtract?" [Why non-example: Leading question, does not reveal student thinking] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: One-on-One Think Aloud
skills.description: Deliver a one-on-one think aloud that makes reasoning explicit, checks understanding, stamps the key takeaway, and transfers to student practice.

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: aligned practice
look_fors.name: Aligned Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students practice the exact focus skill and/or concept just modeled or from the lesson's objective
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Practice task requires the same skill or concept that was modeled, introduced, or specified in the lesson's objective
- Task targets that skill directly, not a related or easier substitute
look_fors.acceptable_variations: - Supportive scaffolds (e.g., sentence starters, exemplars) may be used as long as the target skill is unchanged
look_fors.strong_examples:
- Teacher models blending /m/ /a/ /p/ → "map"; students then blend new words (/s/ /u/ /n/ → "sun")
- Objective states students will add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators; practice includes a set of three addition and three subtraction problems with unlike denominators that are different than the problems modeled by the teacher
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- Teacher models blending CVC words; practice only has students identify the first sound
- Objective states students will explain the relationship between cooling time and crystal size in igneous rocks; practice has students identify igneous rocks and explain how they were formed, but does not explicitly require an explanation of the relationship between cooling time and crystal size
look_fors.non_examples:
- Teacher models segmenting phonemes; practice instead has students clap syllables
- Objective states students will be able to calculate density; practice instead has students determine if objects sink or float

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 1: frame the purpose of the think aloud
look_fors.name: Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview what will happen and state clear focus for student thinking and engagement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews what teacher and/or students will do
* States clear purpose, target question, or learning focus
* Gives students specific task or role during activity (listen for, analyze, record, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May check for understanding of the framing before beginning the activity
* Student task may be note-taking, analyzing, comparing, evaluating, or other cognitive engagement
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I have noticed that our understanding of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' sometimes breaks down because of all the pronouns that Zora Neale Hurston uses. When texts have tons of pronouns, there are steps readers can follow to avoid confusion. I will show you how I make sense of the pronouns so I can follow along with the story. As I am thinking aloud for you, I want you to record notes on the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean. Before I start sharing my thinking, remind me - what are you doing as I am thinking aloud for you?"

* "I want to highlight DeAndre's response. As I read it, think about what makes his argument strong." <Reads>

* "I'm going to show you each characteristic of parallel lines with examples. As I do, record the characteristic and an example in your notes. You will use your notes later to practice identifying examples and non-examples of parallel lines based on these characteristics."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "I am going to show you both methods for the sake of putting it out there, whichever you prefer. So let's start by using slope-intercept form. Which form are we starting with?" [Why attempting: Purpose unclear, no student task/goal]
- "This think aloud will be about dividing fractions." [Why attempting: States topic but not purpose or goal]
- "Take a look up here quickly and just pause what you're doing. I want to highlight a student response." [Why attempting: missing why they are highlighting specific student response]
- “Today we are going to continue our focus on fluency. I want you all to sit where you are and listen, then I want to hear you all read. [Why attempting: Fluency is too broad, purpose should be more specific]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, listen to me think aloud." [Why non-example: No framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "I'm going to show you how to do this. Pay attention." [Why non-example: 'Pay attention' too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as compliance (e.g., "Complete this task to earn your participation points for the day", "You must read") [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as for grades or test performance only (e.g., "This is on the state exam", "This exit ticket is like a quiz for your grade") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 4: guided practice
look_fors.name: Guided Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students time to apply learning with guidance.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Provides task that applies specific content and/or skills to a new but related context or problem
- Offers scaffolding (e.g., checklist, guiding questions, reference material, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Level of guidance varies based on student need: heavy scaffolding to light check-ins
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph." <Displays new paragraph> "Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here and how do you know?" <Student responds> "Good - you skimmed the previous paragraph for clues. Show me - where exactly did you find that clue?" <Student points> "Excellent. What will you do now to check if that makes sense?" <Continues using questions to scaffold>

- "As you revise your lab conclusions, you can always look back to our exemplar from yesterday's lab for a strong example of how to use evidence." <Circulates> "What evidence could you include here?" "Why did you choose that data to support your conclusion?" <Checks in with multiple students>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Don't forget the steps I just took to determine the central idea" [Why attempting: minimal/vague guidance]
 * "Try another problem like this one. Raise your hand if you need help." [Why attempting: Reactive rather than proactive guidance]
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Finishes think aloud> "Okay, moving on to our next topic..." [Why non-example: No practice]
* "Now complete this worksheet silently." <Sits at desk, doesn't monitor> [Why non-example: No guidance or scaffolding]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 2: narrate thinking; may be interspersed with Right Question
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 2: may be interspersed with Narrate Your Thinking or follow it
look_fors.name: Right Question (CFU)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that reveals what you need to know about student understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question directly targets the learning objective/goal or related key concept or skill from the lesson
* Question reveals whether students can demonstrate the specific knowledge or skill being taught
* Question is aligned with the cognitive demand of the learning objective from the lesson (or scaffolds toward it) 
* When available, learning objective/goal from the lesson must be: 
===BEGIN LEARNING OBJECTIVE(S)/GOAL(S)===
[Learning Objective(s)/Goal(s) from external source]
{{learning_objective_s__goal_s_}}
===END LEARNING OBJECTIVE(S)/GOAL(S)===
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* For selected response questions, question includes appropriate number of answer choices for the concept being assessed
* Question may be related to prior knowledge (e.g., from an earlier lesson) necessary for success with the current lesson's objective
* Question may require less cognitive demand if used in a way that scaffolds toward the full cognitive demand of the lesson (e.g., teacher checks for student ability to identify figurative language types like metaphors before having students analyze an author's use of figurative language)
* Any question that asks students to demonstrate understanding (e.g., explain, apply learning to a new scenario, etc.) as opposed to doing something else like predicting can be a check for understanding question
* Student tasks themselves, when framed around prompts or questions that require students to demonstrate understanding, may be checking for understanding questions
* Questions may come directly from lesson plan or materials
* Questions may ask for students to respond verbally, in writing, in pictures, etc
* Questions may target anticipated misconceptions
* Do nows are often checks for understanding of prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how metamorphic rocks form. Teacher first asks students to define temperature and pressure in their own words [scaffold] before asking "How are metamorphic rocks formed? Use today’s key vocabulary words in your answer."
* Learning objective is to compare and contrast two characters; teacher asks "What are two similarities and two differences between Character A and Character B?"
* Learning objective is to compare and contrast two characters; teacher asks students to identify the character traits of the first character. Transcript or lesson plan indicates that later in lesson teacher asks students to compare and contrast two characters. [Why strong: Question scaffolds directly toward objective]
* Learning objective is "SWBAT determine why constellations in the night sky vary by season by using and analyzing a model". Teacher references specific questions for students to answer in writing in their handout. Uploaded lesson plan shows these questions to be: "Will someone in Buenos Aires ever see Ursa Major?", "Will someone in New York City ever see The Southern Cross?", "Would constellations still change throughout the year if the Earth did not revolve around the Sun?" and "Why don’t we see constellations during the day?" [Why strong: These questions require full understanding of the spatial reasoning required to master the objective and also require nuanced understanding relative to the objective]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how sedimentary rocks are formed. Teacher asks students to identify specific sedimentary rocks based on grain size [Why attempting: Related to objective and may imply formation environment, but does not directly align to objective]
* Learning objective is to solve two-step equations; teacher asks students to solve a one-step equation and does not move on to a two-step equation next or indicate it is a stepping stone to two-step equations [Why attempting: Lower cognitive demand than objective]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Learning objective is to explain how metamorphic rocks form; teacher asks "What is your favorite type of rock?" [Why non-example: Doesn't target learning objective] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks vague question (e.g., "Any questions?", "Does that make sense?", etc.) [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 3: stamp the transferable takeaway
look_fors.name: Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Articulate key learning in transferable terms.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States clear and accurate key point(s)
* Emphasizes when, why, how, or where to apply the learning
* Often framed as a next step
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher states takeaway OR asks students to state it OR co-creates with students
* Takeaway may be verbal only or in conjunction with writing on the board, anchor chart, and/or student writing
* Focus may be on content understanding, procedural steps, strategic approach, or transferable skill
* May connect specific example to broader principle or strategy
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When you are determining the central idea, always make sure it covers the entire text and references the specific topic."

* "Now that you have seen my model, what will you do next time you get stuck on a unit conversion?" <Student responds> "Yes - set up the conversion factor by putting the unit you want to get rid of in the denominator. That strategy is key for unit conversions."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember, in this problem we used slope-intercept form." [Why attempting: Specific to single problem, does not include when/why/how for transfer]
* "What did you learn from this?" [Why non-example: Too vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, let's move on to the next problem." [Why non-example: No takeaway]
* "So the answer is 42." [Why non-example: Specific answer without transferable principle]
* "Do you feel better about solving these on your own now?" [Why non-example: No takeaway]

skills.name: Organized Time
skills.description: Clearly define each part of tutorial, give concise instructions, and make tight transitions to maximize learning time.

look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.name: Linked Transition
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Transition to the next part of the lesson by linking it directly to what just happened.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Moves from one major lesson task or segment to the next with a clear transition statement and without unrelated commentary
- Names the specific learning just completed
- States how the prior learning connects to or will be used in the upcoming task
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- May reference the immediately preceding activity or an earlier example/activity from the lesson
- What's referenced may be a strategy, pattern, skill, or specific piece of information
- Applies to transitions between major activities/parts of the session; not required for quick time checks, reminders, or brief redirections within the same activity
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "That opening reminded us how to combine like terms. We'll use that skill now to solve an equation."
- "You just noticed a pattern in those examples. Let's see if that same pattern helps us solve the next problem."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
"Now that we've finished our opening, let's move to equations." [Why attempting: names the prior lesson segment but doesn't connect it to the next task]

"You just completed three do now questions in the opening. Let's see, yep, two multiple choice and one open ended response. So the opening required you to combine like terms and you did that. Good job! Next, you'll use combining like terms like you did in the opening to solve equations because you often have to combine like terms to solve equations." [Why attempting: connects to prior skill but lacks concision]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Time's up. Let's move on." [Why non-example: no link to what was just done or learning]
- "Next, you need to complete questions in part B." [Why non-example: jumps to next task without connecting to prior work]

look_fors.name: Specific Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell students exactly what they should be doing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Tells students what to do (not what not to do)
* Directions include necessary details for task success
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Routine tasks may require less specificity. New or complex tasks, routines or procedures, or routines or procedures that need to be retaught may require more specificty. 
* For multi-step routines or procedures, specificity should apply to each step
* Necessary details for task success might include components like time length, task location in room or on paper/screen, voice/volume level, task goal or criteria for success, task rationale or what to do if finished early. Specific directions only need the components from this list that are needed for student success; they do not need to include ALL components all the time.
* When given as feedback during a task, directions may target only the specific portion of the task the student is struggling with rather than the full task.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Take 5 minutes to independently find key evidence that supports the author's claim in the text. When you find a key piece of evidence, underline it."
* "Before you move on to question 2, add a diagram to your response for question 1."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Find the key evidence in the text and underline it." [Why attempting: Missing time, independent/group mode, specification of key evidence in context]
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't just underline everything." [Why non-example: What not to do, vague]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if a lesson plan has been uploaded for the session. Not required if no lesson plan is provided.
look_fors.name: Lesson Fidelity
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Follow your lesson plan's sequence, content, and structure moment-to-moment with strategic adjustments as needed
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Delivers content, activities, and sequence as specified in the uploaded lesson plan.
* Deviations from the plan, when present, fall into recognizable categories: responding to the needs of a specific student or students, scaffolded supports added that don't reduce the rigor of the lesson, or in-the-moment adjustments responding to student thinking or understanding
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Wording of scripted language may be changed so long as intent, content, and rigor are not altered
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher follows the plan's sequence and content
* Teacher temporarily breaks the plan's rigorous analysis question ("Why did the character's actions lead to this outcome?") into two smaller supporting questions when students struggle, then returns to the original question and has students answer it in full
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Lesson plan calls for a partner discussion on character motivation; teacher asks one student to share instead [Why attempting: preserves content, but not intent of engaging all students]
* Lesson plan's question asks students to analyze how and why a character changed over the course of the story; teacher instead asks "What did the character do at the beginning, middle, and end of the story?"; after students respond, teacher explains how the character changed [Why attempting: somewhat aligned but lowers rigor]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lesson plan calls for a partner discussion on character motivation; teacher skips it entirely with no rationale
* Lesson plan's question asks students to analyze why a character changed over the course of the story; teacher instead asks "Who were the characters?" and never returns to original question [Why non-example: Significantly lower rigor than initial plan]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when routine, procedure, or logistics directions include 3 or more steps where order matters; not required for short directions (1-2 steps) or when order does not affect success. NOT required and should NEVER be applied to content-task directions. NOT required and should NEVER be applied to breaking down the steps of an academic task.
look_fors.name: Sequential Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break complex, multi-step directions down into sequential, logically ordered steps.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Multi-step directions for routines, procedures, or logistics broken into ordered steps that are made explicit by the teacher through numbers or words like "first," "next," and "then"
- This look-for applies to routine, procedural, or logistical directions (e.g., steps for transitions, steps for materials use or clean-up, steps for engaging in complex engagement routines or activities like turn and talk or Socratic seminar, etc.); does not apply to breaking down the steps to solve an academic task or problem
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Breaking down how to solve an academic task or problem into steps (e.g., "first find the common denominator, then multiply, then simplify") is out of scope for this look-for. This is a separate, often valid instructional move  and should not be scored as either evidence or non-evidence of Sequential Directions.
look_fors.strong_examples: “First, fill out your name and group number at the top of your handout. Second, identify your variables and write a hypothesis. Third, write a procedure that will test your hypothesis. Next, once you have all sections from the top of your lab handout through the procedure complete, raise your hand. I will come check your work and clear you to get materials from the counter. Finally, walk to get your materials from the counter and bring them back to your table.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first part of your experiment is to identify your hypothesis and variables. Your procedure should come from the hypothesis and variables. Once you have those components, raise your hand for my clearance, and then you can get materials. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your paper." [Why attempting: Some sequential language, steps still disordered]
look_fors.non_examples: "Materials are on the counter for you. You can get your materials once you have the top part of your lab handout done, but you have to check in with me before you get materials. Write your procedure and identify your hypothesis and variables. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your lab handout." [Why non-example: Steps out of order, no sequential language]

skills.name: Phonological & Phonemic Awareness Instruction
skills.description: Teach phonological and phonemic awareness by targeting a sound unit and producing and isolating sounds precisely

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
Depending on the phonological or phonemic unit of the lesson….
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name(s) ("em") or "muh"
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces digraphs and vowel teams accurately (/ch/, /ee/, etc.)
* Segments syllables accurately
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
"Listen: /mmm/-op. The first sound is /mmm/."
"What is another word that sounds like 'bat'?"
"Which one doesn't belong? Weed, bead, pill, seed?"
"/tae/ /bl/ What's the word?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first sound in 'top' is /tuh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
"The first sound in 'mop' is 'em.'" [Why non-example: says letter not sound]
"There are five sounds in 'cheese': /c/, /h/, /e/, /e/, /z/" [Why non-example: not accurately pronouncing digraph /ch/ nor vowel team /ee/]
"Tiger has two syllables: /tieg/ /r/" [Why non-example: syllables not divided correctly]

look_fors.name: Isolate the Target Sound
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pull the target sound out of the word so students can hear it distinctly.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Separates the target sound from the rest of the word 
- Stretches or repeats the word to make the target audible (e.g., /sss/un)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
* In Spanish, the target unit may also be a sinfón (consonant blend treated as one unit, e.g., /tr/, /bl/); onset-rime framing does not apply in Spanish, since open syllables make rime less salient.
look_fors.strong_examples: "Listen to the first sound: /sss/…un. /s/. Now you say just the first sound." "What is the first sound you hear in: 'cat'?" "I'm going to segment the onset and rime in the word cat, /k/ /at/" "The word napkin has two syllables: /nap/ /kin/" "How many words do you hear? I went to the store."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Isolates the first sound on some words but blends it back in on others within the same task. [Why attempting: inconsistent isolation]
look_fors.non_examples: "Sun starts with /s/." <said quickly; the sound is never separated from the word>

look_fors.name: Target the Right Phonological Unit
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Work at the sound unit the lesson targets: word, syllable, onset-rime, or phoneme.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Activity operates at the intended unit (e.g., clapping syllables for syllable work, isolating phonemes for phoneme work)
Does not substitute a different grain (e.g., syllables when the objective is phonemes)
look_fors.strong_examples:
Syllable lesson: "Let's clap the beats in Jordan's name: Jor (clap) dan (clap). Two syllables."
Phoneme lesson: "Say each sound in 'sun': /s/ /u/ /n/."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Syllable lesson: Teacher claps syllables but calls them "sounds," blurring the syllable and phoneme levels.
look_fors.non_examples: Objective is phoneme blending, but the teacher has students clap syllables instead.

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the task uses a physical anchor for the sound unit (e.g., clapping syllables, tapping phonemes); not required for purely oral tasks such as rhyme
look_fors.name: Sound-to-Movement Mapping
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pair each sound unit with one matching movement
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Assigns one physical motion to each sound unit (e.g., one clap per syllable, one tap per phoneme)
Keeps the movement-to-unit match consistent; no extra or missing motions
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Movement may be clapping, stomping, tapping, touching boxes on the board, moving magnets on the board, or similar
* Tapping and sweeping: one tap per sound followed by a single continuous sweep under the whole word to cue blending; the blend sweep is one glide across all sounds, not one motion per unit
* In Spanish, a sinfón (consonant blend) receives one motion as a single blended unit (e.g., one clap for the /gr/ in "grande"), not one motion per consonant within the blend.
look_fors.strong_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ms. (clap) Ah (clap) med (clap). Three claps for three syllables. Now let's stomp it: Ms. (stomp) Ah (stomp) med (stomp)."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ma (tap)(tap) ya (tap)" [Why attempting: motion-to-unit match inconsistent]
look_fors.non_examples: Claps several times while saying a word without matching one clap to each beat.

skills.name: Phonological & Phonemic Awareness Instruction (Spanish)
skills.description: Teach Spanish language phonological and phonemic awareness by targeting a sound unit, producing and isolating sounds precisely, and following correct Spanish developmental progression.

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production (Spanish)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target Spanish sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name ("eme") or an added vowel ("muh")
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces the five Spanish vowel sounds consistently; pronunciation is always the same, never variable by word
* Segments syllables accurately, respecting Spanish syllable structure (open: ma-pa; closed: pan)
* Pronounces Spanish-specific digraphs (e.g., ll, rr, ch) and the ñ sound accurately
* Produces a sinfón as one blended onset, not two separated sounds (/bl/ in blanco, not /b/-/l/)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target sounds vary by lesson focus: sílabas (ma-pa) for chunking; phoneme /m/ for phoneme work; sinfón /tr/ for blend work; rhyming words (pan/gran) when used.
* Regional pronunciation (seseo vs. distinción, aspirated /s/) is a valid variation, not an error.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Escuchen: /mmm/-esa. El primer sonido es /mmm/."
* "¿Qué otra palabra suena como 'pan'?"
* "'Blanco' empieza con el sinfón /bl/, dos sonidos juntos."
* "'Tigre' tiene dos sílabas: ti-gre."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "El primer sonido en 'pan' es /puh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "El primer sonido en 'mesa' es 'eme.'" [says the letter name, not the sound]
* "'Chico' tiene cinco sonidos: /c/ /h/ /i/ /c/ /o/" [Why non-example: fails to treat /ch/ as one digraph sound]
* "'Tigre' tiene tres sílabas: /ti/ /gr/ /e/" [Why non-example: syllables divided incorrectly; the sinfón gr belongs with the following vowel: ti-gre]
* "Leamos 'idea'. /ai/ /de/ /a/" [Why non-example: incorrect Spanish pronunciation of /i/]

look_fors.name: Isolate the Target Sound
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pull the target sound out of the word so students can hear it distinctly.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Separates the target sound from the rest of the word 
- Stretches or repeats the word to make the target audible (e.g., /sss/un)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
* In Spanish, the target unit may also be a sinfón (consonant blend treated as one unit, e.g., /tr/, /bl/); onset-rime framing does not apply in Spanish, since open syllables make rime less salient.
look_fors.strong_examples: "Listen to the first sound: /sss/…un. /s/. Now you say just the first sound." "What is the first sound you hear in: 'cat'?" "I'm going to segment the onset and rime in the word cat, /k/ /at/" "The word napkin has two syllables: /nap/ /kin/" "How many words do you hear? I went to the store."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Isolates the first sound on some words but blends it back in on others within the same task. [Why attempting: inconsistent isolation]
look_fors.non_examples: "Sun starts with /s/." <said quickly; the sound is never separated from the word>

look_fors.name: Target the Right Phonological Unit (Spanish)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Work at the sound unit the lesson targets (i.e., sílaba, sinfón, or fonema) following the Spanish developmental sequence, not an English onset-rime or phoneme-first sequence.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Activity operates at the intended unit (clapping syllables for syllable work, isolating sinfones for blend work, isolating phonemes for phoneme work)
* When multiple phonological units are included in instruction, syllables precede sinfones and sinfones precede phonemes
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Syllable work may use open (ma-pa) or closed (pan-tas) syllables
* Sinfón work should isolate the blend as one unit (/bl/, /gr/, /tr/), not split into separate consonants.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Syllable lesson: "Vamos a aplaudir las sílabas en 'Mariana': Ma (aplauso) ri (aplauso) a (aplauso) na (aplauso). Cuatro sílabas."
* Sinfón lesson: "Escuchen el sinfón en 'grande': /gr/. ¿Qué otras palabras empiezan con /gr/?"
* Phoneme lesson: "Digan cada sonido en 'sol': /s/ /o/ /l/."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Syllable lesson: teacher claps syllables but calls them "sonidos," blurring the syllable and phoneme levels.
look_fors.non_examples:
* Objective is sinfón isolation, but the teacher has students clap syllables instead.
* Teacher leads an English-style onset-rime task as the phonological awareness activity for a Spanish lesson.
* Teacher treats sinfones as phonemes during instruction

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the task uses a physical anchor for the sound unit (e.g., clapping syllables, tapping phonemes); not required for purely oral tasks such as rhyme
look_fors.name: Sound-to-Movement Mapping
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Pair each sound unit with one matching movement
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Assigns one physical motion to each sound unit (e.g., one clap per syllable, one tap per phoneme)
Keeps the movement-to-unit match consistent; no extra or missing motions
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Movement may be clapping, stomping, tapping, touching boxes on the board, moving magnets on the board, or similar
* Tapping and sweeping: one tap per sound followed by a single continuous sweep under the whole word to cue blending; the blend sweep is one glide across all sounds, not one motion per unit
* In Spanish, a sinfón (consonant blend) receives one motion as a single blended unit (e.g., one clap for the /gr/ in "grande"), not one motion per consonant within the blend.
look_fors.strong_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ms. (clap) Ah (clap) med (clap). Three claps for three syllables. Now let's stomp it: Ms. (stomp) Ah (stomp) med (stomp)."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Syllable lesson: "Ma (tap)(tap) ya (tap)" [Why attempting: motion-to-unit match inconsistent]
look_fors.non_examples: Claps several times while saying a word without matching one clap to each beat.

skills.name: Picture Walk
skills.description: Guide students through a text's cover and key images before reading to build background knowledge and curiosity.

look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.name: Connect to Prior Knowledge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Activate students' existing knowledge of the topic or content.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Prompts students to recall what they already know about the topic or concept
* Links new content to previously learned content or familiar real-world concepts
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Background knowledge may be drawn from prior lessons or common experience
* May ask students questions, have them complete a practice item to demonstrate a previous skill, or otherwise engage students in the relevant prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "This story is about seeds. Remember when we learned how seeds grow into plants? Look, this character is planting a seed right here. What do you already know about what a seed needs?"
* "Today we will learn to calculate density. Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month, so your do now today is a speed problem. Pay attention to how you figure out the units in your answer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This story is about the ocean. Who has seen a picture the ocean or a picture of it?" <A few students raise hands and teacher moves on> [Why attempting: superficial connection to prior knowledge]
* "Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month. You divide one number by another and keep the units." [Why attempting: teacher-led connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "This story is about the ocean." [Why non-example: no connection to prior knowledge]

look_fors.name: Engage All Students
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt every student to respond, not just volunteers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts every student to respond, not only volunteers or hand-raisers
* Every student produces a response (spoken, written, gestured, or signaled)
* Teacher follows up with non-responders rather than accepting partial participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Participation may be simultaneous — choral response, whiteboards, everybody writes / stop and jot, or turn and talk — or sequential (every student takes a turn)
* A student may pass in the moment if the teacher returns to them before the segment ends
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard. Then, when I say show me, hold it up." <Pauses, scans boards> "Dani, Sam, give me your best guess" <Pauses until all students have answer written> "Show me." <Scans all boards> "I've got all but three boards up, let's get to 100%" <Waits until all boards are up>
- "We're going around the circle — everyone gives one word describing the narrator. If you need time, say 'come back to me.'" <Every student contributes; teacher returns to the two who passed>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard." <Teacher scans the front two tables> "Great, moving on." <Several boards in the back are blank> [Why attempting: no follow-up on non-responders]
- "Talk to your partner. Partner closest to the door: share how you categorized the example and why. You have 1 minute." <Students talk; teacher never has second partner share> [Why attempting: Only tells one partner to share]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Who can tell me the theme of this chapter?" <Four hands raise; teacher calls on one student, affirms the answer, and moves on>
- "Look at this book. What do you see?" [Why non-example: No clear expectation that everyone responds, or for how to respond]

look_fors.name: Explain Unfamiliar Terms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explain unfamiliar terms to support content understanding and vocabulary development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Defines new or unfamiliar words
- Provides synonyms or familiar language for unfamiliar terms
- NOT required when term is part of a classroom routine or procedure (e.g., "phonics time") or refers to a skill likely used repeatedly in a grade/subject (e.g., "calculate," "solve," "blend," etc.) unless the teacher indicates this is the first time with the routine or skill
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May provide or connect to word(s) in students' home language(s) to support explanation of target word when teaching multilingual learners
look_fors.strong_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries where earth’s plates move away from each other.”
- “A cake is the baked dessert in this picture. Cake in Spanish is ‘pastel’.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- “There are some new words that you're going to learn in this book. Same, recipe,  and unique. Alright, let’s get started and see what happens.” [Why non-example; Names but does not explain new terms]
look_fors.non_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- I am using expression, so you hear my voice. I have intonation and inflection. [Why non-example: expression is just more than hearing voice; no definition of intonation or inflection]

look_fors.name: Highlight Only What Matters
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Feature high-impact images and text features rather than previewing every page.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews a purposeful subset of pages and images (e.g., those that introduce critical vocabulary, tricky concepts, or unfamiliar settings), not every page and image
* Skips pages not essential to comprehension
look_fors.strong_examples: <Turns to two pages> "I want to show you two pages. First, here's the marketplace. It is a busy place where people buy food. Second, here's Amir looking out the bus window. He looks nervous." <Closes the book>
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Previews the cover and most pages, lingering on several that aren't central to the story>
look_fors.non_examples: "Let me show you every page so you know the story before we read." <Walks through all pages in order, narrating each>

look_fors.name: Leave Some Mystery
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview enough of a story to support comprehension and spark curiosity without revealing the ending.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Withholds the story's resolution or key plot twists
* Frames the preview as a glimpse that builds curiosity
