* Stops previewing before the climax or ending pages
look_fors.strong_examples: "We've seen the bear getting hungrier and hungrier while his friends keep bringing food. I wonder if he'll ever get full… let's read to find out."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Maybe the food bear's friends keep bringing will help him sleep at the end." [Why attempting: previews story ending as a 'maybe', leaves little curiosity]
- Shows picture on cover of book, explains three new vocabulary words that students will encounter in the book, then starts reading. [Why attempting: Previews story to support comprehension without giving away the story, but does not explicitly spark curiosity]
look_fors.non_examples: "And at the very end, the bear finally falls asleep and all his friends tuck him in. Now let's read it."

look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.name: Text Preview
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Guide students through key images and text features before reading.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Displays the cover and names the title, author, and/or illustrator
* Turns through chosen pages, drawing attention to key features and images
* Points to or describes what is visible in the images (e.g., characters, setting, actions)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May include text features like headings, captions, chapters, and diagrams
look_fors.strong_examples: <Holds up the cover> "Our book is Bear Wants More by Karma Wilson." <Turns to a key page> "Look! Here's the bear waking up in spring. And here he is down by the river." <Turns to another> "Now look at all his friends gathered around."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Holds up the cover, points to bear and Author name> "This is Bear Wants More by Karma Wilson" <Opens book and begins reading> [Why attempting: previews cover only]
look_fors.non_examples: "Our book is Bear Wants More." <Opens to page one and begins reading without showing any illustrations>

look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Predictions/Observations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to make their own predictions and/or observations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides time and structure for students to form predictions
* Explicitly invites student predictions/observations as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student predictions by revisiting or testing them against new information
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Predictions/observations may be gathered from a subset of students or the whole group
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Looking at this cover, what do you think might happen in this story? Turn and tell your partner your prediction." <Students predict; teacher notes a few and tells students they will return to them after reading>
* "Before we run the experiment, write down what you predict will happen to the balloon in the hypothesis box." <Students write> "Let's test it and see."
* "Take a moment to look at this photograph. What do you notice about the bear's fur? Turn and tell your partner what you notice. Say, I notice…" <Students share observations, teacher notes a few and tells students they will learn something special about bears' fur when they read>
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What do you think happens next?" <Accepts one or two predictions and moves on> [Why attempting: doesn't create broad prediction-generation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher states what will happen and/or what they see; students only listen
* "What do you think will happen?" with no time or structure for students to respond

look_fors.name: Cultivate Student Questions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structured opportunities for students to generate their own questions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides dedicated time and structure for students to formulate questions
* Explicitly invites student questions as a learning move, not just a check-in
* Honors student-generated questions by using them to drive learning (e.g., discussion or investigation)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student questions may be verbal or written
* Use of student questions may focus in on a small subset or consider all questions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading." <Students write> "Share your question with a partner." <Students discuss> Teacher uses student questions to frame the class discussion.
 * "We've been studying the water cycle. What's a question a scientist might still be trying to answer?" <Students generate questions> "I love this one — let's investigate it together."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What questions do you have?" and accepts and answers 1 to 2 student questions and moves on [Why attempting: doesn't create broad student question-generation]
 "Before we discuss, take 2 minutes to write down one thing you're still wondering after the reading" <Teacher moves on immediately> [Why attepting: Students have opportunity to ask questions, but they are not used for learning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher asks all questions; students only answer
* "Any questions?" with no time or structure for students to formulate them

look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Participation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Vary the modes students use to respond.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses 2+ participation modes (e.g., saying, writing, gesturing, drawing, moving) across the lesson or lesson segment
* Varies the mode across activities or segments rather than defaulting to one
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May offer choice in how students communicate or demonstrate their understanding; this still counts as 2+ modes
* A single mode is fine in a moment, but multiple modes should be used across time
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Write your prediction on your sticky note." <Students write> "Now stand up and put your sticky note on the chart under the heading you picked." <Students move to chart> "Turn and tell your partner why you chose that one."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone write your answer in your notebook. If you finish early, you can draw a quick sketch of it." [Why attempting: second mode only for early finishers]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Every prompt across the lesson or lesson segment asks students to respond in writing with no opportunities for other modes like drawing or speaking
* "Turn and tell your partner what you predict." <Later> "Turn and tell your partner what surprised you."

look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Positive Redirection
skills.description: Recognize behaviors outside tutorial pod expectations and use positive techniques to address them.

look_fors.name: Positive Narration
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Name specific actions of individuals and groups that are meeting the expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific students/groups meeting expectations
* Narration describes specific actions (not general praise like "good job")
* Actions are framed in terms of what to do, not what not to do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* May use shorter but less specific narration ("table 3 has it") when most students already working
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “I can tell tables 2, 3, and 5 are ready to start the experiment because they have all their materials set up to match the diagram on page 2”
* “Jenn, Abhi and Alice have already started underlining key details in the text”
 * “Lequite, Dave, and Eric are referring back to their timeline notes to help them get started”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Good job Lequite, Dave, and Eric” [Why attempting: vague praise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Most of us are not on task, let's get to it." [Why non-example: Negative/vague]
* ""Kiara, you shouldn't be on your phone right now." [Why non-example: Names student, what not to do]
* "I'll wait." [Why non-example: Passive-aggressive, vague]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if the tutor enters a 1:1 interaction with a student to address behavior. Else not required.
look_fors.name: Curious 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: At the start of an interaction with a student not meeting expectations, ask a question to try to understand their barrier or unmet need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks question to understand barrier (e.g., "What's going on?", "Can you tell me about that?")
* Question is asked before giving directions or solutions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “Everything ok?”
* “Looks like you’re stuck. Can you tell me about that?”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone else is getting started, why aren't you?" [Why attempting: negative framing]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Problem 2 is tough. Let me give you the first step I would take" [Why non-example: no question]
* "Are you seriously off task again?" [Why non-example: judgmental not curious question}

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if the tutor enters a 1:1 interaction with a student to address behavior. Else not required.
look_fors.name: Private 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use body language and voice to make the 1:1 interaction feel private in the full class setting.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Physically lowers to student level or leans in close
* Uses quiet/whisper voice
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher kneels down to student level and uses whisper voice to redirect
look_fors.attempting_examples: Teacher leans in close but uses normal speaking voice [Why attempting: Body language but not voice]
look_fors.non_examples: Teacher redirects student from across the room in a loud voice

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if the tutor enters a 1:1 interaction with a student to address behavior. Else not required.
look_fors.name: Quick 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: During full group time, keep 1:1 interactions short. If more extended interaction seems needed, name a time and place when you will circle back to the student.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Leeps comments concise
* Full interaction less than 30-45 seconds
* If issue requires more time, teacher names when they'll circle back
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition or slowed rate of speech for English Language Learners may extend time slightly
look_fors.strong_examples: “Thanks for sharing that. To refocus now, take a quick stretch break if you need it. I’d love to learn more about the argument on the playground later so I can support you and your classmates in working it out. Let’s check in and talk more at the start of independent reading time.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Thanks for sharing that, can you give me a quick summary of what happened between you and your friend on the playground?" [Why attempting: Asks for detail, doesn't name time to circle back]
look_fors.non_examples: “Thanks for sharing that. Let’s revisit our school norms of respect, safety, and inclusion. Tell me exactly what you said and then what your friend said on the playground and connect to our school norms. Were you upholding the norms? Was your friend?” [Why non-example: Invites extended private conversation in full group setting]

look_fors.name: Anonymous Group Reminders
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give a brief, positively framed reminder and/or anonymized statement of encouragement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States expectation positively without naming specific students (e.g., "we are silently doing..."; "waiting on X number" or "I have almost everyone")
 * May include brief rationale
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You are talking quietly to one partner about the prompt on the board for another minute,”
* “Remember to independently add your evidence in the left hand column so you can reference it later”
* “We are only waiting on two. Almost there!”
* “I have got about 80% of the class, can we can get to 100% in the next 5 seconds?.”
* “Staying silent helps everyone concentrate on their independent thinking and writing”
* “Make sure to add units to your measurement, otherwise others won’t know if you mean 4 inches or 4 miles”.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Only three classmates are still off task" [Why attempting: Anonymous but framed negatively]
 * "We're almost there, just waiting on Mayme and Diana" [Positive but not anonymous]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “Tables 3 and 5, you’re not following directions, pay attention”
 * “Forest, we’re waiting for you”
 * “Not showing your work means you lose points”
 * “If you can’t be quiet, I’m going to start giving demerits”

look_fors.name: Leverage the Workspace (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use visual cues in the shared workspace to direct attention or organize information without interrupting the flow of conversation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Highlights or circles part of the problem, text, or task to direct attention
- Color-codes or marks related parts of a problem to show how they connect
- In the virtual environment, adds a typed note to redirect or refocus (e.g., "You should move on to #3.")
- Places a supportive sticker, checkmark, or quick reminder in the workspace or on a student's paper
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Online: highlighting, circling, chat messages, digital emoji/reactions, or digital stickers
- In-person: circling or pointing on a shared paper/whiteboard, a written sticky note, physical stamp/sticker, pointing on student's paper
- Cue may organize or connect information, clarify focus, celebrate success, or help a student re-engage with the task
look_fors.strong_examples:
- Highlights the row in the table where the sign error occurred and asks, "What do you notice here?"
- Types in chat: "Move on to #3."
- Circles the step on the shared paper and taps it twice to draw attention
- Places a sticker next to a completed problem with the note "Nice work — keep going!"
look_fors.attempting_examples: Types "Focus please" in the chat with no highlight or reference point [Why attempting: Vague, no visual anchor]
look_fors.non_examples: "Come on, guys, let's focus — we're on number 3." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.name: Mindful Break
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Guide a brief low-effort breathing, sensory, or movement pause
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Pauses instruction/practice for a short guided mindfulness activity (e.g., breathing, sensory noticing, or mindful movement) 
- Gives simple, low-cognitive-load directions (no problem-solving or content review) 
- Frames around present-moment awareness or noticings
- Keeps the activity brief (roughly 1-3 minutes)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May or may not explicitly name the activity as "meditation" or "mindfulness"
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's take a mindful minute. Close your eyes if you're comfortable. Breathe in for four counts... hold... breathe out for four counts." <repeats 2-3 times>
- "Let's stand up and stretch. A quick reset like this helps clear your head before we keep going. As you reach up, notice how the stretch feels in your arms and shoulders."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Let's pause for a second. Take a deep breath in... and out." <pauses briefly and moves on> [Why attempting: mindfulness element minimal]
look_fors.non_examples: "Alright, quick break. While we pause, think about how you'd solve the next problem differently." [Why non-example: demands cognitive effort, not mental rest]

look_fors.name: Offer Choice to Re-focus
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer a student choice to help them exercise some autonomy while meeting the expectation
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Presents multiple options to a student not meeting an expectation; the options allow the student to make a real (often small) choice, but still hold the expectation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Offering a student a brief break (e.g., a sip of water, a quick stretch) before returning to the expectation still counts as holding it
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "It looks like you are having trouble getting started on your do now. You can choose to answer in writing or draw a picture. See if that helps you get unstuck."
- "I can see you're having a tough time staying in line. Let’s keep moving as a class. Do you want to walk next to me or hold the door?”
- "Remember, right now we are silently listening. If you need to stand up in the back or to the side to help you focus, you can.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "It's time to join us on the carpet. You can sit criss-cross or kneel, but you need to be with the group right now." [Why attempting: choice offered, but focuses more on time pressure than choice]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Do you want to complete your do now or catch up tomorrow?" [Why non-example: lowers expectation]
- "Do you want to complete your do now now, or sit in detention?" [Why non-example: second option is a consequence]

look_fors.name: Positive Redirection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Restate the expectation clearly, maintaining a high expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Restates the expectation, without lowering it, clearly
* Expecation is framed in what to do (not what not to do)
* Does NOT scold or reprimand
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* Individual redirections should generally be private; in rare cases they may be full group if anonymous/full group redirection given first and then individual redirection is a quick, warm, reminder
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You’ve got three minutes left to organize your materials and identify your variables and constants”
 * “Clear your table fully by putting away those last two papers”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Stop doodling and start problem 2" [Why attempting: mixes positive and negative framing]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, since you're behind already, you can just do…." [Why non-example: Lowers expectations]
* "I already told you not to talk," "stop getting distracted by what's going on in the hallway" [Why non-example: Negative, scolding]

look_fors.name: Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use non-verbal physical cues to remind students of expectations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Uses gesture or other physical cue to redirect attention or remind of an expectation (e.g., point, hand signal, proximity)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be paired with a brief related verbal reminder or delivered silently
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Points to the area of a worksheet a student should be working on
* Taps twice on desk near a student who's drifted off-task as a quiet redirect
* Makes shh sign to student talking during independent work time
look_fors.attempting_examples: Gives non-verbal cue with an unclear meaning (e.g., shrug for student off-task)
look_fors.non_examples: Reprimanding a student immediately before trying a non-verbal reminder

skills.name: Positive Relationships (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Foster culturally responsive relationships through caring interactions that honor and affirm students' identities, race, and cultural backgrounds.

look_fors.name: Honor Student Identities
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Connect to and affirm various aspects of students' identities and personal backgrounds (e.g., race, culture, religion, language, gender, etc.)
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References students' racial and/or cultural backgrounds or experiences in instruction
* Uses students' home languages when applicable
* Creates space for students to share their racial and/or cultural identities or stories
* Includes examples (e.g., readings, historical figures, etc.) from diverse racial and/or cultural backgrounds, including those representative of student identities

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Honor Student Identities: 
### Note: the following list of behaviors are related to oher look-fors, but they do NOT count as evidence for Honoring Student Identities
* Differentiating for specific learning needs or offering choice unrelated to identity markers such as race or culture
* Inclusion of multiple forms of communication or participation
* Providing supports or messaging that communicate all students can succeed
* Treating mistakes as learning opportunities
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Can happen through content connections, instructional examples, or explicit opportunities for sharing
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher of multilingual learners (English and Spanish speakers) provides key directions in English and Spanish and references the benefits of knowing or learning multiple languages.
* In a lesson on personal narratives, teacher has students compare and contrast their experiences and traditions around names with the experience shared in a short narrative the class reads.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Who celebrates Lunar New Year?" <one student raises hand> "Great! We celebrate lots of different holidays and that's great." <moves on without further discussion> [Why attempting: Acknowledges diversity but misses opportunity to honor or explore the student's culture]
* I know a lot of you were into K-Pop Demon Hunters this year, so this problem is about Rumi!"[Why attempting: Connects to known student interest, but superficial]
* "In this class, all are welcome" [Why attempting: Messages general inclusion, but vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Discusses family traditions but only references dominant cultural holidays (Thanksgiving, Christmas) without acknowledging students' diverse backgrounds [type: missed opportunity]
* Invalidates or dismisses part of a student's identity (e.g., misgenders a student, calls a student by the wrong name repeatedly or without adjustment, "in this country we speak English," "you're the only one who celebrates Diwali Lily so pick a menorah or a Christmas tree to decorate today," etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Predominantly calls on or praises students only from certain identity groups (e.g., only girls, only white students, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Stereotypes a part of a student’s identity (e.g, “You are so articulate!” or “Where are you really from?” to a student of color) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Predominantly admonishes or gives consequences to students only from certain identity groups (e.g., only boys, only students of color, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.type_explanation: Either this look for OR Model Identity Awareness and Self-Reflection is required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Facilitate Identity and Equity Discussions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Include and productively navigate discussions about identity, power, bias, and systemic issues
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Creates space for discussions about equity, power dynamics, or systemic issues (e.g., "Let's talk about why some voices are heard more than others," "What patterns do you notice about who gets to tell this story?")
* Responds productively when identity-related tensions or questions arise rather than avoiding or dismissing
* Validates student experiences with inequity or bias without minimizing
* Addresses microaggressions or biased comments as learning opportunities
* Asks questions that surface equity or power dynamics in content
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Discussions can be brief moments or extended conversations depending on context
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher shares example of racism in the history of science (Samuel Morton's skull measurements) and facilitates discussion on the scientists represented in the class textbook, who are mostly white and male, asking: "How does representation in our textbook connect to the Samuel Morton example in history?" "Why is lack of representation a problem today?"
* Student makes comment with bias or a mircroagression to another student (e.g., asks "but where are you really from?" to a student of color who shared they are from the city the school is in). Teacher addresses calmly and directly in the moment (e.g., explaining why the statement causes harm by the assumption it communicates, asking a follow up question of the student who made the statement such as 'What do you mean by that question?,' or sharing their own experience 'e.g., in my experience, white people never get asked that question. I know when I've been asked that question in the past it makes me feel like I don't belong.'). Teacher may also invite a follow up individual conversation to help the student who made the comment learn.
* Class reading features character experiencing racism. Teacher facilitates multiple rounds of discussion on the questions: "What systems or patterns allowed this to happen?," "Who had power in this situation? Who didn't?," "How does that connect to what we see today?"
* Student shares full group: "People always assume I'm good at math because I'm Asian." Teacher responds: "Thank you for sharing that. That's an example of a stereotype. Even when stereotypes seem 'positive,' they can be harmful." <Teacher may follow up by asking class or small group additional questions such as "why are stereotypes harmful?" "how can we combat stereotypes?"; the teacher does not expect the student who shared to teach the rest of the class by directing questions only to them>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks why all the scientists in textbook are white men. Teacher says: "That's a good question and it's not fair. Plenty of other cultures contributed to scientific knowledge" but moves on without discussion [Why attempting: Acknowledges but doesn't facilitate productive conversation]
* Student makes comment with bias or a mircroagression (e.g., asks "but where are you really from?" to a student of color who shared they are from the city the school is in). Teacher gives generic reminder ("Why would you ask that? Be respectful") without addressing the bias [Why non-example: Doesn't navigate identity-related harm]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Student raises question about fairness or bias (e.g., "Why are AP classes so white?"). Teacher responds: "Let's not get into that now" or "That's not what we're here to talk about" [Why non-example: Avoids identity/equity discussion] [type: relational harm, severe]
* Student shares experience with discrimination (e.g., "I always get followed in that store because I'm Black." Teacher responds: "I'm sure they don't mean it to feel the way it does for you" or "Everyone has challenges" [Why non-example: Dismisses or minimizes inequity] [type: relational harm, severe]
* Student makes comment with bias or a mircroagression (e.g., asks "but where are you really from?" to a student of color who shared they are from the city the school is in). Teacher ignores it. [Why non-example: Doesn't navigate identity-related harm] [type: relational harm, severe]
* During discussion of historical injustice, teacher presents "both sides have good points" without acknowledging power imbalances [Why non-example: False equivalence obscures systemic issues] [type: learning harm, severe]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Facilitate Student-to-Student Relationships
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structures and opportunities for students to interact positively with each other
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses instructional structures that require student interaction (turn and talks, partner work, group discussions)
* Creates opportunities for students to give each other recognition
* Students demonstrate respect when peers speak or share
* Students show care for each other (affirming comments, applause, support)
* Students demonstrate knowledge of one another as individuals (e.g., interests, events, traditions, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student-to-student interactions can occur through structured academic tasks, classroom routines, or social-emotional activities
* Can involve brief partner interactions or extended collaborative work
* May include sentence or question frames for productive discussion (e.g., "Can you explain...?," "I agree because...," "I disagree because...," etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Students respond positively to peers who share (e.g., hand signals to show encouragement, building on each others' ideas, etc.)
* "Let's take a moment for shout-outs. Who noticed someone doing something kind or helpful today?" <multiple students recognize peers>
* Teacher structures lesson with multiple turn-and-talks and small group work. Students proactively demonstrate respect for each other by not interrupting each other, waiting for speakers to finish, and building on each other's ideas. Students appear comfortable engaging with various classmates.
* Teacher or students refer to class norms either for praise or positively framed reminders
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Students work in pairs or groups but some students dominate the conversation or students do not recognize or encourage each other [Why attempting: Structure exists but lacks intentional development of positive relationships]
* Student-to-student interactions are rarely hostile or dismissive, but when a negative interaction does occur teacher does not respond
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lesson consists entirely of teacher-led instruction with no student-to-student interaction opportunities [type: missed opportunity]
* Student-to-student interactions are sometimes or often hostile or dismissive (e.g., "Ha, you don't know what you're talking about," "Ugh, do I have to work with Mariana?," students interrupt each other, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Any form of bullying goes unaddressed [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.type_explanation: Either this look for OR Facilitate Identity and Equity Discussions is required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Model Identity Awareness and Self-Reflection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share own identity and positionality; model self-reflection about biases and patterns
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Shares own identity or positionality when relevant to content (e.g., race, class, language, gender, ability, etc.)
* Explicitly connects own identity to privilege, access, or systemic patterns
* Names own biases or patterns in real-time when they surface
* Models accountability when recognizing own bias or mistake related to identity/equity
* Reflects aloud on how own identity shapes perspective or experiences
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Level of personal disclosure depends on context
* Can share identity aspects without requiring vulnerability about difficult personal experiences
* Self-reflection can address patterns noticed over time or in-the-moment realizations
look_fors.strong_examples:
*<During discussion on systemic racism and privilege> "My great grandfather was a white World War II veteran and was able to buy a house because of the GI bill. However, Black veterans were often denied access to the same benefits, like affordable home loans, that they were due. This and other similar examples of racism have led to generational wealth gaps and that are evident today."
* "I've noticed that I've been hearing more from girls in full group discussions. I think that reflects an unconscious bias on my part in terms of who I am calling on first. I'm going to be more intentional about that." <models self-reflection and accountability in real-time>
* Teacher mispronounces student's name. Student corrects. Teacher responds: "Thank you for correcting me. I should have asked you to teach me the correct pronunciation from the beginning. That was my mistake." <models accountability without defensiveness>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher shares: "I grew up in a middle-class family" but doesn't connect to how that shaped their access, experiences, or perspectives
* Teacher notices own pattern (e.g., calling on boys more) but only mentions it privately or in reflection, not modeling the self-awareness for students [Why attempting: Self-reflects but doesn't model it publicly]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks students an identity-related question without sharing own example [type: missed opportunity]
* Makes statement indicating lack of awareness of structural bias related to identity (e.g., "I don't see color" or "I may be white but I didn't have any privilege growing up") [type: relational harm, severe]
* Makes statement indicating lack of personal growth or accountability (e.g., "I don't see color," or "I welcome everyone but I'm old school and just can't adjust to call someone they," or responds defensively with something like "don't take it so personally" or "you know that's not what I meant" when called on something biased or offensive) [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.name: Build Personal Rapport
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Show care for students beyond academic content
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References personal information about students (interests, family, experiences)
* Shares appropriate personal information or experiences to connect
* Demonstrates knowledge of students as individuals
* Creates opportunities for personal sharing
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Can occur through one-on-one interactions, or small or whole-group discussions or activities
* Personal connections can be brief check-ins/references or extended sharing opportunities
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <One-on-one> "I know you'll be writing your personal narrative about when your dad passed away. I'm honored you feel comfortable sharing something so meaningful with our class. That takes courage."
* Teacher shares personal coping strategy when discussing managing challenging days: "When I'm frustrated, I take three deep breaths. Let me show you." <models technique> "What strategies help you when you're having a tough day?"
* Students share personal information comfortably. This may include connections between content and personal experiences or challenges, or celebrations of good things outside of the classroom (family member visit, sports event, concert, etc.), for example.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher asks, "How was your weekend?" to whole class at start of Monday. One student shares briefly. Teacher says "Nice" and immediately transitions to lesson. [Why attempting: Creates opening but doesn't meaningfully engage]
* Teacher calls on student with December birthday when asking about next month but doesn't acknowledge the connection [Why attempting: Shows awareness but misses opportunity to build rapport]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher only discusses academic content, never asking about or referencing students' lives, interests, or experiences [Why non-example: Purely transactional, no personal connection] [type: missed opportunity]
* Student mentions birthday and teacher responds, "Okay, let's get back to the lesson" [Why non-example: Dismisses personal information, missed connection opportunity] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Emotional Regulation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Maintain a supportive, asset-based approach consistently throughout interactions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Responds to disruptions or misbehavior with positive, proactive, and anonymized strategies to support students (e.g., proximity, positive narration, anonymous group reminder, etc.) BEFORE consequences or individual redirections
* Consistently messages high expectations and belief in students' ability to meet them
* Assumes the best of students and seeks to understand (e.g., asks an off-task student what they are stuck on or if they need anything rather than assuming student is being deliberately defiant)
* Allows students to complete responses before redirecting or transitioning to the next student

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Emotional Regulation: 
* Calm or neutral tone alone
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Individual teachers will have different tones according to their communication style; variations are expected from teacher to teacher
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's pause for a moment. We can't hear what Christina is sharing now. Let's give our silent attention to her so we can learn from her thinking." <Pauses> "Thank you. Go ahead Christina."
- Positively narrates ("Table 6 is silently starting the do now, Aricely is reviewing her notes from yesterday to help her with problem 1") and gives an anonymous whole-group reminder ("We've got almost everyone working independently on the do now. Let's see if we can get to 100% in the next 15 seconds")
- <Leans down and speaks quietly> "Aaron, you seem distracted. Is everything ok?" <continues instruction without dwelling on behavior when Aaron gets back on task>
- Uses anonymous reminder after one student calls out answer "Remember, raise your hand to share"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember, we raise our hands. I need you to remember that. Don't just call out" [Why attempting: Words may imply frustration, but also positive and anonymous reminder to start]
* Let's get this problem set done today. I don't want a repeat of yesterday's off-task behavior, and I know you can do it." [Why attempting: Mix of negative and positive framing and language]
look_fors.non_examples:
* When student speaks out of turn, immediately says: "I said raise your hand! Why can't you follow simple directions?" [type: relational harm, severe]
* When student speaks out of turn, immediately publicly redirects ("Aidan, stop calling out") or gives consequence ("You are losing a point") [type: relational harm]
* <Teacher sighs heavily and rolls eyes when student asks to use bathroom> "Again? You just went an hour ago." [Why non-example: Exasperation, lack of empathy] [type: relational harm, severe]
* "Let's see if we can get through this problem set today without a repeat of yesterday" [Why non-example: Does not message high expectations and belief in students] [type: relational harm]
* Interrupts or talks over student(s) [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create conditions where students attempt challenging work safely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly invites students to try even if unsure (e.g., "Give it a shot, even if you're not certain, this will help you learn and help me see your thinking")
* Recognizes attempts and effort, not just correct answers
* Provides support structures that allow productive struggle (think time, partner talk, resources)

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
* Student shares incorrect answer [rationale: not clear evidence that student feels safe, they may have thought their answer was correct]
* Teacher asks follow up questions or asks students to build on others' thinking [rationale: not a bad practice, but does not explicitly create safe conditions for risk-taking]
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* When applicable, includes statements like "There's no right answer" or "Multiple approaches work here"
* May celebrate "wrong" answers that show sophisticated reasoning
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I want to hear your thinking even if you're not 100% sure. Your ideas will help us all learn"
* "We're figuring things out together rather than just looking for the 'right' answer"
* "Try it out in your voice and we can all learn from each other's writing" 
* "Turn and talk with a partner to share thinking before we discuss as a class"
* Remember, you have a toolbox for when you feel stuck. Consult the rubric or phone a friend!"  
* "I actually expect some of your first attempts to be unsuccessful. If you finish this without running into a single issue, you probably didn't take a big enough risk. I'm looking for how you pivot when things get messy, not just the final product."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you get it wrong" [Why attempting: no connection to learning value]
* "Be sure everyone participates!" [Why attempting: generic participation encouragement instead of explicitly encouraging academic risk taking]
* Validates partially correct answers [Why attempting: Implies recognition of effort, but not explicit]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher consistently calls on same few students who raise hands with confidence [type: missed opportunity]
* "Don't worry, this one is easy" [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarrass or demotivate a student from taking future risks (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Normalize Mistakes as Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state that errors are part of learning and respond to mistakes or misconceptions as opportunities to learn
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States that mistakes help learning 
* Responds to errors with curiosity rather than clarification alone
* Publicly acknowledges own mistakes as learning opportunities
* Thanks students for sharing mistakes that help class learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May frame revision as normal part of learning process
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections. Let's look at what this mistake can teach us"
* <Teacher makes and catches own error> "Oops! Can anyone find the mistake I just made?" <Student answers> "Thanks! Next time I will..."
*  <Student work shows two divided by zero is two> Teacher: "Oooh, interesting thinking here! Walk me through why you think two divided by zero is two." <Listens to student thinking, and connects to thinking when providing clarification>
* "This is a really interesting misconception. I used to think that the seasons were caused by Earth's distance from the sun, too. This is a logical guess, but it's not what's actually happening, which blew my mind a little when I learned the real answer!"<Teacher demonstrates misconception clarification and comes back to original student to share updated thinking>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you make a mistake" [Why attempting: Reassures but doesn't frame mistakes as valuable]
* <Student gives partially correct answer.> Teacher: "Good start. You're getting there" <does not explain why, calls on another student>. [Why attempting: Somewhat affirming but doesn't use error as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
- <student gives wrong answer> "No, that's not right. Who else?" [Why non-example: Dismisses error without learning value] [type: relational harm]
- Only acknowledges correct answers with praise [type: missed opportunity]
- "You mixed up the numerator and denominator AGAIN" <exasperated tone> [Why non-example: judgmental of error] [type: relational harm]
- Tells one student to explain to another why they are wrong [Why non-example: Negatively framed with emphasis on wrong vs. correct instead of what can be learned] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Oral Tradition Learning Modes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Incorporate learning modes rooted in oral traditions (e.g., storytelling, call and response, visual art, movement, and music) as vehicles for learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses one or more oral tradition learning modes as part of instruction: storytelling, call and response, music/rhythm, movement/kinesthetic response, or visual/artistic expression 
* Positions these modes as ways to learn or demonstrate understanding, not only as transitions, rewards, or breaks
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Mode selection depends on content and context 
* Can be teacher-led (teacher tells story, leads call and response) or student-led (students create, perform, move) 
* Teacher may name the learning value of the mode (e.g., "Stories help us remember and connect to what we're learning," "Music helps our brains remember," "Movement helps ideas stick")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Students act out a historical event, using movement and dialogue to demonstrate understanding of perspectives and sequence 
* "Instead of writing your answer, you're going to teach your partner through a short story that includes the three new vocabulary words we learned" 
* Teacher uses call and response to practice mathematical language: "When I say numerator, you say top number. Numerator!" "Top number!" 
* Students create visual representations of a concept and gallery walk to learn from peers' interpretations
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher reads a story to begin a lesson, then shifts entirely to worksheet [Why attempting: Story used as hook but not key learning mode]
* "You can add a picture if you have time after you finish writing" [Why attempting: Secondary/optional to the main learning activity] 
* "Let's do a dance break before we get back to work" [Why attempting: Dance used as transition; movement break likely to support student learning but dance is not the learning mode itself]
look_fors.non_examples: * Lesson relies exclusively on text-based and verbal-analytical modes (reading, writing, hand-raising discussion) with no integration of story, call and response, art, movement, or music [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Practice
skills.description: Provide structured opportunities for students to apply the target skill

look_fors.name: Aligned Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students practice the exact focus skill and/or concept just modeled or from the lesson's objective
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Practice task requires the same skill or concept that was modeled, introduced, or specified in the lesson's objective
- Task targets that skill directly, not a related or easier substitute
look_fors.acceptable_variations: - Supportive scaffolds (e.g., sentence starters, exemplars) may be used as long as the target skill is unchanged
look_fors.strong_examples:
- Teacher models blending /m/ /a/ /p/ → "map"; students then blend new words (/s/ /u/ /n/ → "sun")
- Objective states students will add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators; practice includes a set of three addition and three subtraction problems with unlike denominators that are different than the problems modeled by the teacher
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- Teacher models blending CVC words; practice only has students identify the first sound
- Objective states students will explain the relationship between cooling time and crystal size in igneous rocks; practice has students identify igneous rocks and explain how they were formed, but does not explicitly require an explanation of the relationship between cooling time and crystal size
look_fors.non_examples:
- Teacher models segmenting phonemes; practice instead has students clap syllables
- Objective states students will be able to calculate density; practice instead has students determine if objects sink or float

look_fors.name: Engage All Students
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt every student to respond, not just volunteers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts every student to respond, not only volunteers or hand-raisers
* Every student produces a response (spoken, written, gestured, or signaled)
* Teacher follows up with non-responders rather than accepting partial participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Participation may be simultaneous — choral response, whiteboards, everybody writes / stop and jot, or turn and talk — or sequential (every student takes a turn)
* A student may pass in the moment if the teacher returns to them before the segment ends
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard. Then, when I say show me, hold it up." <Pauses, scans boards> "Dani, Sam, give me your best guess" <Pauses until all students have answer written> "Show me." <Scans all boards> "I've got all but three boards up, let's get to 100%" <Waits until all boards are up>
- "We're going around the circle — everyone gives one word describing the narrator. If you need time, say 'come back to me.'" <Every student contributes; teacher returns to the two who passed>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard." <Teacher scans the front two tables> "Great, moving on." <Several boards in the back are blank> [Why attempting: no follow-up on non-responders]
- "Talk to your partner. Partner closest to the door: share how you categorized the example and why. You have 1 minute." <Students talk; teacher never has second partner share> [Why attempting: Only tells one partner to share]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Who can tell me the theme of this chapter?" <Four hands raise; teacher calls on one student, affirms the answer, and moves on>
- "Look at this book. What do you see?" [Why non-example: No clear expectation that everyone responds, or for how to respond]

look_fors.name: Guided Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students time to apply learning with guidance.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Provides task that applies specific content and/or skills to a new but related context or problem
- Offers scaffolding (e.g., checklist, guiding questions, reference material, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Level of guidance varies based on student need: heavy scaffolding to light check-ins
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph." <Displays new paragraph> "Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here and how do you know?" <Student responds> "Good - you skimmed the previous paragraph for clues. Show me - where exactly did you find that clue?" <Student points> "Excellent. What will you do now to check if that makes sense?" <Continues using questions to scaffold>

- "As you revise your lab conclusions, you can always look back to our exemplar from yesterday's lab for a strong example of how to use evidence." <Circulates> "What evidence could you include here?" "Why did you choose that data to support your conclusion?" <Checks in with multiple students>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Don't forget the steps I just took to determine the central idea" [Why attempting: minimal/vague guidance]
 * "Try another problem like this one. Raise your hand if you need help." [Why attempting: Reactive rather than proactive guidance]
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Finishes think aloud> "Okay, moving on to our next topic..." [Why non-example: No practice]
* "Now complete this worksheet silently." <Sits at desk, doesn't monitor> [Why non-example: No guidance or scaffolding]

look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Participation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Vary the modes students use to respond.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses 2+ participation modes (e.g., saying, writing, gesturing, drawing, moving) across the lesson or lesson segment
* Varies the mode across activities or segments rather than defaulting to one
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May offer choice in how students communicate or demonstrate their understanding; this still counts as 2+ modes
* A single mode is fine in a moment, but multiple modes should be used across time
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Write your prediction on your sticky note." <Students write> "Now stand up and put your sticky note on the chart under the heading you picked." <Students move to chart> "Turn and tell your partner why you chose that one."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone write your answer in your notebook. If you finish early, you can draw a quick sketch of it." [Why attempting: second mode only for early finishers]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Every prompt across the lesson or lesson segment asks students to respond in writing with no opportunities for other modes like drawing or speaking
* "Turn and tell your partner what you predict." <Later> "Turn and tell your partner what surprised you."

look_fors.name: Classify Examples and Non-Examples
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students decide whether items are examples or non-examples of the concept or skill.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher presents items and asks students to judge each as an example or non-example
* Students sort or label the items and explain what makes each one fit or not
look_fors.strong_examples: "I'll show ten shapes. Thumbs up if it's a polygon, thumbs down if not, and be ready to explain how you know." <Students respond and justify each>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Asks one student to classify a single item, then moves on. [Why attempting: only one student classifies]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher lists which shapes are polygons and which are not while students watch.
* Teacher asks students to explain why a set of shapes are examples of polygons.

skills.name: Practice (ECE)
skills.description: Provide structured opportunities for students to apply the target skill, moving from supported group attempts toward individual practice.

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the skill involves a physical or movement-based response that maps onto the concept being practiced; not required for purely verbal or written practice tasks
look_fors.name: Total Physical Response (TPR)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: A visual method of checking for or supporting understanding where, on the teacher's cue, each student responds to a question or prompt at the same time using their whole body or physical movements in a way that conveys meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt and directs students to respond with physical movement
* Physical movement clearly corresponds to concept being taught or assessed
* Prompts students to do the movement at the same time
* Students do movement simultaneously
* Scans student movements
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* If using to check for understanding, must have more than one possible response and be in response to a question (e.g., "Imagine the UV light is here in the room and you are a plant. When I say go, use your body to show the direction you will grow")
* If using to convey meaning, may have single motion without a question (e.g., "frigid means really cold. cross your arms and shake your body to show brrrrrrrrr...frigid!")
* If using to convey meaning, exact simultaneous response less important
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Let's clap the beats in Christopher's name. Ready? Chris (clap) to (clap) pher (clap). Three claps for three syllables. Now let's stomp it: Chris (stomp) to (stomp) pher (stomp). Each stomp matches one beat."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Clap once if you think you know the answer." [Why attempting: Physical response but no conceptual connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Tell me how many syllables are in 'butterfly.'" [Why non-example: Verbal response only]

skills.name: Praise Effort Not Achievement
skills.description: Specifically praise students' effort, persistence, and willingness to take risks rather than their achievement or innate ability.

look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Promote Growth Mindset
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame ability as developable through effort
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses words like "yet," "so far," "not yet," when students struggle
* Emphasizes progress and improvement over fixed ability
* References brain growth or learning as a process
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May teach explicitly about neuroplasticity and brain development
* Can highlight individual student growth over time
* May use metaphors about building skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can't do this yet, but with practice your brain will build new connections"
* "You've shown such growth since the beginning of the year. Look how far you've come"
* "This is challenging work, and you're learning to handle it. Every time you struggle through hard problems, your brain gets stronger"
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "You can do it if you try hard" [Why attempting: Emphasizes effort but doesn't explicitly frame ability as developable]
* Uses "yet" occasionally but inconsistently
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Some people are just good at math"
* "You either get it or you don't"
* Implies ability is fixed ("You're a natural")

skills.name: Private Redirection
skills.description: When a student continues to struggle to meet expectations after proactive support, address behavior privately with curiosity, clarity, and confidence in the student's ability to succeed.

look_fors.name: Affirmation/Assurance
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Express confidence in student's ability to be successful
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in students' abilities (e.g., "I know you can do this," "You're capable of this work")
* May reference growth over time (e.g., "You already figured out..., now you just have to...")
* May be used after redirection, when giving feedback, or during instruction
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address whole class or individual students
* If used after a redirection, walks away rather than lingering to check compliance
* Redirect affirmations may be more concise (e.g., "You got this")
* Often paired with communicating high expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* After redirection: "You've got this - I'm excited to see your thinking when I come around again later" <walks away>
* During instruction: "I know you can master this concept"
* When giving feedback: "I'm giving you this feedback because I know you're capable of meeting high standards."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Okay great, get to work" [Why attempting: Positive and directive but not affirming]
* "Good job" [Why attempting: Generic praise]
* "You can do this if you focus" [Why attempting: Conditional]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Let's see if you can actually do it this time" [Why non-example: Doubts capability]
- "Just give it your best and see what you can do" [Why non-example: No affirmation/assurance of student's ability]
- States what student did wrong (e.g., “that’s not solving the equation”) without any follow up

look_fors.name: Curious 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: At the start of an interaction with a student not meeting expectations, ask a question to try to understand their barrier or unmet need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks question to understand barrier (e.g., "What's going on?", "Can you tell me about that?")
* Question is asked before giving directions or solutions
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “Everything ok?”
* “Looks like you’re stuck. Can you tell me about that?”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Everyone else is getting started, why aren't you?" [Why attempting: negative framing]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Problem 2 is tough. Let me give you the first step I would take" [Why non-example: no question]
* "Are you seriously off task again?" [Why non-example: judgmental not curious question}

look_fors.name: Positive Redirection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Restate the expectation clearly, maintaining a high expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Restates the expectation, without lowering it, clearly
* Expecation is framed in what to do (not what not to do)
* Does NOT scold or reprimand
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* Individual redirections should generally be private; in rare cases they may be full group if anonymous/full group redirection given first and then individual redirection is a quick, warm, reminder
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You’ve got three minutes left to organize your materials and identify your variables and constants”
 * “Clear your table fully by putting away those last two papers”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Stop doodling and start problem 2" [Why attempting: mixes positive and negative framing]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, since you're behind already, you can just do…." [Why non-example: Lowers expectations]
* "I already told you not to talk," "stop getting distracted by what's going on in the hallway" [Why non-example: Negative, scolding]

look_fors.name: Private 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use body language and voice to make the 1:1 interaction feel private in the full class setting.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Physically lowers to student level or leans in close
* Uses quiet/whisper voice
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher kneels down to student level and uses whisper voice to redirect
look_fors.attempting_examples: Teacher leans in close but uses normal speaking voice [Why attempting: Body language but not voice]
look_fors.non_examples: Teacher redirects student from across the room in a loud voice

look_fors.name: Quick 1:1 Interaction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: During full group time, keep 1:1 interactions short. If more extended interaction seems needed, name a time and place when you will circle back to the student.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Leeps comments concise
* Full interaction less than 30-45 seconds
* If issue requires more time, teacher names when they'll circle back
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition or slowed rate of speech for English Language Learners may extend time slightly
look_fors.strong_examples: “Thanks for sharing that. To refocus now, take a quick stretch break if you need it. I’d love to learn more about the argument on the playground later so I can support you and your classmates in working it out. Let’s check in and talk more at the start of independent reading time.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Thanks for sharing that, can you give me a quick summary of what happened between you and your friend on the playground?" [Why attempting: Asks for detail, doesn't name time to circle back]
look_fors.non_examples: “Thanks for sharing that. Let’s revisit our school norms of respect, safety, and inclusion. Tell me exactly what you said and then what your friend said on the playground and connect to our school norms. Were you upholding the norms? Was your friend?” [Why non-example: Invites extended private conversation in full group setting]

skills.name: Productive Struggle (Saga)
skills.description: Create the conditions for students to persist through challenges in a way that supports rigorous learning.

look_fors.name: Affirmation/Assurance
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Express confidence in student's ability to be successful
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in students' abilities (e.g., "I know you can do this," "You're capable of this work")
* May reference growth over time (e.g., "You already figured out..., now you just have to...")
* May be used after redirection, when giving feedback, or during instruction
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address whole class or individual students
* If used after a redirection, walks away rather than lingering to check compliance
* Redirect affirmations may be more concise (e.g., "You got this")
* Often paired with communicating high expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* After redirection: "You've got this - I'm excited to see your thinking when I come around again later" <walks away>
* During instruction: "I know you can master this concept"
* When giving feedback: "I'm giving you this feedback because I know you're capable of meeting high standards."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Okay great, get to work" [Why attempting: Positive and directive but not affirming]
* "Good job" [Why attempting: Generic praise]
* "You can do this if you focus" [Why attempting: Conditional]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Let's see if you can actually do it this time" [Why non-example: Doubts capability]
- "Just give it your best and see what you can do" [Why non-example: No affirmation/assurance of student's ability]
- States what student did wrong (e.g., “that’s not solving the equation”) without any follow up

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame tasks as challenging yet worthy while maintaining rigorous standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Acknowledges difficulty/high expectations but doesn't frame as worthy (e.g., "This is hard" or "Oooh, a spicy problem!")
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
* Assigning easier work to struggling students without scaffolding the grade-level content [Why non-example: Reduces rigor]

look_fors.name: Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create conditions where students attempt challenging work safely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly invites students to try even if unsure (e.g., "Give it a shot, even if you're not certain, this will help you learn and help me see your thinking")
* Recognizes attempts and effort, not just correct answers
* Provides support structures that allow productive struggle (think time, partner talk, resources)

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
* Student shares incorrect answer [rationale: not clear evidence that student feels safe, they may have thought their answer was correct]
* Teacher asks follow up questions or asks students to build on others' thinking [rationale: not a bad practice, but does not explicitly create safe conditions for risk-taking]
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* When applicable, includes statements like "There's no right answer" or "Multiple approaches work here"
* May celebrate "wrong" answers that show sophisticated reasoning
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I want to hear your thinking even if you're not 100% sure. Your ideas will help us all learn"
* "We're figuring things out together rather than just looking for the 'right' answer"
* "Try it out in your voice and we can all learn from each other's writing" 
* "Turn and talk with a partner to share thinking before we discuss as a class"
* Remember, you have a toolbox for when you feel stuck. Consult the rubric or phone a friend!"  
* "I actually expect some of your first attempts to be unsuccessful. If you finish this without running into a single issue, you probably didn't take a big enough risk. I'm looking for how you pivot when things get messy, not just the final product."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you get it wrong" [Why attempting: no connection to learning value]
* "Be sure everyone participates!" [Why attempting: generic participation encouragement instead of explicitly encouraging academic risk taking]
* Validates partially correct answers [Why attempting: Implies recognition of effort, but not explicit]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher consistently calls on same few students who raise hands with confidence [type: missed opportunity]
* "Don't worry, this one is easy" [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarrass or demotivate a student from taking future risks (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Normalize Mistakes as Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state that errors are part of learning and respond to mistakes or misconceptions as opportunities to learn
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States that mistakes help learning 
* Responds to errors with curiosity rather than clarification alone
* Publicly acknowledges own mistakes as learning opportunities
* Thanks students for sharing mistakes that help class learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May frame revision as normal part of learning process
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections. Let's look at what this mistake can teach us"
* <Teacher makes and catches own error> "Oops! Can anyone find the mistake I just made?" <Student answers> "Thanks! Next time I will..."
*  <Student work shows two divided by zero is two> Teacher: "Oooh, interesting thinking here! Walk me through why you think two divided by zero is two." <Listens to student thinking, and connects to thinking when providing clarification>
* "This is a really interesting misconception. I used to think that the seasons were caused by Earth's distance from the sun, too. This is a logical guess, but it's not what's actually happening, which blew my mind a little when I learned the real answer!"<Teacher demonstrates misconception clarification and comes back to original student to share updated thinking>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you make a mistake" [Why attempting: Reassures but doesn't frame mistakes as valuable]
* <Student gives partially correct answer.> Teacher: "Good start. You're getting there" <does not explain why, calls on another student>. [Why attempting: Somewhat affirming but doesn't use error as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
- <student gives wrong answer> "No, that's not right. Who else?" [Why non-example: Dismisses error without learning value] [type: relational harm]
- Only acknowledges correct answers with praise [type: missed opportunity]
- "You mixed up the numerator and denominator AGAIN" <exasperated tone> [Why non-example: judgmental of error] [type: relational harm]
- Tells one student to explain to another why they are wrong [Why non-example: Negatively framed with emphasis on wrong vs. correct instead of what can be learned] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Promote Growth Mindset
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame ability as developable through effort
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses words like "yet," "so far," "not yet," when students struggle
* Emphasizes progress and improvement over fixed ability
* References brain growth or learning as a process
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May teach explicitly about neuroplasticity and brain development
* Can highlight individual student growth over time
* May use metaphors about building skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can't do this yet, but with practice your brain will build new connections"
* "You've shown such growth since the beginning of the year. Look how far you've come"
* "This is challenging work, and you're learning to handle it. Every time you struggle through hard problems, your brain gets stronger"
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "You can do it if you try hard" [Why attempting: Emphasizes effort but doesn't explicitly frame ability as developable]
* Uses "yet" occasionally but inconsistently
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Some people are just good at math"
* "You either get it or you don't"
* Implies ability is fixed ("You're a natural")

skills.name: Purpose and Motivation (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Help students connect to the purpose and value of their learning by framing goals, communicating high expectations, and making content relevant.

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations

look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"

look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
