look_fors.type_explanation: Required if teacher can demonstrate in the flow of the lesson or practice (e.g., student brings up identity, content can connect to diverse examples); else not required
look_fors.name: Honor Student Identities
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Connect to and affirm various aspects of students' identities and personal backgrounds (e.g., race, culture, religion, language, gender, etc.)
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References students' racial and/or cultural backgrounds or experiences in instruction
* Uses students' home languages when applicable
* Creates space for students to share their racial and/or cultural identities or stories
* Includes examples (e.g., readings, historical figures, etc.) from diverse racial and/or cultural backgrounds, including those representative of student identities

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Honor Student Identities: 
### Note: the following list of behaviors are related to oher look-fors, but they do NOT count as evidence for Honoring Student Identities
* Differentiating for specific learning needs or offering choice unrelated to identity markers such as race or culture
* Inclusion of multiple forms of communication or participation
* Providing supports or messaging that communicate all students can succeed
* Treating mistakes as learning opportunities
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Can happen through content connections, instructional examples, or explicit opportunities for sharing
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher of multilingual learners (English and Spanish speakers) provides key directions in English and Spanish and references the benefits of knowing or learning multiple languages.
* In a lesson on personal narratives, teacher has students compare and contrast their experiences and traditions around names with the experience shared in a short narrative the class reads.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Who celebrates Lunar New Year?" <one student raises hand> "Great! We celebrate lots of different holidays and that's great." <moves on without further discussion> [Why attempting: Acknowledges diversity but misses opportunity to honor or explore the student's culture]
* I know a lot of you were into K-Pop Demon Hunters this year, so this problem is about Rumi!"[Why attempting: Connects to known student interest, but superficial]
* "In this class, all are welcome" [Why attempting: Messages general inclusion, but vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Discusses family traditions but only references dominant cultural holidays (Thanksgiving, Christmas) without acknowledging students' diverse backgrounds [type: missed opportunity]
* Invalidates or dismisses part of a student's identity (e.g., misgenders a student, calls a student by the wrong name repeatedly or without adjustment, "in this country we speak English," "you're the only one who celebrates Diwali Lily so pick a menorah or a Christmas tree to decorate today," etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Predominantly calls on or praises students only from certain identity groups (e.g., only girls, only white students, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Stereotypes a part of a student’s identity (e.g, “You are so articulate!” or “Where are you really from?” to a student of color) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Predominantly admonishes or gives consequences to students only from certain identity groups (e.g., only boys, only students of color, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required during opening
Else, optional
look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Learning Goal(s)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to learning goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or points to learning goal
* Uses language like "Today you'll learn..." or "By the end of this activity, you'll be able to..."
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use to frame full lesson or activity in a lesson
* May reference during in struction to highlight connection (e.g., this helps us achieve today's goal of simplifying fractions by...")
* Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
* Learning goal may be for unit, lesson, or activity
* May refer to learning goal using different terminology such as objective, outcome, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you will learn how to identify the main idea and supporting details in nonfiction text. This will help you understand what authors want you to remember most"
* "By the end of this activity, you will be able to identify and explain each stage of the water cycle"
* "Our goal today is to master adding fractions with unlike denominators"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "We're going to learn about fractions" [Why attempting: Vague; does not specify specific goal related to fractions]
* "The objective is on the board" <points but doesn't read or discuss> [Why attempting: Doesn't actively frame or reference]
* “Show your mastery of today’s objective on this exit ticket!” [Why attempting: References objective, but not in a way that reinforces the specific goal]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: Focuses on what students will do not learn]

look_fors.name: Connect Learning to Student Interests and Lives
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Make content relevant to students' experiences and interests
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses examples from students' lives or communities
* Asks students to make personal connections to content
* Incorporates student interests into lesson examples or activities
* Shows real-world applications relevant to students
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May reference current events meaningful to students
* Can invite students to share their own examples
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Many of you mentioned you love The Grizzlies in our beginning of year survey. Let's use player statistics to practice calculating percentages"
* "How does this connect to what you see in your own neighborhood or family?"
* "What's something you do when you are feeling mad?" 
* "Next, we will apply what we learned to classify plants in our school's community garden"
* "We know that the ocean moderates the climate of cities on the coast. Let's now look at some data to see if Lake Michigan is big enough to moderate climate here."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This might be interesting to you" [Why attempting: Suggests relevance but doesn't explicitly connect]
 * Uses one example at start of unit but doesn't sustain connections
look_fors.non_examples:
* Uses only generic or teacher-selected examples
* Dismisses student attempts to make personal connections
* Never asks how content relates to students' lives

look_fors.name: Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview what will happen and state clear focus for student thinking and engagement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews what teacher and/or students will do
* States clear purpose, target question, or learning focus
* Gives students specific task or role during activity (listen for, analyze, record, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May check for understanding of the framing before beginning the activity
* Student task may be note-taking, analyzing, comparing, evaluating, or other cognitive engagement
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I have noticed that our understanding of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' sometimes breaks down because of all the pronouns that Zora Neale Hurston uses. When texts have tons of pronouns, there are steps readers can follow to avoid confusion. I will show you how I make sense of the pronouns so I can follow along with the story. As I am thinking aloud for you, I want you to record notes on the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean. Before I start sharing my thinking, remind me - what are you doing as I am thinking aloud for you?"

* "I want to highlight DeAndre's response. As I read it, think about what makes his argument strong." <Reads>

* "I'm going to show you each characteristic of parallel lines with examples. As I do, record the characteristic and an example in your notes. You will use your notes later to practice identifying examples and non-examples of parallel lines based on these characteristics."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "I am going to show you both methods for the sake of putting it out there, whichever you prefer. So let's start by using slope-intercept form. Which form are we starting with?" [Why attempting: Purpose unclear, no student task/goal]
- "This think aloud will be about dividing fractions." [Why attempting: States topic but not purpose or goal]
- "Take a look up here quickly and just pause what you're doing. I want to highlight a student response." [Why attempting: missing why they are highlighting specific student response]
- “Today we are going to continue our focus on fluency. I want you all to sit where you are and listen, then I want to hear you all read. [Why attempting: Fluency is too broad, purpose should be more specific]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, listen to me think aloud." [Why non-example: No framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "I'm going to show you how to do this. Pay attention." [Why non-example: 'Pay attention' too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as compliance (e.g., "Complete this task to earn your participation points for the day", "You must read") [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as for grades or test performance only (e.g., "This is on the state exam", "This exit ticket is like a quiz for your grade") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Rationale
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share how the routine, procedure, or task supports learning and/or the classroom community.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Explains purpose of routine, procedure, or task relative to learning and/or classroom community
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May include connection to classroom norms or goals, real world application or importance, or students' interests or identities
look_fors.strong_examples: “We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today because we will be constantly talking to our peers to share our great ideas, and I want us all to have the opportunity to share without slowing down the class.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today. This is an important procedure for our classroom culture and learning." [Why attempting: Generic importance]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today.”
* "This is an important procedure so I do not have to give so many consequences" [Why non-example: Negative, emphasizes compliance]
* "This routine is important for the state exam" [Why non-example: Not rooted in learning or community]

look_fors.name: Student Goal-Setting
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in establishing and tracking goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Facilitates process for students to set personal or collective goals
* Provides structure for students to monitor or reflect on progress toward goals
* Conferences with students about their goals
* Celebrates progress toward student-identified goals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Goals may be academic, behavioral, or both
* Can be short-term (daily/weekly) or long-term (unit/semester)
* May use goal-setting templates, trackers, or reflection protocols
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you'll each set a goal for what you want to improve. We'll check in on Fridays to see your progress"
* "Look at your data from the last assessment. Based on that, what's one skill you want to strengthen?"
* Students maintain goal-tracking sheets and regularly reflect on progress
* "Now that we've identified group strengths relative to our class norms, take 2 minutes to write a personal goal relative to our class norms. Refer to the examples on the board if you need some inspiration!"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What do you want to work on today?" [Why attempting: Vague]
* "Here are our class goals. Raise your hand if you would like propose any changes or additions" [Why attempting: Teacher-led with student input]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All goals set by teacher without student input
* Goals never referenced

skills.name: Ratio (Saga)
skills.description: When supporting students, move from less to more teacher-directed scaffolds in succession to keep as much thinking on the student(s) as possible.

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B (Intervention 2 — Quick Cue/Hint): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group B before advancing to Intervention 3
look_fors.name: Cue Missing or First Step
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Highlight a skipped step or emphasize which step comes first.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly states which step was missed or which step should be first
* Uses language like "first step," "remember to," or "before you [next step]"
* Provides time for students to take first step or add the missing step
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used to help students get started on procedure, process, or sequence OR in response to a procedural error
* Teacher may or may not provide additional explanation depending on student needs
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Don’t forget the first step. Check the anchor chart if you need to.” 
* "Remember that the first step is to check if the source is a primary source or secondary source."
* "Don't forget step 3, which is to convert to moles if needed. I see a few of us skipped this step in the ammonia example, so go back and check your own work and revise if needed."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * “Don’t forget to do all the steps. Double check your work.”
look_fors.non_examples: "You're missing something." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B (Intervention 2 — Quick Cue/Hint): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group B before advancing to Intervention 3
look_fors.name: Cue with Anchor Chart or Notes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Direct students to reference visual aids or notes.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs student attention to specific anchor chart, poster, or notes
* Provides time for students to review and apply information
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may or may not provide additional explanation depending on student needs
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Reference our anchor chart if you need to remind yourself of each part in FOIL on problem 6."
* "Look at our chart to remember how to line up your ruler with the object."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Take two minutes to first look back at your notes at our definition of fitness and then silently adjust your answer. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Check the board as you work."
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't forget to use your resources if you need help." [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B (Intervention 2 — Quick Cue/Hint): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group B before advancing to Intervention 3
look_fors.name: Cue with Definition, Rule or Procedure
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Remind students of a definition, rule or procedure to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or references a previously taught definition, rule or procedure
* Directs students to apply the definition, rule, or procedure
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may explain/provide the definition, rule or procedure or ask students to recall or find it
* General rather than specific cues (e.g., “Remember that we always read in one direction”) can put more cognitive lift on students, but teacher should get more specific if students do not self-correct after first cue
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Always measure the volume in a graduated cylinder by getting eye level and reading from the bottom of the meniscus. Everyone check your most recent volume measurement." <Students self-correct; Teacher moves on>
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle> “Ok, let’s get a little more specific. Remember that we always read from left to right. Watch my finger as I read on this page" <Teacher reads, moving finger from left to right>. "Now, turn the page and put your finger where you will start reading." <Teacher scans and circulates> "Next, move your finger in the direction you will read." <Teacher scans and circulates>
* "Remember, like terms have the same variable and exponent. Go back and make sure you have only combined like terms" <Students self-correct; teacher moves on>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle; Teacher repeats same cue>
* "Remember like terms share letters or variables, and also share exponents. That is, the exponents have to be the same" [Why attempting: Definition imprecise, no direction as to what to apply]
look_fors.non_examples: "Remember to measure carefully." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B (Intervention 2 — Quick Cue/Hint): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group B before advancing to Intervention 3
look_fors.name: Cue with Example
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Reference specific examples to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References specific example(s) of knowledge and/or skill of focus in the moment
* Prompts students to apply the example
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may explain the example(s) or ask students to do so
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's revise our definitions of a prime number. Remember, one example is 7. Another is 11."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Let's think back to our examples of the sea turtle and the gray whale. The sea turtle had a lot more offspring, but what did the gray whale have that the sea turtle did not? Take 1 minute and turn and talk with your partner at a level two voice. Go." <Student turn and talk, teacher circulates>. "Alright, based on the conversation you had with your partner, take one minute to adjust your answer."
* "2 is more than 1. 1 is less than 2. Is 3 more than 4 or less than 4?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "It seems we are torn on this one. Think back to our sea turtle and gray whale example and then revise your answer" [Why attempting: References example but doesn't explicitly connect to misconception or guide students to do so]
look_fors.non_examples: "Think about what we learned before." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A (Intervention 1 — Questioning): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group A before advancing to Intervention 2
look_fors.name: Follow up Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use questions to push student thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Asks students to elaborate, explain reasoning, or provide evidence
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May direct follow-ups to original speaker OR redirect to other students
* May invite students to agree, disagree, or add on to peer responses ("Do you agree with ___? Why?")
* May ask for clarification or specificity ("What do you mean by...", "Can you show me where...")
* May probe connections between ideas ("How does this relate to...", "Why does this matter?")
* May scaffold incorrect responses toward correct understanding with targeted questions
* May focus on process ("How did you figure that out?") OR product ("Why is this answer stronger?")
* May be paired with a variety of question response formats (e.g., turn and talk, cold call, everybody writes, etc.)
* Often involves a sequence of questions to push for deeper thinking, but may not need multiple questions if initial student response is strong and detailed
* May be posed as a standalone/initiating question, not only in reaction to a prior student response
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Which student's response did you choose and why?" <Student: "Student B because it has more details"> "Say more about that - what kind of details make Student B's response stronger?" <Student explains> "Good. Maya, do you agree with that? Why or why not?" <Maya responds> "So you're both noticing that Student B shows what Amos actually did. How does that connect to our goal of using strong evidence?"

* "Why did I substitute in the values of x and y from the point given in the problem?" <Student: "Because it was in the problem"> "You're right that I used information from the problem. But why did I need to substitute those specific values? What was I trying to find?" <Student: "The b"> "Yes! I was solving for b, the y-intercept. I knew I could substitute 5 for x and 1 for y because the problem told me the point (5, 1) was on the line. So let's try again - why did I substitute those values into the equation?"

* "Water has a positive and negative side, but methane doesn't. How might that structural difference impact how each interacts with oil?" <Posed as an opening question, not in reaction to a prior student response>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Walk us through your answer [Why attempting: Too vague]
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus" [Why attempting: builds on one students' response, but doesn't require explanation of thinking]
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here?" <Points> [Why attempting: Provides related practice but doesn't ask students to explain their thinking process]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts first response and moves on without probing
* Asks vague check for understanding question rather than probing specific thinking (e.g., "does that make sense?", "do you have any questions?", etc.)
* Asks simple yes/no or recall question (e.g., "Did I figure out the pronoun correctly?", "What does precipitation mean?", "What value did I get for b?", etc.)

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP C (Intervention 3 — Teacher Support): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group C if Interventions 1–2 have not resolved the student's confusion
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP B (Intervention 2 — Quick Cue/Hint): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group B before advancing to Intervention 3
look_fors.name: Playback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes a mistake, simply restate what the student said in a neutral tone, allowing them to hear their response and self-correct.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher repeats answer in neutral tone
* Teacher pauses (2-5 seconds)
* Student often self-corrects
look_fors.acceptable_variations: If playback doesn't work, use different strategy
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "3 + 4 is 8." Teacher: "You're saying 3 + 4 is 8." <pause> Student: "Oh wait, no, it's 7." Teacher: "Yes, 7."
* Student: "The answer is 52." Teacher: "52." <pause, looks at student> Student: <recalculates> "Actually, I think it's 62." Teacher: "Let me see your work. Yes, 62 is correct - nice job catching that."
* Student: "The setting is in a school." Teacher: "You said the setting is in a school." <pause> Student: "Well, it's in a classroom specifically." Teacher: "A classroom - that's more precise. Good."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student: "The capital of California is Los Angeles." Teacher: "Los Angeles? Common mistake, it's Sacramento." [Why non-example: No opportunity for student to self-correct first]
* Student: "7 times 8 is 54." Teacher: "You're saying 7 times 8 is 54..." <says it with a doubtful tone> [Why attempting: Playback but tone not neutral]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Are you sure about that?" [Why non-example: No playback] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Let me tell you the right answer..." [Why non-example: No opportunity for student to self-correct] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A (Intervention 1 — Questioning): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group A before advancing to Intervention 2
look_fors.name: Probing Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student makes an error or reveals a misconception, ask follow-up questions to understand the student's thinking and the root cause of the misunderstanding.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student gives incorrect answer
* Teacher asks follow-up question about student's thinking
* Teacher uses curious, non-judgmental language
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May probe publicly or privately
* May ask series of questions to get to root cause
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Student: "The answer is 24." Teacher: "You got 24. Can you walk me through how you solved it?" Student: "I multiplied 3 times 8." Teacher: "You multiplied 3 times 8. What made you decide to multiply instead of add?" Student: "Because the problem said 'each' so I thought that meant times." Teacher: "You saw the word 'each' and knew that was a clue. Let's look at the problem together and figure out if multiplication is the right operation here."
* Student: "I think the main idea is that the girl went to the store." Teacher: "You said the main idea is that she went to the store. What part of the text made you think that was the main idea?" Student: "It was in the first sentence." Teacher: "Got it. How should we use the text to find the main idea?”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Check your answer against the key now. What would you change?" [Why attempting: Does not necessarily reveal student thinking]
* "And in step 3 did you multiply or divide?" [Why attempting: Does not reveal student thinking; may be leading]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Immediately corrects the student without asking any questions [type: missed opportunity]
* "Really? You think it's 7?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you remember we talked about this yesterday?" [Why non-example: Judgmental] [type: relational harm]
* "Don't you think you should add instead of subtract?" [Why non-example: Leading question, does not reveal student thinking] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP A (Intervention 1 — Questioning): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group A before advancing to Intervention 2
look_fors.name: Scaffolding Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student is stuck or makes an error, ask a simpler or more foundational question to get them thinking, then use their response to bridge back to the original task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student is stuck or has made an error
* Teacher asks a simpler, more foundational, or more manageable question related to the original task or question
* Teacher connects the student's response back to the original task or question
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require more than one scaffolding question before returning to the original task
* Scaffolding question may break the task into a smaller chunk (e.g., "What's the first step?") rather than stepping down in conceptual complexity 
* Bridge back may be a statement rather than a question (e.g., "Ok, now that you've identified you need to multiply length x width, do that to find the area and finish the problem")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Let's start with what area means. What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something."  Teacher: "Yes, and why does that help us here?" Student: "Because we need to find how much space the rectangle takes up." Teacher: "Exactly. So what information does the problem give you that might help you figure that out?"
 * Student: <identifies an incorrect theme> Teacher: "What actually happens to the main character by the end of the story?" Student: "She decides to go back and help even though it's hard." Teacher: "Good. So what do you think the author wants us to learn from that choice? That's your theme."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something." Teacher: "It's the size, or how much space the rectangle takes up. Now find the area of this rectangle." [Why attempting: Asks one scaffolding question but does not check to see if student needs more in order to complete the problem]
look_fors.non_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Remember, the area of a rectangle is length x width" [Why non-example: Provides a cue rather than asking a question; thinking stays with teacher]

look_fors.type_explanation: OPTIONAL GROUP C (Intervention 3 — Teacher Support): Teacher must demonstrate at least 1 look-for from Group C if Interventions 1–2 have not resolved the student's confusion
look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
* Feedback may address content, process, or self-regulation
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Your thesis clearly states your position. To strengthen paragraph 2, add textual evidence like you did in paragraph 1, then explain how it supports your claim"
* "You accurately identified the problem. Now show your work step-by-step so I can see your mathematical thinking. Look at the example on the anchor chart for the format"
" Now, I want you to try holding your scissors with just your thumb and pointer finger from your right hand."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Your evidence is weak. Add more quotes" [Why attempting: Identifies issue but doesn't explain how to select strong evidence]
* "Nice work on the intro. The body needs more details" [Why attempting: Names strength and area for improvement but lacks concrete next steps]
* "This is better than last time" [Why attempting: Acknowledges growth but not specific about what improved or next steps]
*  "Keep working. Make sure that you use the visual anchors around the classroom to help you." [Why attempting: Lacks specificity as to what to improve or how to use visual anchors]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Good job" [Why non-example: Generic without specifics] [type: missed opportunity]
* "This needs work" [Why non-example: Identifies problem but no actionable steps] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You're not there yet - keep trying" [Why non-example: No specific guidance for improvement] [type: missed opportunity]
* Only marking errors without explanation or guidance [Why non-example: No actionable next steps] [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Respectful Routines
skills.description: Build productive behavioral and academic expectations using routines that respect students' humanity.

look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.name: Rationale
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share how the routine, procedure, or task supports learning and/or the classroom community.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Explains purpose of routine, procedure, or task relative to learning and/or classroom community
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May include connection to classroom norms or goals, real world application or importance, or students' interests or identities
look_fors.strong_examples: “We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today because we will be constantly talking to our peers to share our great ideas, and I want us all to have the opportunity to share without slowing down the class.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today. This is an important procedure for our classroom culture and learning." [Why attempting: Generic importance]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “We are going to learn and practice the procedure for a turn-and-talk today.”
* "This is an important procedure so I do not have to give so many consequences" [Why non-example: Negative, emphasizes compliance]
* "This routine is important for the state exam" [Why non-example: Not rooted in learning or community]

look_fors.name: Specific Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell students exactly what they should be doing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Tells students what to do (not what not to do)
* Directions include necessary details for task success
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Routine tasks may require less specificity. New or complex tasks, routines or procedures, or routines or procedures that need to be retaught may require more specificty. 
* For multi-step routines or procedures, specificity should apply to each step
* Necessary details for task success might include components like time length, task location in room or on paper/screen, voice/volume level, task goal or criteria for success, task rationale or what to do if finished early. Specific directions only need the components from this list that are needed for student success; they do not need to include ALL components all the time.
* When given as feedback during a task, directions may target only the specific portion of the task the student is struggling with rather than the full task.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Take 5 minutes to independently find key evidence that supports the author's claim in the text. When you find a key piece of evidence, underline it."
* "Before you move on to question 2, add a diagram to your response for question 1."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Find the key evidence in the text and underline it." [Why attempting: Missing time, independent/group mode, specification of key evidence in context]
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't just underline everything." [Why non-example: What not to do, vague]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when routine, procedure, or logistics directions include 3 or more steps where order matters; not required for short directions (1-2 steps) or when order does not affect success. NOT required and should NEVER be applied to breaking down the steps of an academic task.
look_fors.name: Sequential Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break complex, multi-step directions down into sequential, logically ordered steps.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Multi-step directions for routines, procedures, or logistics broken into ordered steps that are made explicit by the teacher through numbers or words like "first," "next," and "then"
- This look-for applies to routine, procedural, or logistical directions (e.g., steps for transitions, steps for materials use or clean-up, steps for engaging in complex engagement routines or activities like turn and talk or Socratic seminar, etc.); does not apply to breaking down the steps to solve an academic task or problem
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Breaking down how to solve an academic task or problem into steps (e.g., "first find the common denominator, then multiply, then simplify") is out of scope for this look-for. This is a separate, often valid instructional move  and should not be scored as either evidence or non-evidence of Sequential Directions.
look_fors.strong_examples: “First, fill out your name and group number at the top of your handout. Second, identify your variables and write a hypothesis. Third, write a procedure that will test your hypothesis. Next, once you have all sections from the top of your lab handout through the procedure complete, raise your hand. I will come check your work and clear you to get materials from the counter. Finally, walk to get your materials from the counter and bring them back to your table.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first part of your experiment is to identify your hypothesis and variables. Your procedure should come from the hypothesis and variables. Once you have those components, raise your hand for my clearance, and then you can get materials. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your paper." [Why attempting: Some sequential language, steps still disordered]
look_fors.non_examples: "Materials are on the counter for you. You can get your materials once you have the top part of your lab handout done, but you have to check in with me before you get materials. Write your procedure and identify your hypothesis and variables. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your lab handout." [Why non-example: Steps out of order, no sequential language]

look_fors.name: Learning Process Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on learning activities, content, or approach
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students for input on learning activities or topics
* Allows students to select their own examples or applications
* Provides choices in task approach during learning
* Invites students to share personal perspectives or connections
* Offers options for how to engage with content
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Choices may be guided or open-ended depending on learning objectives
* Can offer choice in sequence, grouping, scaffolds, or specific activities
* Student input may shape current or future lessons
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Choose which historical figure you want to research based on your interests"
* "When I say go, move to one of the three tables on the window side of the room if you prefer to work with a partner, and one of the three tables on the door side of the room if you prefer to work alone"
* "What examples should we use for this concept? Who has an idea from your own experience?"
* "You can choose if and when you use one of the available supports, such as the exemplar lab report from last week, the sentence starters for hypotheses, or the hint card with an image of one way to set up your materials" 
* "For today's homework, you can listen to the podcast OR complete the reading on this topic"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can work independently instead of with a partner. Teacher says yes. [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* "If you feel like the problems with fractions with different denominators are too hard, you can just choose the ones with the same denominators" [Why attempting: Offers choice, but lowers expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher selects all examples and applications without student input
* All students engage with content in identical way
* Dismisses student suggestions for how to approach learning
* Never asks students what interests them or connects to their experiences
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.name: Learning Product Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on how to demonstrate learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Offers choices in demonstration method (written, oral, visual, performance, etc.)
* Provides options for final product format
* Invites student input on how they want to show what they know
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Student input may be solicited before task or as options are presented
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can show your understanding by writing an explanation, creating a diagram, or explaining it aloud to a partner"
* "Would you like to present your findings as a poster, a speech, or a written report?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can do a presentation instead of write an essay for their final product. Teacher says yes.  [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* Offers one alternative option but frames it as "easier"
look_fors.non_examples:
* All students complete identical task in identical format with no variation
* Teacher selects all demonstration methods without offering alternatives
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

skills.name: Rich Tasks
skills.description: Choose tasks that allow for conceptual understanding, problem-solving, and mathematical reasoning.

look_fors.name: Connect Learning to Student Interests and Lives
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Make content relevant to students' experiences and interests
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses examples from students' lives or communities
* Asks students to make personal connections to content
* Incorporates student interests into lesson examples or activities
* Shows real-world applications relevant to students
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May reference current events meaningful to students
* Can invite students to share their own examples
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Many of you mentioned you love The Grizzlies in our beginning of year survey. Let's use player statistics to practice calculating percentages"
* "How does this connect to what you see in your own neighborhood or family?"
* "What's something you do when you are feeling mad?" 
* "Next, we will apply what we learned to classify plants in our school's community garden"
* "We know that the ocean moderates the climate of cities on the coast. Let's now look at some data to see if Lake Michigan is big enough to moderate climate here."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This might be interesting to you" [Why attempting: Suggests relevance but doesn't explicitly connect]
 * Uses one example at start of unit but doesn't sustain connections
look_fors.non_examples:
* Uses only generic or teacher-selected examples
* Dismisses student attempts to make personal connections
* Never asks how content relates to students' lives

look_fors.name: Connecting Representations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Guide students to connect and compare two mathematical representations based on the underlying mathematics
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents two different, but related mathematical representations (e.g., multiple diagrams that could be used to answer the same word problem; choosing an image from 2 similar options to represent a specific equation)
* Asks students to articulate connections between the representations (e.g., identify corresponding elements or values, identify equivalent forms, match to underlying math/rules, etc.)
* Guides students to explain the underlying mathematics that links the representations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be two different representations of the exact same rule/concept (e.g., equation) or related representations where one must be matched to a specific rule, example, or concept
* May include more than 2 representations
* May follow 5-part structure: Launch → Connect Representations → Share and Study Connections → Create a Representation → Meta-Reflection
look_fors.strong_examples: * <Displays two distance vs. time graphs side by side> "These two graphs show related mathematical relationships. I want you to think about: How are these representations connected? What corresponds between Graph A and Graph B?" <think and partner time> "What connections did you find?" <Student: "Graph A goes up then down, like a hill. Graph B does the same thing"> "Can you be more specific about which features correspond?" <Student: "The peak in Graph A at time 5 matches the peak in Graph B at time 5. And where Graph A starts and ends at zero, Graph B does too"> "Excellent - you're identifying corresponding structural features."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Shows graph and table and asks "What's the same about these?" [Why attempting: Prompts comparison but question is vague about mathematical connection]
 * "Look at Graph A and Graph B. Can someone tell me how they're connected?" <calls on one student, accepts answer, moves on> [Why attempting: Asks for connection but doesn't guide class to articulate underlying mathematics]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks students to describe a single representation
* Shows multiple representations but does not ask students to connect

look_fors.name: Critique, Correct, and Clarify
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Present flawed mathematical writing for students to analyze, improve, and clarify
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a partial, incorrect, incomplete, or ambiguous mathematical argument, explanation, or solution
* Prompts students to identify errors, ambiguities, or areas needing clarification
* Students improve response
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often combines with a think/pair/share structure followed by individual revisions
* Teacher may model respectful critique language
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I tried to explain why 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 2, and I wrote: 'When you divide fractions you flip the second one and multiply, so 1/2 × 4/1 = 2.' Can you help me improve my explanation? First, on your own, identify what's unclear or incorrect about my reasoning. Then work with your partner to write an improved explanation that clarifies the mathematical thinking." <individual work time> <pair work time> "Let's hear some improved explanations." <pairs share> "Now take a minute to refine your own explanation one more time based on what you heard."
 * <Displays written work> "A student wrote: 'The slope is 3 because you go up 3.' Take 2 minutes individually to identify what's ambiguous or incomplete about this explanation. What mathematical details are missing?" <individual time> "Now work with your partner to rewrite this explanation with precise mathematical language and complete reasoning." <pair work> <pairs share improved versions> "Refine your explanation one final time."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Presents flawed work and asks students to identify what's wrong but doesn't have them improve the response
look_fors.non_examples:
* Presents correct, complete student work for analysis
* "This answer is wrong. Can someone give me the right answer?" [Why non-example: No analysis]

look_fors.name: Examples and Non-Examples
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Clarify concepts by showing both what they are and what they aren't
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides example(s) that demonstrate the concept
* Provides non-example(s) that contrast with the concept
* Explicitly identifies which are examples and which are non-examples
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Examples and non-examples may be presented verbally, visually, or with manipulatives
* May be teacher-led demonstration or student-directed exploration
* May present examples first or non-examples first depending on instructional purpose
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's look at functions and non-functions. This is a function: each input has exactly one output. <shows table> See how input 2 only pairs with output 5? Now here's a non-function: <shows different table> Notice how input 3 pairs with both output 7 and output 9. That makes this a non-function because one input has multiple outputs."
 * "I'm going to show you four tables. Two show proportional relationships and two do not. First, these two are proportional - notice the constant rate in both. Now these two are not proportional - see how the rate changes? That's how we know they're non-proportional."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Look at these tables. Some show proportional relationships and some don't. Examples A and C are proportional, but B, D, and E are not." [Why attempting: Examples and non-examples but no connection to concept/why]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Here's a function: y = 2x + 3. Got it?" [Why non-example: Only one example, no non-example provided]
 * "These are all functions" <shows multiple examples but no non-examples> [Why non-example: No contrast provided]

look_fors.name: Manipulatives/Visual Representations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use concrete models and visuals to clarify concepts
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses concrete objects or visual representations to illustrate concepts
* Models use of precise vocabulary while demonstrating with manipulatives or visuals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Manipulatives and visuals can be used during initial instruction, during guided practice, or during independent work
* May be teacher-led demonstration or student-directed exploration
* Applies to both vocabulary development and conceptual understanding
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's use these base-ten blocks to understand place value. This cube represents one unit. This rod represents ten units - see how it's made of ten unit cubes? And this flat represents one hundred. Watch as I show you 234 using these blocks." <Models with blocks while narrating><Asks students to make different 3 different numbers with blocks after modeling>
 * "Let me show you how a proportional relationship works using this diagram. <Points to table on screen> In a proportional relationship, there's a constant rate between the two quantities. Look at 'Hours Worked' and 'Money Earned.' When we work 1 hour, we earn $15. Notice this arrow showing times 15. Now watch what happens with 2 hours - we earn $30. That's still times 15. <Points to each arrow> See how every single relationship is times 15? 3 hours gives us $45, 4 hours gives us $60, and 5 hours gives us $75. The rate stays constant - it's always times 15. That constant rate is what makes this proportional. <Points to checkmark> That's why this diagram shows 'proportional' at the bottom."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Here's a function. See how the input is on the left side of the chart and the output is on the left? That's a function" [Why attempting: Visual, but concept imprecise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "A function is when you have one unique output for any input." [Why non-example: Verbal explanation only, no visual support]
 * <Shows a visual on screen but doesn't reference it or explain it>

look_fors.name: Open Middle
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Present a problem with one starting point, one answer or solution type, and multiple solution paths involving varying degrees of optimization
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents problem with closed beginning (same starting point for all students)
* Problem has closed end (same answer, answer type, or goal)
* Problem has open middle (multiple valid approaches or solutions)
* Problem inludes optimization component (easy to get an answer, challenging to get best answer)
* Prompts students to share their thinking and solution methods
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May have single optimal answer or multiple equally valid optimal answers
look_fors.strong_examples: * "Given the point (3,5), use the digits 1-9, at most one time each, to find a point that minimizes the slope of the line passing through the two points. The slope cannot be undefined. Think about your strategy and be ready to share how you know you found the minimum slope." <Teacher uses think/pair/share strategy with question>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Use the digits 1-9 to create two 2-digit numbers. Find their sum." [Why attempting: Has closed beginning and end but no optimization; too easy]
 * "Given the point (3,5), find another point that creates a line with small slope" <doesn't specify optimization criteria or constraints> [Why attempting: Lacks clear optimization goal or constraints]
* Gives strong prompt but does not have students share thinking
look_fors.non_examples:
* Simple multiple choice item not involving optimization 
* "Create any equation you want and solve it" [Why non-example: Open beginning]

look_fors.name: Require Reasoning or Justification
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Establish the norm that answers must include reasoning or evidence
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sets or reinforces the expectation that students explain thinking, not just give answer
* Provides and references supports for reasoning and justification (e.g., sentence starters, posted norms)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Reasoning standard may be content-specific ("use evidence from the text") or general ("tell me how you know")
* May use follow up questions to push students who answer without reasoning to explain; however, for look-for to be strong, the expectation for reasoning or justification must be proactively established
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I don't just want to know what you think, I want to know why. So, remember to use our sentence frame: I think ___, because ___"
 * Student: "The answer is 12" Teacher: "You might be right — but I need the how you got there. Walk me through your reasoning." <student responds with reasoning> Teacher: "That's the kind of thinking I want to hear every time."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Can you say more?" [Why attempting: prompts elaboration but doesn't establish reasoning as a standing expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts correct answers without asking for reasoning (e.g., "Great answer! Who else?")
* Only asks for justification when an answer is wrong

look_fors.name: Which One Doesn't Belong
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Present 3+ mathematical representations and ask which doesn't belong
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents 3+ mathematical representations (figures, graphs, expressions, etc.) to students
* Asks "Which one doesn't belong?"
* Prompts students to explain rationale for their choice
* Creates space for multiple valid answers with different mathematical reasoning
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Number of options may vary depending on instructional purpose, always 3+ options, generally 3-4
* May use geometric figures, graphs, expressions, diagrams, or other mathematical representations
* May be used at various points in lesson
look_fors.strong_examples: * <Displays four graphs> "Which one doesn't belong? Think about your answer and your reasoning." <Gives think time and then asks students to turn and talk to a partner> "Let's hear different ideas. Which one doesn't belong and why?" <Student: "C doesn't belong because it's not a straight line"> "What mathematical language could make that more precise?" <Student: "C doesn't belong because it's nonlinear while A, B, and D are linear"> "Another idea?" <Student: "I think B doesn't belong because it has a negative slope"> "So we have multiple valid answers depending on which mathematical feature we focus on."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Presents four graphs and asks "Which one doesn't belong?" <one student shares> "Good, Graph C. That's right." [Why attempting: Validates single answer, shuts down multiple rationales]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Presents only two options
* Presents options: 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and X [Why non-example: Only one obvious answer; not mathematically significant; no opportunity for precise language]

skills.name: Set and Support Clear Expectations
skills.description: Give clear, concise directions and support on-task engagement with a sequence of positive supports when students struggle to meet expectations.

look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.name: Positive Narration
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Name specific actions of individuals and groups that are meeting the expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific students/groups meeting expectations
* Narration describes specific actions (not general praise like "good job")
* Actions are framed in terms of what to do, not what not to do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* May use shorter but less specific narration ("table 3 has it") when most students already working
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “I can tell tables 2, 3, and 5 are ready to start the experiment because they have all their materials set up to match the diagram on page 2”
* “Jenn, Abhi and Alice have already started underlining key details in the text”
 * “Lequite, Dave, and Eric are referring back to their timeline notes to help them get started”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Good job Lequite, Dave, and Eric” [Why attempting: vague praise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Most of us are not on task, let's get to it." [Why non-example: Negative/vague]
* ""Kiara, you shouldn't be on your phone right now." [Why non-example: Names student, what not to do]
* "I'll wait." [Why non-example: Passive-aggressive, vague]

look_fors.name: Specific Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell students exactly what they should be doing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Tells students what to do (not what not to do)
* Directions include necessary details for task success
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Routine tasks may require less specificity. New or complex tasks, routines or procedures, or routines or procedures that need to be retaught may require more specificty. 
* For multi-step routines or procedures, specificity should apply to each step
* Necessary details for task success might include components like time length, task location in room or on paper/screen, voice/volume level, task goal or criteria for success, task rationale or what to do if finished early. Specific directions only need the components from this list that are needed for student success; they do not need to include ALL components all the time.
* When given as feedback during a task, directions may target only the specific portion of the task the student is struggling with rather than the full task.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Take 5 minutes to independently find key evidence that supports the author's claim in the text. When you find a key piece of evidence, underline it."
* "Before you move on to question 2, add a diagram to your response for question 1."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Find the key evidence in the text and underline it." [Why attempting: Missing time, independent/group mode, specification of key evidence in context]
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't just underline everything." [Why non-example: What not to do, vague]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if Positive Narration has already been attempted and students are still not meeting expectations; not required if expectations are already being met
look_fors.name: Anonymous Group Reminders
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give a brief, positively framed reminder and/or anonymized statement of encouragement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States expectation positively without naming specific students (e.g., "we are silently doing..."; "waiting on X number" or "I have almost everyone")
 * May include brief rationale
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You are talking quietly to one partner about the prompt on the board for another minute,”
* “Remember to independently add your evidence in the left hand column so you can reference it later”
* “We are only waiting on two. Almost there!”
* “I have got about 80% of the class, can we can get to 100% in the next 5 seconds?.”
* “Staying silent helps everyone concentrate on their independent thinking and writing”
* “Make sure to add units to your measurement, otherwise others won’t know if you mean 4 inches or 4 miles”.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Only three classmates are still off task" [Why attempting: Anonymous but framed negatively]
 * "We're almost there, just waiting on Mayme and Diana" [Positive but not anonymous]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “Tables 3 and 5, you’re not following directions, pay attention”
 * “Forest, we’re waiting for you”
 * “Not showing your work means you lose points”
 * “If you can’t be quiet, I’m going to start giving demerits”

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if Anonymous Group Reminders has already been attempted and students are still not meeting expectations; not required if expectations are already being met
look_fors.name: Positive Redirection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Restate the expectation clearly, maintaining a high expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Restates the expectation, without lowering it, clearly
* Expecation is framed in what to do (not what not to do)
* Does NOT scold or reprimand
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* Individual redirections should generally be private; in rare cases they may be full group if anonymous/full group redirection given first and then individual redirection is a quick, warm, reminder
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You’ve got three minutes left to organize your materials and identify your variables and constants”
 * “Clear your table fully by putting away those last two papers”
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Stop doodling and start problem 2" [Why attempting: mixes positive and negative framing]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, since you're behind already, you can just do…." [Why non-example: Lowers expectations]
* "I already told you not to talk," "stop getting distracted by what's going on in the hallway" [Why non-example: Negative, scolding]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when directions include 3 or more steps where order matters; not required for short directions (1-2 steps) or when order does not affect success
look_fors.name: Sequential Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break complex, multi-step directions down into sequential, logically ordered steps.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Multi-step directions for routines, procedures, or logistics broken into ordered steps that are made explicit by the teacher through numbers or words like "first," "next," and "then"
- This look-for applies to routine, procedural, or logistical directions (e.g., steps for transitions, steps for materials use or clean-up, steps for engaging in complex engagement routines or activities like turn and talk or Socratic seminar, etc.); does not apply to breaking down the steps to solve an academic task or problem
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Breaking down how to solve an academic task or problem into steps (e.g., "first find the common denominator, then multiply, then simplify") is out of scope for this look-for. This is a separate, often valid instructional move  and should not be scored as either evidence or non-evidence of Sequential Directions.
look_fors.strong_examples: “First, fill out your name and group number at the top of your handout. Second, identify your variables and write a hypothesis. Third, write a procedure that will test your hypothesis. Next, once you have all sections from the top of your lab handout through the procedure complete, raise your hand. I will come check your work and clear you to get materials from the counter. Finally, walk to get your materials from the counter and bring them back to your table.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first part of your experiment is to identify your hypothesis and variables. Your procedure should come from the hypothesis and variables. Once you have those components, raise your hand for my clearance, and then you can get materials. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your paper." [Why attempting: Some sequential language, steps still disordered]
look_fors.non_examples: "Materials are on the counter for you. You can get your materials once you have the top part of your lab handout done, but you have to check in with me before you get materials. Write your procedure and identify your hypothesis and variables. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your lab handout." [Why non-example: Steps out of order, no sequential language]

look_fors.name: Observable Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Describe what student success looks and/or sounds like.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Directions describe what success looks like or sounds like in a way that students can envision
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Directions only need to be observable enough for students to understand expectations. After that, additional observability cues are not necessary.
look_fors.strong_examples: “When I say go, silently stand up behind your chair to show me you’re ready for recess. I will know you are ready when your chair is pushed in and your walking feet are pointed toward the door. Go!”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Stand up behind your chair to show me you’re ready for recess”
look_fors.non_examples: “Get ready for recess”

look_fors.acceptable_variations: Breaking down how to solve an academic task or problem into steps (e.g., "first find the common denominator, then multiply, then simplify") is out of scope for this look-for. This is a separate, often valid instructional move  and should not be scored as either evidence or non-evidence of Sequential Directions.
look_fors.strong_examples: “First, fill out your name and group number at the top of your handout. Second, identify your variables and write a hypothesis. Third, write a procedure that will test your hypothesis. Next, once you have all sections from the top of your lab handout through the procedure complete, raise your hand. I will come check your work and clear you to get materials from the counter. Finally, walk to get your materials from the counter and bring them back to your table.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first part of your experiment is to identify your hypothesis and variables. Your procedure should come from the hypothesis and variables. Once you have those components, raise your hand for my clearance, and then you can get materials. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your paper." [Why attempting: Some sequential language, steps still disordered]
look_fors.non_examples: "Materials are on the counter for you. You can get your materials once you have the top part of your lab handout done, but you have to check in with me before you get materials. Write your procedure and identify your hypothesis and variables. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your lab handout." [Why non-example: Steps out of order, no sequential language]

look_fors.type_explanation:
More important for new or complex directions and multilingual learners
Less important for routine or simple directions
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

skills.name: Sight Recognition
