skills.description: Teach students to recognize a word accurately and effortlessly by mapping its sounds to its spelling and explicitly teaching any irregular parts, so the word is stored for instant retrieval.

look_fors.name: Accurate Sound Production
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say target sounds accurately and precisely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the target sound in isolation correctly
Depending on the phonological or phonemic unit of the lesson….
* Says the sound (/m/), not the letter name(s) ("em") or "muh"
* Stretches continuous sounds (/mmm/) and clips stop sounds (/t/) without adding a vowel
* Pronounces digraphs and vowel teams accurately (/ch/, /ee/, etc.)
* Segments syllables accurately
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., syllables /nap/ /kin/ when focus is on chunking; sound /b/ when focus is phonemes; words "bat" and "cat" when focus is rhyming; sounds /m/ /at/ when focus is onset-rime; etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
"Listen: /mmm/-op. The first sound is /mmm/."
"What is another word that sounds like 'bat'?"
"Which one doesn't belong? Weed, bead, pill, seed?"
"/tae/ /bl/ What's the word?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first sound in 'top' is /tuh/." [Why attempting: adds a vowel to a stop sound]
look_fors.non_examples:
"The first sound in 'mop' is 'em.'" [Why non-example: says letter not sound]
"There are five sounds in 'cheese': /c/, /h/, /e/, /e/, /z/" [Why non-example: not accurately pronouncing digraph /ch/ nor vowel team /ee/]
"Tiger has two syllables: /tieg/ /r/" [Why non-example: syllables not divided correctly]

look_fors.name: Map Letters to Sounds
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Say the correct sound for each letter or letter pattern.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Produces the correct sound while showing a letter or letter pattern
* Treats a letter team or digraph as one sound (e.g., English "sh" says /sh/; Spanish "ch" says /tʃ/)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Target sounds may be at different phonological units depending on lesson focus (e.g., /c/ and /at/ for an onset-rime focus)
look_fors.strong_examples: <Shows "sh"> "These two letters work together. They say /sh/." <Points> "/sh/. Now let's read it in this word /sh/, /i/, /n/, shin."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "a"> "That says /a/, or sometimes /ay/." <does not specify which for this word> [Why attempting: gives a sound and letter, but leaves out of context of word]
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Shows the word "shine"> "The word is shine." [Why non-example: no mapping of specific letters to sounds]
* With no visuals: "Listen to me say /sh/. Now listen to me say /sh/ ine. Shine." [Why non-example: no connection to the actual letters, sound only]

look_fors.name: Read the Word as a Whole
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Read the whole word as a single unit, accurately and effortlessly, rather than sounding it out each time.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Reads the whole word as a unit after its parts are mapped, not sound-by-sound
* Returns to the word so it is read on sight, accurately and without re-decoding
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Recognition is built over repeated encounters; early attempts may still require some decoding before the word is read as a whole.
look_fors.strong_examples: <After mapping the parts of "said"> "Now read the whole word." <Students> "said." <Later, returning to it> "And this word?" <Students read "said" instantly, without sounding out.>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Blends the sounds to read the word once but never returns to read it as a whole unit.
look_fors.non_examples: Sounds the word out letter-by-letter every time it appears, never reading it as a whole.

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the word has an irregular part that does not follow expected sound-spelling patterns; else not required
look_fors.name: Flag the Tricky Part
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Identify the irregular part of the word that must be remembered, and separate it from the parts that follow expected patterns.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the part(s) of the word that follow the expected sound-spelling pattern
* Points out or marks the irregular part that does not follow the pattern and must be remembered
look_fors.acceptable_variations: The irregular part may be marked visually (e.g., underlined, circled, marked with a heart) or named aloud.
look_fors.strong_examples: <Shows "said"> "We read /s/ and /d/ just like we expect. The tricky part is 'ai' here <points>; it says /e/, not what we would guess. That is the part to remember."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <Shows "said"> "The tricky part is in the middle." <does not say what is regular or what to remember>
look_fors.non_examples: <Shows "said"> "This is a word you just have to memorize."

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the word shares a salient, teachable spelling-sound pattern with other high-frequency words; not required when no useful pattern can be leveraged
look_fors.name: Group Words by Pattern
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach the word alongside others that share its spelling-sound pattern, rather than in isolation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Connects the target word to other words that share the same spelling-sound pattern
* Names the shared pattern so students can apply it to related words
look_fors.acceptable_variations: The pattern may be a rime or word family (e.g., he/she/me/we/be) or a shared tricky element (e.g., could/would/should).
look_fors.strong_examples: "We just learned 'he.' Look how 'she,' 'we,' 'me,' and 'be' all work the same way; the e says its name. Let's read them together."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Teaches "could," then "would," then "should" in a row but never names the shared pattern.
look_fors.non_examples: Teaches several unrelated sight words one after another with no connection between them.

skills.name: Specific Expectations (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Provide clear, actionable directions and support students to meet expectations while encouraging student choice in learning.

look_fors.name: Concision
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use only necessary words and steps; do not include details students do not need.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Includes only words and steps necessary for student understanding
* No extraneous details or over-explanation
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Strategic repetition for English Language Learners is acceptable
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Step 2 of our lab procedure is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials."
* "A habitat is where an organism, like a plant or an animal, lives. A habitat includes what the organism needs to survive, like food, water, and shelter. For example, a frog's habitat is a pond. The pond habitat includes living things like the insects the frog eats and other animals and plants. The pond habitat also includes non-living things like the water the frog needs for life."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials so we need to have space to work with them safely. So, step 2 is to put away all materials except something to write with so you have space to work safely with lab materials. Be sure to put away books and any other materials you have out." [Why attempting: Some unnecessary words and repetition]
* "So, a habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism can be a plant or it can be an animal. A habitat includes the different things that the organism needs in order to survive - things like food that it eats, water that it drinks, and shelter where it can be safe. So for example, if we think about a frog, a frog's habitat would be a pond. In the pond habitat there are living things, like the insects that the frog eats for its food, and there are also other animals that live there and plants that grow there. And the pond habitat also has non-living things too, like the water that the frog needs to live and also rocks and mud that are in the pond." [Why attempting: Unnecessary words and phrases throughout]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Ok, so it's time to get ready for step 2 of our lab procedure. Our labs always involve materials. That might be graduated cylinders, balances, specimens to observe, or substances to measure - you name it. Working with materials is always fun! To be able to have space to work with materials, step 2 is to be sure to clear off the area in front of you on your table. There should be nothing there. Put away your books from silent reading time. If the last activity involved any materials, be sure to put those away. If you have anything else out, find a place for it so we have enough space for our lab materials." [Why non-example: Excessive details, tangential comments]
* "Habitat - so this is a really important word. A habitat is basically where something, an organism, lives, like where an animal or a plant lives. It's kind of like their home, but the word is habitat not home. So a habitat includes things around them, that is the organism, the plant or animal, that they need. Like, for example, if you think about a frog, right, a frog lives in a pond, so the pond is the frog's habitat. It includes the things the frog needs. And in the pond there are living things - like there are insects that the frog eats, and there are other animals, and there are plants and stuff like that. And then there are also non-living things in the habitat too, like the water - frogs need water to live - and the mud and rocks and things like that in the pond. So the habitat is all of this stuff together, water, mud, rocks, insects, plants, other animals." [Why non-example: Excessive filler words, redundant explanations]

look_fors.name: Positive Narration
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Name specific actions of individuals and groups that are meeting the expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific students/groups meeting expectations
* Narration describes specific actions (not general praise like "good job")
* Actions are framed in terms of what to do, not what not to do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* May use shorter but less specific narration ("table 3 has it") when most students already working
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “I can tell tables 2, 3, and 5 are ready to start the experiment because they have all their materials set up to match the diagram on page 2”
* “Jenn, Abhi and Alice have already started underlining key details in the text”
 * “Lequite, Dave, and Eric are referring back to their timeline notes to help them get started”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Good job Lequite, Dave, and Eric” [Why attempting: vague praise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Most of us are not on task, let's get to it." [Why non-example: Negative/vague]
* ""Kiara, you shouldn't be on your phone right now." [Why non-example: Names student, what not to do]
* "I'll wait." [Why non-example: Passive-aggressive, vague]

look_fors.name: Specific Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell students exactly what they should be doing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Tells students what to do (not what not to do)
* Directions include necessary details for task success
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Routine tasks may require less specificity. New or complex tasks, routines or procedures, or routines or procedures that need to be retaught may require more specificty. 
* For multi-step routines or procedures, specificity should apply to each step
* Necessary details for task success might include components like time length, task location in room or on paper/screen, voice/volume level, task goal or criteria for success, task rationale or what to do if finished early. Specific directions only need the components from this list that are needed for student success; they do not need to include ALL components all the time.
* When given as feedback during a task, directions may target only the specific portion of the task the student is struggling with rather than the full task.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Take 5 minutes to independently find key evidence that supports the author's claim in the text. When you find a key piece of evidence, underline it."
* "Before you move on to question 2, add a diagram to your response for question 1."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Find the key evidence in the text and underline it." [Why attempting: Missing time, independent/group mode, specification of key evidence in context]
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't just underline everything." [Why non-example: What not to do, vague]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if the teacher has already used look-fors from the Optional group and/or Positive Narration and students are still not meeting expectations; not required if expectations are already being met
look_fors.name: Anonymous Group Reminders
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give a brief, positively framed reminder and/or anonymized statement of encouragement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States expectation positively without naming specific students (e.g., "we are silently doing..."; "waiting on X number" or "I have almost everyone")
 * May include brief rationale
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You are talking quietly to one partner about the prompt on the board for another minute,”
* “Remember to independently add your evidence in the left hand column so you can reference it later”
* “We are only waiting on two. Almost there!”
* “I have got about 80% of the class, can we can get to 100% in the next 5 seconds?.”
* “Staying silent helps everyone concentrate on their independent thinking and writing”
* “Make sure to add units to your measurement, otherwise others won’t know if you mean 4 inches or 4 miles”.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Only three classmates are still off task" [Why attempting: Anonymous but framed negatively]
 * "We're almost there, just waiting on Mayme and Diana" [Positive but not anonymous]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “Tables 3 and 5, you’re not following directions, pay attention”
 * “Forest, we’re waiting for you”
 * “Not showing your work means you lose points”
 * “If you can’t be quiet, I’m going to start giving demerits”

look_fors.type_explanation: Required if the direction is complex and new; not required for familiar or routine directions; not required for simple directions
look_fors.name: Directions Check for Understanding
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Asks a question or asks a student to demonstrate to check for understanding of complex or new directions before students begin task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Asks question about directions or asks student to model/demonstrate part of the directions before students begin
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May also occur after students begin if many students are confused. In this situation, teacher should call on student who is meeting expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Which partner shares first?"
* "How long will you have for your table discussion?"
* "Everyone pick up your scissors and show me how you hold them safely"
* Ellie, you set up your t-chart correctly. Can you show your paper to the class?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: *"Everyone got that? [Why attempting: vague question; may be rhetorical]
look_fors.non_examples: No check for understanding of a new, complex direction

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Learning Process Choice or Learning Product Choice is required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Learning Process Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on learning activities, content, or approach
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students for input on learning activities or topics
* Allows students to select their own examples or applications
* Provides choices in task approach during learning
* Invites students to share personal perspectives or connections
* Offers options for how to engage with content
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Choices may be guided or open-ended depending on learning objectives
* Can offer choice in sequence, grouping, scaffolds, or specific activities
* Student input may shape current or future lessons
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Choose which historical figure you want to research based on your interests"
* "When I say go, move to one of the three tables on the window side of the room if you prefer to work with a partner, and one of the three tables on the door side of the room if you prefer to work alone"
* "What examples should we use for this concept? Who has an idea from your own experience?"
* "You can choose if and when you use one of the available supports, such as the exemplar lab report from last week, the sentence starters for hypotheses, or the hint card with an image of one way to set up your materials" 
* "For today's homework, you can listen to the podcast OR complete the reading on this topic"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can work independently instead of with a partner. Teacher says yes. [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* "If you feel like the problems with fractions with different denominators are too hard, you can just choose the ones with the same denominators" [Why attempting: Offers choice, but lowers expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher selects all examples and applications without student input
* All students engage with content in identical way
* Dismisses student suggestions for how to approach learning
* Never asks students what interests them or connects to their experiences
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Learning Process Choice or Learning Product Choice is required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Learning Product Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on how to demonstrate learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Offers choices in demonstration method (written, oral, visual, performance, etc.)
* Provides options for final product format
* Invites student input on how they want to show what they know
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Student input may be solicited before task or as options are presented
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can show your understanding by writing an explanation, creating a diagram, or explaining it aloud to a partner"
* "Would you like to present your findings as a poster, a speech, or a written report?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can do a presentation instead of write an essay for their final product. Teacher says yes.  [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* Offers one alternative option but frames it as "easier"
look_fors.non_examples:
* All students complete identical task in identical format with no variation
* Teacher selects all demonstration methods without offering alternatives
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when the activity involves materials, movement, or writing/drawing in multiple locations; else not required
look_fors.name: Model/Demonstrate Task
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Model or demonstrate what success looks like for a task, routine, or procedure.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Demonstrates (e.g., physically models, shows on paper or screen, etc.) or has student demonstrate what success looks like
- Model/demonstration is accurate
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- For multi-step tasks, routines, or procedures, model is presented step-by-step
- Can use student volunteer to demonstrate with teacher guidance
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on as shown in our safety gear image. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why strong: Uses visual and body motion/modeling in addition to verbal]
- Teacher demonstrates turn and talk in specific steps (e.g., face each other, decide who goes first, etc.) with student volunteers while rest of class observes and checks off steps on handout. After model, teacher narrates what was done well and highlights hardest part.
- “Watch my mouth” <points to mouth> “B says /b/. Watch again for how I press my lips together. /b/.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- <Teacher asks for two volunteers to model turn and talk> "Thanks Randy and Rochely. Ok, show me the turn and talk procedure" [Why attempting: Not specific, not broken down into steps for longer procedure]
- "Look how strong table 3's lab set-up is" [Why attempting: References exemplar but vague about what makes it strong]
- “Listen to me. B says /b/” [Why attempting: accurate model but verbal only]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution." [Why non-example: Verbal only, no demonstration]
- “Listen to me. B says buh”  [Why non-example: model inaccurate and verbal only]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required for a score of 90+; else not required
look_fors.name: Preempt Anticipated Challenge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Name a specific point of difficulty in the activity before or as it comes up, along with how to handle it.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names a specific part of the activity, task, or process likely to be difficult (e.g., a tricky step, common wrong turn, time crunch, or common misconception)
* Pairs the named challenge with guidance, a strategy, or a resource for navigating it
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be named before the activity begins or in the moment as students reach that point
* Challenge may be conceptual, procedural, or logistical
* Guidance may be given directly or elicited from students (e.g., "What might make this tricky? What could you do about it?")
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "When you get to combining like terms, it's easy to accidentally combine an x term with a constant. Before you do that step, circle your x terms in one color and your constants in another."
- "Some groups run out of time on the last question because they spend too long on the first two. I'd suggest setting a 5-minute cap for each of the first two problems."
- "What do you think might trip you up when you're building your circuit?" <Student: "Maybe getting the batteries backwards"> "Good thinking. That's why we labeled the contacts in the battery holder. What can you look for on the battery to know how to line it up with the contacts?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: - "Step 3 can be tricky, so check your work." [Why attempting: lacks specificity about the difficulty or how to address it]
look_fors.non_examples: - "This next part might be hard." <No guidance or strategy offered>

look_fors.type_explanation: Required for directions with 3 or more sequential steps; not required for short directions (1-2 steps) or when order does not affect success
look_fors.name: Sequential Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break complex, multi-step directions down into sequential, logically ordered steps.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Multi-step directions for routines, procedures, or logistics broken into ordered steps that are made explicit by the teacher through numbers or words like "first," "next," and "then"
- This look-for applies to routine, procedural, or logistical directions (e.g., steps for transitions, steps for materials use or clean-up, steps for engaging in complex engagement routines or activities like turn and talk or Socratic seminar, etc.); does not apply to breaking down the steps to solve an academic task or problem
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Breaking down how to solve an academic task or problem into steps (e.g., "first find the common denominator, then multiply, then simplify") is out of scope for this look-for. This is a separate, often valid instructional move  and should not be scored as either evidence or non-evidence of Sequential Directions.
look_fors.strong_examples: “First, fill out your name and group number at the top of your handout. Second, identify your variables and write a hypothesis. Third, write a procedure that will test your hypothesis. Next, once you have all sections from the top of your lab handout through the procedure complete, raise your hand. I will come check your work and clear you to get materials from the counter. Finally, walk to get your materials from the counter and bring them back to your table.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "The first part of your experiment is to identify your hypothesis and variables. Your procedure should come from the hypothesis and variables. Once you have those components, raise your hand for my clearance, and then you can get materials. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your paper." [Why attempting: Some sequential language, steps still disordered]
look_fors.non_examples: "Materials are on the counter for you. You can get your materials once you have the top part of your lab handout done, but you have to check in with me before you get materials. Write your procedure and identify your hypothesis and variables. Don't forget to fill out your name and group number at the top of your lab handout." [Why non-example: Steps out of order, no sequential language]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Circulate, Scan, Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues, Affirming Non-Verbal Cues, or Multi-Modal Instruction must be demonstrated
look_fors.name: Affirming Non-Verbal Cues
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use non-verbal cues to acknowledge and encourage students in the moment.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Uses gesture, facial expression, or other physical cue that acknowledges or encourages a specific student action (e.g., thumbs up, nod, smile)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be paired with a brief verbal acknowledgment or delivered silently
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Nods and gives a thumbs up to a student who just worked through a tricky step on their own
* Directs spirit fingers at a student thinking through an answer to show support
look_fors.attempting_examples: Gives a general, undirected affirming cue rather than one tied to a specific student action (e.g., smiles at the whole class, gives a thumbs up as a generic "go ahead" signal after directions rather than in response to something a student did)
look_fors.non_examples: Gives only negative cues (e.g., finger shaking, cut it out gesture)

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Circulate, Scan, Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues, Affirming Non-Verbal Cues, or Multi-Modal Instruction must be demonstrated
look_fors.name: Circulate
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Move throughout different areas of the room.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Moves position/location in room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may stand still briefly to do things like read a slide, help a specific student, or model
* Circulation may be strategic (e.g., proximity to students who need support)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher moves throughout the room, visiting different areas and standing near different student groups
 * Circulating throughout the room, standing near students who are not yet on task
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher walks to back of room once but stays there [Why attempting: Moves but doesn't circulate throughout]
 * Teacher paces in front of room only [Why attempting: Movement but limited to one area]
look_fors.non_examples: Standing in one place for an extended period of time

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Circulate, Scan, Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues, Affirming Non-Verbal Cues, or Multi-Modal Instruction must be demonstrated
look_fors.name: Multi-Modal Instruction
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use multiple modes to deliver instruction.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Instruction delivered through 2+ methods (verbal + visual / demonstration / gesture, verbal + written, etc.)
- Multiple modes used simultaneously or in quick succession
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Multi-modal instruction is useful for both content delivery and directions
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Watch me do the cleanup procedure first. Then it will be your turn. First, check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Ok I have my goggles on my face and not at the top of my head and both gloves on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink as I am doing here. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Verbal + physical modeling]
- "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you each step on this diagram. <Points to diagram> Plants take in carbon dioxide here through the leaves and water here through the roots. Then they use sunlight - represented by these arrows - to produce glucose, which they store here, and oxygen, which exits here." [Verbal + visual with specific references]
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container. Watch me do this step and notice how slowly I am pouring so the solution does not splash." [Why attempting: Model/visual only at end]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Let me show you on this diagram what happens during photosynthesis." <Points to diagram but doesn't explain the steps shown> [Why attempting: References visual but doesn't integrate it with explanation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "When I say go, first check that your goggles and gloves are still on. Next, place the safe disposal container in the sink. Finally, slowly pour the solution into the container." [Why non-example: Verbal only]
* "Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert sunlight into energy. Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Circulate, Scan, Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues, Affirming Non-Verbal Cues, or Multi-Modal Instruction must be demonstrated
look_fors.name: Scan
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Visually monitor students across different areas of the room.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Eyes move across different students/areas
* Teacher's body orientation changes to face different parts of room
* Visual monitoring occurs whether teacher is standing still or moving
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Teacher may focus gaze and body orientation when interacting with a specific student or group or piece of content (e.g., on the board)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* While helping one student, teacher periodically looks up to scan rest of class
* Teacher turns body to face different sections of room, making eye contact with students in each area
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher glances up briefly but returns focus to materials [Why attempting: Minimal scanning]
 * Teacher scans one section of room but not others [Why attempting: Incomplete coverage]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher looks down at materials without looking at students [Why non-example: no scan]
* Teacher faces board/screen for extended period without turning to scan students [Why non-example: no scan]
* Teacher stares at one student/area only [Why non-example: Not scanning across room]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Circulate, Scan, Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues, Affirming Non-Verbal Cues, or Multi-Modal Instruction must be demonstrated
look_fors.name: Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use non-verbal physical cues to remind students of expectations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Uses gesture or other physical cue to redirect attention or remind of an expectation (e.g., point, hand signal, proximity)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be paired with a brief related verbal reminder or delivered silently
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Points to the area of a worksheet a student should be working on
* Taps twice on desk near a student who's drifted off-task as a quiet redirect
* Makes shh sign to student talking during independent work time
look_fors.attempting_examples: Gives non-verbal cue with an unclear meaning (e.g., shrug for student off-task)
look_fors.non_examples: Reprimanding a student immediately before trying a non-verbal reminder

skills.name: Strong Open/Close
skills.description: Engage students promptly at the start and close tutorial, leaving students feeling successful.

look_fors.name: Connect to Prior Knowledge
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Activate students' existing knowledge of the topic or content.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Prompts students to recall what they already know about the topic or concept
* Links new content to previously learned content or familiar real-world concepts
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Background knowledge may be drawn from prior lessons or common experience
* May ask students questions, have them complete a practice item to demonstrate a previous skill, or otherwise engage students in the relevant prior knowledge
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "This story is about seeds. Remember when we learned how seeds grow into plants? Look, this character is planting a seed right here. What do you already know about what a seed needs?"
* "Today we will learn to calculate density. Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month, so your do now today is a speed problem. Pay attention to how you figure out the units in your answer"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "This story is about the ocean. Who has seen a picture the ocean or a picture of it?" <A few students raise hands and teacher moves on> [Why attempting: superficial connection to prior knowledge]
* "Calculating density is a little bit like calculating speed, which we did last month. You divide one number by another and keep the units." [Why attempting: teacher-led connection]
look_fors.non_examples: * "This story is about the ocean." [Why non-example: no connection to prior knowledge]

look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Agenda
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to lesson agenda to reinforce key vocabulary and/or preview learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Refers to written agenda or schedule
* Makes connection to what students are learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
look_fors.strong_examples: “Let’s move on to our next activity on the agenda for today: the debrief. Our debrief discussion will help us explain how array models help us multiply.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Let's move on to our next activity [Why attempting: Vague]
* The agenda is on the board <points but doesn't read or reference specifics] [Why attempting: doesn't actively frame or reference]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: No information on flow of time or learning activities]

look_fors.name: Reference or Frame Learning Goal(s)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview or refer back to learning goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or points to learning goal
* Uses language like "Today you'll learn..." or "By the end of this activity, you'll be able to..."
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use to frame full lesson or activity in a lesson
* May reference during in struction to highlight connection (e.g., this helps us achieve today's goal of simplifying fractions by...")
* Should not reference so much that it disrupts flow of lesson
* Learning goal may be for unit, lesson, or activity
* May refer to learning goal using different terminology such as objective, outcome, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you will learn how to identify the main idea and supporting details in nonfiction text. This will help you understand what authors want you to remember most"
* "By the end of this activity, you will be able to identify and explain each stage of the water cycle"
* "Our goal today is to master adding fractions with unlike denominators"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "We're going to learn about fractions" [Why attempting: Vague; does not specify specific goal related to fractions]
* "The objective is on the board" <points but doesn't read or discuss> [Why attempting: Doesn't actively frame or reference]
* “Show your mastery of today’s objective on this exit ticket!” [Why attempting: References objective, but not in a way that reinforces the specific goal]
look_fors.non_examples: * You will work in groups today [Why non-example: Focuses on what students will do not learn]

look_fors.name: Relational Check-In
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Briefly check in with students on feelings or personal context.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Poses a brief feelings/life check-in prompt 
- Pauses for student response(s) before moving on 
- Acknowledges or responds to what student(s) shared
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Verbal, written, or nonverbal (e.g., pointing to a feelings chart) response format 
- Individual, small-group, or whole-class delivery 
- Use of a structured tool (e.g., mood meter) or a direct verbal question
look_fors.strong_examples:
- <projects mood meter at start of class> "Take a second, where are you on the meter today?" <students respond> "I see a lot of us are low energy, let's start with a quick stretch."
- “Turn and talk with your partner for 2 minutes, and share your rose, thorn, and bud from the weekend." <students turn and talk> <teacher circulates, listening in>
look_fors.attempting_examples: <holds up mood meter> "Point to how you're feeling today." <students point> "Ok, thanks for letting me know, let's get started." [Why attempting: response to what students shared is superficial]
look_fors.non_examples: "How's everyone doing?" <no pause, moves directly into content>

look_fors.name: Student Goal-Setting
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in establishing and tracking goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Facilitates process for students to set personal or collective goals
* Provides structure for students to monitor or reflect on progress toward goals
* Conferences with students about their goals
* Celebrates progress toward student-identified goals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Goals may be academic, behavioral, or both
* Can be short-term (daily/weekly) or long-term (unit/semester)
* May use goal-setting templates, trackers, or reflection protocols
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you'll each set a goal for what you want to improve. We'll check in on Fridays to see your progress"
* "Look at your data from the last assessment. Based on that, what's one skill you want to strengthen?"
* Students maintain goal-tracking sheets and regularly reflect on progress
* "Now that we've identified group strengths relative to our class norms, take 2 minutes to write a personal goal relative to our class norms. Refer to the examples on the board if you need some inspiration!"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What do you want to work on today?" [Why attempting: Vague]
* "Here are our class goals. Raise your hand if you would like propose any changes or additions" [Why attempting: Teacher-led with student input]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All goals set by teacher without student input
* Goals never referenced

look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Monitoring and Self-Reflection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to do metacognitive checks or reflections on their own learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts students to monitor their own understanding, confidence, or progress
* Students pause to meta-cognitively reflect on their own learning in-the-moment or after a specific lesson, task, or goal is completed
* Students often identify when they're stuck, confused, or need help
* Students describe how their understanding or confidence has changed over time
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Monitoring tools vary by context (e.g., emoji check-ins for confidence ratings, answer keys for accuracy, progress trackers for completion, targeted questions for considering response quality, etc.)
* Students may track their own progress using provided tools (e.g., confidence scales, answer keys, completion trackers)
* May be embedded as a recurring routine (e.g., a daily exit ticket format, weekly reflection protocol) rather than a one-time prompt
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <At the end of a lesson> "Take 2 minutes to complete the statement 'I used to think... now I know...' based on what you have learned today."
* "On a scale of 1-5, how confident are you that you understand why the character made that choice?" <Students show fingers, teacher sees mix of 2s and 4s> "Turn to your partner and explain why you chose that number." <Students discuss their confidence levels>
* What was most challenging for you today? What helped you work through it?"
* "Place your green, yellow, or red circle on the top of the stack on your desk to indicate if you are ready to move on, need a little help, or are completely stuck"
* "Take a moment to reflect: What strategy did you use? How well did it work? What might you try differently next time?"
* "Now that you have peer feedback on your essay, turn and talk to a new partner about one major strength of your current essay and one next step you will take to revise it"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "During the work time, raise your hand if you need help" [Why attempting:Students are invited to self-monitor, but question is unlikely to lead to all students engaging in metacognitive monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Does everyone understand?" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher circulates and identifies confused students but students don't self-identify [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Student Agency and Pride in Work (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Create structures and opportunities that develop student ownership over their learning and contributions to classroom culture.

look_fors.name: Academic Discourse Norms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach how students should engage in academic conversations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly teaches and uses sentence stems or protocols for academic discussion
* Establishes and refers to expectations for listening and building on ideas
* Establishes and refers to expectations for ensuring all voices are heard
* Redirects discourse violations with reference to established norms
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Norms may be co-created with students or taught by teacher
* Can include visual anchor charts with discussion expectations
* May practice norms through fishbowl or role-play
* May model norms before use
* Norms may include distinct expectations for speakers and non-speakers (e.g., conduct norms for speakers, note-taking or listening norms for non-speakers)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When we disagree, we use the stem 'I disagree because...' and explain our thinking with evidence"
* "Our discussion norms are: listen to understand, build on ideas, and ask clarifying questions. Let's practice"
* Student: "I respectfully disagree because..." Teacher: "Notice how Tucker used our sentence stem for disagreement to express his response to Vanessa productively. What do you think Anya?"
* Student: "What do you think, Patrice?" <Student invites participation from other student>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Be respectful when you talk to each other" [Why attempting: Vague]
* Posts discussion norms but never references or reinforces them
* Several students use sentence starters for academic discourse, but conversation is limited to the same few students
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students interrupt or talk over each other without redirection
* The same few students dominate conversation
* Allows dismissive comments about peers' ideas ("That's dumb")
* No norms, sentence stems, or protocols related to academic discourse present

look_fors.name: Foster Student Ownership of Culture
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Involve students in creating and maintaining classroom norms
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Co-creates classroom expectations or agreements with students
* Asks students to reflect on or evaluate classroom culture
* Invites student input on how to improve learning environment
* References shared norms that students helped establish
* Has students lead culture-building activities
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use different terminlogy (e.g., norms, values, acronym the class comes up with like ROAR or SHINE that covers co-created norms, etc.)
* May have students create visual representations of norms
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's reflect on how we're doing with our classroom agreements. What's working well? What do we need to strengthen?"
* "As a class, what norms should we establish for our discussions so everyone feels heard?"
* "You all decided respect and collaboration were important. I noticed that slipping today. How can we reset?"
* Students hold each other accountable to shared norms without teacher intervention
* "Who has a shout out for a peer who is exemplifying our classroom values?
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Don't forget our norms." 
* Rarely disscusses or references shared classroom culture norms or expectations
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher establishes rules without student input
* Never disscusses or references shared classroom culture norms or expectations
* Treats norms as teacher's expectations only

look_fors.name: Jigsaw
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use jigsaw protocol where students become experts and teach peers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns students to "expert" groups to learn one piece of content
* Then reassigns students to "teaching" groups where each person teaches their section
* Structures activity so every student is responsible for teaching peers
* Provides clear expectations for both expert and teaching phases
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Expert groups may read, research, solve, or analyze different content
* Teaching groups may be called "home groups" or "mixed groups"
* May provide teaching guides or sentence stems for expert teaching
* Can be done with pairs (pair jigsaw) or larger groups
look_fors.strong_examples: "In expert groups, you'll have 10 minutes to become the class expert on your assigned topic. Then you'll teach it to three other students who learned different topics. I will give details on how to do this after the expert round" <Gives specific directions for expert round> <At transition point from expert to eaching groups, teacher gives specific directions for teaching round>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Table 1 will learn topic A, table 2 will learn topic B" but never regroups for teaching [Why attempting: Expert phase only, no jigsaw]
* Jigsaw structure set up but students unclear about teaching expectations [Why attempting: Structure incomplete]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Students work in groups but everyone learns same content together
* Teacher teaches all content; students never teach peers

look_fors.name: Learning Process Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on learning activities, content, or approach
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students for input on learning activities or topics
* Allows students to select their own examples or applications
* Provides choices in task approach during learning
* Invites students to share personal perspectives or connections
* Offers options for how to engage with content
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Choices may be guided or open-ended depending on learning objectives
* Can offer choice in sequence, grouping, scaffolds, or specific activities
* Student input may shape current or future lessons
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Choose which historical figure you want to research based on your interests"
* "When I say go, move to one of the three tables on the window side of the room if you prefer to work with a partner, and one of the three tables on the door side of the room if you prefer to work alone"
* "What examples should we use for this concept? Who has an idea from your own experience?"
* "You can choose if and when you use one of the available supports, such as the exemplar lab report from last week, the sentence starters for hypotheses, or the hint card with an image of one way to set up your materials" 
* "For today's homework, you can listen to the podcast OR complete the reading on this topic"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can work independently instead of with a partner. Teacher says yes. [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* "If you feel like the problems with fractions with different denominators are too hard, you can just choose the ones with the same denominators" [Why attempting: Offers choice, but lowers expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher selects all examples and applications without student input
* All students engage with content in identical way
* Dismisses student suggestions for how to approach learning
* Never asks students what interests them or connects to their experiences
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.name: Learning Product Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on how to demonstrate learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Offers choices in demonstration method (written, oral, visual, performance, etc.)
* Provides options for final product format
* Invites student input on how they want to show what they know
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Student input may be solicited before task or as options are presented
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can show your understanding by writing an explanation, creating a diagram, or explaining it aloud to a partner"
* "Would you like to present your findings as a poster, a speech, or a written report?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can do a presentation instead of write an essay for their final product. Teacher says yes.  [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* Offers one alternative option but frames it as "easier"
look_fors.non_examples:
* All students complete identical task in identical format with no variation
* Teacher selects all demonstration methods without offering alternatives
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.name: Student Agency for Learning Needs
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in voicing needs and making adjustments to their learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher asks students what they need (e.g., "What would help you right now?", "What resources do you need?")
* Teacher responds to student-initiated requests for support, resources, or changes
* Students articulate specific learning needs (e.g., "I need more examples," "I am stuck on the unit conversion," etc.)
* Students make adjustments to their approach based on self-monitoring or self-assessment (e.g., choose different resources, modify their strategy, seek help)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Needs may relate to: pacing, resources, supports, task modifications, clarification, or different learning pathways
* Teacher may offer menu of options or students may self-select without prompting
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During independent work, student raises hand: "If the photosphere is the visible surface of the sun, why is it on the inside of the diagram?" Teacher: "The key is the word visible. The photosphere is what the human eye can see. What do you think that means about the chronosphere?" Student "Oh, ok, it's above the photosphere but we can't see it". <Student goes back to work>.
* Student: "I'm stuck. I can't figure out why I keep getting my unit conversions wrong." Teacher: "Can you think of anything that would help you get unstuck?" Student: "Can I see another example of the joules to ergs conversion?" <Teacher directs student to exemplar, student reviews it and then goes back to their own problem set.>
* Students review criteria for success and make edits to their own work based on their self-evaluations.
* Teacher says "Some of you finished early and some need more time. Decide what you need: more practice, start the extension, or revise your work." <Students make different choices based on their self-assessment>
* During writing conference, student says: "I'm stuck on my introduction. Can I start with my body paragraphs first and come back to it?" Teacher affirms: "That's a great strategy - many writers do that." <Student adjusts their approach>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Student asks "Can you help me?" Teacher helps but doesn't prompt student to identify specific need [Why attempting: Student initiates but doesn't articulate specific need]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher assigns all students the same intervention or support without asking what they need [type: missed opportunity]
* Student says "I don't get it" or "I"m stuck" and waits for teacher to fix it [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks if there are any questions and moves on immediately or after a couple students say no [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Goal-Setting
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in establishing and tracking goals
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Facilitates process for students to set personal or collective goals
* Provides structure for students to monitor or reflect on progress toward goals
* Conferences with students about their goals
* Celebrates progress toward student-identified goals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Goals may be academic, behavioral, or both
* Can be short-term (daily/weekly) or long-term (unit/semester)
* May use goal-setting templates, trackers, or reflection protocols
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Today you'll each set a goal for what you want to improve. We'll check in on Fridays to see your progress"
* "Look at your data from the last assessment. Based on that, what's one skill you want to strengthen?"
* Students maintain goal-tracking sheets and regularly reflect on progress
* "Now that we've identified group strengths relative to our class norms, take 2 minutes to write a personal goal relative to our class norms. Refer to the examples on the board if you need some inspiration!"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What do you want to work on today?" [Why attempting: Vague]
* "Here are our class goals. Raise your hand if you would like propose any changes or additions" [Why attempting: Teacher-led with student input]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All goals set by teacher without student input
* Goals never referenced

look_fors.name: Student Leadership
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Allow students to lead activities, discussions, or demonstrations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Invites students to lead parts of lesson or activity
* Has students teach or demonstrate for the class
* Assigns formal or informal leadership roles
* Student takes charge while teacher observes or supports
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May scaffold leadership with preparation or support first
* Leadership may be brief (leading one example) or extended (leading full activity/presentation)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Jamal, will you come up and lead the class through your example?"
* "Who can be the teacher and explain this to the class?"
* Student leads call and response letter-sound review while teacher observes
* Teacher assigns student to lead small group through specific protocol or procedure
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student comes to board to share answer but teacher talks through most of the solution [Why attempting: Teacher still leading most]
* Leadership opportunities only for select students [Why attempting: Not equitable access]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher directs all activities and discussions
* Students only respond when called upon, never take charge
* "Who wants to share?"  [Why non-example: Invites participation but not leadership]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Support Student-to-Student Discourse
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Route conversation through students rather than always through teacher
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs students to respond to each other and build on peer ideas in discussion 
* Steps back during student-to-student exchanges
* As needed, reminds students to respond to each other ("What do you think about Maya's idea?")
* As needed, reminds students to build on peer ideas ("Add on to what Marcus said")
* Students respond to and build on each other's ideas
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May provide supports such as initial model or academic discourse norms
 * Can use structured prompts ("Do you agree or disagree with...?")
 * May redirect specific students to each other or open it to whole class
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Ok, let's discuss our key question for the day. For the next three minutes, I will step to the side unless I need to give a quick reminder. Use our academic discourse norms to discuss the key question as a group. In particular, Don't forget to respond to and build on each other's ideas and monitor your air time." 
 * "Marcus, what do you think about Keisha's explanation? Do you agree or see it differently?"
 * "Who can add to that idea?" <student responds to peer's thinking, not restating own idea>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus and a thumbs down if you do not" <most students give thumbs up, a couple give thumbs down> Teacher: "Yes, Marcus was correct" <teacher moves on> [Why attempting: Missed opportunity for student-to-student discussion]
 * <One student gives response> Teacher: "What do you think, Kim?" [Why attempting: Implies potential peer-to-peer response, but unclear]
look_fors.non_examples:
* All student responses go to teacher who then responds or calls on next student
 * "I’m sure we all agree with Marcus's great point about…" [Why non-example: Assumes student response rather than students giving response]

skills.name: Student Autonomy and Responsibility (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Students carry out established classroom routines with minimal prompting and have a voice in shaping them.

look_fors.name: Routine Cue
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: For an established routine, give a brief cue or direction instead of restating full steps.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Gives a short cue (a word, number, phrase, direction, countdown, or signal) rather than restating the routine's steps with details
- Cue prompts students to independently carry out a previously-taught routine, in part or in full
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Cue may be verbal (word, number, direction, phrase), a countdown, or a non-verbal signal
- Cue may launch the full routine at once, mark movement between steps students already know, or briefly reference a single step (e.g., a short reminder) without restating that step's full details
- Cue may include specifics that change each time the routine is used (e.g., in a turn and talk, cue may include question or task, time, and who talks first)
- Applies to both behavioral/logistical routines (e.g., class entry/exit) and academic-engagement routines (e.g., turn and talk)
- Applies only to routines that recur regularly (e.g., classroom entry, do now, materials, exit ticket, classroom exit) once they've already been taught; new or unfamiliar routines and activity directions are out of scope
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Ok, let's transition to centers." <Students hesitate and several ask where to go> [Why attempting: Brief cue given, but routine not yet automatic]
- "OK now turn and talk." [Why attempting: cue is brief, but lacks key information, such as time and topic, for student success]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "First, put away your materials. Remember, your folder goes in your backpack and pencils go in the central caddy. Then, stand up and push your chair in silently like I am doing right now. Finally, walk to the door with your hands to yourselves to line up. Before we begin, what’s the first step?" [Why non-example: Re-teaches rather than cueing]
- <A few students forget to push in their chairs> "Everyone pause. Let's review — when you stand up, push your chair all the way in so it's out of the walking path. Watch me do it." [Why non-example: Pauses to reteach the full class a routine step over a few students missing a piece, rather than giving a brief individualized reminder]
- "A turn and talk is where you talk to one partner about a question I give you. Each time I tell you to turn and talk, you will face your partner, knee to knee, and talk in an inside voice. I will tell you the amount of time you have and which partner should go first. For example, I might say, 'turn and talk about the differences between the two characters for three minutes. You have three minutes and the partner with the longer hair goes first.'" [Why non-example: Full explanation rather than brief cue/direction]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Foster Student Ownership of Culture, Solicit Student Feedback, or Implement Student Feedback is required for a score of 90+; below that, demonstrating or partially demonstrating one of these three also satisfies the Optional Look-For Rule
look_fors.name: Foster Student Ownership of Culture
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Involve students in creating and maintaining classroom norms
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Co-creates classroom expectations or agreements with students
* Asks students to reflect on or evaluate classroom culture
* Invites student input on how to improve learning environment
* References shared norms that students helped establish
* Has students lead culture-building activities
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use different terminlogy (e.g., norms, values, acronym the class comes up with like ROAR or SHINE that covers co-created norms, etc.)
* May have students create visual representations of norms
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's reflect on how we're doing with our classroom agreements. What's working well? What do we need to strengthen?"
* "As a class, what norms should we establish for our discussions so everyone feels heard?"
* "You all decided respect and collaboration were important. I noticed that slipping today. How can we reset?"
* Students hold each other accountable to shared norms without teacher intervention
* "Who has a shout out for a peer who is exemplifying our classroom values?
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Don't forget our norms." 
* Rarely disscusses or references shared classroom culture norms or expectations
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher establishes rules without student input
* Never disscusses or references shared classroom culture norms or expectations
* Treats norms as teacher's expectations only

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Foster Student Ownership of Culture, Solicit Student Feedback, or Implement Student Feedback is required for a score of 90+; below that, demonstrating or partially demonstrating one of these three also satisfies the Optional Look-For Rule
look_fors.name: Implement Student Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Make a visible change to routines, culture, or supports based on student feedback.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- References specific feedback previously shared by students or responds to in-the-moment feedback from student(s)
- Describes or enacts a change made in response to that feedback
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Feedback referenced may have been gathered on a previous day or given in the moment
- Change may be to a routine, a classroom culture practice, or a learning support
- Change may be announced to the whole class or applied for an individual or small group
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "In your survey last week, a bunch of you said the centers rotation felt rushed. So starting today, each rotation is five minutes instead of three."
- Student: "Can we talk about ideas at our table before we write a procedure?" Teacher: "Good idea. Let's take two minutes for discussion before you start writing." 
- "You all mentioned in our discussion that the caddies are distracting when we're not using them. I moved the caddies to the front table they are easy to find when we need them and out of the way when we don't need them."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "I heard some of you wanted an easier way to line up. Let's just try lining up by table today." [Why attempting: change made, but link to specific prior feedback is vague]
look_fors.non_examples: - "Some of you didn't like the seating chart. Do your best to get along with your group today." [Why non-example: names feedback but doesn't implement a change]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Foster Student Ownership of Culture, Solicit Student Feedback, or Implement Student Feedback is required for a score of 90+; below that, demonstrating or partially demonstrating one of these three also satisfies the Optional Look-For Rule
look_fors.name: Solicit Student Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students for input on classroom routines, culture, or learning supports.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Poses a question or provides a survey/prompt asking for student input
- Input requested concerns classroom routines, procedures, culture, or learning supports
- Question is open enough to surface a range of student perspectives or suggestions
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered via written survey, digital form, discussion, or informal verbal check-in
* May be directed to the whole class, small groups, or an individual
* May ask about something specific (e.g., a particular routine) or open-ended (e.g., what would help you learn better)
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Any thoughts on how centers are going?" [Why attempting: vague prompt, unlikely to surface actionable input]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Survey asks only about student interests or identity (e.g., "What's your favorite subject?") [Why non-example: personal interest, not feedback on the learning environment]
* "Does everyone like how we do morning routine?" <No response solicited or expected> [Why non-example: rhetorical, not a genuine ask]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Student Agency for Learning Needs, Student Leadership, Foster Student Ownership of Culture, Solicit Student Feedback, or Implement Student Feedback must be demonstrated or partially demonstrated
look_fors.name: Student Agency for Learning Needs
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in voicing needs and making adjustments to their learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher asks students what they need (e.g., "What would help you right now?", "What resources do you need?")
* Teacher responds to student-initiated requests for support, resources, or changes
* Students articulate specific learning needs (e.g., "I need more examples," "I am stuck on the unit conversion," etc.)
* Students make adjustments to their approach based on self-monitoring or self-assessment (e.g., choose different resources, modify their strategy, seek help)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Needs may relate to: pacing, resources, supports, task modifications, clarification, or different learning pathways
* Teacher may offer menu of options or students may self-select without prompting
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During independent work, student raises hand: "If the photosphere is the visible surface of the sun, why is it on the inside of the diagram?" Teacher: "The key is the word visible. The photosphere is what the human eye can see. What do you think that means about the chronosphere?" Student "Oh, ok, it's above the photosphere but we can't see it". <Student goes back to work>.
* Student: "I'm stuck. I can't figure out why I keep getting my unit conversions wrong." Teacher: "Can you think of anything that would help you get unstuck?" Student: "Can I see another example of the joules to ergs conversion?" <Teacher directs student to exemplar, student reviews it and then goes back to their own problem set.>
* Students review criteria for success and make edits to their own work based on their self-evaluations.
* Teacher says "Some of you finished early and some need more time. Decide what you need: more practice, start the extension, or revise your work." <Students make different choices based on their self-assessment>
* During writing conference, student says: "I'm stuck on my introduction. Can I start with my body paragraphs first and come back to it?" Teacher affirms: "That's a great strategy - many writers do that." <Student adjusts their approach>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Student asks "Can you help me?" Teacher helps but doesn't prompt student to identify specific need [Why attempting: Student initiates but doesn't articulate specific need]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher assigns all students the same intervention or support without asking what they need [type: missed opportunity]
* Student says "I don't get it" or "I"m stuck" and waits for teacher to fix it [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks if there are any questions and moves on immediately or after a couple students say no [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: At least one of Student Agency for Learning Needs, Student Leadership, Foster Student Ownership of Culture, Solicit Student Feedback, or Implement Student Feedback must be demonstrated or partially demonstrated
look_fors.name: Student Leadership
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Allow students to lead activities, discussions, or demonstrations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Invites students to lead parts of lesson or activity
* Has students teach or demonstrate for the class
* Assigns formal or informal leadership roles
* Student takes charge while teacher observes or supports
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May scaffold leadership with preparation or support first
* Leadership may be brief (leading one example) or extended (leading full activity/presentation)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Jamal, will you come up and lead the class through your example?"
* "Who can be the teacher and explain this to the class?"
* Student leads call and response letter-sound review while teacher observes
* Teacher assigns student to lead small group through specific protocol or procedure
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student comes to board to share answer but teacher talks through most of the solution [Why attempting: Teacher still leading most]
* Leadership opportunities only for select students [Why attempting: Not equitable access]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher directs all activities and discussions
* Students only respond when called upon, never take charge
* "Who wants to share?"  [Why non-example: Invites participation but not leadership]

skills.name: Student Explanation
skills.description: Prompt students to elaborate on their learning and explain their thinking.

look_fors.name: Follow up Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use questions to push student thinking
look_fors.observable_behaviors: * Asks students to elaborate, explain reasoning, or provide evidence
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May direct follow-ups to original speaker OR redirect to other students
* May invite students to agree, disagree, or add on to peer responses ("Do you agree with ___? Why?")
* May ask for clarification or specificity ("What do you mean by...", "Can you show me where...")
* May probe connections between ideas ("How does this relate to...", "Why does this matter?")
* May scaffold incorrect responses toward correct understanding with targeted questions
* May focus on process ("How did you figure that out?") OR product ("Why is this answer stronger?")
* May be paired with a variety of question response formats (e.g., turn and talk, cold call, everybody writes, etc.)
* Often involves a sequence of questions to push for deeper thinking, but may not need multiple questions if initial student response is strong and detailed
* May be posed as a standalone/initiating question, not only in reaction to a prior student response
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Which student's response did you choose and why?" <Student: "Student B because it has more details"> "Say more about that - what kind of details make Student B's response stronger?" <Student explains> "Good. Maya, do you agree with that? Why or why not?" <Maya responds> "So you're both noticing that Student B shows what Amos actually did. How does that connect to our goal of using strong evidence?"

* "Why did I substitute in the values of x and y from the point given in the problem?" <Student: "Because it was in the problem"> "You're right that I used information from the problem. But why did I need to substitute those specific values? What was I trying to find?" <Student: "The b"> "Yes! I was solving for b, the y-intercept. I knew I could substitute 5 for x and 1 for y because the problem told me the point (5, 1) was on the line. So let's try again - why did I substitute those values into the equation?"

* "Water has a positive and negative side, but methane doesn't. How might that structural difference impact how each interacts with oil?" <Posed as an opening question, not in reaction to a prior student response>
