look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Walk us through your answer [Why attempting: Too vague]
* "Give a thumbs up if you agree with Marcus" [Why attempting: builds on one students' response, but doesn't require explanation of thinking]
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here?" <Points> [Why attempting: Provides related practice but doesn't ask students to explain their thinking process]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts first response and moves on without probing
* Asks vague check for understanding question rather than probing specific thinking (e.g., "does that make sense?", "do you have any questions?", etc.)
* Asks simple yes/no or recall question (e.g., "Did I figure out the pronoun correctly?", "What does precipitation mean?", "What value did I get for b?", etc.)

look_fors.name: Prompt Evaluation or Judgment
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to assess, critique, or make judgments about claims, work, or ideas
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students to evaluate the quality, accuracy, or strength of something (e.g., an argument, solution, peer response, or source)
* Asks students to weigh options, make a decision, and justify their choice
* Invites students to agree or disagree with a claim and explain why
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Target of evaluation may vary (e.g., teacher-generated examples, student work, texts, or real-world claims)
* May be structured (written criteria) or open-ended (verbal judgment)
* May ask students to evaluate whether evidence is sufficient or complete, not only its quality or strength
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Here are two student responses to the essay prompt. Which is stronger, and what makes it stronger? Use our rubric to decide." 
* "The author claims social media is making teens less happy. Is that argument convincing? What evidence would you need to be sure?"
* "We got two different answers to this problem. Can both be right? How would you decide which one to trust?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Do you agree or disagree?" with no follow-up for reasoning [Why attempting: invites a stance but not evaluation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Asks students to recall or describe rather than evaluate (e.g., "What did the author say?")
* Asks recall questions

look_fors.name: Prompt Generalization Assessment
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask whether a pattern or rule holds true in other cases
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks whether a pattern, rule, or relationship the student identified holds true in a new, hypothetical, or more general case
* Asks student to apply current thinking or a stated rule to a different case or situation
* Question extends beyond the specific instance or task at hand
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May reference a hypothetical scenario or an actual different case, not only the current task
* May be posed as a standalone/initiating question or follow directly from the immediate task
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "You noticed water has a positive and negative side. Do all molecules have a positive and negative side? Why or why not?"
* "You found this triangle's angles add up to 180. Is that always true for triangles? How do you know?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Does this pattern happen with other molecules?" [Why attempting: Yes/no, doesn't ask for reasoning or transfer]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher: "So this pattern would also happen with other nonpolar molecules." [Why non-example: States rather than asks]
* Student: "The angles add up to 180." Teacher: "Great, next problem." [Why non-example: Misses opportunity to extend]

look_fors.name: Require Reasoning or Justification
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Establish the norm that answers must include reasoning or evidence
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Sets or reinforces the expectation that students explain thinking, not just give answer
* Provides and references supports for reasoning and justification (e.g., sentence starters, posted norms)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Reasoning standard may be content-specific ("use evidence from the text") or general ("tell me how you know")
* May use follow up questions to push students who answer without reasoning to explain; however, for look-for to be strong, the expectation for reasoning or justification must be proactively established
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I don't just want to know what you think, I want to know why. So, remember to use our sentence frame: I think ___, because ___"
 * Student: "The answer is 12" Teacher: "You might be right — but I need the how you got there. Walk me through your reasoning." <student responds with reasoning> Teacher: "That's the kind of thinking I want to hear every time."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Can you say more?" [Why attempting: prompts elaboration but doesn't establish reasoning as a standing expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Accepts correct answers without asking for reasoning (e.g., "Great answer! Who else?")
* Only asks for justification when an answer is wrong

skills.name: Student Feedback (OnYourMark)
skills.description: Give students immediate, individual-specific feedback that names what they are doing well and what to adjust, while keeping the thinking and talk on the student.

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame tasks as challenging yet worthy while maintaining rigorous standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Acknowledges difficulty/high expectations but doesn't frame as worthy (e.g., "This is hard" or "Oooh, a spicy problem!")
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
* Assigning easier work to struggling students without scaffolding the grade-level content [Why non-example: Reduces rigor]

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
* Feedback may address content, process, or self-regulation
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Your thesis clearly states your position. To strengthen paragraph 2, add textual evidence like you did in paragraph 1, then explain how it supports your claim"
* "You accurately identified the problem. Now show your work step-by-step so I can see your mathematical thinking. Look at the example on the anchor chart for the format"
" Now, I want you to try holding your scissors with just your thumb and pointer finger from your right hand."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Your evidence is weak. Add more quotes" [Why attempting: Identifies issue but doesn't explain how to select strong evidence]
* "Nice work on the intro. The body needs more details" [Why attempting: Names strength and area for improvement but lacks concrete next steps]
* "This is better than last time" [Why attempting: Acknowledges growth but not specific about what improved or next steps]
*  "Keep working. Make sure that you use the visual anchors around the classroom to help you." [Why attempting: Lacks specificity as to what to improve or how to use visual anchors]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Good job" [Why non-example: Generic without specifics] [type: missed opportunity]
* "This needs work" [Why non-example: Identifies problem but no actionable steps] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You're not there yet - keep trying" [Why non-example: No specific guidance for improvement] [type: missed opportunity]
* Only marking errors without explanation or guidance [Why non-example: No actionable next steps] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required when feedback needs to direct the student's next action (what to do / how to do it); else not required
look_fors.name: Specific Directions
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Tell students exactly what they should be doing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Tells students what to do (not what not to do)
* Directions include necessary details for task success
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Routine tasks may require less specificity. New or complex tasks, routines or procedures, or routines or procedures that need to be retaught may require more specificty. 
* For multi-step routines or procedures, specificity should apply to each step
* Necessary details for task success might include components like time length, task location in room or on paper/screen, voice/volume level, task goal or criteria for success, task rationale or what to do if finished early. Specific directions only need the components from this list that are needed for student success; they do not need to include ALL components all the time.
* When given as feedback during a task, directions may target only the specific portion of the task the student is struggling with rather than the full task.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Take 5 minutes to independently find key evidence that supports the author's claim in the text. When you find a key piece of evidence, underline it."
* "Before you move on to question 2, add a diagram to your response for question 1."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Find the key evidence in the text and underline it." [Why attempting: Missing time, independent/group mode, specification of key evidence in context]
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't just underline everything." [Why non-example: What not to do, vague]

skills.name: Student Metacognition
skills.description: Create structures and opportunities for students to monitor their own understanding, evaluate their work quality, and advocate for their learning needs.

look_fors.name: Student Agency for Learning Needs
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in voicing needs and making adjustments to their learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher asks students what they need (e.g., "What would help you right now?", "What resources do you need?")
* Teacher responds to student-initiated requests for support, resources, or changes
* Students articulate specific learning needs (e.g., "I need more examples," "I am stuck on the unit conversion," etc.)
* Students make adjustments to their approach based on self-monitoring or self-assessment (e.g., choose different resources, modify their strategy, seek help)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Needs may relate to: pacing, resources, supports, task modifications, clarification, or different learning pathways
* Teacher may offer menu of options or students may self-select without prompting
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During independent work, student raises hand: "If the photosphere is the visible surface of the sun, why is it on the inside of the diagram?" Teacher: "The key is the word visible. The photosphere is what the human eye can see. What do you think that means about the chronosphere?" Student "Oh, ok, it's above the photosphere but we can't see it". <Student goes back to work>.
* Student: "I'm stuck. I can't figure out why I keep getting my unit conversions wrong." Teacher: "Can you think of anything that would help you get unstuck?" Student: "Can I see another example of the joules to ergs conversion?" <Teacher directs student to exemplar, student reviews it and then goes back to their own problem set.>
* Students review criteria for success and make edits to their own work based on their self-evaluations.
* Teacher says "Some of you finished early and some need more time. Decide what you need: more practice, start the extension, or revise your work." <Students make different choices based on their self-assessment>
* During writing conference, student says: "I'm stuck on my introduction. Can I start with my body paragraphs first and come back to it?" Teacher affirms: "That's a great strategy - many writers do that." <Student adjusts their approach>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Student asks "Can you help me?" Teacher helps but doesn't prompt student to identify specific need [Why attempting: Student initiates but doesn't articulate specific need]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher assigns all students the same intervention or support without asking what they need [type: missed opportunity]
* Student says "I don't get it" or "I"m stuck" and waits for teacher to fix it [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks if there are any questions and moves on immediately or after a couple students say no [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Self-Monitoring and Self-Reflection
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to do metacognitive checks or reflections on their own learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts students to monitor their own understanding, confidence, or progress
* Students pause to meta-cognitively reflect on their own learning in-the-moment or after a specific lesson, task, or goal is completed
* Students often identify when they're stuck, confused, or need help
* Students describe how their understanding or confidence has changed over time
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Monitoring tools vary by context (e.g., emoji check-ins for confidence ratings, answer keys for accuracy, progress trackers for completion, targeted questions for considering response quality, etc.)
* Students may track their own progress using provided tools (e.g., confidence scales, answer keys, completion trackers)
* May be embedded as a recurring routine (e.g., a daily exit ticket format, weekly reflection protocol) rather than a one-time prompt
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <At the end of a lesson> "Take 2 minutes to complete the statement 'I used to think... now I know...' based on what you have learned today."
* "On a scale of 1-5, how confident are you that you understand why the character made that choice?" <Students show fingers, teacher sees mix of 2s and 4s> "Turn to your partner and explain why you chose that number." <Students discuss their confidence levels>
* What was most challenging for you today? What helped you work through it?"
* "Place your green, yellow, or red circle on the top of the stack on your desk to indicate if you are ready to move on, need a little help, or are completely stuck"
* "Take a moment to reflect: What strategy did you use? How well did it work? What might you try differently next time?"
* "Now that you have peer feedback on your essay, turn and talk to a new partner about one major strength of your current essay and one next step you will take to revise it"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "During the work time, raise your hand if you need help" [Why attempting:Students are invited to self-monitor, but question is unlikely to lead to all students engaging in metacognitive monitoring]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Does everyone understand?" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher circulates and identifies confused students but students don't self-identify [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Support and Perseverance (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Build a classroom culture where students feel safe to take risks, persist through challenges, and support one another.

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required for exemplary rating on Danielson 2b: Support and Perseverence
Else not required
look_fors.name: Facilitate Student-to-Student Relationships
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create structures and opportunities for students to interact positively with each other
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses instructional structures that require student interaction (turn and talks, partner work, group discussions)
* Creates opportunities for students to give each other recognition
* Students demonstrate respect when peers speak or share
* Students show care for each other (affirming comments, applause, support)
* Students demonstrate knowledge of one another as individuals (e.g., interests, events, traditions, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Student-to-student interactions can occur through structured academic tasks, classroom routines, or social-emotional activities
* Can involve brief partner interactions or extended collaborative work
* May include sentence or question frames for productive discussion (e.g., "Can you explain...?," "I agree because...," "I disagree because...," etc.)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Students respond positively to peers who share (e.g., hand signals to show encouragement, building on each others' ideas, etc.)
* "Let's take a moment for shout-outs. Who noticed someone doing something kind or helpful today?" <multiple students recognize peers>
* Teacher structures lesson with multiple turn-and-talks and small group work. Students proactively demonstrate respect for each other by not interrupting each other, waiting for speakers to finish, and building on each other's ideas. Students appear comfortable engaging with various classmates.
* Teacher or students refer to class norms either for praise or positively framed reminders
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Students work in pairs or groups but some students dominate the conversation or students do not recognize or encourage each other [Why attempting: Structure exists but lacks intentional development of positive relationships]
* Student-to-student interactions are rarely hostile or dismissive, but when a negative interaction does occur teacher does not respond
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lesson consists entirely of teacher-led instruction with no student-to-student interaction opportunities [type: missed opportunity]
* Student-to-student interactions are sometimes or often hostile or dismissive (e.g., "Ha, you don't know what you're talking about," "Ugh, do I have to work with Mariana?," students interrupt each other, etc.) [type: relational harm, severe]
* Any form of bullying goes unaddressed [type: relational harm, severe]

look_fors.name: Emphasize Collective Success
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame learning as community endeavor where all contribute
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses "we" language when discussing learning and progress
* Frames individual success as benefiting the group
* Teacher and students celebrate whole-class achievements or growth
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May use class goals or challenges
* May highlight how diverse perspectives strengthen collective understanding
* May create accountability to peers, not just to teacher
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We're all learning together, and each person's ideas make us all smarter. With that in mind, let's here from a few different perspectives to help us interpret the evidence we collected"
* "Our collective effort helped us reach this milestone. Everyone contributed"
* Creates team game structure where students work together toward shared goal
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Use of we/our language without explicit connection to goals, collective work, classroom community, etc. (e.g., "Welcome to our classroom!", "Today we will work together to learn....", etc.)
* Let's here from a few different perspectives on this one" [Why attempting: Implies but does not make explicit individual contribution to strengthen whole group learning]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Only individual competition or achievement recognized
* "My classroom" language
* Emphasizes individual success without connecting to community

look_fors.name: Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Create conditions where students attempt challenging work safely
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly invites students to try even if unsure (e.g., "Give it a shot, even if you're not certain, this will help you learn and help me see your thinking")
* Recognizes attempts and effort, not just correct answers
* Provides support structures that allow productive struggle (think time, partner talk, resources)

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Encourage Academic Risk-Taking
* Student shares incorrect answer [rationale: not clear evidence that student feels safe, they may have thought their answer was correct]
* Teacher asks follow up questions or asks students to build on others' thinking [rationale: not a bad practice, but does not explicitly create safe conditions for risk-taking]
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* When applicable, includes statements like "There's no right answer" or "Multiple approaches work here"
* May celebrate "wrong" answers that show sophisticated reasoning
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I want to hear your thinking even if you're not 100% sure. Your ideas will help us all learn"
* "We're figuring things out together rather than just looking for the 'right' answer"
* "Try it out in your voice and we can all learn from each other's writing" 
* "Turn and talk with a partner to share thinking before we discuss as a class"
* Remember, you have a toolbox for when you feel stuck. Consult the rubric or phone a friend!"  
* "I actually expect some of your first attempts to be unsuccessful. If you finish this without running into a single issue, you probably didn't take a big enough risk. I'm looking for how you pivot when things get messy, not just the final product."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you get it wrong" [Why attempting: no connection to learning value]
* "Be sure everyone participates!" [Why attempting: generic participation encouragement instead of explicitly encouraging academic risk taking]
* Validates partially correct answers [Why attempting: Implies recognition of effort, but not explicit]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher consistently calls on same few students who raise hands with confidence [type: missed opportunity]
* "Don't worry, this one is easy" [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarrass or demotivate a student from taking future risks (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Group Roles
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Assign and support specific roles to student group members to support collaboration
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Assigns or has students assign specific roles within groups
* Names roles and responsibilities (e.g., facilitator, recorder, timekeeper, materials manager, reporter)
* Refers to roles during activity to support accountability
  Roles distribute responsibility across all group members
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Roles can vary based on task (discussion roles vs. task roles)
* May provide role cards or descriptions
* In a tutoring context, there may only be one group and group may be small (e.g., 2 students only)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "In your groups, assign these roles: facilitator to keep discussion moving, recorder to capture ideas, timekeeper to monitor pace, and reporter to share findings. Each person is essential to your success"
* "Today's roles are: reader, materials manager, and checker. I'll explain each job and then you will decide who will do what in your group." 
 * "You'll need a question-asker and a summarizer in each pair. Take 10 seconds to decide who does what"
 * Provides role cards with specific responsibilities for each group member
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Assigns only one role ("Someone be the recorder") 
* "Make sure each person in your group contributes something to the discussion"
look_fors.non_examples: * "Work with your table group" <no roles or structure provided>

look_fors.name: Normalize Mistakes as Learning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state that errors are part of learning and respond to mistakes or misconceptions as opportunities to learn
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States that mistakes help learning 
* Responds to errors with curiosity rather than clarification alone
* Publicly acknowledges own mistakes as learning opportunities
* Thanks students for sharing mistakes that help class learning
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May frame revision as normal part of learning process
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections. Let's look at what this mistake can teach us"
* <Teacher makes and catches own error> "Oops! Can anyone find the mistake I just made?" <Student answers> "Thanks! Next time I will..."
*  <Student work shows two divided by zero is two> Teacher: "Oooh, interesting thinking here! Walk me through why you think two divided by zero is two." <Listens to student thinking, and connects to thinking when providing clarification>
* "This is a really interesting misconception. I used to think that the seasons were caused by Earth's distance from the sun, too. This is a logical guess, but it's not what's actually happening, which blew my mind a little when I learned the real answer!"<Teacher demonstrates misconception clarification and comes back to original student to share updated thinking>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "It's okay if you make a mistake" [Why attempting: Reassures but doesn't frame mistakes as valuable]
* <Student gives partially correct answer.> Teacher: "Good start. You're getting there" <does not explain why, calls on another student>. [Why attempting: Somewhat affirming but doesn't use error as learning opportunity]
look_fors.non_examples:
- <student gives wrong answer> "No, that's not right. Who else?" [Why non-example: Dismisses error without learning value] [type: relational harm]
- Only acknowledges correct answers with praise [type: missed opportunity]
- "You mixed up the numerator and denominator AGAIN" <exasperated tone> [Why non-example: judgmental of error] [type: relational harm]
- Tells one student to explain to another why they are wrong [Why non-example: Negatively framed with emphasis on wrong vs. correct instead of what can be learned] [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Promote Growth Mindset
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame ability as developable through effort
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses words like "yet," "so far," "not yet," when students struggle
* Emphasizes progress and improvement over fixed ability
* References brain growth or learning as a process
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May teach explicitly about neuroplasticity and brain development
* Can highlight individual student growth over time
* May use metaphors about building skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can't do this yet, but with practice your brain will build new connections"
* "You've shown such growth since the beginning of the year. Look how far you've come"
* "This is challenging work, and you're learning to handle it. Every time you struggle through hard problems, your brain gets stronger"
* "Making mistakes means your brain is working hard and making new connections"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "You can do it if you try hard" [Why attempting: Emphasizes effort but doesn't explicitly frame ability as developable]
* Uses "yet" occasionally but inconsistently
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Some people are just good at math"
* "You either get it or you don't"
* Implies ability is fixed ("You're a natural")

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Supporting Expectations
skills.description: Use proactive and responsive techniques to help students meet established expectations

look_fors.name: Affirming Non-Verbal Cues
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use non-verbal cues to acknowledge and encourage students in the moment.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Uses gesture, facial expression, or other physical cue that acknowledges or encourages a specific student action (e.g., thumbs up, nod, smile)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be paired with a brief verbal acknowledgment or delivered silently
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Nods and gives a thumbs up to a student who just worked through a tricky step on their own
* Directs spirit fingers at a student thinking through an answer to show support
look_fors.attempting_examples: Gives a general, undirected affirming cue rather than one tied to a specific student action (e.g., smiles at the whole class, gives a thumbs up as a generic "go ahead" signal after directions rather than in response to something a student did)
look_fors.non_examples: Gives only negative cues (e.g., finger shaking, cut it out gesture)

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required if has already attempted circulate and/or scan, support/reminder non-verbal cues, affirming non-verbal cues, and positive narration and there are still students not meeting the expectation. 
Else not required.
look_fors.name: Anonymous Group Reminders
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give a brief, positively framed reminder and/or anonymized statement of encouragement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States expectation positively without naming specific students (e.g., "we are silently doing..."; "waiting on X number" or "I have almost everyone")
 * May include brief rationale
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “You are talking quietly to one partner about the prompt on the board for another minute,”
* “Remember to independently add your evidence in the left hand column so you can reference it later”
* “We are only waiting on two. Almost there!”
* “I have got about 80% of the class, can we can get to 100% in the next 5 seconds?.”
* “Staying silent helps everyone concentrate on their independent thinking and writing”
* “Make sure to add units to your measurement, otherwise others won’t know if you mean 4 inches or 4 miles”.
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Only three classmates are still off task" [Why attempting: Anonymous but framed negatively]
 * "We're almost there, just waiting on Mayme and Diana" [Positive but not anonymous]
look_fors.non_examples:
* “Tables 3 and 5, you’re not following directions, pay attention”
 * “Forest, we’re waiting for you”
 * “Not showing your work means you lose points”
 * “If you can’t be quiet, I’m going to start giving demerits”

look_fors.name: Circulate
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Move throughout different areas of the room.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Moves position/location in room
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may stand still briefly to do things like read a slide, help a specific student, or model
* Circulation may be strategic (e.g., proximity to students who need support)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher moves throughout the room, visiting different areas and standing near different student groups
 * Circulating throughout the room, standing near students who are not yet on task
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher walks to back of room once but stays there [Why attempting: Moves but doesn't circulate throughout]
 * Teacher paces in front of room only [Why attempting: Movement but limited to one area]
look_fors.non_examples: Standing in one place for an extended period of time

look_fors.name: Positive Narration
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Name specific actions of individuals and groups that are meeting the expectation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific students/groups meeting expectations
* Narration describes specific actions (not general praise like "good job")
* Actions are framed in terms of what to do, not what not to do
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Brief "what not to do" acceptable if phrasing this way increases clarity (e.g., safety reminders, reminder to avoid a common error/pitfall, etc.) and delivery is warm
* May use shorter but less specific narration ("table 3 has it") when most students already working
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “I can tell tables 2, 3, and 5 are ready to start the experiment because they have all their materials set up to match the diagram on page 2”
* “Jenn, Abhi and Alice have already started underlining key details in the text”
 * “Lequite, Dave, and Eric are referring back to their timeline notes to help them get started”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Good job Lequite, Dave, and Eric” [Why attempting: vague praise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Most of us are not on task, let's get to it." [Why non-example: Negative/vague]
* ""Kiara, you shouldn't be on your phone right now." [Why non-example: Names student, what not to do]
* "I'll wait." [Why non-example: Passive-aggressive, vague]

look_fors.name: Support/Reminder Non-Verbal Cues
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use non-verbal physical cues to remind students of expectations.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Uses gesture or other physical cue to redirect attention or remind of an expectation (e.g., point, hand signal, proximity)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May be paired with a brief related verbal reminder or delivered silently
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Points to the area of a worksheet a student should be working on
* Taps twice on desk near a student who's drifted off-task as a quiet redirect
* Makes shh sign to student talking during independent work time
look_fors.attempting_examples: Gives non-verbal cue with an unclear meaning (e.g., shrug for student off-task)
look_fors.non_examples: Reprimanding a student immediately before trying a non-verbal reminder

look_fors.type_explanation:
Required if expectation/direction is new or complex. 
Else not required.
look_fors.name: Directions Check for Understanding
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Asks a question or asks a student to demonstrate to check for understanding of complex or new directions before students begin task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors: Asks question about directions or asks student to model/demonstrate part of the directions before students begin
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May also occur after students begin if many students are confused. In this situation, teacher should call on student who is meeting expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Which partner shares first?"
* "How long will you have for your table discussion?"
* "Everyone pick up your scissors and show me how you hold them safely"
* Ellie, you set up your t-chart correctly. Can you show your paper to the class?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: *"Everyone got that? [Why attempting: vague question; may be rhetorical]
look_fors.non_examples: No check for understanding of a new, complex direction

look_fors.name: Scan
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Visually monitor students across different areas of the room.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Eyes move across different students/areas
* Teacher's body orientation changes to face different parts of room
* Visual monitoring occurs whether teacher is standing still or moving
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Teacher may focus gaze and body orientation when interacting with a specific student or group or piece of content (e.g., on the board)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* While helping one student, teacher periodically looks up to scan rest of class
* Teacher turns body to face different sections of room, making eye contact with students in each area
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher glances up briefly but returns focus to materials [Why attempting: Minimal scanning]
 * Teacher scans one section of room but not others [Why attempting: Incomplete coverage]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher looks down at materials without looking at students [Why non-example: no scan]
* Teacher faces board/screen for extended period without turning to scan students [Why non-example: no scan]
* Teacher stares at one student/area only [Why non-example: Not scanning across room]

skills.name: Text-Dependent Questioning
skills.description: Ask and facilitate text-dependent questions that require students to return to the text for evidence, building in complexity from explicit recall toward inferential and evaluative understanding.

look_fors.type_explanation: Elaborative question; often the culminating, highest-order question in the sequence
look_fors.name: Elaborative Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that gets at the text's deeper understanding, theme, or overall meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question asks students to synthesize across the text (not a single detail) to identify a theme, lesson, or overall understanding
* Requires students to use evidence from the text to support a broader interpretive claim
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May ask students to state and defend a theme, lesson, or big-picture interpretation
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is this story teaching us about hard work? Use evidence from the text to explain."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What is the theme of this story?" <accepts a one-word answer with no evidence> [Why attempting: elaborative question, but no textual support required]
look_fors.non_examples: "Do you think hard work is important?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Should be applied with EVERY text-dependent question
look_fors.name: Engage All Students
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt every student to respond, not just volunteers
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher prompts every student to respond, not only volunteers or hand-raisers
* Every student produces a response (spoken, written, gestured, or signaled)
* Teacher follows up with non-responders rather than accepting partial participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Participation may be simultaneous — choral response, whiteboards, everybody writes / stop and jot, or turn and talk — or sequential (every student takes a turn)
* A student may pass in the moment if the teacher returns to them before the segment ends
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard. Then, when I say show me, hold it up." <Pauses, scans boards> "Dani, Sam, give me your best guess" <Pauses until all students have answer written> "Show me." <Scans all boards> "I've got all but three boards up, let's get to 100%" <Waits until all boards are up>
- "We're going around the circle — everyone gives one word describing the narrator. If you need time, say 'come back to me.'" <Every student contributes; teacher returns to the two who passed>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "Everyone write your answer on your whiteboard." <Teacher scans the front two tables> "Great, moving on." <Several boards in the back are blank> [Why attempting: no follow-up on non-responders]
- "Talk to your partner. Partner closest to the door: share how you categorized the example and why. You have 1 minute." <Students talk; teacher never has second partner share> [Why attempting: Only tells one partner to share]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Who can tell me the theme of this chapter?" <Four hands raise; teacher calls on one student, affirms the answer, and moves on>
- "Look at this book. What do you see?" [Why non-example: No clear expectation that everyone responds, or for how to respond]

look_fors.type_explanation: Explicit question; generally comes earliest in the questioning sequence
look_fors.name: Explicit Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question whose answer is directly stated in the text ("right there").
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question can be answered by locating information stated outright in the text
* Answer does not require inference or interpretation beyond locating/paraphrasing what is stated
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May ask students to quote the exact text or paraphrase what is stated, or locate it within the text
* May be posed before, during, or after reading a passage
look_fors.strong_examples: "What did Mary's mother do after her father died?" (Answer: she sold everything — directly stated in the text)
look_fors.attempting_examples: "What happened in this chapter?" [Why attempting: text-dependent, but too broad to pinpoint a specific explicitly-stated detail]
look_fors.non_examples: "What does 'sold' mean?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Implicit question; generally increases in complexity after explicit questions
look_fors.name: Implicit Text-Dependent Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question whose answer requires inference, because it is not directly stated in the text.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question cannot be answered by locating a single stated sentence
* Requires students to combine information from the text with their own knowledge and analysis to infer an answer
* Teacher asks students to point to what in the text supports the inference
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require inferring feelings, motivation, or an unstated cause/effect
* May draw on multiple parts of the text combined
look_fors.strong_examples: "The text never tells us how the hen felt when her friends said no. Based on what she did next, how do you think she felt, and what in the text makes you think that?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "How do you think the hen felt?" <accepts a one-word answer without asking what in the text supports it> [Why attempting: inferential question, but no textual support required]
look_fors.non_examples: "How do people usually feel when their friends reject them?" [Why non-example: doesn't require the text to answer]

look_fors.type_explanation: Applies throughout instructional sequence
look_fors.name: Lesson Fidelity
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Follow your lesson plan's sequence, content, and structure moment-to-moment with strategic adjustments as needed
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Delivers content, activities, and sequence as specified in the uploaded lesson plan.
* Deviations from the plan, when present, fall into recognizable categories: responding to the needs of a specific student or students, scaffolded supports added that don't reduce the rigor of the lesson, or in-the-moment adjustments responding to student thinking or understanding
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Wording of scripted language may be changed so long as intent, content, and rigor are not altered
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher follows the plan's sequence and content
* Teacher temporarily breaks the plan's rigorous analysis question ("Why did the character's actions lead to this outcome?") into two smaller supporting questions when students struggle, then returns to the original question and has students answer it in full
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Lesson plan calls for a partner discussion on character motivation; teacher asks one student to share instead [Why attempting: preserves content, but not intent of engaging all students]
* Lesson plan's question asks students to analyze how and why a character changed over the course of the story; teacher instead asks "What did the character do at the beginning, middle, and end of the story?"; after students respond, teacher explains how the character changed [Why attempting: somewhat aligned but lowers rigor]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lesson plan calls for a partner discussion on character motivation; teacher skips it entirely with no rationale
* Lesson plan's question asks students to analyze why a character changed over the course of the story; teacher instead asks "Who were the characters?" and never returns to original question [Why non-example: Significantly lower rigor than initial plan]

look_fors.type_explanation: Not governed by the Explicit/Implicit/Elaborative progression; may occur at any point
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group A look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group A look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group A look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Scaffolding Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student is stuck or makes an error, ask a simpler or more foundational question to get them thinking, then use their response to bridge back to the original task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student is stuck or has made an error
* Teacher asks a simpler, more foundational, or more manageable question related to the original task or question
* Teacher connects the student's response back to the original task or question
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require more than one scaffolding question before returning to the original task
* Scaffolding question may break the task into a smaller chunk (e.g., "What's the first step?") rather than stepping down in conceptual complexity 
* Bridge back may be a statement rather than a question (e.g., "Ok, now that you've identified you need to multiply length x width, do that to find the area and finish the problem")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Let's start with what area means. What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something."  Teacher: "Yes, and why does that help us here?" Student: "Because we need to find how much space the rectangle takes up." Teacher: "Exactly. So what information does the problem give you that might help you figure that out?"
 * Student: <identifies an incorrect theme> Teacher: "What actually happens to the main character by the end of the story?" Student: "She decides to go back and help even though it's hard." Teacher: "Good. So what do you think the author wants us to learn from that choice? That's your theme."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something." Teacher: "It's the size, or how much space the rectangle takes up. Now find the area of this rectangle." [Why attempting: Asks one scaffolding question but does not check to see if student needs more in order to complete the problem]
look_fors.non_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Remember, the area of a rectangle is length x width" [Why non-example: Provides a cue rather than asking a question; thinking stays with teacher]

look_fors.type_explanation: Group A (Scaffolds): teacher must demonstrate 1-3 Group A look-fors if students struggle to respond
look_fors.name: Text Chunking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Break the text into smaller, manageable parts to support comprehension of a longer or more complex sentence or passage.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Displays or reads aloud one chunk (word, phrase, sentence, or short section) of the text at a time, rather than the full sentence/passage at once
* Asks a question or prompts thinking about that specific chunk before moving to the next chunk
* Builds toward the meaning of the full sentence or passage across the chunks
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Chunk size may vary (word, phrase, or sentence) depending on text complexity and student need
* May chunk visually (sentence strips, highlighting, revealing text progressively) or verbally (reading and pausing)
look_fors.strong_examples: Teacher displays and reads: "Mary" <pause> "Who is the sentence about?" <student responds: "Mary"> Teacher then displays and reads: "had few friends," and asks the following sequence of questions, taking student responses for each: "What did Mary have?"; "How many friends is 'few'?"; "What if we added the word a in front of few? Would that change the meaning? How?"; "Can you say this chunk in your own words? How?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: <displays the full sentence at once> "Let's break this down. Who is it about? Mary. What problem did she have? Few friends. Why? Because of her family's poverty and the teasing." [Why attempting: connection to exact text chunks implied instead of explicit]
look_fors.non_examples: "Mary had few friends because of her family's poverty and the other children's teasing. What does this sentence mean?" [Why non-example: full sentence given at once, no chunking]

skills.name: Think Aloud
skills.description: Deliver a think aloud of your thought process that makes reasoning explicit, engages students in noticing your thinking, stamps the key takeaway, and transfers to student practice.

look_fors.type_explanation: May interleave with Narrate Your Thinking or follow it; may fall before or after Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.name: Aligned Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students practice the exact focus skill and/or concept just modeled or from the lesson's objective
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Practice task requires the same skill or concept that was modeled, introduced, or specified in the lesson's objective
- Task targets that skill directly, not a related or easier substitute
look_fors.acceptable_variations: - Supportive scaffolds (e.g., sentence starters, exemplars) may be used as long as the target skill is unchanged
look_fors.strong_examples:
- Teacher models blending /m/ /a/ /p/ → "map"; students then blend new words (/s/ /u/ /n/ → "sun")
- Objective states students will add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators; practice includes a set of three addition and three subtraction problems with unlike denominators that are different than the problems modeled by the teacher
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- Teacher models blending CVC words; practice only has students identify the first sound
- Objective states students will explain the relationship between cooling time and crystal size in igneous rocks; practice has students identify igneous rocks and explain how they were formed, but does not explicitly require an explanation of the relationship between cooling time and crystal size
look_fors.non_examples:
- Teacher models segmenting phonemes; practice instead has students clap syllables
- Objective states students will be able to calculate density; practice instead has students determine if objects sink or float

look_fors.type_explanation: May interleave with Narrate Your Thinking or follow it; may fall before or after Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.name: Check What Students Noticed
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask a question that checks students' thinking or understanding relative to a specific question or focus you gave them when you framed an activity like a think aloud or model.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Question directly addresses the task, focus, or thinking question stated during framing (e.g., what to listen for, notice, analyze, predict, or record)
* Question is answerable based on what students observed, heard, or noticed during the framed activity itself
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Applies to analysis of think alouds, demonstrations, worked examples, videos, etc.
* May check understanding of the framed task/question itself, or a specific detail/noticing from within the activity
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "As I think aloud, record the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean." <During think aloud, teacher asks>: "What clue did I use to figure out who 'her' was talking about?"
* "Notice what makes DeAndre's argument strong as I read it aloud" <Teacher reads DeAndre's work aloud> "Ok, what did you notice that made DeAndre's argument strong? Turn and talk to your elbow partner for 1 minute"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "As I think aloud, record the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean." <Teacher thinks aloud> <After think aloud>: "Did you notice my steps?" [Why attempting: yes/no framing doesn't surface a specific detail]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Regardless of the teacher framing the task, asks a vague or broad question like "Does that make sense?" or "Did you enjoy the reading?"
* Teacher does not frame the task with a focus area

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 1: frame activity purpose comes first
look_fors.name: Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Preview what will happen and state clear focus for student thinking and engagement.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Previews what teacher and/or students will do
* States clear purpose, target question, or learning focus
* Gives students specific task or role during activity (listen for, analyze, record, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May check for understanding of the framing before beginning the activity
* Student task may be note-taking, analyzing, comparing, evaluating, or other cognitive engagement
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "I have noticed that our understanding of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God' sometimes breaks down because of all the pronouns that Zora Neale Hurston uses. When texts have tons of pronouns, there are steps readers can follow to avoid confusion. I will show you how I make sense of the pronouns so I can follow along with the story. As I am thinking aloud for you, I want you to record notes on the steps I take to figure out what the pronouns mean. Before I start sharing my thinking, remind me - what are you doing as I am thinking aloud for you?"

* "I want to highlight DeAndre's response. As I read it, think about what makes his argument strong." <Reads>

* "I'm going to show you each characteristic of parallel lines with examples. As I do, record the characteristic and an example in your notes. You will use your notes later to practice identifying examples and non-examples of parallel lines based on these characteristics."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- "I am going to show you both methods for the sake of putting it out there, whichever you prefer. So let's start by using slope-intercept form. Which form are we starting with?" [Why attempting: Purpose unclear, no student task/goal]
- "This think aloud will be about dividing fractions." [Why attempting: States topic but not purpose or goal]
- "Take a look up here quickly and just pause what you're doing. I want to highlight a student response." [Why attempting: missing why they are highlighting specific student response]
- “Today we are going to continue our focus on fluency. I want you all to sit where you are and listen, then I want to hear you all read. [Why attempting: Fluency is too broad, purpose should be more specific]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, listen to me think aloud." [Why non-example: No framing] [type: missed opportunity]
* "I'm going to show you how to do this. Pay attention." [Why non-example: 'Pay attention' too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as compliance (e.g., "Complete this task to earn your participation points for the day", "You must read") [type: missed opportunity]
* States purpose as for grades or test performance only (e.g., "This is on the state exam", "This exit ticket is like a quiz for your grade") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: May interleave with Narrate Your Thinking or follow it; may fall before or after Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.name: Guided Practice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students time to apply learning with guidance.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Provides task that applies specific content and/or skills to a new but related context or problem
- Offers scaffolding (e.g., checklist, guiding questions, reference material, etc.)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Level of guidance varies based on student need: heavy scaffolding to light check-ins
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph." <Displays new paragraph> "Who is 'him' in the second sentence right here and how do you know?" <Student responds> "Good - you skimmed the previous paragraph for clues. Show me - where exactly did you find that clue?" <Student points> "Excellent. What will you do now to check if that makes sense?" <Continues using questions to scaffold>

- "As you revise your lab conclusions, you can always look back to our exemplar from yesterday's lab for a strong example of how to use evidence." <Circulates> "What evidence could you include here?" "Why did you choose that data to support your conclusion?" <Checks in with multiple students>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's apply what you just learned to this paragraph. Don't forget the steps I just took to determine the central idea" [Why attempting: minimal/vague guidance]
 * "Try another problem like this one. Raise your hand if you need help." [Why attempting: Reactive rather than proactive guidance]
look_fors.non_examples:
* <Finishes think aloud> "Okay, moving on to our next topic..." [Why non-example: No practice]
* "Now complete this worksheet silently." <Sits at desk, doesn't monitor> [Why non-example: No guidance or scaffolding]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 2: core of the think aloud, comes after Frame Activity Purpose
look_fors.name: Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Share your internal thought process aloud as you work.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Speaks in first person about mental processes ("I'm thinking...", "I notice...", "I'm wondering...")
* Articulates decisions and reasoning as they occur ("I'm going to try this because...")
* Makes thinking visible by voicing questions, connections, and strategy choices
* Connects procedural steps to conceptual understanding when applicable
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May include self-correction and mistakes as part of authentic thinking
* May be continuous throughout modeling a task OR break up with other strategies like short student practice opportunities or checking for understanding techniques
* May use visuals while narrating (points to text, writes steps, demonstrates on screen)
look_fors.strong_examples: "Ok. I'm going to start with this sentence: 'The people all saw her come because it was sundown.' I know that a pronoun is a word used to replace a noun. The first pronoun I see here is **her**, so I'm going to highlight that. Now, I need to figure out who **her** is referring to. Hmm… I'm going to ask myself: What clues are there in the story to help me figure this out? Let me skim the previous paragraph to see if there is a clue there… This paragraph is about an old woman so I think that the old woman must be her. I'm going to jot that down and underline that clue. Let me reread the sentence now: 'The people all saw **her** come because it was sundown.' Let me make sure that makes sense: 'The people all saw **the old woman** come because it was sundown.' Yes, I think that makes sense so far."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Let's start by using slope-intercept form. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slope of the first line was three-fifths so I know the new slope is three-fifths. That is the m in y=mx + b. The problem gives us the point 5, 1, so let's plug in 5 for x and 1 for y. Watch me solve for b…first I plug in my known values and get 1 = 3 + b. Then subtract 3 from both sides. B is -2. Now, our full equation is y = 3/5x - 2." [Why attempting: Explains steps but limited internal monologue]
* Interrupts flow of internal monologue frequently (e.g., with unrelated asides or questions or jumping around with statements like “oh I forgot to tell you earlier that I…”)
look_fors.non_examples:
* "To complete the task, first label the parts of the diagram. Then, write a description of what is happening at each arrow." [Why non-example: Giving instructions, not narrating thinking] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You swapped x and y in your practice problem here. Try again." [Why non-example: Telling student what's wrong, not modeling thinking process] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Her in this text is the old woman." [Why non-example: Stating answer without showing thought process] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Step 3: comes after Narrate Your Thinking
look_fors.name: Stamp Transferable Takeaway
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Articulate key learning in transferable terms.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States clear and accurate key point(s)
* Emphasizes when, why, how, or where to apply the learning
* Often framed as a next step
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher states takeaway OR asks students to state it OR co-creates with students
* Takeaway may be verbal only or in conjunction with writing on the board, anchor chart, and/or student writing
* Focus may be on content understanding, procedural steps, strategic approach, or transferable skill
* May connect specific example to broader principle or strategy
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "When you are determining the central idea, always make sure it covers the entire text and references the specific topic."

* "Now that you have seen my model, what will you do next time you get stuck on a unit conversion?" <Student responds> "Yes - set up the conversion factor by putting the unit you want to get rid of in the denominator. That strategy is key for unit conversions."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember, in this problem we used slope-intercept form." [Why attempting: Specific to single problem, does not include when/why/how for transfer]
* "What did you learn from this?" [Why non-example: Too vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Okay, let's move on to the next problem." [Why non-example: No takeaway]
* "So the answer is 42." [Why non-example: Specific answer without transferable principle]
* "Do you feel better about solving these on your own now?" [Why non-example: No takeaway]

skills.name: Timely, Constructive Feedback (Danielson-Aligned)
skills.description: Deliver or facilitate specific feedback that supports student improvement and learning

look_fors.type_explanation: Required either alone or in conjuction with Student Self-Evaluation for exemplary on Danielson row: Timely, Constructive Feedback
look_fors.name: Peer Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Structure opportunities for students to assess and provide strengths and/or improvement suggestions on classmates' work using criteria or standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides students with criteria, rubric, or protocol for giving feedback
* Students reference success criteria when evaluating peer work
* Students identify specific strengths and areas for growth in peer work
* Students use peer feedback to revise their own work
* May involve written comments, verbal exchanges, or structured protocols
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Feedback may be reciprocal (partners exchange) or one-directional (one student receives from multiple peers)
* May use protocols like "two stars and a wish," "TAG" (tell, ask, give), or subject-specific rubrics
* Teacher may model feedback expectations before student practice
* Feedback may be written or verbal
* Feedback may be anonymous
* Students in grade 2 and earlier may not use specific standards or criteria yet
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher distributes thesis checklist and models giving feedback: "I'm looking at criterion 2 - does the thesis state a clear position? Yes, it says 'schools should have longer recess.' To strengthen it, add why - compare to the exemplar." <Teacher gives directions for peer feeedback> During feedback activity, one student says to another: "Using our thesis checklist, I see your thesis states a clear position. To strengthen it, add a preview of your two main reasons like the exemplar shows" <Students revise own work after feedback activity>
* Teacher introduces "Glow & Grow" and names what to listen for: "For your glow, tell one thing you learned or one detail that was interesting. For your grow, give an idea for what they could add next time." Models with sample: "My glow is I learned that dolphins sleep with one eye open. My grow is you could tell us where dolphins live." Students practice with partners. Student feedback: "My glow is I learned about how wolves live in packs. My grow is you could what wolves eat"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Teacher provides rubric but students say "You did good on this part" without specifics [Why attempting: Has structure but feedback lacks specificity]
* Students identify what's missing but not how to improve it 
* Peer feedback happens but students don't use it to revise or reflect
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Tell your partner what you think about their work" without criteria or structure [Why non-example: Too vague]
* "Give your partner a compliment like good job!" [Why non-example: Not specific or actionable]

look_fors.type_explanation: Required either alone or in conjuction with Student Self-Evaluation for exemplary on Danielson row: Timely, Constructive Feedback
look_fors.name: Student Self-Evaluation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide criteria and time for students to evaluate their work quality.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher provides rubric, success criteria, or exemplar work
* Teacher allocates time for students to compare their work to the standard
* Students review their work against provided rubric, criteria, or work
* Students identify specific strengths and/or gaps in their work
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Criteria, rubric, or exemplar may be provided by teacher or co-created with students
* May occur formatively during revision or summatively after completion
* Students may annotate their work, score themselves, or explain what's present or missing
* Students may work individually or in pairs;
* Peer-to-peer feedback or evaluation is acceptable so long as the student must also reflect on their own work (e.g., identify what they will revise)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher displays three responses to a writing prompt (emerging, proficient, exemplary). "With your group, decide which is strongest and record what you see in that response that's missing in others." <Students discuss and identify specific elements> "Now look at your own draft. Which of those elements do you have? Which are you missing?" <Students compare their drafts to the identified elements>
* Teacher distributes rubric: "Read the criteria for 'Evidence from Text.' Put a star next to the descriptor that matches your essay. If you're between two levels, mark both." <Students read rubric, some students mark Proficient but note they need more specific quotes>
* Before turning in lab reports, teacher says "Compare your conclusion to the checklist. You should have: a claim, three pieces of evidence, and a connection to your hypothesis. Check off each one you included." <Students review their work, one student realizes they forgot the hypothesis connection and adds it>
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Use the rubric to self-evaluate as you complete your lab report" [Why attempting: somewhat vague]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Check that you did your best work" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* Resource such as rubric, exemplar, or success criteria is displayed but no time or direction is given for student use [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher completes evaluation (e.g., "I will come around and give you the score you would get on the hypothesis rubric row if you turned in your lab report right now") [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Affirmation/Assurance
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Express confidence in student's ability to be successful
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in students' abilities (e.g., "I know you can do this," "You're capable of this work")
* May reference growth over time (e.g., "You already figured out..., now you just have to...")
* May be used after redirection, when giving feedback, or during instruction
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address whole class or individual students
* If used after a redirection, walks away rather than lingering to check compliance
