* Redirect affirmations may be more concise (e.g., "You got this")
* Often paired with communicating high expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* After redirection: "You've got this - I'm excited to see your thinking when I come around again later" <walks away>
* During instruction: "I know you can master this concept"
* When giving feedback: "I'm giving you this feedback because I know you're capable of meeting high standards."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Okay great, get to work" [Why attempting: Positive and directive but not affirming]
* "Good job" [Why attempting: Generic praise]
* "You can do this if you focus" [Why attempting: Conditional]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Let's see if you can actually do it this time" [Why non-example: Doubts capability]
- "Just give it your best and see what you can do" [Why non-example: No affirmation/assurance of student's ability]
- States what student did wrong (e.g., “that’s not solving the equation”) without any follow up

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame tasks as challenging yet worthy while maintaining rigorous standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Acknowledges difficulty/high expectations but doesn't frame as worthy (e.g., "This is hard" or "Oooh, a spicy problem!")
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
* Assigning easier work to struggling students without scaffolding the grade-level content [Why non-example: Reduces rigor]

look_fors.name: Name the Error or Misconception
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly state what was incorrect or misunderstood.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States the specific error, mistake, or gap in thinking clearly
* Contrasts the error with the correct understanding
* Connects the error to the root cause when possible
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May directly explain the correct understanding and/or root cause of the error or ask students to do so
* May use student work or examples to illustrate the error OR describe it generally without specific examples
* May be used reactively (in response to observed errors) or proactively (addressing predicted common misconceptions in advance)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "The misconception I'm seeing is that you're confusing mass and weight. This is a distinction I struggled with for a long time too! You said the object's mass would be different on the moon, but mass stays the same no matter where you are - that's the amount of matter in an object. What changes on the moon is weight, which is the force of gravity pulling on that mass."
* "Looking at Student A's response, the error is that this answer is too general. What makes Student B's response stronger?" <Student responds> "Yes, response A says 'Amos is determined' but doesn't prove it with specific evidence from the text. Looking at Student B's response, this answer includes specific actions such as 'worked on his boat in the daytime and studied navigation at night'. This shows us exactly how Amos demonstrated determination. The key difference is that Student A stated the trait without proof, while Student B connected the trait to specific textual evidence."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "You made a calculation error here." [Why attempting: Names that there's an error but doesn't specify what kind or where the thinking went wrong]
* "Remember, you need to show your work." [Why attempting: States what's missing but doesn't explain the underlying thinking error]
* "This isn't quite right yet." [Why attempting: Acknowledges incorrectness but doesn't name the specific error or misconception]
* "You swapped x and y. Try again." [Why attempting: Identifies the procedural error but doesn't explain why this matters or connect to conceptual understanding]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Vague feedback without naming a specific error or misconception (e.g.,"This needs improvement.", "Good try! Let's keep working on it.", "You didn't follow the directions", etc.) [type: missed opportunity]
* Shows correct work without addressing the error [type: missed opportunity]
* Calls out error in a way that could embarass or demotivate a student (e.g., "Let's look at what Amira did wrong") [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Specific Praise
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Acknowledge specific actions, effort, or thinking rather than general performance
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names the specific action, behavior, or thinking being praised
* Connects praise to observable student work or participation
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Praise can focus on academic content, behavioral expectations, or effort/persistence
* Can be brief for simple tasks or skills, so long as it is aligned and specific (e.g., "Yes, /sh/" after student correctly says /sh/ phoneme)
* May include details about what made the contribution valuable, especially for more complex tasks or skills
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Kaliah, I appreciate how you used the number line to show your thinking. That helped us all see your strategy clearly."
* "I noticed how you worked through that challenging problem without giving up. That sustained effort is exactly what mathematicians do."
* <After student shares answer> "That's a strong observation. You connected the evidence directly to the author's main claim."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "I like what you're thinking." [Why attempting: Acknowledges thinking but lacks specificity]
look_fors.non_examples: * General praise with no specific detail about what was done well (e.g., "Good job!"; "Nice work everyone!") [type: missed opportunity]

skills.name: Use a Calm, Neutral, Assertive Voice
skills.description: Deliver directions and respond to behavior with a calm, neutral, and assertive tone that preserves student dignity.

look_fors.name: Be Direct
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: State directions as clear statements, not disguised questions or choices.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Delivers directions as declarative/imperative statements
* Avoids phrasing non-optional actions as questions (e.g., "Can you...?") or false choices (e.g., "Do you want to...?") when the action isn't actually optional
* Avoids hesitant or hedging language when giving directions
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Genuine choice may be offered declaratively/imperatively without violating this look-for (e.g., "Choose to work independently or with a partner.")
look_fors.strong_examples: "Take out your notebook now."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Can you sit down for me?" [Why attempting: attempt at supportive phrasing with a directive, but student may misinterpret as a question]
* "I think it might be a good time to start your independent work now." [Why attempting: declarative but qualified/hesitant]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Are you ready to take out your notebook yet?" [Why non-example: framed as question, may convey annoyance]
* "Um, maybe you guys could kind of start working whenever you're ready?" [Why non-example: hesitant, non-assertive]

look_fors.name: Emotional Regulation
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Maintain a supportive, asset-based approach consistently throughout interactions
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Responds to disruptions or misbehavior with positive, proactive, and anonymized strategies to support students (e.g., proximity, positive narration, anonymous group reminder, etc.) BEFORE consequences or individual redirections
* Consistently messages high expectations and belief in students' ability to meet them
* Assumes the best of students and seeks to understand (e.g., asks an off-task student what they are stuck on or if they need anything rather than assuming student is being deliberately defiant)
* Allows students to complete responses before redirecting or transitioning to the next student

## Behaviors that are NOT evidence of Emotional Regulation: 
* Calm or neutral tone alone
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Individual teachers will have different tones according to their communication style; variations are expected from teacher to teacher
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "Let's pause for a moment. We can't hear what Christina is sharing now. Let's give our silent attention to her so we can learn from her thinking." <Pauses> "Thank you. Go ahead Christina."
- Positively narrates ("Table 6 is silently starting the do now, Aricely is reviewing her notes from yesterday to help her with problem 1") and gives an anonymous whole-group reminder ("We've got almost everyone working independently on the do now. Let's see if we can get to 100% in the next 15 seconds")
- <Leans down and speaks quietly> "Aaron, you seem distracted. Is everything ok?" <continues instruction without dwelling on behavior when Aaron gets back on task>
- Uses anonymous reminder after one student calls out answer "Remember, raise your hand to share"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember, we raise our hands. I need you to remember that. Don't just call out" [Why attempting: Words may imply frustration, but also positive and anonymous reminder to start]
* Let's get this problem set done today. I don't want a repeat of yesterday's off-task behavior, and I know you can do it." [Why attempting: Mix of negative and positive framing and language]
look_fors.non_examples:
* When student speaks out of turn, immediately says: "I said raise your hand! Why can't you follow simple directions?" [type: relational harm, severe]
* When student speaks out of turn, immediately publicly redirects ("Aidan, stop calling out") or gives consequence ("You are losing a point") [type: relational harm]
* <Teacher sighs heavily and rolls eyes when student asks to use bathroom> "Again? You just went an hour ago." [Why non-example: Exasperation, lack of empathy] [type: relational harm, severe]
* "Let's see if we can get through this problem set today without a repeat of yesterday" [Why non-example: Does not message high expectations and belief in students] [type: relational harm]
* Interrupts or talks over student(s) [type: relational harm]

look_fors.name: Affective Statements
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Communicate how a student's specific actions affected you or others to build awareness and empathy
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Identifies a specific feeling (e.g., "I feel frustrated," "I was scared," "It makes me feel proud")
* Names the specific action or behavior that caused the feeling (
* Does NOT label character (e.g., as disrespectful, unmotivated, uncaring, incapable of listening/sitting still/doing a task, etc.)
* Connects the feeling to the impact of the behavior on self, others, or the community
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be used to reinforce positive behaviors or redirect negative behaviors
* May address impact on teacher, peers, or the broader community
* May be delivered privately to preserve student dignity (e.g., asking the student to sit next to you)
* May be delivered from one student to another
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "James, I feel upset that you ripped the pages out of your library book. When you rip the pages out, other students cannot enjoy the book after you."
* "Marcellus, I am excited to hear the thoughts you shared in the discussion. It helped me know that you understood the passage."
* Student to another student: ““Malachi, I am feeling frustrated by your tapping. When you tap like that, I cannot concentrate on my reading.”
* Student to another student: “Samaya, thanks for asking me to share my answer. It made me feel like you value my thinking.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Alia shared she was feeling supported when you did that" [Why attempting: Missing specific behavior and impact]
* "When you rip pages, other students can't use the book" [Why attempting: Missing feeling/how affected]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "You're being disrespectful" [Why non-example: Labels character, not behavior]
* "You need to stop doing that" [Why non-example: No feeling or impact stated]
* "I'm so frustrated with this class!" [Why non-example: No specific behavior identified; not calm]
* "You're always causing problems" [Why non-example: Attacks who the student is rather than what they did]

skills.name: Various Strategies and Scaffolds
skills.description: Use various instructional strategies and individualized scaffolds so each student reaches their zone of productive struggle.

look_fors.name: Align to Lesson / Objective
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Target instruction, tasks, and questions to the lesson's objective, reaching its full rigor by the end of the lesson.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Instruction, tasks, questions, and activities focus on the lesson's content or objective, not a tangential or off-objective substitute
* The cognitive demand of what the teacher and students do matches the rigor of the objective, or deliberately scaffolds toward it
* By the end of the lesson, students work at the full rigor of the objective, not only a lower-demand version of it
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * May target the full objective or a prerequisite/lower-demand step, as long as it scaffolds toward and the lesson reaches the objective's full rigor
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Objective: infer a character's motivation from textual evidence; prompt: "What does Maria's choice in paragraph 4 reveal about what she wants, and which line shows it?"
* Objective: add fractions with unlike denominators; the task presents three such sums different from those modeled
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Objective: students explain how cooling rate affects crystal size; the task asks students to label rock types [Why attempting: related content, not the objective's relationship]
look_fors.non_examples: * Objective: students compare two strategies; the task instead has students copy the steps of one strategy [Why non-example: no comparison; off-objective]

look_fors.name: Cue with Anchor Chart or Notes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Direct students to reference visual aids or notes.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Directs student attention to specific anchor chart, poster, or notes
* Provides time for students to review and apply information
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may or may not provide additional explanation depending on student needs
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Reference our anchor chart if you need to remind yourself of each part in FOIL on problem 6."
* "Look at our chart to remember how to line up your ruler with the object."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Take two minutes to first look back at your notes at our definition of fitness and then silently adjust your answer. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Check the board as you work."
look_fors.non_examples: "Don't forget to use your resources if you need help." [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Cue with Definition, Rule or Procedure
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Remind students of a definition, rule or procedure to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States or references a previously taught definition, rule or procedure
* Directs students to apply the definition, rule, or procedure
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Teacher may explain/provide the definition, rule or procedure or ask students to recall or find it
* General rather than specific cues (e.g., “Remember that we always read in one direction”) can put more cognitive lift on students, but teacher should get more specific if students do not self-correct after first cue
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Always measure the volume in a graduated cylinder by getting eye level and reading from the bottom of the meniscus. Everyone check your most recent volume measurement." <Students self-correct; Teacher moves on>
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle> “Ok, let’s get a little more specific. Remember that we always read from left to right. Watch my finger as I read on this page" <Teacher reads, moving finger from left to right>. "Now, turn the page and put your finger where you will start reading." <Teacher scans and circulates> "Next, move your finger in the direction you will read." <Teacher scans and circulates>
* "Remember, like terms have the same variable and exponent. Go back and make sure you have only combined like terms" <Students self-correct; teacher moves on>
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Remember that we always read in one direction. Start again on page three." <Students continue to struggle; Teacher repeats same cue>
* "Remember like terms share letters or variables, and also share exponents. That is, the exponents have to be the same" [Why attempting: Definition imprecise, no direction as to what to apply]
look_fors.non_examples: "Remember to measure carefully." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Cue with Example
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Reference specific examples to help students clarify thinking.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* References specific example(s) of knowledge and/or skill of focus in the moment
* Prompts students to apply the example
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Often used in response to a specific misconception or mistake or in advance of a predicted misconception or mistake
* Teacher may explain the example(s) or ask students to do so
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's revise our definitions of a prime number. Remember, one example is 7. Another is 11."
* "It seems we are torn on this one. Let's think back to our examples of the sea turtle and the gray whale. The sea turtle had a lot more offspring, but what did the gray whale have that the sea turtle did not? Take 1 minute and turn and talk with your partner at a level two voice. Go." <Student turn and talk, teacher circulates>. "Alright, based on the conversation you had with your partner, take one minute to adjust your answer."
* "2 is more than 1. 1 is less than 2. Is 3 more than 4 or less than 4?"
look_fors.attempting_examples: "It seems we are torn on this one. Think back to our sea turtle and gray whale example and then revise your answer" [Why attempting: References example but doesn't explicitly connect to misconception or guide students to do so]
look_fors.non_examples: "Think about what we learned before." [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Leverage the Workspace (Saga)
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use visual cues in the shared workspace to direct attention or organize information without interrupting the flow of conversation.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Highlights or circles part of the problem, text, or task to direct attention
- Color-codes or marks related parts of a problem to show how they connect
- In the virtual environment, adds a typed note to redirect or refocus (e.g., "You should move on to #3.")
- Places a supportive sticker, checkmark, or quick reminder in the workspace or on a student's paper
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Online: highlighting, circling, chat messages, digital emoji/reactions, or digital stickers
- In-person: circling or pointing on a shared paper/whiteboard, a written sticky note, physical stamp/sticker, pointing on student's paper
- Cue may organize or connect information, clarify focus, celebrate success, or help a student re-engage with the task
look_fors.strong_examples:
- Highlights the row in the table where the sign error occurred and asks, "What do you notice here?"
- Types in chat: "Move on to #3."
- Circles the step on the shared paper and taps it twice to draw attention
- Places a sticker next to a completed problem with the note "Nice work — keep going!"
look_fors.attempting_examples: Types "Focus please" in the chat with no highlight or reference point [Why attempting: Vague, no visual anchor]
look_fors.non_examples: "Come on, guys, let's focus — we're on number 3." [Why non-example: Verbal only]

look_fors.name: Manipulatives/Visual Representations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use concrete models and visuals to clarify concepts
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses concrete objects or visual representations to illustrate concepts
* Models use of precise vocabulary while demonstrating with manipulatives or visuals
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Manipulatives and visuals can be used during initial instruction, during guided practice, or during independent work
* May be teacher-led demonstration or student-directed exploration
* Applies to both vocabulary development and conceptual understanding
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Let's use these base-ten blocks to understand place value. This cube represents one unit. This rod represents ten units - see how it's made of ten unit cubes? And this flat represents one hundred. Watch as I show you 234 using these blocks." <Models with blocks while narrating><Asks students to make different 3 different numbers with blocks after modeling>
 * "Let me show you how a proportional relationship works using this diagram. <Points to table on screen> In a proportional relationship, there's a constant rate between the two quantities. Look at 'Hours Worked' and 'Money Earned.' When we work 1 hour, we earn $15. Notice this arrow showing times 15. Now watch what happens with 2 hours - we earn $30. That's still times 15. <Points to each arrow> See how every single relationship is times 15? 3 hours gives us $45, 4 hours gives us $60, and 5 hours gives us $75. The rate stays constant - it's always times 15. That constant rate is what makes this proportional. <Points to checkmark> That's why this diagram shows 'proportional' at the bottom."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Here's a function. See how the input is on the left side of the chart and the output is on the left? That's a function" [Why attempting: Visual, but concept imprecise]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "A function is when you have one unique output for any input." [Why non-example: Verbal explanation only, no visual support]
 * <Shows a visual on screen but doesn't reference it or explain it>

look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.name: Scaffolding Question
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: When a student is stuck or makes an error, ask a simpler or more foundational question to get them thinking, then use their response to bridge back to the original task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Student is stuck or has made an error
* Teacher asks a simpler, more foundational, or more manageable question related to the original task or question
* Teacher connects the student's response back to the original task or question
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May require more than one scaffolding question before returning to the original task
* Scaffolding question may break the task into a smaller chunk (e.g., "What's the first step?") rather than stepping down in conceptual complexity 
* Bridge back may be a statement rather than a question (e.g., "Ok, now that you've identified you need to multiply length x width, do that to find the area and finish the problem")
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Let's start with what area means. What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something."  Teacher: "Yes, and why does that help us here?" Student: "Because we need to find how much space the rectangle takes up." Teacher: "Exactly. So what information does the problem give you that might help you figure that out?"
 * Student: <identifies an incorrect theme> Teacher: "What actually happens to the main character by the end of the story?" Student: "She decides to go back and help even though it's hard." Teacher: "Good. So what do you think the author wants us to learn from that choice? That's your theme."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "What is area?" Student: "It's like... the size of something." Teacher: "It's the size, or how much space the rectangle takes up. Now find the area of this rectangle." [Why attempting: Asks one scaffolding question but does not check to see if student needs more in order to complete the problem]
look_fors.non_examples: * <Student stuck on finding area of rectangle> Teacher: "Remember, the area of a rectangle is length x width" [Why non-example: Provides a cue rather than asking a question; thinking stays with teacher]

look_fors.name: Word Banks
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Give students a set of target words to draw from in their response.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Provides a specific set of words students can use to answer a question or complete a task
* Directs students to use the bank as they write or speak
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Bank may be paired with sentence frames for more support, or provided on its own for less
* Support may be faded over time, from bank plus frames, to bank alone, to no bank
look_fors.strong_examples:
* <Displays: played, sang, liked, started, heard> "Use one of these words to finish the sentence. 'Nina Simone ______.' Which one fits what the text says about her music?"
* <Displays: sum, difference, equation, variable> "When you explain your steps, use at least two of these words. I will be looking for them in your answer."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * <Posts a list of twenty words from the unit> "Here are some words you could use." [Why attempting: bank is not targeted to the question students are answering]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Use good vocabulary words in your answer." <No words provided>

skills.name: Vocabulary Instruction
skills.description: Teach a target word's meaning accurately, defining it in student-friendly language, showing it in meaningful contexts, and giving students active opportunities to use the word.

look_fors.name: Explain Unfamiliar Terms
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explain unfamiliar terms to support content understanding and vocabulary development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
- Defines new or unfamiliar words
- Provides synonyms or familiar language for unfamiliar terms
- NOT required when term is part of a classroom routine or procedure (e.g., "phonics time") or refers to a skill likely used repeatedly in a grade/subject (e.g., "calculate," "solve," "blend," etc.) unless the teacher indicates this is the first time with the routine or skill
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May provide or connect to word(s) in students' home language(s) to support explanation of target word when teaching multilingual learners
look_fors.strong_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries where earth’s plates move away from each other.”
- “A cake is the baked dessert in this picture. Cake in Spanish is ‘pastel’.”
look_fors.attempting_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- “There are some new words that you're going to learn in this book. Same, recipe,  and unique. Alright, let’s get started and see what happens.” [Why non-example; Names but does not explain new terms]
look_fors.non_examples:
- “Volcanoes are commonly found at divergent plate boundaries”
- I am using expression, so you hear my voice. I have intonation and inflection. [Why non-example: expression is just more than hearing voice; no definition of intonation or inflection]

look_fors.name: Word in Context
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Show the target word used in a meaningful sentence or context.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Uses the target word in a clear example sentence
Ties the example to a familiar situation or the text being read
look_fors.strong_examples: "Curious means you really want to know about something. I was curious about the noise outside, so I went to look. Tell your partner about a time you felt curious."
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Curious means you really want to know about something. Now use it in a sentence." [Why attempting: asks for context but provides no example]
look_fors.non_examples: "Curious is an adjective. It has three syllables." [Why non-example: describes the word but never uses it in meaningful context]

look_fors.type_explanation: Connect Word Meaning is required when the word's meaning is best clarified through related words or word parts (e.g., a morphologically transparent or easily confused word); not required for simple, concrete words
look_fors.name: Connect Word Meaning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Connect the word to related words or word parts to sharpen its meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Links the word to synonyms, antonyms, or closely related words
Connects to word parts (prefix, root, suffix) when the word's structure carries meaning
look_fors.strong_examples: For "rebuild": "Re- means again. We saw it in rewrite and redo. So rebuild means to build something again."
look_fors.attempting_examples: For "rebuild": "Re- means again, so rebuild means build again." <does not connect to other re- words>
look_fors.non_examples: For "rebuild": "Rebuild means to build something again." [Why non-example: no connection to the prefix re- or related words that would generalize the meaning]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Gestures for Meaning
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use gestures to demonstrate the meaning of a concept or a word, supporting understanding and language development.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Uses hand movements, body language, or facial expressions that illustrate meaning
* Gestures match/support verbal content
look_fors.strong_examples:
* “These are all different types of acute angles that I am making with my arms”
* “Stand up for lava and duck down for magma”
look_fors.attempting_examples: “As I read, give a thumbs up every time you hear the word amendment" (Why non-example: Not clearly connected to meaning)
look_fors.non_examples:
* Does not use gestures
* “Give me a thumbs up if you understand” (Why non-example: Not paired with concept or word)

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Graphic Organizers
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Ask students to fill in a structured visual organizer to support and.or show their understanding
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear prompt/purpose for graphic organizer
* Clear directions for parts of graphic organizer (e.g, sections of t-chart, Venn diagram areas of overlap and non-overlap, etc.) and completion (e.g., time, individual vs. pair/group work, etc.)
* Organizer matches prompt/concept/thinking skill
* Students fill out
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
- Different types of graphic organizer
- Graphic organizers familiar to students may require less specific directions (e.g., "Fill out the t-chart to compare and contrast facts and opinions. Try to get at least three items for each")
- Semantic and concept maps are types of graphic organizer particularly useful for vocabulary development
look_fors.strong_examples:
- "You each have a Venn diagram on your desk. In the left circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for amphibians. In the right circle, write characteristics that are ONLY true for reptiles. In the middle overlapping section, write characteristics they both share. Try to include at least 3 items in each section. You have 4 minutes to work with a partner."
- "On your paper, you have a cause-and-effect chart with three boxes. In the left column, write three causes of World War I. In the right column, write one effect for each cause. Be specific - use dates or events when you can. You have 3 minutes, silent and solo."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Fill in this Venn diagram comparing amphibians and reptiles." [Why attempting: Uses organizer but lacks specificity for organizer or completion]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Do your graphic organizer" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]
* "Show the steps of mitosis in the Venn diagram" [Why non-example: Organizer does not match concept/prompt] [type: learning harm]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Mentor Texts
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use a high-quality text as a model for students to analyze and emulate.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Presents a high-quality text excerpt as a model
Directs students to examine specific craft features (e.g., word choice, sentence structure, organization)
Names what makes the example effective or prompts students to identify it
Connects the model to what students will read or write
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
May be a full passage, a single sentence, or a short excerpt
May be from published work, teacher exemplar, or strong student work
look_fors.strong_examples: "Here is our mentor sentence: 'The night Max wore his wolf suit and made mischief of one kind and another, his mother called him WILD THING.' What do you notice about how the author describes Max?" <collects noticings> "Now let us try that same pattern in our own writing."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Shows a strong sentence and says "Notice the author's word choice" but does not name the move or connect it to what students will do
look_fors.non_examples: Reads a passage aloud without drawing attention to any craft move or connecting it to student work

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Model Language
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Explicitly model specific language before you ask students produce language.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Demonstrates desired language structure or response before students produce it
* May provide sentence starters or frames
look_fors.acceptable_variations: None
look_fors.strong_examples: “Try using the sentence frame: According to ‘source name’... For example, if I was using that sentence frame with source 1, I might say ‘According to Roosevelt’s 1933 Inaugural Address, Roosevelt thought the government should hire more people directly.’ Turn and talk to your partner using that same sentence frame with source 2.”
look_fors.attempting_examples: "Try using the sentence frame: According to 'source name'... to describe source 2 to your partner" [Why attempting: Frame provided, not modeled]
look_fors.non_examples: “Describe source 2 to your partner”

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Picture Talk
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Use a shared image or experience to engage students with target vocabulary in context.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Prompts students to observe and describe what they notice in a shared image, illustration, or experience
Introduces or surfaces target words in the context of the image or experience
Students use the target words as they talk or write about it
look_fors.acceptable_variations: The anchor may be a photo, book illustration, projected image, or a shared class experience (e.g., a demo or field trip)
look_fors.strong_examples: <shows image of Gran at the beach> "Take a look at this picture. What do you notice?" <invites observations> "Yes, she is on an adventure. Adventure means doing something new and exciting. Turn to your partner and use adventure in your own sentence."
look_fors.attempting_examples: <shows image of Gran at the beach> "Take a look at this picture. What do you notice?" <invites observations> "Yes, she is on an adventure. Adventure means doing something new and exciting.” [Why attempting: no student engagement with specific target word]
look_fors.non_examples: <shows image of Gran at the beach> "Take a look at this picture. Gran is on an adventure!” <Moves on> [Why non-example: Minimal connection to target word; no student engagement]

look_fors.type_explanation: Rate Optional Group B look-fors and consider in scoring whenever evidence is present
look_fors.name: Point out Cognates
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Point out cognates in a student’s home language to help them learn new vocabulary words more quickly and easily.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly states when a word is similar in student's home language
* Makes connection between languages (e.g., "In Spanish, this word sounds similar")
look_fors.acceptable_variations: Use of cognates may be more or less frequent depending on instructional language and student's home language (e.g., more cognates between English and Spanish than English and Chinese)
look_fors.strong_examples: When applicable, points out cognates for key words (e.g., “Today we will share family traditions. In Spanish, we say tradiciones familiares - notice how similar tradiciones in Spanish is to traditions in English, and how familiares and family also start with the same sounds”).
look_fors.attempting_examples: When applicable, references cognates for key words (e.g., "Today, we will share family traditions, tradiciones familiares") [Why attempting: States cognate, doesn't highlight similarity]
look_fors.non_examples: Misses an opportunity to share a cognate for a key word.

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Semantic Gradients
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students order related words along a continuum by shade of meaning or intensity.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Presents a set of related words that vary by degree, intensity, or shade of meaning
Directs students to arrange the words in order along a continuum
Prompts students to explain the difference between adjacent words
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
The continuum may run between two antonyms or from weakest to strongest
Words may be teacher-provided or student-generated
look_fors.strong_examples: Asks students to name words for a character’s feelings in a book, then chooses two (mad, annoyed) and adds three more (infuriated, grumpy, and fuming). Asks students to put them in order of intensity and explain their reasoning.
look_fors.attempting_examples: Explains that the following set of words varies in intensity from less to more intense: grumpy, annoyed, mad, fuming, infuriated [Why attempting only teacher-led, no nuance]
look_fors.non_examples: “Infuriated means really mad” [Why non-example: focuses on definition not shades of mean]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Stop & Jot / Everybody Writes
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt student to reflect on a task or prompt in writing.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents clear writing question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (most often time)
* All students writing simultaneously
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May incorporate graphic organizers or annotations
* Expectations may include things like materials to reference, criteria for success, what to do if you finish early, etc.
look_fors.strong_examples: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to independently write your answer in the box in the middle of today's handout <points>. If you need help getting started, use the sentence frames on the board: Rules and laws both... However, rules..., and laws.... Go ahead."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "What happened in the story?" [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
* "You have 1 minute to write the main idea. Go." [Why attempting: Strong prompt but could be clearer about where to write]
* "Take 5 minutes to answer items 1-3 in your interactive handout. You may work with your small group" [Why attempting: group work direction somewhat confusing and may be difficult to ascertain individual understanding unless paired with listen in]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Write down your thoughts" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Synonym Work
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students choose the most precise or vivid synonym, not just any word with the same meaning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Presents a target word and prompts students to produce or select synonyms
Provides or builds a synonym chart for a common word
Prompts students to choose the synonym that best fits a sentence's meaning or tone
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
Synonyms may be student-generated or selected from a provided chart or bank
May focus on replacing a vague word (e.g., good, said, went) with a more precise one
look_fors.strong_examples: "The word good does not tell us much. Look at our synonym chart: excellent, outstanding, impressive, terrific. Pick the one that best fits your sentence about the dog and read it to your partner."
look_fors.attempting_examples: “What are some synonyms of good?” [Why attempting: no application to context, meaning, or tone]
look_fors.non_examples: “Angry is a synonym of mad” [Why non-example: no student involvement or attention to precise meaning]

look_fors.type_explanation: Rate Optional Group B look-fors and consider in scoring whenever evidence is present
look_fors.name: Teach Multiple Forms of New Words
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Teach multiple forms of new words to support students’ ability to use the word in context.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents related forms of new vocabulary (e.g., predict, prediction, predictable)
* Shows how word changes with different endings or uses
* Uses different forms of word in context (e.g., sentences)
look_fors.acceptable_variations: May prioritize key vocabulary for teaching multiple forms rather than doing this for ALL words that may be new to students
look_fors.strong_examples: Teaches multiple forms of new words in context with examples of use.
look_fors.attempting_examples: References multiple forms of new words, but does not provide in context examples of use for each form.
look_fors.non_examples: Teaches only one form of a new word.

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Turn & Talk / Partner Discussion
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Prompt students to turn to a partner or a small group and engage in a brief discussion about a specific question or task.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Presents a clear question or prompt
* Gives clear expectations (partner, time, voice level, etc.)
* Student partners/small groups all discuss at the same time, generally for 30 secs-3 mins depending on complexity
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Partners and small groups are both acceptable
* Think-pair-share is a common acceptable variation. Students think first, then discuss with a partner, then teacher calls on a few students to share whole group.
* May specify which partner speaks first or let students decide.
* May use sentence stems to support.
* Almost always paired with circulation & listen in.
look_fors.strong_examples:
* Teacher: "What is the difference between rules and laws? Take 2 minutes to turn and talk to your desk partner with a level 2 voice. Go!" 
* "First, take 15 seconds to think silently about this question: How are rectangles and squares related?" <pause for 15 seconds> "Now, turn to your partner and share your thinking. You have 1 minute total - 30 seconds each. The person with longer hair goes first. Go."
look_fors.attempting_examples: * "Turn to your partner and discuss what happened in the story." [Why attempting: Broad prompt, no time expectation]
look_fors.non_examples: * "Discuss with your partner" [Why non-example: Too vague] [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Vocabulary Notebook
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Have students record new words with defined components in a vocabulary notebook.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Directs students to record the new word in a notebook or journal
Prompts students to add a student-friendly definition
Prompts students to add an example sentence
Prompts students to add a visual or personal connection
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
Not every entry must include all components; the teacher may prioritize specific ones
May be a dedicated notebook, vocabulary section, or recurring template
look_fors.strong_examples: "In your vocabulary notebook, write the word relieved. Next to it, write what it means in your own words. Then write one sentence using relieved, and draw a quick picture or note a time you felt that way."
look_fors.attempting_examples: Has students copy the word and definition but does not prompt for an example sentence or personal connection [Why attempting: records word and definition only, missing usage or connection]
look_fors.non_examples: Tells students to "write down the word" with no definition, example, or connection

look_fors.type_explanation: Teacher must demonstrate 1-3 look-fors from Optional Group A to actively engage students with target word(s)
look_fors.name: Word Wall Engagement
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Direct students to actively use word(s) form a posted word wall to make meaning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
Directs students to a posted collection of words (the word wall)
Prompts students to use words from the word wall in context or in relation to each other, in writing, speech, or diagraming
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
May involve physical manipulation of words into categories, continuums, semantic maps, etc.
May combine with other strategies like turn and talk, stop & jot, gallery walk, etc.
May add or reference specific words on the wall during instruction, but should still engage students actively
look_fors.strong_examples:
“With your partner, sort the orange word cards into three categories: predators, prey, or non-living things. Each time you categorize a word, explain WHY it goes in that category to your partner”
“Now that you have mapped our focus words for the day from the word wall, use at least three of them to write a paragraph about the push and pull factors that drove the Great Migration”.
look_fors.attempting_examples: “Use the word paradox in a sentence” <points to word on word wall> [Why attempting: missed opportunity for deeper engagement with word in context, word in relationship to other words, or shades of meaning of the word]
look_fors.non_examples: Defines paradox and points to it on the word wall [Why non-example: no student engagement]

skills.name: Voice and Choice (Saga)
skills.description: Engage student voice and choice in learning

look_fors.name: Learning Process Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on learning activities, content, or approach
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Asks students for input on learning activities or topics
* Allows students to select their own examples or applications
* Provides choices in task approach during learning
* Invites students to share personal perspectives or connections
* Offers options for how to engage with content
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Choices may be guided or open-ended depending on learning objectives
* Can offer choice in sequence, grouping, scaffolds, or specific activities
* Student input may shape current or future lessons
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Choose which historical figure you want to research based on your interests"
* "When I say go, move to one of the three tables on the window side of the room if you prefer to work with a partner, and one of the three tables on the door side of the room if you prefer to work alone"
* "What examples should we use for this concept? Who has an idea from your own experience?"
* "You can choose if and when you use one of the available supports, such as the exemplar lab report from last week, the sentence starters for hypotheses, or the hint card with an image of one way to set up your materials" 
* "For today's homework, you can listen to the podcast OR complete the reading on this topic"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can work independently instead of with a partner. Teacher says yes. [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* "If you feel like the problems with fractions with different denominators are too hard, you can just choose the ones with the same denominators" [Why attempting: Offers choice, but lowers expectation]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher selects all examples and applications without student input
* All students engage with content in identical way
* Dismisses student suggestions for how to approach learning
* Never asks students what interests them or connects to their experiences
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.name: Learning Product Choice
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Offer students choice or input on how to demonstrate learning
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Offers choices in demonstration method (written, oral, visual, performance, etc.)
* Provides options for final product format
* Invites student input on how they want to show what they know
* Maintains high expectations while offering choice
look_fors.acceptable_variations: * Student input may be solicited before task or as options are presented
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "You can show your understanding by writing an explanation, creating a diagram, or explaining it aloud to a partner"
* "Would you like to present your findings as a poster, a speech, or a written report?"
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student asks if they can do a presentation instead of write an essay for their final product. Teacher says yes.  [Why attempting: Allows choice reactively, but not proactive for all students]
* Offers one alternative option but frames it as "easier"
look_fors.non_examples:
* All students complete identical task in identical format with no variation
* Teacher selects all demonstration methods without offering alternatives
* Choice is not meaningful (e.g., working with pencil vs. pen)

look_fors.name: Student Agency for Learning Needs
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Support students in voicing needs and making adjustments to their learning.
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Teacher asks students what they need (e.g., "What would help you right now?", "What resources do you need?")
* Teacher responds to student-initiated requests for support, resources, or changes
* Students articulate specific learning needs (e.g., "I need more examples," "I am stuck on the unit conversion," etc.)
* Students make adjustments to their approach based on self-monitoring or self-assessment (e.g., choose different resources, modify their strategy, seek help)
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* Needs may relate to: pacing, resources, supports, task modifications, clarification, or different learning pathways
* Teacher may offer menu of options or students may self-select without prompting
look_fors.strong_examples:
* During independent work, student raises hand: "If the photosphere is the visible surface of the sun, why is it on the inside of the diagram?" Teacher: "The key is the word visible. The photosphere is what the human eye can see. What do you think that means about the chronosphere?" Student "Oh, ok, it's above the photosphere but we can't see it". <Student goes back to work>.
* Student: "I'm stuck. I can't figure out why I keep getting my unit conversions wrong." Teacher: "Can you think of anything that would help you get unstuck?" Student: "Can I see another example of the joules to ergs conversion?" <Teacher directs student to exemplar, student reviews it and then goes back to their own problem set.>
* Students review criteria for success and make edits to their own work based on their self-evaluations.
* Teacher says "Some of you finished early and some need more time. Decide what you need: more practice, start the extension, or revise your work." <Students make different choices based on their self-assessment>
* During writing conference, student says: "I'm stuck on my introduction. Can I start with my body paragraphs first and come back to it?" Teacher affirms: "That's a great strategy - many writers do that." <Student adjusts their approach>
look_fors.attempting_examples: Student asks "Can you help me?" Teacher helps but doesn't prompt student to identify specific need [Why attempting: Student initiates but doesn't articulate specific need]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher assigns all students the same intervention or support without asking what they need [type: missed opportunity]
* Student says "I don't get it" or "I"m stuck" and waits for teacher to fix it [type: missed opportunity]
* Teacher asks if there are any questions and moves on immediately or after a couple students say no [type: missed opportunity]

look_fors.name: Student Leadership
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Allow students to lead activities, discussions, or demonstrations
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Invites students to lead parts of lesson or activity
* Has students teach or demonstrate for the class
* Assigns formal or informal leadership roles
* Student takes charge while teacher observes or supports
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May scaffold leadership with preparation or support first
* Leadership may be brief (leading one example) or extended (leading full activity/presentation)
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Jamal, will you come up and lead the class through your example?"
* "Who can be the teacher and explain this to the class?"
* Student leads call and response letter-sound review while teacher observes
* Teacher assigns student to lead small group through specific protocol or procedure
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* Student comes to board to share answer but teacher talks through most of the solution [Why attempting: Teacher still leading most]
* Leadership opportunities only for select students [Why attempting: Not equitable access]
look_fors.non_examples:
* Teacher directs all activities and discussions
* Students only respond when called upon, never take charge
* "Who wants to share?"  [Why non-example: Invites participation but not leadership]

skills.name: Wise Feedback
skills.description: Deliver feedback that combines three essential components: affirmation of the student's capability, communication of high expectations for rigorous work, and specific actionable guidance for improvement.

look_fors.name: Affirmation/Assurance
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Express confidence in student's ability to be successful
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* States confidence in students' abilities (e.g., "I know you can do this," "You're capable of this work")
* May reference growth over time (e.g., "You already figured out..., now you just have to...")
* May be used after redirection, when giving feedback, or during instruction
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address whole class or individual students
* If used after a redirection, walks away rather than lingering to check compliance
* Redirect affirmations may be more concise (e.g., "You got this")
* Often paired with communicating high expectations
look_fors.strong_examples:
* After redirection: "You've got this - I'm excited to see your thinking when I come around again later" <walks away>
* During instruction: "I know you can master this concept"
* When giving feedback: "I'm giving you this feedback because I know you're capable of meeting high standards."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Okay great, get to work" [Why attempting: Positive and directive but not affirming]
* "Good job" [Why attempting: Generic praise]
* "You can do this if you focus" [Why attempting: Conditional]
look_fors.non_examples:
- "Let's see if you can actually do it this time" [Why non-example: Doubts capability]
- "Just give it your best and see what you can do" [Why non-example: No affirmation/assurance of student's ability]
- States what student did wrong (e.g., “that’s not solving the equation”) without any follow up

look_fors.name: Communicate High Expectations
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Frame tasks as challenging yet worthy while maintaining rigorous standards
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Explicitly names that work is challenging or rigorous OR clearly states a rigorous goal for the lesson/work
* Frames difficulty or goal as worthy of student effort rather than insurmountable
* Connects challenging work to meaningful outcomes or skill development (e.g., "This skill will help you when...")
* Maintains standards rather than lowering expectations
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May address individual students or whole class
* May frame less rigorous tasks or goals as stepping stones to more rigorous tasks or goals
* Often paired with affirmation/assurance of student's capability
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "We’re ready to write strong arguments. Writing a strong argument requires you to analyze evidence and make logical connections. This skill will help you think critically in many subjects and we will get there together"
* "Today we will solve multi-step equations and build your mathematical reasoning. We will break it into steps to achieve our goal"
* "We have claims and evidence down, so I'm asking you to push your thinking to the next level here with reasoning"
look_fors.attempting_examples: * Acknowledges difficulty/high expectations but doesn't frame as worthy (e.g., "This is hard" or "Oooh, a spicy problem!")
look_fors.non_examples:
* Lowers expectations (e.g., "This is really hard, so just try your best. If you don’t get all the way there, that’s ok.")
* Assigning easier work to struggling students without scaffolding the grade-level content [Why non-example: Reduces rigor]

look_fors.name: Specific, Actionable Feedback
look_fors.teacher_facing_explanation: Provide clear next steps for improvement tied to standards or success criteria
look_fors.observable_behaviors:
* Names specific strengths in student work (what was done well)
* Identifies specific areas for improvement with concrete suggestions
* Provides clear next steps or strategies student can implement
* References standards, criteria, or learning objectives
* May direct students to resources or examples to support revision
look_fors.acceptable_variations:
* May be delivered verbally, in writing, or both
* May reference exemplars or success criteria to clarify expectations
* May include questions that prompt student thinking rather than direct corrections
* Feedback may address content, process, or self-regulation
look_fors.strong_examples:
* "Your thesis clearly states your position. To strengthen paragraph 2, add textual evidence like you did in paragraph 1, then explain how it supports your claim"
* "You accurately identified the problem. Now show your work step-by-step so I can see your mathematical thinking. Look at the example on the anchor chart for the format"
" Now, I want you to try holding your scissors with just your thumb and pointer finger from your right hand."
look_fors.attempting_examples:
* "Your evidence is weak. Add more quotes" [Why attempting: Identifies issue but doesn't explain how to select strong evidence]
* "Nice work on the intro. The body needs more details" [Why attempting: Names strength and area for improvement but lacks concrete next steps]
* "This is better than last time" [Why attempting: Acknowledges growth but not specific about what improved or next steps]
*  "Keep working. Make sure that you use the visual anchors around the classroom to help you." [Why attempting: Lacks specificity as to what to improve or how to use visual anchors]
look_fors.non_examples:
* "Good job" [Why non-example: Generic without specifics] [type: missed opportunity]
* "This needs work" [Why non-example: Identifies problem but no actionable steps] [type: missed opportunity]
* "You're not there yet - keep trying" [Why non-example: No specific guidance for improvement] [type: missed opportunity]
* Only marking errors without explanation or guidance [Why non-example: No actionable next steps] [type: missed opportunity]
